text.text:
Question፦ To begin, if a person is married, must they constantly attend Holy Communion with their spouse?  Because my mother really wants to partake in holy communion and has already confessed her sins when we went to Ethiopia and she did timket, but my father doesn't go to church and only follows church services from home, is it possible for my mother to take Kurban without my father or do they have to do it together because she really wants to partake in holy communion (they are married)?  

Answer፦

text:
The question is regarding a husband and wife who are living together but are not united in their spiritual life. One of them wants to partake of Holy Communion but the other is not attending church regularly.

The first issue is that the penance fathers have not provided adequate guidance and discipline to the couple to help them walk together in their spiritual journey. This is a problem that affects many faithful believers and is a failure on the part of the penance fathers. They should show the right path and teach the way so that people can live by the teachings of the Church.  

Secondly, couples must start their marriage with a focus on their spiritual life rather than solely on material wealth and property. They should not be driven by materialistic desires, but rather by their faith. Even if they give tithes or attend church, it should not be out of obligation but rather out of love for God. It is important to seek God's kingdom and righteousness first, and all other things will be added.

Regarding the question of whether the wife can receive Holy Communion alone, the answer is no. As long as they are living together and sharing a bed, one cannot receive Holy Communion alone. If the man is not able to adjust his position and come back to the faith, and if they have exhausted all efforts to reconcile, the woman may choose to separate and receive Holy Communion alone. However, it is important to try to keep the couple together and give them advice so that they can be together until the end.

The couple should seek guidance from elders and penance fathers to avoid any unwanted issues in their relationship that may lead to separation. The father is not going to church because he lacks a Christian education but not because he hates salvation, so it is important to involve responsible fathers in this process so they can pull him into the church using the wisdom that has been given to them. 

In conclusion, it is important to prioritize one's spiritual life and seek guidance from penance fathers to walk together with one's spouse. Holy Communion entails unity in flesh and should only be received together as a couple.

They should show the right path and teach the way so that people can live by the teachings of the Church.  

Secondly, couples must start their marriage with a focus on their spiritual life rather than solely on material wealth and property. They should not be driven by materialistic desires, but rather by their faith. Even if they give tithes or attend church, it should not be out of obligation but rather out of love for God. It is important to seek God's kingdom and righteousness first, and all other things will be added.

Regarding the question of whether the wife can receive Holy Communion alone, the answer is no. As long as they are living together and sharing a bed, one cannot receive Holy Communion alone. If the man is not able to adjust his position and come back to the faith, and if they have exhausted all efforts to reconcile, the woman may choose to separate and receive Holy Communion alone. However, it is important to try to keep the couple together and give them advice so that they can be together until the end.

The couple should seek guidance from elders and penance fathers to avoid any unwanted issues in their relationship that may lead to separation. The father is not going to church because he lacks a Christian education but not because he hates salvation, so it is important to involve responsible fathers in this process so they can pull him into the church using the wisdom that has been given to them. 

In conclusion, it is important to prioritize one's spiritual life and seek guidance from penance fathers to walk together with one's spouse. Holy Communion entails unity in flesh and should only be received together as a couple.

text:
Beloved members of John's Repentance spiritual service, on this most hallowed day, we gather in holy reverence to celebrate the feats and miracles of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Our Lady, the Theotokos, and we turn our gaze towards the narrative of the Apostle Matthias, as well as the commemoration of other venerable saints.

Let us, therefore, commence our discourse in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, our Triune God, unto whom be all glory and honor.

On this day, the 31st day of October, we commemorate the miraculous deeds of the Virgin Mary in delivering the Apostle Matthias from the darkened pit of imprisonment, amidst a land of savages and cannibals. Lo! How wondrous are the ways of the Lord, and how benevolent is the intercession of the Theotokos on behalf of those who serve the Gospel with fervor and devotion.

The Apostle Matthias, having been chosen by lot to preach the Good News to the ends of the earth, found himself in a barbarous land named Askutes, believed by the chroniclers of the Church to be Russia. The custom of this people was vile and horrendous; they would blind the eyes of strangers, imprison them, and, after thirty days, cruelly slaughter them to partake of their flesh.

Brethren, imagine the desolation of the Apostle, his eyes taken from him, languishing in prison, his heart crying out to the Lord and His Blessed Mother for deliverance. And lo! The mercies of the Lord are never far from His faithful servants. Before the thirtieth day came to pass, the Virgin Mary, in her boundless compassion, sent the Apostle Andrew to the rescue of Matthias.

Andrew, by the grace of God and the intercession of the Theotokos, entered the prison miraculously, restoring sight to Matthias and leading him out of captivity. With divine might, they caused water to flow from the prison’s very foundation, flooding the land and bringing the barbarians to the brink of destruction.

In that moment of divine retribution, the apostles appeared before them, preaching the Gospel of salvation, revealing the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven, and calling them to repentance and faith in our Lord. By the prayers of the Theotokos, they turned away from their brutish ways, were baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and became gentle, sincere, and compassionate.

So, brethren, let us take heed of this wondrous tale, let us venerate the Theotokos, for she is a fervent intercessor and a steadfast protector of all who call upon her name with faith and love. Let her prayers be a fortress for us, guiding us in the path of righteousness, and leading us to the Heavenly Kingdom.

May the blessings of the Theotokos be upon us all, and may her intercessions guide us in the path of salvation. Amen.

text:
Beloved members of John's Repentance, When we speak of the divinity of Christ, we tread upon holy ground, for this is a matter of utmost importance and profound mystery. It is not a doctrine that is grasped by the intellect alone, but rather, it is understood through the heart, in the light of divine revelation and with the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

The heretics and the reformers, in their limited understanding and their departure from the true faith, have put forth the notion that Jesus Christ is merely a mediator, a bridge between God and man. But let us refute this false teaching with the words of the Scriptures and the teachings of the Church Fathers.

In the Gospel according to John, Jesus speaks clearly of His divine nature. He declares, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). These words are not the words of a mere mediator or prophet. These are the words of God Himself, speaking in the flesh. And when the Jews took up stones to stone Him, accusing Him of blasphemy, He responded, “Do you say of Him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, ‘You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” (John 10:36).

The Apostle Paul, in his letter to the Philippians, speaks of Christ’s divine nature, saying, “Though He was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied Himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men” (Philippians 2:6-7). Here, we see that Christ, though He is God, took on human flesh, humbling Himself for our sake.

Christ came into the world not to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many (Matthew 20:28). He is the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world (John 1:29). He is the Good Shepherd, who lays down His life for the sheep (John 10:11). And by His death and resurrection, He has trampled down death, and has opened to us the gates of paradise.

Furthermore, the miracles of Christ attest to His divinity. He healed the sick, gave sight to the blind, and raised the dead. He calmed the storm and walked on water. He fed the five thousand with five loaves and two fish. These are not the deeds of a mere man, but of God Himself, working wonders in our midst.

In conclusion, dear brethren, let us hold fast to the orthodox teaching of the Church, affirming the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ. He is true God and true man, the Word made flesh, the second person of the Holy Trinity. Let us worship Him, adore Him, and give thanks to Him, for He is worthy of all praise and honor, now and forever, unto the ages of ages. Amen.

text.text: : the great martyr and warrior for the faith
Beloved members of John's Repentance spiritual service, in the Lord, grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Today is the monthly feast of St. George and hence let us read about him and partake of his blessings.
👉 Inquiry: What is the significance of this iconic depiction of Saint George?

text:
: We have spoken at length, dear brethren, on the sacred art of iconography, its origins steeped in Holy Tradition, its sanctified practice endorsed by the guardians of the Faith, and its necessity as a window to the divine. The image of the martyr Saint George, resplendent on his steed, lance in hand, plunging into the dragon, is not a mere depiction of mortal combat but a rich set of spiritual truth.

This scene is an edifying spectacle, illustrating not only Saint George's noble upbringing but also his spiritual ascent. Consider the young saint, who, at the tender age of ten, had already mastered the spear. This weapon, both in physical and spiritual terms, symbolizes the Word of God, sharp and double-edged, piercing the very soul and spirit. And as he grew in stature, he sojourned among the pagans proclaiming, "

text.text: Behold, I am George, servant of Christ the King.

text:
"

Saint George relinquished the earthly titles bestowed upon him at his father’s demise, seeking instead the celestial crown offered by the King of kings. On reaching the age of maturity, the governor of his land wished to tether him to worldly concerns through marriage, but the Holy Spirit destined him for a heavenly union. When the governor perished, Saint George journeyed to Beirut, where providence led him to a maiden bound to a tree.

This maiden, destined for the maw of the draconic beast, represents the soul ensnared by sin, awaiting the deliverance only Christ can offer. The dragon, an embodiment of the evil one, exhibits traits of ferocity and deception. Its defeat at the hands of Saint George was a foreshadowing of the ultimate victory over evil through Christ.

Saint George, upon encountering the weeping maiden, hearkened not to his own safety but rather declared, "I may lack a beard, yet the One who stands with me shall triumph." This declaration is a testament to the indwelling power of the Triune God, for in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, he engaged the beast.

The ensuing victory over the dragon was more than a physical conquest; it was a demonstration of divine power. Saint George implored the onlookers to turn from their idolatry and embrace the truth of God. Upon their assent, he dispatched the dragon and raised a church as a beacon of faith.

Thus, the image of Saint George slaying the dragon is not a mere depiction of heroism; it is a narrative icon that speaks of salvation, of the warrior saint’s sacrificial spirit, and of the transformative power of God's grace.

Brethren, let us then regard the figure of Saint George not simply as a subject of artistic portrayal but as an exemplar of virtue. In the visage of this saint, we are reminded that our own lives are to be a living icon, manifesting Christ to the world through our actions, our sufferings, and our steadfast faith.

May the deeds of Saint George inspire us to combat the dragons of our time—sin, despair, and faithlessness—with the spear of truth and the shield of faith. And let us, in our veneration, echo the faith of our forebears: honoring not only the saint but the One who crowned him, even unto death on the battlefield of this world.

text.text: Brethren in the Lord, who stand steadfast in the unwavering Orthodox faith, grace unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ. Today we will be learning about the holy Eucharist, which stands as the pinnacle of our redemption and the very lifeblood of the Church.
✍ The Incarnation: The Prologue to the Eucharist

text:
Before we venture into the holy of holies, let us lay a foundation by reflecting upon the Incarnation, which is the cornerstone of all Christian doctrine. In the fullness of time, God, in His inscrutable wisdom, willed to be united with man. "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14). This is not a mere visitation but an abiding union. The Godhead was pleased to dwell bodily (Colossians 2:9), and in this union, the natures of divinity and humanity are neither confounded nor separated but are united without mixture or change.

text.text: The Eucharist: The Apex of Theology

text:

This Sacrament is not a mere remembrance but an anamnesis, a making present of the one sacrifice of Calvary. In the Divine Liturgy, we are lifted above time and space, and the events of our redemption are made present to us, that we might partake of the fruits of the Tree of Life which is Christ Himself.

text.text: ✍ The Eucharist: The Medicine of Immortality

text:

To partake of the Eucharist unworthily is to eat and drink judgment upon oneself (1 Corinthians 11:29). Hence, the Church, as a loving mother, calls her children to approach with a pure heart, having confessed and repented, that they might be made partakers of divine nature (2 Peter 1:4).

text.text: Conclusion: The Call to Union with Christ

text:
The Eucharist calls us to a life of holiness and union with Christ. It is not an end in itself but the means to our sanctification and salvation. To commune is to abide in Christ and to have Christ abide in us. Here, the faithful are invited to partake of the divine banquet, to enter into the joy of their Master, and to be transformed into the image of the One who gave Himself up for us all.

Let us, therefore, draw near with faith and with an ardent desire to be united with Christ, to be healed by His touch, and to be sanctified by His life-giving Body and Blood. May this Holy Sacrament be for us a pledge of the world to come and a haven of salvation in this present age.

In the words of our beloved Saint John Chrysostom, "O taste and see that the Lord is good" (Psalm 34:8), and let us partake of this banquet with the angels, making earth

 join with heaven, in the unending hymn of praise.

Through the prayers of our Holy Fathers, Lord Jesus Christ our God, have mercy on us. Amen.

of eyes and thoughts

👉 Question፦ What is meant by fornication of thought and eyes?

Answer፦

text:
The fornication of thought and eyes, my dear member, is a profound ailment of the soul, where one entertains impure thoughts and allows the gaze to fall upon things that inflame passions and lead one astray from the path of righteousness. In the Holy Scriptures, we are called to purity not only in deed but in heart and mind as well. Our Lord Jesus Christ said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

This sin of the mind and eyes is a deviation from the sacred covenant we are to keep with our bodies and souls as temples of the Holy Spirit. The antidote to such temptation is vigilance in our thoughts and discipline in our sight. We are to "set no wicked thing before [our] eyes" (Psalm 101:3) and to take captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ (2 Corinthians 10:5).

To cultivate purity, one must immerse oneself in prayer, the reading of Holy Scripture, and the lives of the saints, whose examples inspire us to greater holiness. A spiritual father or guide, as provided through our ministry, is invaluable in this struggle, for they can help direct your gaze towards the “author and finisher of our faith” (Hebrews 12:2).

Remember, our battle is not against the flesh, but against “principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world” (Ephesians 6:12). Guarding our senses is not simply an act of personal piety but a warfare against these spiritual forces.

Now, dear soul, what step will you take to guard your heart and eyes, to draw nearer to the purity to which Christ calls you?

text:
Consider, my beloved, the Scriptures that recount the creation of man. "And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness" (Genesis 1:26). In these words lies a mystery profound: that man was fashioned as a mirror of God’s own liberty, bestowed with the ability to choose—a faculty divine in its root. Man does not live by constraint, but by freedom, and this is the very essence of his glory, surpassing all other creatures.

Yet, with the subtlety of a serpent, the question slithers into the garden of our mind: What is this free will? It is, I tell you, the power to incline oneself towards the good or to descent towards evil. But mark this well: though the choice is ours, the capacity to choose the good and the very notion of good comes from God. For, as the Apostle James teaches, "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above" (James 1:17).

Now, some do err, thinking death and sin as natural to man as his very flesh. But this is not so. For sin is not the coin of our realm, nor death our native country. These are but intruders, unnatural guests that have darkened our doorstep through the misuse of our sacred gift. We were, as the holy Apostle Paul declares, predestined for life and salvation. But predestination without free will is like a painter without a canvas—it cannot manifest.

Oh, the deep wisdom of Saint Athanasius! For he did perceive the ignoble fall of man who, by his will, descends to the depths, ensnared by his own choices, and thus is ruled by passions as by cruel taskmasters. Consider then the gravity of sin: it is a voluntary servitude, a bondage self-imposed, and therein lies its tragedy.

And what of the words of the wise Solomon? They resound as a warning to our souls: we must not court death through our misdeeds or usher in ruin by our actions. For in so doing, we yield to the basest element of ourselves and deny our God-given nature.

Consider further, brethren, the angels, those ministering spirits, who likewise bear the responsibility for their actions. For freedom is not the sole province of humanity; it is shared with the heavenly hosts. And in freedom, there is accountability. Only a free agent can be subject to judgment, for only he can truly choose.

Here, too, must we ponder the harsh truth that our will can become enslaved—enslaved by desire which, when it has conceived, brings forth sin, and sin, when it is finished, brings forth death, as Saint James the Just teaches. Thus, the will itself can become the very source of death.

Yet, do not despair, for the devil indeed plays upon our will but cannot coerce it. We may be tempted, yet by our free will, we can resist. By saying "no" to sin, we assert the divine image within us.

In conclusion, though the struggle between the carnal and the spiritual is fierce, there is hope. If we, by our free will, submit to God’s will and walk in the path of righteousness, let us be steadfast in prayer and fasting. For the Lord has promised: "Ask, and it shall be given you" (Matthew 7:7). And in asking for divine aid, we do not abdicate our freedom but perfect it, aligning our will with the divine will, which is our true liberation.

Thus, may the Almighty God, who in His infinite wisdom has granted us this precious gift of free will, cut asunder the cords of sin that bind us, that we may freely choose the good and in so doing, find our rest in Him. Amen.

👉 Question፦ Greetings in the Lord, I have a question about something that has been on my mind lately! I read books written by Eastern Orthodox authors and their saints. They have been a great source of spiritual support in my journey, however I wonder if this will cause issues for me as Oriental Orthodox! Does our church have any sort of rules about reading or using resources from churches we aren't in Communion with? Are their saints, specifically modern saints that lived after the schism considered saints in our church?

Answer፦

text:
Greetings to you in the peace and love of our Lord Jesus Christ,

It is a joy to hear of your diligence in seeking spiritual nourishment through the writings of the holy ones who have walked the path of faith before us. The quest for understanding and the enrichment of one’s faith through the writings of saints and learned authors is indeed commendable.

In the embrace of the Orthodox tradition, both Eastern and Oriental, we find common ground in the veneration of saints who lived before the Chalcedonian schism. These holy men and women belong to both our families and provide us with a shared heritage of faith and piety.

When considering modern saints recognized after the schism, there is a space for nuanced appreciation. Question፦ Bless me Father. I am a convert. I have a profound love for Our Lady Dingil Maryam. I heard it said that She is the gate to Zion. How should we properly approach Our Lady Maryam? How should we understand her?

Answer፦

text:
Blessed are you, dear child, in your journey towards the embrace of Holy Orthodoxy. Our Lady, the Theotokos and Ever-Virgin Mary, holds a place of high honor in our faith, for she is the gate through which the Light of the World has entered. As it is written: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel" (Isaiah 7:14).

In approaching Our Lady Maryam, we do so with utmost reverence and love, recognizing her as the pure vessel of salvation, chosen by God to bear His only-begotten Son. We venerate her, not as a deity, but as the Mother of God, honoring her unique and singular role in the history of our salvation.

To understand her is to reflect upon her life - her humility, her obedience, and her unyielding faith. She stands as the supreme model of submission to God's will, a beacon of light guiding us towards her Son, Jesus Christ. We approach her with prayerful hearts, through the many beautiful Akathists and hymns written in her honor, through contemplation of her icons, and by emulating her virtues in our lives.

Remember, dear child, that devotion to the Theotokos is a journey towards Christ. For every honor we give to Mary directs us to the ultimate worship of God. Let us ask ourselves: how might we, like the Blessed Virgin, become bearers of Christ in our world?

text:
Brethren in Christ, as we commemorate the annual feast of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ (November 7), let us take a moment and learn more about Him and the Devine gifts He has given us. Jesus Christ is both fully man fully God. He is perfect in His divinity and perfect in His humanity. This is no mere titular union, nor a confounding of natures as the heretics have vainly asserted, but a true and indissoluble union, one Person of two natures, unaltered, unconfused, undivided, and inseparable. He is of two natures, which undergo no confusion, no change, no division, no separation; at no point was the difference between the natures taken away through the union, but rather the property of each nature is preserved and comes together to form one person and subsistence.

Consider, O faithful, that the Word became flesh not by a mere appearance or diminution of His divine nature; rather, He remained what He was and assumed what He was not, for our sake and for our salvation. In the unfathomable abyss of His mercy, He who is beyond eternity entered time, He whom the heavens cannot contain was contained in a virgin’s womb, He who upholds the universe was held in the arms of a mother.

Behold the Eucharist, that venerable and most divine Sacrament of His Body and Blood. As the Incarnation unites divinity with humanity, so does the Holy Eucharist unite Christ with us, and us with Christ. This is not a mere symbol, as some have erroneously taught, but the true Body and the true Blood, offered for the life of the world and for its salvation. As St. John Damascene declares, "The bread and wine are not a foreshadowing of the body and blood of Christ—by no means!—but the deified body of the Lord, because the Lord has said, 'This is my body', not, 'This is a symbol of my body', and 'My blood', not, 'A symbol of my blood'."

And what, dear brethren, is the Church but the Body of Christ, the fullness of Him who fills all in all? Within the embrace of the Church lies the fulness of truth and the treasures of grace, dispensed through the sacraments. In her, heaven and earth are joined, and the eschatological reality of the Kingdom is made present. The Church, both visible and invisible, temporal and eternal, is the context in which the mysteries of God are made manifest and efficacious.

The incarnate Logos, Jesus Christ our Lord, is the center and culmination of all history, the Alpha and Omega, the One in whom all things hold together. By His Incarnation, life, death, resurrection, and ascension, He has recapitulated all things, offering us a path to deification, that we may become by grace what He is by nature.

In this salvific narrative, we must not overlook the kenotic movement of the Incarnation: He who was in the form of God took the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men, and being found in human form, He humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross. This self-emptying is not a forsaking of His divine nature, but the expression of His divine love, a love which calls us to communion, to theosis, to partake of the divine nature.

Therefore, let us approach this great mystery with awe and with humility, with repentance and with love. Let us embrace the risen Christ with a faith not blind but seeing beyond sight, discerning the Word made flesh for our sake. As we partake of the Holy Mysteries, let us be transformed, becoming what we receive, the body of Christ, to the praise of His glorious grace.

text.text:
Question፦ Hello, I was wondering what the church says about dinosaurs and tectonic plates in relation to the timeline of the earth/universe according to science and the events that occurred compared to biblical timeline of the universe. Did dinosaurs exist & if so, when did they actually exist if the world hasn't been existing for millions of years according to the bible. How long has the universe been existing? is it in thousands or in millions?  Someone asked me this questions & i am not sure how to respond. Thank you!

Answer፦

text:
Dear seeker of truth,

Your inquiry touches upon the harmony between faith and science, a topic that has long intrigued both believers and scholars. The Orthodox Church, while deeply rooted in the spiritual understanding of creation as revealed in Scripture, does not oppose scientific discovery or the study of the natural world. In fact, the Church Fathers often encouraged the study of God's creation as a means to better understand and appreciate the Creator Himself.

Regarding dinosaurs and tectonic plates, the Church does not have an official position on scientific matters such as these. However, it is important to remember that the Bible, particularly the Book of Genesis, is not a scientific textbook but a theological and spiritual document. Its purpose is to convey the truth of God’s relationship with the world and humanity, rather than to provide a detailed account of the physical development of the universe.

Saint Basil the Great, in his "Hexaemeron," which is a series of homilies on the six days of creation, affirms that the creation of the world is an act of God, but he does not delve into specific scientific explanations. He writes, “What sort of day was it then? It was one without the succession of day and night, a day not measured by the sun, a day which had no need of any luminary.”

As for the age of the universe, the Church allows for a variety of understandings. While some may interpret the days of creation in Genesis as literal 24-hour periods, others view them as symbolic of longer epochs. The Church does not bind its faithful to a specific interpretation, as the essence of our faith lies in the Creator, not in the details of His creation.

Regarding the existence of dinosaurs, it is entirely possible, within the framework of Orthodox theology, to acknowledge their existence in the ancient past, as uncovered by scientific research. Did dinosaurs exist & if so, when did they actually exist if the world hasn't been existing for millions of years according to the bible. How long has the universe been existing? is it in thousands or in millions?  Someone asked me this questions & i am not sure how to respond. Thank you!

Your inquiry touches upon the harmony between faith and science, a topic that has long intrigued both believers and scholars. The Orthodox Church, while deeply rooted in the spiritual understanding of creation as revealed in Scripture, does not oppose scientific discovery or the study of the natural world. text: Beloved in Christ, we gather today to contemplate a mystery profound, An event both in time and beyond time: the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the Theotokos, our spiritual mother. This narrative is not merely a story of the past but a living fountain of spiritual wisdom and grace, flowing into the hearts of the faithful.

In the fullness of time, a moment chosen by Providence, the world witnessed the birth of Mary, a pivotal event in the history of salvation. Her nativity signifies not just the birth of a saintly figure, but the dawning of a new era in divine-human relations. The earth, long cursed to bear thorns and thistles, offered its first and most splendid fruit in Mary. Herein, we behold a divine paradox: the infinite God preparing a finite creature to become His dwelling place.

text.text: The Righteous Ancestors: Joachim and Anna

text: Consider Joachim and Anna, her venerable parents. In them, we see a living testament to faith and righteousness. Their lives, marked by piety and adherence to the law, were a prelude to the grace they would receive. Their daughter, Mary, was not merely the fruit of their lineage but a gift of grace, a testament to the power of God working through human fidelity. They were chosen not for their nobility or riches but for their humility and devotion, proving that God exalts the lowly and fills the hungry with good things.

text.text: The Conception and Birth of Mary

text: In the conception and birth of Mary, we witness the intersection of divine providence and human cooperation. This event was not an ordinary occurrence but a divine intervention, marking the beginning of the fulfillment of ancient prophecies. The birth of Mary was the dawn before the rising Sun, Christ Himself. She was born not of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.

text.text: Mary: The Fulfillment of the Law

text: The nativity of Mary is not merely an isolated event but a critical juncture in the divine plan. She stands as the fulfillment of the Law, embodying its purity and righteousness. In her, the virtues extolled in the Old Testament find their perfect expression. Thus, in venerating Mary, we venerate the culmination of the law’s promise, the bridge between the old and the new.

text.text: The Virginity of Mary: A Sign of Divine Favor

text: The perpetual virginity of Mary is a sign of her unique role in salvation history. She was chosen, not consumed by earthly desires, but dedicated entirely to God's purpose. Her virginity is not a mere physical attribute but a symbol of her total consecration to God. In giving birth to Christ, she remains a virgin, signifying the miraculous nature of Christ's birth and the divine mystery encompassing it.

In her birth, Mary was given to humanity as a gift of grace, and through her, we received Christ, the greater gift. By bearing Christ, she becomes not only His mother but also the spiritual mother of all who follow Him. In her, we find our spiritual lineage, our connection to the divine. She is a mother to all, nurturing us in the faith and guiding us toward her Son.

text.text: Mary's Birth: A Challenge to Ancient Philosophies

text: The nativity of Mary confronts the ancient philosophies that viewed the material world with suspicion or contempt. In her, we see that creation can be sanctified and raised to divine dignity. Her purity and holiness challenge our perceptions of the physical world, revealing that it is not matter that is corrupt, but our misuse of it.

The birth of Mary is a cause for universal rejoicing. It marks the end of a long period of spiritual barrenness and the beginning of our redemption. Just as a mother forgets her labor pains for the joy of bringing a child into the world, so too does the birth of Mary turn our sorrow into joy. In her birth, we see the promise of our own rebirth in Christ, the dawn of a new creation.

text: Prayer, in the Orthodox tradition, is not merely a ritual or a set of words recited mechanically. It is the breath of the soul, a dialogue with the Divine. It transcends mere spoken language, reaching into the depths of the heart where the spirit communes with God. This communion is akin to a mystical union, where the soul, stripped of worldly distractions, stands naked and humbled before its Creator.

text.text: True Prayer: The Heart's Dialogue with God

text: True prayer is characterized by humility, love, and a deep yearning for God's presence. It is not merely the utterance of words but a state of the heart. In the words of St. John Chrysostom, "Prayer does not mean simply to pour out one's heart. It means rather to find the way to God and to speak with Him, whether the soul is full of joy or despair." Thus, true prayer is the lifting of the heart and mind to God, transcending the boundaries of earthly concerns.

The Orthodox tradition emphasizes the need for unceasing prayer. As St. Paul urges, "pray without ceasing" (1 Thessalonians 5:17). This constant prayer is not a ceaseless utterance of words but a continual orientation of the heart towards God. It's about maintaining a state of spiritual alertness, always being in God's presence, and being aware of His omnipresence.

text.text: The Role of the Jesus Prayer

text: In Orthodox spirituality, the Jesus Prayer ("Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner") holds a special place. It is a simple yet powerful tool that assists in the journey towards continuous prayer. By repeating this prayer, one is constantly calling upon the name of Jesus, thereby fostering an intimate relationship with Him.

text.text: The Liturgical and Personal Dimensions of Prayer

text: Orthodox worship is deeply liturgical, and these communal prayers serve as a model for personal prayer. The Divine Liturgy, the pinnacle of Orthodox worship, is not only a communal celebration but also a personal encounter with the living God. Similarly, personal prayer is not isolated from the liturgical life of the Church but is intimately connected to it.

Prayer, in the Orthodox understanding, is transformative. It changes us, molds us, and brings us closer to the likeness of God. As St. John Chrysostom eloquently puts it, "Prayer is the light of the soul, the true knowledge of God and man, the healer of vices, the physician of diseases, the peace of the soul, the heavenly guide which lifts men from earth to heaven."

In conclusion, prayer in the Orthodox tradition is a journey of transformation, a continuous dialogue with God that takes place in the heart. It is an ascent of the soul towards God, a means of entering into the divine mystery, and a path to becoming partakers of the divine nature. May this understanding of prayer enrich and deepen the spiritual lives of all who seek to draw nearer to God.

text: In the heart of Orthodox spirituality lies the pursuit of a deep, personal relationship with God. This relationship is nurtured not just through intellectual understanding but through a life lived in accordance with God's will. Spiritual wisdom, therefore, is more than knowledge; it is the lived experience of God's presence in our lives.

text.text: 1. The Pursuit of Humility and Truth

text: The first step towards acquiring spiritual wisdom is the embrace of humility. In the Orthodox tradition, humility is not weakness but a recognition of our dependence on God. It is the fertile ground where wisdom takes root. As we humble ourselves, acknowledging our limitations and our need for divine guidance, we become receptive to the truths God reveals to us. These truths are not always in harmony with the world's wisdom, but they are anchored in a higher understanding that transcends human reasoning.

text.text: 2. The Role of the Holy Spirit

text: Orthodox spirituality emphasizes the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, the Comforter, who guides us into all truth. This Spirit reveals the mysteries of the divine and makes known the deep things of God. He is the one who enlightens our minds and hearts, enabling us to grasp the profound realities of the Christian faith. The Holy Spirit also aids us in discerning the truth, helping us distinguish between what is genuinely of God and what is not.

text.text: 3. Wisdom in Action: The Orthodox Way of Life

text: In Orthodoxy, wisdom is not merely an intellectual exercise but is demonstrated through action. It involves living out the teachings of Christ in daily life. This means practicing virtues such as love, patience, kindness, and forgiveness. It also means participating in the sacramental life of the Church, through which grace is imparted to believers. The Eucharist, confession, prayer, and fasting are not just rituals but means of grace that cultivate spiritual wisdom within us.

text.text: 4. The Significance of Suffering and Trials

text:
The Orthodox perspective views suffering and trials as opportunities for spiritual growth. In the midst of difficulties, believers are called to cling to God and trust in His providence. These challenging moments are seen as purifying fires that refine our faith and deepen our understanding of God's ways. text.text: The Sacred Vision of Saint Lalibela

text: In the heart of Ethiopia, under the divine guidance of the Holy Spirit, arose a king whose spiritual vision transcended the bounds of his earthly kingdom.  King St. Lalibela, moved by the plight of his people who could no longer embark on pilgrimages to Jerusalem, was graced with a heavenly vision. This vision was not merely a replica of the earthly Jerusalem but an embodiment of the celestial city, the New Jerusalem, as revealed to Saint John the Theologian in his Revelation. Herein, Saint Lalibela was called to create a spiritual oasis, a Jerusalem in Ethiopia, that would be a beacon of faith and hope for his people and all who sought the divine.

text.text: The Intersection of Holiness and Kingship

text: The life of Saint Lalibela stands as a testament to the harmonious blending of royal authority and sanctity. He was not merely a temporal ruler but a spiritual beacon, embodying the ideal of the priest-king. His reign was marked by an unyielding devotion to God, a devotion that transcended mere ritualistic observance and penetrated the very essence of his being. His was a rule guided by divine wisdom, where the scepter of governance and the staff of spiritual authority were held in a harmonious balance.

The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela are not merely architectural marvels but are imbued with deep theological significance. Each structure, carved with painstaking devotion and divine inspiration, stands as a living sermon in stone. These churches are a manifestation of Saint Lalibela's deep spiritual communion with God, a physical testament to an invisible reality. They are, in their very essence, a microcosm of the heavenly Jerusalem, a tangible encounter with the divine mystery.

text.text: The Trials and Triumphs of Faith

text: The life of Saint Lalibela was marked by trials and tribulations, moments where the darkness of human malice sought to overshadow the light of divine purpose. Yet, in every instance, these trials were transformed into triumphs of faith. The poison intended to end his life became a means of divine revelation and physical healing, echoing the words of Christ that His followers would handle serpents and drink deadly poison without harm (Mark 16:18). This miraculous deliverance is a testament to the power of faith and the protective hand of God over His chosen ones.

Saint Lalibela's life was marked by divine promises, each a covenantal seal of his divine mission. These promises were not mere words but were living realities that shaped his reign and his spiritual journey. They were assurances of divine favor, guiding him in his earthly mission and assuring him of his eternal reward.

The legacy of King St. Lalibela transcends the boundaries of time and space. His life, his works, and his spiritual vision continue to inspire and guide not only the faithful in Ethiopia but all who seek a deeper understanding of the divine mystery. His churches stand as silent yet eloquent witnesses to a faith that is both ancient and ever new, a faith that calls each believer to a pilgrimage not just to a physical location but to the very heart of God.

In conclusion, the life and works of King St. Lalibela are a mosaic of divine grace, earthly wisdom, and spiritual vision. They beckon us to look beyond the visible and seek the face of the invisible God, reminding us that our ultimate pilgrimage is not to a place of stone and mortar but to the heavenly Jerusalem, the eternal abode of God and His saints. This is the legacy of King St. Lalibela, a legacy that calls each of us to a deeper, more profound faith.

text.text:
👉 Question፦ Will we be judged for killing animals like Rodents?

Answer፦

text:
Beloved in Christ,

In our contemplation of life and its sacredness, we are reminded of the profound words in Genesis 1:26, where God says, "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth." This dominion is not of tyranny but of stewardship, a call to care for God's creation with love and respect.

In the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, as well as in the broader Orthodox Christian tradition, the relationship between humans and animals is viewed through the lens of stewardship and compassion. All creatures are part of God's creation, and as such, they are to be treated with respect and care. While the Church does not explicitly condemn the killing of animals for necessary purposes, such as for food, it does encourage mindfulness and respect for all life.

The act of killing rodents, or any other animal should always be approached with a sense of responsibility and, when necessary, with a spirit of regret for the loss of life. We are reminded to always seek the most humane and compassionate solutions in our interactions with all of God's creatures.

Reflecting on our actions and their impact on the world around us is an essential part of our spiritual journey. In doing so, we align ourselves more closely with God's will, fostering a spirit of humility and love. As you consider this aspect of your life, ask yourself: How can I exercise compassionate stewardship in all my interactions with God's creation?

text.text: About the Holy family's return to the Holy land.

text: Beloved members of John's Repentance spiritual service, today we celebrate the Holy family's return from Egypt to Israel. We call this feast 'Debre Kuskwam' or Mount of Kuskwam. Let us learn about this Holy day and partake from it's blessings.

text.text: The Departure from Egypt: A Symbol of Spiritual Liberation

text: The journey of the Holy Family from Egypt to Israel mirrors the exodus of the Israelites from the land of bondage. Just as Moses led God's chosen people out of slavery into the Promised Land, so too did Joseph guide the Holy Family from the land of Egypt, symbolizing a departure from the spiritual bondage of sin and idolatry. This journey represents the Christian's path from the bondage of sin to the freedom of grace.

text.text: The Suffering and Endurance: A Lesson in Humility and Trust

text: The trials and tribulations faced by the Holy Family during their exile in Egypt and their journey back to Israel serve as a testament to their humility and unwavering trust in God's providence. Their hardships, akin to the tribulations faced by every Christian soul on its journey towards salvation, are a reminder of the suffering Christ Himself would endure for the redemption of mankind.

text.text: The Reception and Hospitality in Ethiopia: Embracing the Universal Church

text: The warm welcome and hospitality the Holy Family received in Ethiopia is emblematic of the universality of Christ's message. Ethiopia, often regarded as a symbol of the Gentile nations in early Christian literature, represents the outreach of the Church to all nations and peoples. The Holy Family's sojourn in Ethiopia and the blessings they bestowed upon the land prefigure the spread of Christianity and the blessings it brings to all corners of the earth.

text.text: The Return to Israel: Fulfillment of Divine Will

text: The return of the Holy Family to Israel signifies the fulfillment of God's will and the completion of a divine journey that began with the Incarnation. This return was not just a physical journey but a spiritual one, marking a full circle from prophecy to fulfillment, from the promise of the Messiah to His living presence among His chosen people.

text.text: The Crossing of the River: A Miraculous Testament

text: The miraculous crossing of the river, facilitated by the divine intervention of Christ, is reminiscent of the crossing of the Red Sea by the Israelites. It signifies the triumph of faith over seemingly insurmountable obstacles and the power of God to make a way where there seems to be no way.

The journey of the Holy Family from Egypt to Israel is not merely a historical event but a spiritual odyssey that encapsulates the essence of the Christian journey. Each step of this journey, marked by faith, hardship, divine intervention, and fulfillment of God's will, offers profound lessons for the faithful. It serves as a microcosm of the Church's pilgrimage through history, a journey from the shadows of sin into the glorious light of Christ's redemption.

In the manner of John Chrysostom, let us reflect deeply on these lessons, drawing from them strength and inspiration for our own spiritual journeys, continually seeking the grace and guidance of the Holy Family in our quest for salvation.

May the blessings of the Holy Mother of God, the Virgin, and the Cross be upon us. Amen.

👉🏾👉🏾👉🏾 About the Holy family's return to the Holy land. 

Beloved members of John's Repentance spiritual service, today we celebrate the Holy family's return from Egypt to Israel. We call this feast 'Debre Kuskwam' or Mount of Kuskwam. Let us learn about this Holy day and partake from it's blessings. 

The Departure from Egypt: A Symbol of Spiritual Liberation

The journey of the Holy Family from Egypt to Israel mirrors the exodus of the Israelites from the land of bondage. Just as Moses led God's chosen people out of slavery into the Promised Land, so too did Joseph guide the Holy Family from the land of Egypt, symbolizing a departure from the spiritual bondage of sin and idolatry. This journey represents the Christian's path from the bondage of sin to the freedom of grace.

The Suffering and Endurance: A Lesson in Humility and Trust

The trials and tribulations faced by the Holy Family during their exile in Egypt and their journey back to Israel serve as a testament to their humility and unwavering trust in God's providence. Their hardships, akin to the tribulations faced by every Christian soul on its journey towards salvation, are a reminder of the suffering Christ Himself would endure for the redemption of mankind.

The Reception and Hospitality in Ethiopia: Embracing the Universal Church

The warm welcome and hospitality the Holy Family received in Ethiopia is emblematic of the universality of Christ's message. Ethiopia, often regarded as a symbol of the Gentile nations in early Christian literature, represents the outreach of the Church to all nations and peoples. The Holy Family's sojourn in Ethiopia and the blessings they bestowed upon the land prefigure the spread of Christianity and the blessings it brings to all corners of the earth.

The Return to Israel: Fulfillment of Divine Will

The return of the Holy Family to Israel signifies the fulfillment of God's will and the completion of a divine journey that began with the Incarnation. This return was not just a physical journey but a spiritual one, marking a full circle from prophecy to fulfillment, from the promise of the Messiah to His living presence among His chosen people.

The Crossing of the River: A Miraculous Testament

The miraculous crossing of the river, facilitated by the divine intervention of Christ, is reminiscent of the crossing of the Red Sea by the Israelites. It signifies the triumph of faith over seemingly insurmountable obstacles and the power of God to make a way where there seems to be no way.

Conclusion: The Everlasting Impact

The journey of the Holy Family from Egypt to Israel is not merely a historical event but a spiritual odyssey that encapsulates the essence of the Christian journey. Each step of this journey, marked by faith, hardship, divine intervention, and fulfillment of God's will, offers profound lessons for the faithful. It serves as a microcosm of the Church's pilgrimage through history, a journey from the shadows of sin into the glorious light of Christ's redemption.

In the manner of John Chrysostom, let us reflect deeply on these lessons, drawing from them strength and inspiration for our own spiritual journeys, continually seeking the grace and guidance of the Holy Family in our quest for salvation.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every language that He has created, today and always.

May the blessings of the Holy Mother of God, the Virgin, and the Cross be upon us. Amen.

text:
. Hence let us delve into this council convened under the auspices of the blessed Emperor Constantine in the year of our Lord 325. This hallowed assembly, gathering in the city of Nicaea, was a beacon of divine illumination, guiding the Church through tumultuous seas of heresy and schism.

318 bishops, shepherds of the faithful, convened in unity of purpose. Among them were luminaries such as Alexander of Alexandria, the venerable overseer of the Egyptian church, and Eustathius of Antioch, a beacon of orthodoxy. They gathered not for earthly gain but to safeguard the sacred doctrine against the ravages of heresy, most notably the teachings of Arius of Alexandria.

Arius, a presbyter whose name has since been etched in infamy, dared to proclaim a Christ diminished, a Son created and not co-eternal with the Father. This was not merely a theological dispute but an affront to the very nature of our Lord Jesus Christ. Such teachings, left unchecked, threatened to rend asunder the very fabric of the Church.

In the spirit of the apostles themselves, these venerable fathers, many scarred by the trials of persecution, gathered to reaffirm the truth of our faith. Emperor Constantine, a servant of God, provided a grand hall for their deliberations, humbling himself before the servants of the Lord. In this sacred space, they debated, prayed, and were guided by the Holy Spirit, crafting a creed that would stand as a bulwark against heresy.

This Nicene Creed, a testament to their faith and unity, articulated the full divinity of Christ: "We believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, begotten from the Father before all ages, God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made; of the same essence as the Father." Through these words, they affirmed that Christ is not a created being but consubstantial with the Father, sharing the same divine essence.

Furthermore, the council established canons for the governance of the Church, addressing issues from the ordination of clergy to the reconciliation of those who had lapsed in faith. These canons reflected a profound understanding of the human condition, offering guidance and discipline while upholding the mercy and grace of God.

The Council of Nicaea stands as a testament to the Church's commitment to truth and unity. The creed formulated there did not merely address the controversies of the day but laid a foundation for all orthodox belief, a beacon of truth shining through the ages.

As we reflect on the legacy of Nicaea, let us hold fast to the truth handed down by these holy fathers. Their teachings, rooted in the apostolic tradition, guide us in our journey towards the Kingdom of Heaven. In their wisdom, let us find our path; in their courage, our inspiration; and in their unity, our strength. To God be the glory, now and forever. Among them were luminaries such as Alexander of Alexandria, the venerable overseer of the Egyptian church, and Eustathius of Antioch, a beacon of orthodoxy. They gathered not for earthly gain but to safeguard the sacred doctrine against the ravages of heresy, most notably the teachings of Arius of Alexandria.

The Council of Nicaea stands as a testament to the Church's commitment to truth and unity. The creed formulated there did not merely address the controversies of the day but laid a foundation for all orthodox belief, a beacon of truth shining through the ages.

As we reflect on the legacy of Nicaea, let us hold fast to the truth handed down by these holy fathers. Their teachings, rooted in the apostolic tradition, guide us in our journey towards the Kingdom of Heaven. In their wisdom, let us find our path; in their courage, our inspiration; and in their unity, our strength. To God be the glory, now and forever. Amen.

text.text: Beloved members of John's Repentance spiritual service, today is the monthly feast of St. Michael. Hence let us read the below text written about him and partake from his blessings.

text:
St. Michael, whose name echoes the divine query, "Who is like God?" stands as a beacon of divine strength and leadership. This mighty Archangel, esteemed in the heavenly hierarchy, is not merely a celestial being but also a symbol of hope and fortitude for the faithful. His role transcends the boundaries of heaven, extending his protective mantle over the faithful on earth.

Let us recall the ancient scriptures and the teachings of the Church Fathers, who spoke of St. Michael with reverence and awe. His presence in pivotal moments of Biblical history underscores his importance. When Joshua, leading the Israelites in the wilderness, encountered a divine figure with a drawn sword, it was none other than St. Michael, the captain of the Lord's host. This encounter, as narrated in the Book of Joshua, reveals the martial and protective aspects of St. Michael's character.

In the exodus from Egypt, where the Israelites were led from bondage to freedom, St. Michael was the guiding light, the angelic shepherd appointed by God Himself to safeguard His people. His role was not only as a guide but also as a guardian, ensuring the fulfillment of God's promises.

Furthermore, in the prophetic visions of Daniel, St. Michael emerges as a powerful intercessor and protector of the faithful. He is depicted as the great prince who stands guard over God's people, a testament to his enduring role in the salvation history.

In the New Testament, St. Michael's presence is equally profound. His role in the cosmic struggle against evil and his intercession for the faithful before the throne of God are themes that resonate throughout Christian theology.

The Orthodox Church, in its liturgical and theological tradition, has always held St. Michael in high esteem. His commemoration on the twelfth day of each month is not merely a ritualistic observance but a testament to his ongoing intercessory role. The Church teaches that St. Michael's prayers bring about the blessings of nature: the timely rains, the fruitful earth, the gentle winds—all are seen as manifestations of his intercession.

In our daily struggles and in the greater spiritual battle against sin and temptation, let us turn to St. Michael for guidance and protection. His example inspires us to stand firm in our faith, to confront the adversities of life with courage, and to remain steadfast in our devotion to God.

As we honor St. Michael, let us remember that his story is not just a tale from the past but a living reality that permeates the life of every Orthodox believer. In our prayers and in our actions, let us emulate his unwavering faith and his unceasing devotion to the will of God. May his intercession strengthen us, may his example guide us, and may his presence among us be a source of comfort and hope.

Thus, beloved in Christ, let us embrace the lessons and the legacy of the Archangel St. Michael. May his blessings be upon us, and may his intercession lead us closer to the divine. In his honor and memory, let us say, "Archangel Michael, pray for us, that we may be worthy of the promises of Christ." Amen.

text.text: Question፦ What is the difference in beliefs about Christ between
? Could you explain the term 'Tax Christ' and 'Common Christ' if they have any significance in Orthodox Christianity? If a person in a

converts to Christianity, what should be their approach in terms of living arrangements and family relationships?

Answer፦

text:
In the grace and peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, I greet you, dear questioner, seeking to illuminate the path of faith for you.

The disagreement between Athanasius and Arius is fundamental in Christian theology, especially in the Orthodox tradition. Saint Athanasius, a staunch defender of Orthodoxy, upheld the belief in the full divinity of Christ. He asserted that Christ is of the same essence (homoousios) as the Father, co-eternal and co-equal. This is foundational to our understanding of the Holy Trinity. In contrast, Arius, a presbyter in Alexandria, argued that the Son was a creation of the Father, and therefore not co-eternal or of the same essence. This view, known as Arianism, was deemed heretical at the First Council of Nicaea in 325 AD.

As for the terms 'Tax Christ' and 'Common Christ', they are not recognized within the Orthodox Christian tradition. Our focus remains on the Christological teachings as affirmed by the Ecumenical Councils.

Regarding conversion from Islam to Christianity, this is a profound and delicate journey. In the Orthodox faith, we encourage love, respect, and patience in all family relationships. It is crucial to maintain peace and honor within the family while steadfastly adhering to one’s newfound faith in Christ. The approach to living arrangements and family relationships should be guided by prayer, the counsel of a spiritual father, and a heartfelt commitment to living a Christ-centered life.

As the Scripture teaches us, “God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him” (1 John 4:16). This love must be the cornerstone of all our relationships, especially within the family.

Now, beloved in Christ, how might you begin to approach these changes in your life with love and patience, while staying true to your faith in our Lord Jesus Christ?

text.text: Question፦ Hi does the Orthodox tewahedo church believe in

text:
Beloved in Christ,

Grace and peace to you. In the Orthodox Tewahedo Church, as in the broader Orthodox Christian tradition, we uphold the sanctity and respect of the human body. This belief stems from the understanding that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19), an integral part of the human person, created in the image and likeness of God.

Therefore, the Church does not endorse cremation. We believe in the resurrection of the body, as professed in the Nicene Creed, and thus maintain the practice of burial, honoring the body as it awaits the resurrection. This is deeply rooted in our theology and liturgical practices, reflecting our reverence for the body as an essential component of human personhood.

In this regard, the Orthodox Church encourages burial as a way of expressing hope in the resurrection and a deep respect for the gift of the body, which God has bestowed upon us. It is a practice that aligns with our understanding of life, death, and the hope of eternal life in Christ.

As you contemplate this teaching, may I ask you to reflect on how you view the body in relation to your spiritual journey? How does this understanding influence your respect for the physical aspect of our human existence, as you walk in faith towards the Kingdom of God?

text.text: Beloved members of John's Repentance spiritual service, today we send you a lesson on the fast of the Prophets which starts on November 24th and ends January 6th so you can read and understand more about this fast.
The Essence of the Prophetic Fast

text: In the richness of Orthodox spirituality, the Fast of the Prophets emerges as a poignant reminder of the yearning and anticipation that prefigured the incarnation of Christ. This fast, spaning 44days, mirrors the fervent prayers and ascetic lives of the prophets who, through divine inspiration, foresaw the coming of the Messiah. Their lives, steeped in prayer and fasting, were beacons pointing towards the great mystery of God becoming man for the salvation of humanity.

This fast is not merely an act of remembrance but a call to spiritual preparation. As the prophets prepared for the coming of Christ through fasting and prayer, so are Christians called to prepare their hearts for the celebration of His Nativity. This period of fasting is an invitation to walk in the footsteps of these holy men, allowing their prophetic visions to illuminate our path towards a deeper understanding of the mystery of the Incarnation.

The Orthodox Church venerates the prophets and apostles as foundational to its faith. Their collective witness forms a continuum that finds its fulfillment in Christ. The Fast of the Prophets, therefore, is not only a preparation for the Nativity of Christ but also a participation in the spiritual legacy of these holy men who were instrumental in God’s salvific plan.

Fasting, in the Orthodox tradition, is not merely an external act but a spiritual discipline aimed at inner transformation. It is a time for Christians to cultivate humility, patience, and charity, aligning their will with God’s. It serves as a reminder of our dependence on God and our need for His grace. The Fast of the Prophets, thus, becomes a journey of spiritual renewal, leading to the joyous celebration of Christ’s birth.

Prayer is the breath of the soul, and in the context of fasting, it assumes an even greater significance. It is through prayer that the fast is sanctified and becomes a true offering to God. The prayers of the faithful during this period are a continuation of the prayers of the prophets, echoing their longing for the Messiah and their devotion to God’s will.

text.text: The Universal Message of the Fast

text: The Fast of the Prophets transcends time and place, inviting all of humanity to partake in the spiritual preparation for the Nativity of Christ. It is a universal call to turn our hearts towards God, to reflect on the mystery of the Incarnation, and to live out the teachings of Christ in our daily lives.

In conclusion, the Fast of the Prophets in the Orthodox Church is a profound spiritual journey that connects believers with the prophetic vision of the Old Testament and prepares them for the celebration of the Nativity of Christ. It is a time of prayer, fasting, and spiritual renewal, echoing the lives and messages of the prophets who foretold the coming of the Messiah. This fast serves as a reminder of the continuous journey towards spiritual awakening and the transformative power of God’s love made manifest in the Incarnation.

In the richness of Orthodox spirituality, the Fast of the Prophets emerges as a poignant reminder of the yearning and anticipation that prefigured the incarnation of Christ. This fast, spaning 44days, mirrors the fervent prayers and ascetic lives of the prophets who, through divine inspiration, foresaw the coming of the Messiah. Their lives, steeped in prayer and fasting, were beacons pointing towards the great mystery of God becoming man for the salvation of humanity.

The Call to Spiritual Preparation

This fast is not merely an act of remembrance but a call to spiritual preparation. As the prophets prepared for the coming of Christ through fasting and prayer, so are Christians called to prepare their hearts for the celebration of His Nativity. This period of fasting is an invitation to walk in the footsteps of these holy men, allowing their prophetic visions to illuminate our path towards a deeper understanding of the mystery of the Incarnation.

The Prophetic and Apostolic Foundation

The Orthodox Church venerates the prophets and apostles as foundational to its faith. Their collective witness forms a continuum that finds its fulfillment in Christ. The Fast of the Prophets, therefore, is not only a preparation for the Nativity of Christ but also a participation in the spiritual legacy of these holy men who were instrumental in God’s salvific plan.

 Fasting: A Spiritual Discipline

Fasting, in the Orthodox tradition, is not merely an external act but a spiritual discipline aimed at inner transformation. It is a time for Christians to cultivate humility, patience, and charity, aligning their will with God’s. It serves as a reminder of our dependence on God and our need for His grace. The Fast of the Prophets, thus, becomes a journey of spiritual renewal, leading to the joyous celebration of Christ’s birth.

Prayer: The Companion of Fasting

Prayer is the breath of the soul, and in the context of fasting, it assumes an even greater significance. It is through prayer that the fast is sanctified and becomes a true offering to God. The prayers of the faithful during this period are a continuation of the prayers of the prophets, echoing their longing for the Messiah and their devotion to God’s will.

 The Universal Message of the Fast

The Fast of the Prophets transcends time and place, inviting all of humanity to partake in the spiritual preparation for the Nativity of Christ. It is a universal call to turn our hearts towards God, to reflect on the mystery of the Incarnation, and to live out the teachings of Christ in our daily lives.

 Conclusion

In conclusion, the Fast of the Prophets in the Orthodox Church is a profound spiritual journey that connects believers with the prophetic vision of the Old Testament and prepares them for the celebration of the Nativity of Christ. It is a time of prayer, fasting, and spiritual renewal, echoing the lives and messages of the prophets who foretold the coming of the Messiah. This fast serves as a reminder of the continuous journey towards spiritual awakening and the transformative power of God’s love made manifest in the Incarnation.

text:
Beloved in Christ,

In the eyes of the Orthodox Church, the focus is always on the state of the heart and the intent behind our actions, rather than the actions themselves in isolation. When it comes to wearing makeup, it is not inherently sinful. It is the intention and the manner in which it is used that matters. As Saint John Chrysostom wisely remarked, "For indeed both wine and intercourse are allowed, but both of these become a sin when they are used improperly and out of season." The same can be applied to wearing makeup.

In 1 Peter 3:3-4, we read: "Do not let your adornment be merely outward—arranging the hair, wearing gold, or putting on fine apparel—rather let it be the hidden person of the heart, with the incorruptible beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is very precious in the sight of God." This scripture invites us to reflect on our intentions. Is the makeup worn to enhance the God-given beauty and to present oneself respectfully, or is it used to draw undue attention or to cultivate vanity? It is the latter that the Church cautions against.

Remember, the Orthodox Church encourages modesty and humility in all aspects of life. Makeup, when used in moderation and with pure intentions, is not considered sinful. It is important, however, to always guard our hearts against vanity and to seek beauty that is "incorruptible" - the beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, rooted in our relationship with God.

As you reflect on this, ask yourself: How can I ensure that my outward appearance is a reflection of the inner beauty of my soul, cultivated through a life of prayer, humility, and love for God?

Question፦ Greetings, our teachers from the Yohannes Nisiha, I pray by Gods Grace you all are well. I wanted to ask a private question about the Celebration of the birth of Our Lord and why we as Orthodox Christians do not put up Christmas Trees in our homes. Many of the faithful in America are starting to use these traditions of the West and I wanted to ask is this accepted by the faith or is this a pagan practice that is against the Celebration of the Incarnation of God. Also, what traditions are encouraged by our Fathers to glorify God in the season of His Holy Birth.

Answer፦

text:
Greetings in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,

Your query touches upon a significant aspect of our faith, especially in these times when cultures intertwine and traditions intermingle. The practice of setting up Christmas trees is indeed a Western tradition and not inherently part of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church or the broader Orthodox Christian tradition. It originated in Germany and gradually became popular in other parts of the world, including America.

In Orthodoxy, we focus on the spiritual essence of feasts, primarily through liturgy, fasting, prayer, and almsgiving. Our emphasis is on the incarnation of Christ, a mystery profoundly expressed in our liturgical celebrations. As St. John Chrysostom says, "The rich man is not one who has much, but one who gives much. For what he gives away remains his forever." This spirit of giving and self-denial is central to our commemoration of Christ's Nativity.

Regarding the Christmas tree, while it is not a traditional Orthodox practice, its use in itself is not considered a pagan or anti-Christian act, as long as it does not detract from the true meaning of the Nativity. However, as Orthodox Christians, we are called to discern and ensure that our practices align with the teachings and traditions of our Church.

Our Fathers encourage traditions that glorify God through increased prayer, participation in the Divine Liturgy, and acts of charity. These practices bring us closer to the mystery of the Incarnation. The Nativity Fast, which we observe, prepares us spiritually for the celebration of Christ's birth. We are also encouraged to read and contemplate the Scriptures, especially the Infancy narratives in the Gospels, and to engage in acts of love and kindness, reflecting the love that God showed by becoming man for our salvation.

In conclusion, while the Christmas tree is a cultural addition rather than an Orthodox tradition, what is most crucial is maintaining a focus on the Incarnation of Christ and living out the virtues that this great feast teaches us. How might you, in this blessed season, deepen your practice of the true spirit of Christ's Nativity in prayer, fasting, and acts of charity?

text.text: Question፦ I have a very hard time forgiving people, what do you advice me?

text:
Beloved in Christ,

Your struggle with forgiveness resonates deeply within the teachings of our faith, and it is a common challenge faced by many, both within and outside the folds of Orthodoxy. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus teaches us, "For if you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." (Matthew 6:14). This verse is a cornerstone in understanding the necessity of forgiveness in our spiritual lives.

text: Beloved members of John's Repentance spiritual service, today is the anual feast of Zion. Hence, let us delve into the profound significance of the Feast of Zion, a pivotal celebration in the Orthodox Tewahedo Church, marked annually on December 1st. This feast, deeply rooted in scriptural and historical contexts, intertwines the sanctity of the Ark of Zion with the reverence for the Virgin Mary, embodying the profound mysteries of faith and divine providence.

text.text: The Ark of Zion: A Testament to God's Presence

text: At the heart of this celebration lies the Ark of Zion, a sacred symbol of God's covenant with His people. The Ark, as recounted in the Holy Scriptures, was entrusted to Moses and later came to reside in the great city of King David. Here, it stood as a beacon of hope and justice for the suffering Israelis, a divine presence amidst their trials and tribulations.

text.text: The Feast of Zion: A Historical Perspective

text:
The narrative of the Ark's journey, particularly its capture and eventual return, is central to the Feast of Zion. This story unfolds with the sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, whose sacrilegious actions in the temple led to dire consequences. Their disrespect towards the sacred rituals, the extinguishing of the temple lamp, and their irreverence in the presence of the Ark invoked divine wrath, fulfilling the prophecy of their simultaneous demise.

The capture of the Ark by the Philistines, a pivotal event, demonstrated the power of God even in foreign lands. The Philistine god Dagon was reduced to rubble in the presence of the Ark, and plagues afflicted the Philistines until they returned the Ark to the Israelites. This return was marked by miraculous events, reinforcing the Ark's divine nature.

text.text: The Virgin Mary: The New Ark

text: In Orthodox theology, the Virgin Mary is venerated as the New Ark, a living sanctuary who bore Christ, the Word made flesh. The Feast of Zion, therefore, is not only a commemoration of the historical Ark but also a celebration of Mary as the Mother of God. This linkage is beautifully encapsulated in the Psalms and the prophecies of Isaiah, which prefigure Mary as Zion, the chosen dwelling of God.

text.text: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and the Ark

text: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church holds a unique connection to the Ark, believing it came to Ethiopia under the auspices of Queen Sheba and King Solomon. This historical belief intertwines with the scriptural narratives, enriching the spiritual tapestry of the Feast of Zion.

text.text: The Feast of Zion: A Call to Spiritual Renewal

text: The Feast of Zion is more than a historical commemoration; it is a call to spiritual renewal, urging the faithful to embody the virtues exemplified by the Virgin Mary. It's a time to reflect on divine justice, mercy, and the transformative power of God's presence in our lives.

As we observe this sacred feast, let us embrace the virtues of love, humility, and service, inspired by the Virgin Mary, the New Ark of the Covenant. May her intercession guide us, and may we find solace and strength in the enduring legacy of the Feast of Zion.

In this manner, the Feast of Zion stands as a profound testament to God's enduring presence and His unyielding commitment to His covenant with humanity. It beckons us to a deeper understanding of our faith and a renewed commitment to live out its precepts in our daily lives.

May the blessings of The Virgin, and the cross be upon us. Amen.
