text:
Hello again , John 11:25-26  says “Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. “ isn’t this referencing us as we were once dead but  now we are  alive in Christ?

Also
How can abiding/beleving in Christ have anything to do with intercession? As our God is pretty straightforward when it comes to what he wants and says as he gave us the commandments and ex. Telling Jonah to go to Nineveh.And can intercession help in getting mercy because it says in Hebrew 4:15(‘Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need’).

The Lord Jesus Christ be with thy spirit.Grace be with you all.Amen

Beloved in Christ,

Your inquiry touches the heart of our faith, the resurrection and life in Jesus Christ, and the mystery of intercession, which are profound yet comforting doctrines of our Holy Church.

Indeed, when our Lord Jesus Christ proclaims, "Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die" (John 11:25-26), He speaks of a spiritual resurrection that precedes the physical one. This spiritual resurrection is our passage from death, the death brought by sin, to life, the eternal communion with God. By believing in Christ, we participate now in this new life, being reborn in spirit, which is a foretaste of the resurrection to come.

Intercession, beloved, is deeply rooted in our relationship with Christ and our communion with the saints. It reflects the unity of the Body of Christ, the Church, where the life and holiness of one member benefits all, and where we are called to bear one another's burdens (Galatians 6:2). In the Orthodox tradition, intercession acknowledges that we are not isolated individuals before God but are part of a holy fellowship, the living and the departed, who are united in Christ.

Our intercession for others and the saints' intercession for us do not negate the direct relationship each person is called to have with God. Rather, they express and deepen this relationship, reflecting the unity and love that should characterize the entire body of believers. As Saint Paul teaches us, we are to pray for one another that we may be healed (James 5:16), indicating that our prayers contribute to the spiritual well-being and salvation of others.

When we approach God with confidence, as advised in Hebrews 4:15, we do so not only on our own behalf but also bringing before Him the needs and sorrows of our brothers and sisters, trusting in His mercy and grace. This act of drawing near to God is both personal and communal, inviting His presence into our lives and our world.

As we reflect on these truths, may we ask ourselves how we are embodying this new life in Christ and participating in the communion of saints through prayer and intercession. Are we willing to deepen our faith by living in accordance with the commandments and actively participating in the life of the Church, thereby drawing nearer to the throne of grace?

May the peace of Christ guide you in your spiritual journey. What will be your next step to live more fully in the resurrected life that Christ offers?

text:
Thanks for answering my previous question.

What does faith look like practically while we wait for the things we pray for? Things like jobs, exams, graduate school and overall success in life. How does one approach these things patiently while having strong faith in God and maintaining a positive mindset.

So in summary,

* What should the mindset of someone who has faith be like? Is faith just a mindset of or it also an action? And if so, what actions do faithful people take?

The practical embodiment of faith, especially in seasons of waiting and anticipation, is a vivid tapestry woven with threads of trust, patience, and active engagement in the life Christ has called us to.

To envisage faith practically, consider the words of St. James the Just, "Faith without works is dead" (James 2:26). This profound truth elucidates that faith, while deeply internal, is also vibrantly external, manifesting through our deeds, our patience, and our steadfastness. Faith is not merely an abstract sentiment or hopeful mindset; it is a dynamic force, compelling us towards love, good works, and unwavering trust in God's providence.

In times of waiting—for a job, for academic success, for any of life's myriad milestones—let your faith be active. Pray unceasingly, as St. Paul exhorts, but also engage with the world as a beacon of Christ's love. Study diligently, prepare thoroughly for your endeavors, and serve others selflessly, embodying the faith you cherish.

Moreover, recall the patience of Job, the perseverance of Abraham, the unwavering trust of the Theotokos. They did not passively await God's promises but lived each day in vibrant faith, anchoring their souls in hope, even amidst trials.

In embracing this active faith, cultivate a mindset of gratitude and trust, recognizing each day as a gift and each challenge as an opportunity to witness the steadfastness of your faith. Such a mindset transcends mere optimism, anchoring you in the profound truth of God's unchanging love and promises.

Now, dear one, as you contemplate your journey, ask yourself: How can I embody my faith today, not just as an internal conviction but as a visible, tangible expression of trust in God's plan for me?

To envisage faith practically, consider the words of St. James the Just, "Faith without works is dead" (James 2:26). This profound truth elucidates that faith, while deeply internal, is also vibrantly external, manifesting through our deeds, our patience, and our steadfastness. Faith is not merely an abstract sentiment or hopeful mindset; it is a dynamic force, compelling us towards love, good works, and unwavering trust in God's providence.

In times of waiting—for a job, for academic success, for any of life's myriad milestones—let your faith be active. Pray unceasingly, as St. Paul exhorts, but also engage with the world as a beacon of Christ's love. Study diligently, prepare thoroughly for your endeavors, and serve others selflessly, embodying the faith you cherish.

Moreover, recall the patience of Job, the perseverance of Abraham, the unwavering trust of the Theotokos. They did not passively await God's promises but lived each day in vibrant faith, anchoring their souls in hope, even amidst trials.

In embracing this active faith, cultivate a mindset of gratitude and trust, recognizing each day as a gift and each challenge as an opportunity to witness the steadfastness of your faith. Such a mindset transcends mere optimism, anchoring you in the profound truth of God's unchanging love and promises.

Now, dear one, as you contemplate your journey, ask yourself: How can I embody my faith today, not just as an internal conviction but as a visible, tangible expression of trust in God's plan for me?

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever, today and always.

May the blessings of the Holy Mother of God, the Virgin, and the Cross be upon us. Amen.

Beloved brethren, today we delve deeply into the essence and paramount importance of peace, a virtue so exalted that it mirrors the Heavenly Kingdom's own tranquility, thereby fostering an abode of serenity within our mortal realm.

The Divine Origin and Earthly Manifestation of Peace

Peace, dear brethren, is not merely an absence of conflict or discord; it is a profound state of spiritual harmony bestowed upon us by the Almighty, an ineffable gift that permeates our very being, anchoring our souls amidst the tumultuous seas of earthly existence.

The Trifold Dimension of Peace:

1. Peace with the Divine: Our first and foremost pursuit should be to establish and maintain peace with God. This sacred communion, realized through prayer, repentance, and the grace of the Holy Sacraments, transforms us, enabling us to reflect the divine peace that surpasses all understanding.

2. Peace with Our Brethren: As children of the same Heavenly Father, it is incumbent upon us to foster peace among ourselves, embodying the Lord's commandment to love our neighbors. This peace extends beyond mere tolerance, urging us to embrace forgiveness, understanding, and unconditional love.

3. Inner Peace: The inner sanctum of our hearts must be consecrated with peace, for without this inner tranquility, we are akin to ships without rudders, tossed by the capricious winds of passion and desire. True inner peace is achieved through self-examination, contemplation, and the nurturing of virtues.

The Indispensable Role of Peace in Our Lives

Without peace, the fabric of our families and societies unravels, giving way to strife and chaos. Peace is the cornerstone upon which the edifice of human civilization is built; it is the harbinger of prosperity, the wellspring of creativity, and the conduit for divine grace.

The Scriptural Illumination of Peace:

Our Lord Jesus Christ, the Prince of Peace, bequeathed this invaluable gift to His disciples, proclaiming, "Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you" (John 14:27). This celestial peace, heralded by the angels at Christ's nativity, is our inheritance and our mission.

In the liturgy, we are repeatedly reminded of this peace, exhorted to share it with one another, thereby weaving an unbreakable bond of communal harmony. The apostolic greetings and exhortations underscore the primacy of peace, echoing through the ages in the epistles and teachings of the Church Fathers.

The Path to Cultivating and Propagating Peace

To be artisans of peace, we must first cultivate it within ourselves, nurturing it through prayer, meditation, and adherence to the divine precepts. As bearers of peace, we are called to diffuse its fragrance in every sphere of our lives, reconciling with those estranged, comforting the afflicted, and standing as beacons of light in a world often shrouded in darkness.

The Reconciliation Imperative:

In moments of conflict or disagreement, our paramount duty is to seek reconciliation, following the Lord's command to make peace with our brethren before approaching the sacred altar. This pursuit of peace must extend to all aspects of our existence, becoming the very air we breathe and the ethos that defines us.

Conclusion: Embracing the Divine Mandate of Peace

In conclusion, dear brethren, let us ardently strive to embody the peace of Christ, which is both our sacred legacy and our divine mandate. In a world fraught with turmoil and strife, let us be the harbingers of peace, radiating its divine light and sowing its seeds in the hearts of all we encounter.

Thus, fortified by divine grace and guided by the luminous examples of the saints and martyrs, let us advance on our earthly pilgrimage with steadfast hearts, resolute in our quest for peace, ever mindful of the Apostle's exhortation: "If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone" (Romans 12:18).

Greetings beloved brother Yohannes Neseha. I am Dcn. Zefre Birhan and I serve at Holy Trinity located in Bronx Ny. I have a question.

My question is now speaking of St. Yared. I am well aware that God took St. Yared into the heavens and that the Holy Spirit filled his mind with the holy Mezmur and Zema.

All though what alarms my mind is how were the melodies of the zema and mezmur of our church. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church created. Please get back to me when you get the chance to.

Sincerely,
Dcn. Zefre Birhan

Beloved Deacon Zefre Birhan,

Before the divine intervention bestowed upon Saint Yared, the worship within the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, like in other early Christian communities, likely utilized simpler chants and hymns. These early melodies and verses would have been more rudimentary, focusing on the Psalms and scriptural canticles, reflecting the Jewish temple worship traditions from which Christian liturgy originated.

In the providence of God, the liturgical music before Saint Yared served its purpose in the divine worship, yet it was through Saint Yared's visionary experience that the Church was endowed with a richer, more profound liturgical expression. This transformation symbolizes a deepening of the Church's liturgical life, a transition from simplicity to a more elaborate, heaven-inspired worship, which has profoundly shaped the spiritual identity of our Church.

Just as King David played his harp and sang the Psalms, enriching the worship of the Old Testament, Saint Yared, through divine inspiration, enhanced the worship of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, embedding within it a heavenly dimension and a deeper mystical resonance.

The tradition of our church teaches us that the melodies and hymns, as received by Saint Yared, were indeed divinely inspired during his rapturous ascent into the heavens. It was in this mystical communion with the Divine that the Holy Spirit imbued him with the celestial melodies and hymns that form the bedrock of our liturgical worship.

In your service, Deacon Zefre, I encourage you to delve deeply into the mystical and spiritual essence of the Zema and Mezmur, allowing their divine melodies to elevate your heart and those of your congregation closer to God. As you guide your flock in the sacred liturgy, remember that you are echoing the angelic choruses of heaven, bridging earth to the divine, and partaking in the heavenly liturgy.

Now, dear brother in Christ, how will you further immerse yourself in the spiritual legacy of Saint Yared to enrich your ministry and deepen your congregation's worship experience?

text.text: The Divine Condescension: The Essence of Zewerede

text: At the heart of Zewerede lies the awe-inspiring truth of the Incarnation, the descent of the Word made flesh, our Lord Jesus Christ, from the celestial heights to our earthly realm. This momentous event, which Zewerede commemorates, is not merely a historical occurrence but a living reality that invites us to contemplate the unfathomable love of God, who, in His infinite mercy, became man to redeem us. As we reflect on this divine condescension, let us remember the words of the Apostle Paul: "But when the fullness of the time had come, God sent forth His Son, born of a woman" (Galatians 4:4). In this sacred act, the divine and human natures are wondrously united, offering us a path to salvation and union with God.

text.text: The Covenant of Salvation: A Bridge Between Testaments

These covenants are not mere agreements but profound expressions of God's steadfast love and commitment to our redemption. In the solemn observance of Zewerede, we are reminded of the continuity between the Old and New Testaments, between the promise made to Adam and its fulfillment in Christ. As we engage in this fast, let us embrace this covenantal relationship with God, allowing it to strengthen our faith and deepen our commitment to His will.

text.text: The Call to Fasting and Prayer: Our Spiritual Armor

text: The practice of fasting during the great lent is not merely an external abstention from food but an inward journey of purification, self-denial, and spiritual renewal. Therefore, let us fast with a pure heart, seeking not only to abstain from bodily pleasures but also to cultivate virtues, to offer prayers of intercession, and to engage in acts of charity and mercy. In this way, our fasting becomes a powerful instrument of divine grace, fortifying us against temptations and drawing us closer to the heart of God.

text.text: The Intercession of the Saints: Our Companions in Prayer

Their lives of holiness and devotion inspire us to persevere in our spiritual endeavors, and their prayers on our behalf are a source of strength and encouragement. In particular, let us invoke the intercession of the Blessed Virgin Mary, who, in her humility and obedience, became the Theotokos, the Mother of God. Through her prayers, may we find the grace to follow Christ more closely and to live in accordance with His teachings.

text.text: Conclusion: A Call to Spiritual Vigilance

May this sacred time be for us a period of reflection, repentance, and spiritual growth, that we may emerge from this Lenten season renewed in spirit and more closely conformed to the image of Christ. And as we journey through these forty days, let us remember the ultimate purpose of our fast: to draw near to God, to experience His transforming love, and to participate in the mystery of our salvation.

May the grace and peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all, now and always. Amen.

In the observance of fasting, a discipline most venerable and ancient, we find ourselves embarking upon a journey that is both deeply personal and universally profound, much akin to the transformative passages detailed in the lives of the saints and the righteous. As we enter this solemn period, particularly marked by the commencement of the Great Lent, it is incumbent upon us to contemplate the manifold trials that accompany this spiritual endeavor, discerning their purpose and the divine wisdom they impart.

The act of fasting, far from being a mere abstention from corporeal nourishment, stands as a profound invocation of spiritual renewal and fortitude. It is a testament to our intrinsic yearning for the divine, a conscious mortification of the flesh to kindle the spirit's flame. Yet, it is in this very act of denial that we often encounter an array of trials, for it is a fundamental truth that the gold is tested by fire, and the faithful by the adversities they face.

Why, then, do these trials emerge with greater intensity as we fast and draw nearer to God? It is a question that resonates with the experiences of many devout souls who, in their pursuit of spiritual elevation, find themselves beset by temptations and tribulations. The answer lies not in the nature of fasting as a cause of these trials but in its capacity to illuminate the struggles inherent in our earthly pilgrimage.

The trials encountered during fasting are not indicators of divine disfavor but rather manifestations of spiritual warfare, wherein the forces that oppose our sanctification intensify their assaults as we strive to ascend the ladder of divine ascent. In fasting, our senses are sharpened, and our spiritual awareness is heightened, rendering us more attuned to the conflict between virtue and vice, light and darkness.

As we navigate the tempestuous waters of these trials, it is imperative to recall the purpose and the transformative power of fasting. It is a discipline that, as the Holy Scriptures and the teachings of the Church Fathers assert, bears the potential to vanquish passions, cultivate virtues, and draw the soul closer to the ineffable presence of God. It is a time of introspection and renewal, a sanctified period wherein the soul, liberated from the fetters of indulgence, soars toward the divine.

Fasting, therefore, should be embraced as a sacred opportunity to fortify the spirit, to confront and conquer the impulses that tether us to our lower nature. It is a call to spiritual arms, an invitation to engage in the noble struggle for holiness and purity of heart. As we persevere through the trials of fasting, let us do so with the assurance that these adversities, however daunting, are instrumental in our spiritual growth, shaping us into vessels more receptive to God's grace.

In conclusion, let the trials of fasting not dishearten us but rather inspire us with a resolute determination to press onward, ever upward, on our journey toward sanctity. Let us embrace these challenges as integral elements of our spiritual maturation, recognizing in them the divine pedagogy that seeks to refine our souls. And in this sacred endeavor, may we find solace in the fellowship of the saints, the guidance of the Church, and the inexhaustible mercy of God, who, in His infinite wisdom, transforms our tribulations into triumphs of the spirit.

May the blessings of the Holy Mother of God, the Virgin, and the Cross be upon us. Amen.

text: The Holy Eucharist, the pinnacle of Christian worship and life, stands as the true embodiment of our Lord Jesus Christ's presence among His faithful. This sacred ritual, often termed the Divine Liturgy in the Orthodox tradition, is not merely a remembrance but a living, mystical participation in the very life, death, and resurrection of Christ.

text.text: 1. The Essence of the Holy Eucharist

text: At the heart of the Eucharist lies the profound mystery of transubstantiation, wherein bread and wine are transformed into the very Body and Blood of Christ. This is not a symbolic act but a divine reality, veiled under the forms of bread and wine. As John Chrysostom himself might say, it is through this divine banquet that heaven and earth embrace, and the faithful are invited to partake in the eternal.

The Eucharist is called a mystery (sacramentum in Latin, mysterion in Greek) because it transcends human understanding. Its truth is apprehended not through intellectual reasoning but through the eyes of faith. In the liturgical celebration, the Church experiences a foretaste of the heavenly kingdom, a mystical participation in the eternal now of God's salvific acts.

The Eucharist is central to the Christian faith because it is the fulfillment of Christ's promise to be with us always (Matthew 28:20). In it, we find the true manna from heaven, the Bread of Life (John 6:35), which nourishes our souls and unites us with the divine nature.

Approaching the Holy Communion demands a heart prepared through prayer, confession, and a sincere desire to amend one's life. The worthy recipient is not one who is sinless but one who recognizes their unworthiness and approaches with humility, repentance, and faith.

The preparation for receiving the Eucharist involves fasting, prayer, and reconciliation with others, reflecting an inner disposition of humility and love. Post-communion, the faithful are called to carry the grace received into the world, living out the Gospel in deeds of love and service.

text.text: The Eucharistic Celebration: An Encounter with the Living Christ

text: The Divine Liturgy is a journey that begins with repentance and culminates in the mystical supper. It is in this sacred meal that the Church experiences the Paschal Mystery of Christ: His suffering, death, resurrection, and glorious ascension. The bread and wine, offered in faith, become by the Holy Spirit the very Body and Blood of Christ.

text.text: The Anamnesis: Remembering the Saving Acts of Christ

text: In the Eucharistic prayer, the Church recalls the life-giving events of Christ's incarnation, death, and resurrection. This memorial (anamnesis) is not a mere recollection but makes present the realities of these salvific events. Through it, the faithful are united with Christ's one, perfect, and sufficient sacrifice on the Cross.

text.text: Communion: The Pledge of Future Glory

text: In receiving the Eucharist, Christians are mystically united with Christ and with one another, forming the Body of Christ, the Church. This communion is a foretaste of the eschatological banquet, the heavenly feast in the Kingdom of God.

The Eucharist as the Source and Summit of Christian Life

The Holy Eucharist stands at the center of Orthodox Christian life. It is the source from which all grace flows and the summit to which all Christian action is directed. In it, the Church finds her identity and mission, to be the sacrament of Christ in the world, proclaiming the Good News and manifesting the Kingdom of God in love, service, and sanctity.

Introduction 

The Holy Eucharist, the pinnacle of Christian worship and life, stands as the true embodiment of our Lord Jesus Christ's presence among His faithful. This sacred ritual, often termed the Divine Liturgy in the Orthodox tradition, is not merely a remembrance but a living, mystical participation in the very life, death, and resurrection of Christ.

1. The Essence of the Holy Eucharist

At the heart of the Eucharist lies the profound mystery of transubstantiation, wherein bread and wine are transformed into the very Body and Blood of Christ. This is not a symbolic act but a divine reality, veiled under the forms of bread and wine. As John Chrysostom himself might say, it is through this divine banquet that heaven and earth embrace, and the faithful are invited to partake in the eternal.

2. The Sacramental Mystery

The Eucharist is called a mystery (sacramentum in Latin, mysterion in Greek) because it transcends human understanding. Its truth is apprehended not through intellectual reasoning but through the eyes of faith. In the liturgical celebration, the Church experiences a foretaste of the heavenly kingdom, a mystical participation in the eternal now of God's salvific acts.

3. The Significance of Holy Communion

The Eucharist is central to the Christian faith because it is the fulfillment of Christ's promise to be with us always (Matthew 28:20). In it, we find the true manna from heaven, the Bread of Life (John 6:35), which nourishes our souls and unites us with the divine nature.

4. The Worthy Reception of Communion

Approaching the Holy Communion demands a heart prepared through prayer, confession, and a sincere desire to amend one's life. The worthy recipient is not one who is sinless but one who recognizes their unworthiness and approaches with humility, repentance, and faith.

5. Preparation and Thanksgiving

The preparation for receiving the Eucharist involves fasting, prayer, and reconciliation with others, reflecting an inner disposition of humility and love. Post-communion, the faithful are called to carry the grace received into the world, living out the Gospel in deeds of love and service.

The Eucharistic Celebration: An Encounter with the Living Christ

The Divine Liturgy is a journey that begins with repentance and culminates in the mystical supper. It is in this sacred meal that the Church experiences the Paschal Mystery of Christ: His suffering, death, resurrection, and glorious ascension. The bread and wine, offered in faith, become by the Holy Spirit the very Body and Blood of Christ.

The Anamnesis: Remembering the Saving Acts of Christ

In the Eucharistic prayer, the Church recalls the life-giving events of Christ's incarnation, death, and resurrection. This memorial (anamnesis) is not a mere recollection but makes present the realities of these salvific events. Through it, the faithful are united with Christ's one, perfect, and sufficient sacrifice on the Cross.

Communion: The Pledge of Future Glory

In receiving the Eucharist, Christians are mystically united with Christ and with one another, forming the Body of Christ, the Church. This communion is a foretaste of the eschatological banquet, the heavenly feast in the Kingdom of God.

Conclusion: The Eucharist as the Source and Summit of Christian Life

The Holy Eucharist stands at the center of Orthodox Christian life. It is the source from which all grace flows and the summit to which all Christian action is directed. In it, the Church finds her identity and mission, to be the sacrament of Christ in the world, proclaiming the Good News and manifesting the Kingdom of God in love, service, and sanctity.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always.

May the blessings of The Virgin, and the cross be upon us. Amen.

text.text: Beloved members of John's Repentance spiritual service, today was the annual feast of Abune Gebre Menfes Kidus where we commemorate his departure from the earth to the heavens. Hence we send you the following lesson so you can read and partake from the day's blessings.

text:
The life and teachings of St. Abune Gebre Menfes Kidus, a revered figure in Orthodox Christianity, offer a profound testament to the power of faith, asceticism, and divine intervention. His story begins in the land of Egypt, where his parents, Simeon and Aklesia, longed for a child for thirty years. In a miraculous occurrence, akin to the biblical stories of old, a divine voice promised them a son whose glory would surpass the heavens. This prophecy was fulfilled with the birth of Abune Gebre Menfes Kidus.

From his infancy, he exhibited signs of divine favor. His actions as a newborn, glorifying the Holy Trinity, and his angelic lifestyle, abstaining from earthly sustenance, marked him as a holy vessel. At the tender age of three, he was visited by Saint Gabriel, who brought blessings from the Virgin Mary and the celestial host. The Abbot Zemedeberhan, recognizing his sanctity, nurtured him in monastic life, where he flourished in spiritual wisdom and miraculous powers. His fame spread far and wide, leading to a pivotal moment when he healed a thousand blind men, a miracle reminiscent of Christ's own healings.

The spiritual journey of St. Abune Gebre Menfes Kidus was marked by profound solitude and communion with God. He was called to a life of seclusion in the forest, where his sustenance was of a heavenly nature, symbolic of man's reliance on divine grace rather than earthly provisions. His time in the wilderness was a testament to his unyielding faith and deep communion with God.

The saint's concern for humanity's salvation was paramount. His intercessions led to the liberation of souls from hell, showcasing his immense spiritual authority. His journey to Ethiopia, carried by Saint Gabriel, was a pivotal moment in his mission. There, he prayed fervently for the nation, an act of love and sacrifice, embodying the heart of a true shepherd.

St. Abune Gebre Menfes Kidus's life was not without trials. His encounter with Satan, who sought to hinder his mission, resulted in his temporary blindness. Yet, in this adversity, he was not forsaken; Saint Michael and Saint Gabriel came to his aid, a testimony to his favored status in the heavenly realms.

His ministry extended to Arabia, where he confronted idolatry and demonstrated the power of Christ through miraculous signs, converting many to Christianity. Even in the face of persecution, his faith remained unshaken, further attesting to his divine calling and steadfastness.

The life of St. Abune Gebre Menfes Kidus culminated in a glorious ascent, taken by angels to Jerusalem, where he was laid to rest. His earthly journey of 562 years, of which 262 was spent in Ethiopia, was marked by unwavering devotion, miraculous deeds, and a deep, transformative love for God and humanity.

This account of St. Abune Gebre Menfes Kidus, steeped in the traditions and teachings of Orthodox Christianity, serves as a beacon of spiritual guidance. His life exemplifies the virtues of faith, humility, and divine communion, offering a path to spiritual enlightenment and closeness to God. In his story, we find a profound reminder of the endless possibilities that faith in God can unlock, and the transformative power of living a life dedicated to divine service and love.

Hello, 

I have a question about something i’ve been hearing about but don’t really understand. What exactly is “metet” and how come there are people in the church (priests and deacons) that do these things using church prayer books? How can something evil be done with a Holy Book & church leaders? And what are people supposed to do to protect themselves from evil things like this that people do. 

Thank you!

Dear seeker of truth,

text: In this temporal existence, no man stands aloof from the stain of sin; it clings to us as the earth to the rain. To acknowledge this is not to embrace despair but to recognize our profound need for Divine mercy. We are brethren in weakness, and in this acknowledgment, we find our common need for God's unending grace.

text.text: The Divine Forbearance Amidst Human Folly

text: Consider the magnanimity of our Creator, who, despite the manifold transgressions of humanity, sustains the cosmos with benevolence. The sun rises, the rain nourishes, and the earth abides, not as recompense for our virtue but as testament to God's forbearance. Were Divine justice to reckon our deeds without mercy, existence itself would falter.

Beware the snare of complacency, for it is the herald of spiritual decay. To don the vestments of faith, to partake in the liturgy, and to frequent the holy sanctuaries are commendable acts. Yet, devoid of a heart inclined towards transformation, they are but hollow rituals. True sanctity and salvation are not garments we don, but states we earnestly strive towards through grace-infused perseverance.

"He who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted" (Luke 14:11). This profound teaching underscores the paradoxical kingdom of Christ, where humility is the scepter and throne. In recognizing our fragility and penchant for sin, we are drawn closer to the Divine, for God dwells not amidst the fanfare of self-righteousness but in the quiet chambers of a contrite heart.

Repentance is the beacon that guides us through the tempests of our baser inclinations. It is not merely the recitation of transgressions but a heartfelt renunciation of sin and a steadfast commitment to divine precepts. True repentance burgeons from the soil of self-awareness, nurtured by the waters of divine grace.

In the Divine gaze, all are equal: the rich and the poor, the sage and the simple. Our offerings are weighed not by their grandeur but by the purity of our intent. Recall the woman taken in adultery, brought before Christ to be judged. In her, we see the embodiment of mercy: "Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more" (John 8:11).

Let us relinquish the mantle of judgment, for it is God alone who discerns the heart's secrets. In humility and love, we are called to bear one another's burdens, mindful of our shared frailty and the infinite mercy that sustains us.

Let us, therefore, gird ourselves with the armor of penitence, treading the narrow path that leads to life eternal. May we, through God's grace, transform our weakness into strength, our despair into hope, and our sin into a clarion call for redemption. In this sacred endeavor, may we find solace in the love of the Almighty, the wellspring of all goodness and the harbinger of our salvation. Amen.

text: Thank you father! :) well since you brought up the topic of one’s calling I’ll go ahead & ask one of my questions related to that which was about discovering ones life calling / discovering our God given gift.

How did you come to discover your divine calling & how can we as believers discover the natural gift God has given to each of us to better serve our church community & find a fulfilling career where we thrive in.

Beloved one, Discovering one's divine calling is a journey of deep reflection, prayer, and engagement with the community and God's word. For many, including myself, the path to understanding our vocation unfolds over time, often through various experiences, challenges, and moments of clarity that God provides along the way.

In my own journey, persistent prayer, meditation on Scripture, and the counsel of wise spiritual elders were instrumental. The sense of calling emerged not as a sudden revelation but as a growing conviction nurtured by these practices and a deep desire to serve God and His people.

For believers seeking to discern their natural gifts and God-given vocation, I would offer the following guidance, rooted in the teachings and traditions of the Church:

1.

: Consistently seek God’s direction in your life through prayer. Ask Him to reveal your gifts and how you can use them for His glory. "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you" (Matthew 7:7).

2.

: The Bible is replete with examples of individuals who discovered their callings through faith and obedience. Reflecting on these stories can offer insights into how God might be working in your own life.

3.

: Often, our God-given talents are revealed through service. By participating in various church and community activities, you can identify what brings you joy and where you make the most impact.

4.

: Consult with spiritual leaders, mentors, or elders within your church. Their wisdom and outside perspective can help you discern your gifts and how they might be used in service to the church and the world.

5.

text.text: Reflect on Your Passions and Talents

text:
: Consider the activities that give you the most joy and fulfillment. Often, our God-given gifts align with our interests and talents. Reflect on how these can be applied in a career or ministry context.

6.

: Discerning your calling is a process that unfolds in God’s timing. Remain faithful and patient, knowing that He will reveal your path in due course.

As you seek to discover your vocation, remember that each believer's calling is unique, and every role within the body of Christ is valuable and needed. In finding and pursuing your divine calling, you not only find fulfillment but also contribute to the edification and growth of the church.

In what ways have you felt drawn to serve or noticed particular talents or passions that might be directed toward a specific calling?

Hello,I have a question? 

Are we are justified by our faith or by our works in the Kingdom of God?

Or is it both?
As faith without works is dead.


Thanks

Beloved in Christ, Your inquiry touches upon the profound mystery of our salvation in the Lord. The Orthodox Church teaches us that faith and works are inseparable in the journey toward the Kingdom of God. As the Apostle James wisely instructs us, "Faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead" (James 2:17). This passage illuminates the truth that genuine faith naturally manifests through loving actions toward God and our neighbor.

In the Orthodox understanding, we are initially justified by grace through faith, which then must be actualized through our deeds. This dynamic synergy between faith and works reflects our cooperation with God's grace, guiding us to grow in holiness and union with Him.

To cultivate this balance, I encourage you to deepen your prayer life, engage in acts of charity, and seek guidance from a spiritual father who can accompany you on your path. By embracing both faith and works, you are actively participating in your own sanctification, drawing nearer to God and His Kingdom.

Now, dear seeker, what step will you take today to demonstrate your faith through loving action?

text: I mean what does the name Orthodox represent in our faith. Henceforth, why do we call our church the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church?

Beloved in Christ, the term "Orthodox" stems from the Greek words "orthos," meaning correct or true, and "doxa," meaning belief or glory. Thus, "Orthodox" signifies "correct belief" or "true worship." This term encapsulates our commitment to preserving the authentic teachings and traditions as handed down from Christ Himself to His Apostles and through them to the Church.

The use of "Orthodox" began in the early Christian era, particularly as a way to distinguish the Church that adhered faithfully to the teachings defined in the Ecumenical Councils from various heretical groups that had diverged from these established doctrines. It was crucial in times of doctrinal disputes to affirm the identity of the Church that remained faithful to the apostolic and patristic teachings. Hence, the term "Orthodox" became a definitive marker of the true Church that maintained fidelity to the Christian faith as it was universally recognized and proclaimed.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church embodies this commitment to orthodoxy, having received the Christian faith in the early Apostolic Age and nurtured it through centuries, steadfast amid various challenges. Our adherence to the term "Orthodox" is a testament to our dedication to uphold the true faith and practices as received from the generations of faithful who preceded us.

The word "Tewahedo" uniquely characterizes our Ethiopian Orthodox faith, signifying the unity of Christ's divine and human natures in one, without division or separation. This profound theological principle is intrinsic to our faith, shaping our worship, our spirituality, and our very identity as followers of Christ in the Ethiopian tradition.

Our Church, bearing the name Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, thus stands as a beacon of the undiluted Christian faith, embracing the unity of Christ and the apostolic teachings preserved and cherished in our tradition.

As you contemplate the meaning behind our Church's name, I encourage you to delve deeper into the richness of the Tewahedo doctrine. How might this understanding of Christ's nature influence your relationship with Him and guide your steps on the path of salvation?

text:
My following question is related to love. 

Ive asked many questions like “where is my Godly spouse?” “When will he come?” “Why is God making me wait?” “How can I learn to be more patient through this process?” “Why am I so pressed or obsessed with the idea of having a man in my life?” “What’s the best way to vet out if a person or an offer is from God or the enemy?” 

I was hoping you could help answer some of these questions.

Beloved one, your heartfelt inquiries about finding a godly spouse are shared by many, and it's beautiful to see your desire to align this aspect of your life with God's will. Your experiences, including the anticipation and the encounters with potential partners, are all part of the journey God is using to shape you, preparing you for the future He has planned.

In addressing your questions and concerns:

While waiting can be challenging, it's important to trust in God's timing. He knows the desires of your heart and is working all things for your good (Romans 8:28). This period of waiting is not passive but an active time of growth, self-discovery, and deepening your relationship with God.

Developing patience can be cultivated through continued trust in God's promises and faithfulness. Reflect on past instances where God has been faithful to you; this can bolster your trust and patience. Remember, "But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint" (Isaiah 40:31).

Your question about being "pressed or obsessed" with finding a partner is insightful. It's beneficial to explore your feelings and desires in prayer and perhaps with a trusted spiritual counselor. Sometimes, understanding deeper motivations can bring clarity and peace, helping you to focus on God's presence and love in the present.

To discern whether someone is a potential spouse sent by God or a distraction, seek alignment with Scriptural principles and godly character traits. Prayer, time, and godly counsel are crucial. Observe their fruits of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22-23), how they treat others, and their commitment to their faith and personal growth.

Use this time to prepare yourself to be the godly spouse you desire to have. Grow in virtues like kindness, patience, and love. Engage in activities that build your character and deepen your faith.

6.

text.text: Being Proactive in a Godly Way

text:
: While waiting on God, it's also okay to be part of Christian groups or activities where you can meet someone with shared values. However, let these interactions be natural and spirit-led rather than forced.

Your journey to finding a godly spouse is also a journey of self-discovery and spiritual growth. Cherish this time with God, knowing that your relationship with Him is the foundation upon which all other relationships are built.

Would you consider taking time to reflect more deeply on what God might be teaching you in this season of waiting and how you might grow through it?

text.text: Brethren in the Lord, who stand steadfast in the unwavering Orthodox faith, grace unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ. Today we will be learning about the holy Eucharist, which stands as the pinnacle of our redemption and the very lifeblood of the Church.
✍ The Incarnation: The Prologue to the Eucharist

text:
Before we venture into the holy of holies, let us lay a foundation by reflecting upon the Incarnation, which is the cornerstone of all Christian doctrine. In the fullness of time, God, in His inscrutable wisdom, willed to be united with man. "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14). This is not a mere visitation but an abiding union. The Godhead was pleased to dwell bodily (Colossians 2:9), and in this union, the natures of divinity and humanity are neither confounded nor separated but are united without mixture or change.

In this mystical union, Christ fully assumed our nature, bearing our griefs, carrying our sorrows, yet without sin. As Saint Cyril rightly proclaimed, the nature that needed salvation was not passed over. Thus, the unblemished Lamb, perfect God and perfect Man, presented Himself as the only sacrifice capable of redeeming our fallen state.

✍

text.text: The Eucharist: The Continuation of Incarnation

text:
The Eucharist, dear faithful, is not separate from this grand narrative; it is the perpetuation of the Incarnation. Just as the divine nature did not obliterate the human in Christ, so the essence of bread and wine is not destroyed when consecrated as the Body and Blood. Here, the Church in her wisdom teaches us that in this Holy Sacrament, there is a mystical but real transformation, akin to the Incarnation itself.

As the Lord Jesus, at His Last Supper, did not speak in parables when He said, "This is my body... This is my blood" (Matthew 26:26-28), we take Him at His divine word, acknowledging a mystery that cannot be fathomed by the human mind but is apprehended by faith.

✍

text.text: The Eucharist: The Apex of Theology

text:
In the Eucharist, we find the sum and summit of all theological truth. It is the tangible expression of God's love, the assurance of His promise, the fulfillment of the covenant. The Eucharist stands as a foretaste of the eschatological feast, where the Church militant and the Church triumphant are united in the worship of the Lamb.

This Sacrament is not a mere remembrance but an anamnesis, a making present of the one sacrifice of Calvary. In the Divine Liturgy, we are lifted above time and space, and the events of our redemption are made present to us, that we might partake of the fruits of the Tree of Life which is Christ Himself.

text.text: ✍ The Eucharist: The Medicine of Immortality

text:
Saint Ignatius of Antioch called the Eucharist the "medicine of immortality," and rightly so. For as much as the body requires bread for sustenance, so too does the soul require the Body of Christ for eternal life. In this Holy Communion, we are united to Christ and through Him to one another, forming one body, of which He is the head.

To partake of the Eucharist unworthily is to eat and drink judgment upon oneself (1 Corinthians 11:29). Hence, the Church, as a loving mother, calls her children to approach with a pure heart, having confessed and repented, that they might be made partakers of divine nature (2 Peter 1:4).

text:

To commune is to abide in Christ and to have Christ abide in us. Here, the faithful are invited to partake of the divine banquet, to enter into the joy of their Master, and to be transformed into the image of the One who gave Himself up for us all.

Let us, therefore, draw near with faith and with an ardent desire to be united with Christ, to be healed by His touch, and to be sanctified by His life-giving Body and Blood. May this Holy Sacrament be for us a pledge of the world to come and a haven of salvation in this present age.

 join with heaven, in the unending hymn of praise.

text: My question is about fear & anxiety. I have struggled with social anxiety for a long time now, and it affects different areas of my life, like work, church, and social events. It affects how I function and interact with others in these different situations. I want to be free and not a prisoner of my mind. I really wanna find the confidence and courage to be able to walk over to someone at work and strike up a conversation, to join in on conversations with my team, to ask questions when I feel stuck or need help, to approach others at church and build that community, to speak up in meetings/groups..etc. I do pray during these situations for God to help me but sometimes I just feel stuck like there is no way for me to become a better version of myself because I can't break out of this cycle. Please help.

Beloved in Christ, the struggle with fear and anxiety, especially in the form of social anxiety, is a heavy burden, but it is one that can be lightened through the grace and peace of our Lord. You are not alone in this battle, and it's a path many faithful have walked before, finding solace and strength in God's presence and promises.

In the Scriptures, we are repeatedly encouraged to cast our anxieties on the Lord, for He cares for us (1 Peter 5:7). The Psalmist also speaks to us in our fears, "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you" (Psalm 56:3). These are not mere words but powerful truths to live by, offering us a foundation of trust in God's providential care.

To address social anxiety and grow in confidence and courage, consider the following steps, deeply rooted in the Orthodox tradition and the teachings of the Church:

1.

: Continue to make prayer your first resort in times of anxiety. Incorporate specific prayers for courage and peace into your daily routine. Engaging with Scripture can also be immensely comforting. Passages like Joshua 1:9, where God commands Joshua to be strong and courageous, can be particularly uplifting.

2.

: The Sacraments, especially Confession and Communion, are sources of grace and healing. Through Confession, we can lay down our burdens and receive counsel, and in Communion, we are united with Christ, who strengthens us.

3.

text.text: Seek Guidance from a Spiritual Father

text:
: Discussing your struggles with a spiritual father can provide not only spiritual guidance but also practical advice tailored to your situation.

4.

: With prayer and trust in God, set small, achievable goals for yourself. For example, you might decide to speak to one person at church this Sunday or ask one question during a meeting at work. Celebrate these small victories, and gradually increase your goals as you become more comfortable.

5.

text.text: Practice Mindfulness and Presence in God’s Creation

text:
: Sometimes, anxiety can stem from being too future-focused or self-centered in our thoughts. Practicing mindfulness—being present in the moment and aware of God’s creation around us—can help shift our perspective and reduce anxiety.

6.

: Engage in church groups or Christian fellowship where you can share your struggles in a safe environment. These settings can also provide opportunities to practice social interactions in a less pressured environment.

7.

text.text: Reflect on the Lives of Saints

text:
: Many saints experienced profound fear and anxiety, yet they found strength in God. Reading their stories can be inspiring and offer practical insights into overcoming fear with faith.

Remember, your worth and identity are rooted in Christ, not in your social performance or perceptions. God loves you infinitely and knows your struggles. With each step you take, no matter how small, you are moving toward the freedom and peace He desires for you.

Would it be possible for you to choose one small goal to achieve this week, as a step toward overcoming social anxiety, trusting that God walks with you in this journey?

text: What is God trying to tell his disciples through this psalm. Also, what is the deep significance behind the reading psalms?

፦ In the heart of the Psalms, we find a reflection of the human soul in all its aspects: joy, sorrow, hope, despair, faith, and doubt. They are prayers that Christ Himself prayed and thereby sanctified, teaching us that in these sacred hymns, we find a direct pathway to commune with God. The Psalms, therefore, are not merely readings; they are the breath of the Church's life, an intimate dialogue between the Creator and His creation.

Consider Psalm 139 (138 in the Septuagint), "O Lord, You have searched me and known me." This Psalm, like many others, reveals the omniscience and omnipresence of God, teaching His disciples about His unfathomable love and the profound knowledge He has of each one of us. It invites us into a deep trust in God, who knows our path and our lying down and is acquainted with all our ways.

The reading of Psalms is deeply significant because it provides us with the words when we have none, elevates our soul, and aligns our heart with the will of God. It teaches us patience, humility, and the profound beauty of repentance. As St. John Chrysostom beautifully articulated, "He who recites the Psalms is uttering them as his own words, and each sings them as if they were written concerning him." They are a mirror to our soul and a guide to our spiritual journey.

As you engage with the Psalms, let them transform you, guide you, and draw you closer to the heart of God. Reflect on how the Psalms resonate with your life and how they call you to live in deeper communion with God. What step will you take today to allow the Psalms to enrich your spiritual journey?

text:
When the church teachings ask us to assess where our treasure is. Does that mean we should prioritize God and have him at the center of our life. 

Or does it mean, we shouldn’t care too much about things like money. For example if a person wants to be a millionaire but puts God first and serves Him. Is that still having God as the treasure or is what God wants for us to leave wealth completely and follow him only? Like the bible story of the guy who did everything but wasn’t able to give up His wealth to follow God.

Beloved in Christ, your inquiry touches upon a foundational teaching of our faith, mirrored in the profound words of our Lord Jesus Christ: "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (Matthew 6:21). This passage invites us to reflect deeply on the orientation of our hearts and the true nature of our desires.

The teachings of the Church, drawing from the wellspring of Holy Scripture and the wisdom of the Fathers, guide us to understand that prioritizing God and centering our lives around Him does not inherently require the abandonment of all material wealth. Rather, it calls for a transformation in how we perceive and utilize such wealth. St. John Chrysostom, a voice echoing through the ages, teaches us that wealth, in itself, is not evil, but it becomes so depending on how we use it. Wealth should be seen as a tool for doing good, for serving the needs of the Church and the poor, thus becoming a means through which we can grow closer to God.

The story of the rich young man in the Gospels (Matthew 19:16-22) serves as a poignant reminder that when material possessions or the pursuit thereof eclipses our love for God and our neighbor, it becomes a barrier to entering the Kingdom of Heaven. It is not wealth itself that is the issue, but the attachment and priority we give it over our relationship with God.

In striving to be a millionaire, one must question: "Is this pursuit drawing me closer to God? Am I seeking wealth to serve Him and others, or is it fostering attachment, pride, and avarice within my heart?" Remember, our Lord Jesus Christ calls us to seek first the Kingdom of God and His righteousness (Matthew 6:33), trusting that all things necessary for our earthly journey will be provided to us according to His divine will.

As you continue to navigate the complexities of living a Christ-centered life in a material world, ask yourself: How can I use the resources and talents God has entrusted to me for the greater glory of His Kingdom? How can I ensure that my heart remains anchored in the love of God, regardless of my material success or failure?

Now, reflecting on these thoughts, what is one step you can take today to align your treasure with the Kingdom of Heaven?

text: Hello I was wondering what are the steps a convert should take when still being new to the faith before and after baptism besides understanding the sacraments and the 5 pillars ?

Beloved in Christ, in the journey you embark upon towards and beyond the holy sacrament of baptism, let us recall the words of St. Paul to the Philippians: "Therefore, my beloved, as you have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your salvation with fear and trembling" (Philippians 2:12).

First and foremost, deepen your relationship with God through prayer. Daily conversation with the Lord opens your heart to His guidance and strengthens your faith. The Jesus Prayer ("Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner") is a precious gem in our tradition, embodying the essence of humility and repentance.

Immerse yourself in Holy Scripture and the writings of the Church Fathers. The Scriptures are the living Word of God, offering nourishment for your soul, while the Fathers provide wisdom that connects us to the early Church.

Attend the Divine Liturgy and other services regularly, as participation in the communal worship of the Church is vital for spiritual growth. This will also connect you with a community of believers who share your journey and can offer support and encouragement.

text: What is the significance of the Tefisihee Mariam that the Deacons say in our church? For example: Antee Wi’itu mesobe werq qeyih ante wisteta mena biruh? I’ve said it myself, but I just don’t know what the importantance of it is in our faith?

Beloved in Christ, the query you have brought forth touches the heart of our liturgical tradition, reflecting the depth and beauty of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. The Tefisihee Mariam, or the Praise of Mary, is a significant hymn chanted by deacons, lauding the Virgin Mary, the Theotokos, for her pivotal role in the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. This hymn exemplifies our veneration of the Mother of God, not as a deity, but as the chosen vessel through whom God became man for our salvation. It embodies our acknowledgment of her virtues and her unique place in our salvation history.

The verse you're referring to "አንቲ ውእቱ መሶበ ወርቅ ንጹሕ እንተ ውስቴታ መና ኅቡዕ ኅብስት ዘወረደ አም ሰምያት ወሀቤ  ሕይወት ለኩኩ ዓለም," which translates to "Thou art the pot of pure gold wherein is hidden the manna, the bread which came down from heaven giving life unto all the world," beautifully articulates the Orthodox Christian belief in Mary as the Ark of the New Covenant. Just as the pot of manna in the Old Testament was kept in the Ark of the Covenant as a testament to God's provision for the Israelites in the desert, Mary is honored as the one who bore Christ, the true Manna from heaven, who gives eternal life to the world.

This verse draws us into the deep typology found in Scripture, where Mary is seen as fulfilling and surpassing the types and symbols of the Old Testament. The pure gold of the pot signifies her purity and the divine choice, while the hidden manna, Christ Himself, is the sustenance for our souls, the Bread of Life, who came down from heaven to nourish and redeem us.

Saint Cyril of Alexandria, a luminary father of the Church, beautifully expounds on this, saying, "Hail, Mary Theotokos, venerable treasure of the whole world... through whom the Holy Trinity is glorified and adored,... through whom the precious Cross is venerated throughout the world, through whom heaven exults, through whom angels and archangels rejoice, through whom demons are put to flight,... through whom the fallen creature is raised up to heaven, through whom the whole creation, possessed by idolatry, has come to the knowledge of the truth."

Thus, the Tefisihee Mariam is not merely a hymn of praise but a profound theological affirmation of the Incarnation and the central role of the Virgin Mary in our salvation. It invites us to marvel at the mystery of God's love and providence, drawing us closer to Him through veneration of His mother.

This understanding and reverence for the Virgin Mary are not mere traditions but are deeply rooted in the Scripture and the teachings of the Church Fathers. They invite us to ponder the mystery of our salvation and the extraordinary role that Mary plays in it, encouraging us to seek her intercessions and to emulate her faith and obedience to God's will.

As you reflect on this, consider how the understanding of Mary as the vessel containing the Bread of Life enriches your faith and draws you closer to Christ. How might this deepen your appreciation for the divine services and your personal devotion to the Theotokos?

text:
Hello I have a question 

Why do we fast until 3pm? Is there a specific reason?

Beloved in Christ, the practice of fasting until 3pm is deeply rooted in the tradition of the Orthodox Church, reflecting our journey of self-denial, repentance, and communion with God. This specific time recalls the hour at which our Lord Jesus Christ gave up His spirit on the Cross for the salvation of the world, as noted in the Gospel of Matthew: "And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, 'Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?' that is, 'My God, My God, why have you forsaken me?'" (Matthew 27:46). By aligning our fast with this momentous hour, we unite ourselves more closely with the sufferings of Christ, remembering His ultimate sacrifice for us.

Fasting until 3pm allows us to exercise discipline over our physical desires, turning our focus towards spiritual nourishment and prayer. It is a tangible expression of our faith, reminding us to rely not on bread alone, "but on every word that comes from the mouth of God" (Matthew 4:4).

As you embark on this journey of fasting, consider how this practice might deepen your relationship with Christ. Reflect on the sacrifices He made for us and how we can offer our own small sacrifices as a way of drawing closer to Him. How might this period of fasting until 3pm enhance your spiritual life and lead you closer to the heart of God?

text.text: : A Reflection on the Third Week of the Great Lent

text:
In the heart of the Great Lent, there comes a week known by the faithful as Mekurab, translating from the ancient tongue as "Synagogue." This designation, while simple in its utterance, carries the weight of centuries, embodying the sacredness of worship and the solemnity of divine communion. It is within this week that the faithful are invited to journey deeper into the mystery of the Incarnation, where Christ Himself, the Word made flesh, enters into the synagogue, not merely as a participant, but as the very fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets.

The Synagogue, historically, stood as the gathering place of the faithful, where the Torah was read and God was worshipped in the beauty of holiness. It was in such a setting that our Lord often found Himself, teaching and revealing the depths of God’s love and commandments. The incident that marks the Mekurab week, as recalled in the sacred narrative, unfolds in the temple, where Christ, with righteous indignation, expels the merchants and money changers, proclaiming, "My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves." This act of purification is not merely an external cleansing of the physical space but an invitation to each soul to cleanse the temple of their own heart, making it a fitting abode for the Divine.

The Church, in her wisdom, has named the weeks of Lent, each carrying a profound spiritual theme that draws the faithful deeper into the mystery of Christ’s Passion and Resurrection. Mekurab, or Synagogue week, thus becomes a focal point where the faithful are called to reflect on the sanctity of God’s house, both the historical temple and the temple of their own hearts, and to recommit themselves to making it a place of true worship, prayer, and divine encounter.

The liturgical life of this week is rich with scriptural readings and hymns that echo the themes of worship, divine zeal, and the call to righteous living. This Sunday's song from

"ቦአ ኢየሱስ ምኩራበ አይሁድ ወመሐረ ቃለ ሃይማኖት..." invites the faithful to contemplate the Lord's teaching in the synagogue, His preference for mercy over sacrifice, and His lordship over the Sabbath. This encapsulates the essence of the Mekurab week, inviting a meditation on how Christ fulfills and transcends the Law, embodying the true Sabbath rest for the souls of the faithful.

Saint Paul’s message to the Colossians, as read in this week, warns against being judged by external observances, reminding the faithful that the substance belongs to Christ. This calls for a deeper understanding that true worship transcends mere ritualistic compliance and finds its essence in the person of Christ. Similarly, the readings from the Epistle of James challenge the faithful to embody their faith through works of mercy and righteousness, reflecting the living faith that justifies.

The liturgical readings culminate in the Gospel narrative of Christ cleansing the temple, a powerful image of divine zeal and the call to purity. The faithful are reminded that the temple, Christ's Body, destroyed and raised up in three days, is the ultimate sign of God's presence and action among His people. Thus, the Mekurab week, through its liturgical and scriptural dimensions, invites the faithful to a profound encounter with Christ, the true Temple, where they are called to become living stones, built up into a spiritual house, offering spiritual sacrifices.

In this holy week of Mekurab, let the faithful be drawn into the heart of worship, where heaven and earth meet in the person of Christ. Let them cleanse the temples of their hearts, making room for the indwelling of the Spirit, and let their lives reflect the beauty of divine worship, not confined to the walls of any synagogue or temple but carried within the temple of the heart, sanctified by the presence of Christ, our Passover Lamb, who invites us all into the eternal Sabbath of His love and peace.

text: Was Jesus born in Ethiopia?

Beloved in Christ, grace to you and peace. Your question touches on the incarnate mystery of our Lord, Jesus Christ, who was born in Bethlehem, as foretold by the prophets of old. The Prophet Micah proclaimed, "But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come for me one who will be ruler over Israel, whose origins are from of old, from ancient times" (Micah 5:2). This prophecy reveals the humility and divine plan of our Lord's nativity, not in Ethiopia, but in the land of Judea.

Ethiopia, however, holds a cherished place in Christian history, being one of the first nations to embrace the faith. The Ethiopian eunuch's baptism by Philip the Evangelist (Acts 8:26-40) signifies the spreading of the Gospel beyond the Jewish community, embracing all nations under the grace of Christ. This story is a testament to Ethiopia's early acceptance and devotion to the teachings of Christ, making it a beacon of faith from the earliest times.

text: Greetings again, I have another question. For me, being a Deacon is amazing. I feel like the Holy Spirit is dwelling with in me so much. I’m always intrigued to read the Holy Bible and to learn the Kidase. All though, I don’t know what a great blessing and significance being a Deacon truly is. Please explain to me the full history of Deaconhood and the history of the first Deacon who was known as St. Steven. Blessings, Goodnight.

Greetings in the peace of Christ,

The Diaconate is a sacred order, rich in history and spiritual significance, embodying service and dedication to the Church and to God’s people.

The role of a Deacon traces back to the early Church, as outlined in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 6. The Apostles, overwhelmed by their responsibilities, sought out seven men "of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom," (Acts 6:3) to assist in serving the widows and the needy. This marked the beginning of the Diaconate. Among these seven was Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit (Acts 6:5), who became the first martyr for Christ, bearing witness to the truth of the Gospel even unto death. His martyrdom highlights the depth of commitment and sacrifice inherent in serving God and His Church.

Being a Deacon, therefore, is not merely a role or a function; it is a vocation to embody the love and service of Christ, to minister to the faithful, and to be a living witness to the Gospel. It is a call to humility, service, and sometimes, sacrifice, as exemplified by St. Stephen. 

Your attraction to the Holy Scriptures and the Kidase (Divine Liturgy) is a foundation upon which your service is built, for through them, you encounter Christ and convey His presence to others. The significance of your role lies in this very act of service and witness, in the footsteps of Christ and His saints.

"Whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your servant, and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be slave of all." (Mark 10:43-44)

Reflecting on the life and martyrdom of St. Stephen, how can you see your service as a Deacon being a reflection of Christ's service to the world?

text:
In the observance of Great Lent, the Church invites us to reflect on the profound narrative of the healing at Bethesda during its fourth week. This week, known as Metsague, derives its name from the story of a man who had been afflicted with illness for thirty-eight years, as recounted in the Gospel of John, chapter 5, verses 1 through 9. This narrative, rich in symbolism and divine truth, serves as a beacon of hope and a call to spiritual awakening, inviting us to delve deeper into the mysteries of faith, healing, and the boundless mercy of God.

In this poignant account, we encounter a figure, Metsague, who embodies the plight of humanity, ensnared by the frailties of the body and the desolation of the spirit. Bethesda, the place of this miraculous healing, with its five porticoes, becomes a symbol of the Church itself, a sanctuary for the ailing, the lost, and the forsaken, awaiting the stirring of the waters of grace. Here, the afflicted gathered, yearning for deliverance, for a touch of the divine that would transform their suffering into salvation.

It was amid this tableau of human misery that Jesus Christ, the Physician of our souls and bodies, approached Metsague. In asking, "Do you want to be healed?" Christ reveals a fundamental truth of our spiritual journey—the necessity of our consent in the work of our own salvation. The man's response, marked by despair and resignation, echoes the condition of many souls who, though desiring deliverance, find themselves paralyzed by their infirmities, unable to reach the healing waters by their own strength.

In commanding Metsague to rise, take up his bed, and walk, Christ demonstrates His authority over sin and death, over all that binds humanity in chains of despair. This act of healing on the Sabbath, which aroused the ire of the legalistic observers, underscores the Lord's message that mercy triumphs over judgment, that the law of love supersedes the letter of the law. Through this miracle, Christ invites us to a Sabbath rest in Him, to find in His mercy and love the true healing of our souls.

Metsague's healing is not merely a historical event but a living testament to the ongoing work of Christ in the world. It beckons us to recognize our own infirmities, our own pools of Bethesda, where we lie in wait for the stirring of the waters. It challenges us to hear Christ's call to rise from our slumber of sin and despair, to embrace the cross of self-denial, and to walk in the newness of life that He offers.

As we journey through the third week of Great Lent, let us meditate upon the profound symbolism of Metsague's healing. Let us contemplate the depth of Christ's mercy, which seeks us out in our infirmities, asking each of us, "Do you want to be healed?" May our hearts respond with a fervent "Yes, Lord," trusting in His power to transform our lives, to bear our infirmities, and to guide us to the still waters of His peace.

In this time of solemn reflection, let us also remember that, like Metsague, we are called to be witnesses to the miracle of grace in our lives, to carry our bed of suffering and follow Christ with resolute faith. For in our healing, we are called not only to salvation but to bear witness to the glory of God, to become beacons of hope and instruments of His mercy in a world yearning for redemption.

May the story of Metsague inspire us to deeper faith, to a more profound understanding of our own need for healing, and to a renewed commitment to follow Christ, our Savior and Healer, through the arduous path of Lent to the glorious dawn of Resurrection.

text:
What does the church advise about careers that consume a lot of your time & potentially limit the amount of time you can spend in church service & activities ? 

For example if i want to become a doctor, the education process will keep me busy and limit the time i can spend in service. In addition, when i start working as a doctor it will be the same. Would this be considered okay as long as i strive to live a sacramental life and serve God with the time I have. Or would the church recommend carefully considering the careers we choose with respect to how that affects our service life. 

Thank you 🙏🏾

Dear beloved in Christ,

Your inquiry touches upon a fundamental aspect of our journey with the Lord, where the balance between worldly duties and spiritual commitments often presents a challenge. The Orthodox Church, deeply rooted in the wisdom of the Holy Scriptures and the teachings of the Fathers, offers a perspective that transcends the apparent dichotomy between secular occupations and spiritual life.

Saint Paul reminds us in Colossians 3:23, "Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men." This verse encapsulates the essence of the Christian approach to work and vocation. The Church does not discourage us from pursuing careers, such as in medicine, that demand a significant portion of our time. Rather, it encourages us to see our professions as arenas for serving Christ and manifesting His love. Being a doctor, you are provided with unique opportunities to serve Christ in the sick and the suffering, embodying the healing ministry of our Lord Jesus.

The key is to ensure that your career does not lead you away from your ultimate goal—the salvation of your soul and union with Christ. It is indeed possible to lead a sacramental life and serve God with the time you have, integrating your faith into your daily work. The challenge is to maintain a prayerful life and participate in the Church's sacraments as much as your circumstances allow.

Consider the words of St. John Chrysostom, who taught that every aspect of our lives could be an offering to God if done in a spirit of love and dedication to His glory. Your career as a doctor, fueled by compassion and the desire to alleviate suffering, can be a powerful ministry and a path to sanctity.

Reflecting on how to balance your career and spiritual life, ask yourself: How can I make my work an offering to God? What steps can I take to ensure that my profession strengthens rather than diminishes my relationship with Christ?

In serving others through your profession, you serve Christ Himself. What will be your first step to integrating your faith with your work, making your life a living testimony of God’s love and mercy?

text:
This feast, which we celebrate today, is rooted deeply in the ethos of our faith, and beckons us to a profound reflection on the Crucifixion, a pivotal moment where divinity intersects with humanity in an act of unparalleled love and redemption.

The narrative of the Crucifixion, as we have inherited through sacred tradition and the Gospel of John, unfolds in the shadow of Gethsemane. It was there, amidst the olive groves, where the tranquility of the night was pierced by the approach of those who sought to capture Jesus of Nazareth. His response, imbued with divine authority, "I am he," caused them to stagger and fall—a testament to the power of His presence and the depth of His willingness to embrace His fate.

This encounter underlines a profound truth: the Crucifixion was not an event borne out of vulnerability or defeat but a conscious sacrifice, chosen by the one who commands the stars and treads upon the waters. In this divine paradox, we find the essence of our faith—the Almighty, bound; the Creator, subjected to His creation; the Giver of Life, embracing death.

As the events of that fateful day unfolded, our Lord, adorned not with regal gold but with a crown of thorns, reveals the heart of God's kingdom: one not of earthly power but of sacrificial love. Mocked and scorned, bearing a cross that symbolized not only His suffering but the weight of humanity's sin, He advanced towards Golgotha. With each step, the reality of His mission became clearer—to reconcile the world unto Himself, transforming an instrument of torture into the beacon of hope.

Upon the hill where Adam's sin cast a long shadow, the New Adam was lifted high. Nailed to the cross, His outstretched arms gathered the expanse of human frailty, offering it up to the Father in an act of ultimate intercession. It was here, at Calvary, that the fountain of mercy was opened, washing away the stains of sin and bridging the chasm wrought by our transgressions.

The cruelty of His tormentors, the indifference of the onlookers, and the tears of the faithful formed the backdrop to this cosmic drama. Yet, beyond the physical torment—a number so vast it numbs the mind—was the spiritual anguish of the Son, forsaken, that the world might be redeemed.

This yearly feast of Medhanialem is not merely a historical remembrance but a living participation in the mystery of the Cross. It invites us to enter into the paradox of Christian life: that in dying we find life, in surrender, victory, and in suffering, joy. As we reflect on the Crucifixion, let us also look beyond, to the Resurrection, where the fullness of God's promise is realized, and the hope of glory shines undimmed.

May the remembrance of Jesus Christ's suffering, His cross, death, and resurrection, not only recall the depths from which we have been lifted but inspire us to live lives worthy of the calling we have received. In this holy contemplation, let us draw near to the heart of God, finding in His wounds our healing, in His death our life, and in His love the strength to carry our crosses with faith, hope, and love. Amen.
