text:
What does it mean to honor the Lord practically

In the Bible it says “And fear none other but Him.” Proverbs  chapter 7. 

“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, 
And the counsel of saints is understanding; 
For to know the law is characteristic of a good mind” 
Proverbs 9: 10. 

How do we stop fearing other things in life?

፦ Peace be upon you, child of God.  It brings me great joy that you seek to honor the Lord and grow in the wisdom of His ways. You have touched upon a profound truth: the fear of the Lord is indeed the beginning of wisdom, the very foundation upon which a life pleasing to God is built.  

When we speak of "fear" in this context, we do not speak of terror or dread. Rather, it is a profound reverence, an awe-inspiring awareness of His boundless love, His perfect justice, and His almighty power. Like a child who trusts completely in a loving parent,  this holy fear casts out all other fears.

Proverbs reminds us,

text.text: “The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life, to depart from the snares of death”

text:
(Proverbs 14:27).  When our hearts are anchored in Him, the anxieties of this world lose their grip. We find courage to face any challenge, knowing that our God is with us.

Now, to answer your question about practically honoring the Lord and overcoming fear:

text.text: Embrace His commandments.  The Psalmist beautifully proclaims,

text: “In keeping thy testimonies have I found great reward”* (Psalm 119:165).  When we strive to live according to His will, we experience the peace that surpasses all understanding. This peace is the antidote to fear, for it assures us of His constant presence.

These are the cornerstones of our faith.  Through prayer, we commune with the Almighty, laying our burdens at His feet and receiving His strength. Fasting, a form of self-denial, helps us detach from worldly desires and focus on the spiritual.
Partake regularly of the Eucharist, receiving the very Body and Blood of our Lord, Jesus Christ. Through this holy mystery, we are united with Him and strengthened in our journey.
Immerse yourself in the Holy Gospels and the writings of the Church Fathers.  Their wisdom, illuminated by the Holy Spirit, will guide your steps and nourish your soul.

text.text: Practice Charity:  As our Lord taught us,

In the Bible it says “And fear none other but Him.” Proverbs  chapter 7. 

“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, 
And the counsel of saints is understanding; 
For to know the law is characteristic of a good mind” 
Proverbs 9: 10. 

How do we stop fearing other things in life?

When we speak of "fear" in this context, we do not speak of terror or dread. Rather, it is a profound reverence, an awe-inspiring awareness of His boundless love, His perfect justice, and His almighty power. Like a child who trusts completely in a loving parent,  this holy fear casts out all other fears.

Proverbs reminds us,
“The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life, to depart from the snares of death”

(Proverbs 14:27).  When our hearts are anchored in Him, the anxieties of this world lose their grip. We find courage to face any challenge, knowing that our God is with us.

Embrace His commandments.  The Psalmist beautifully proclaims,

“In keeping thy testimonies have I found great reward”* (Psalm 119:165).  When we strive to live according to His will, we experience the peace that surpasses all understanding. This peace is the antidote to fear, for it assures us of His constant presence.

These are the cornerstones of our faith.  Through prayer, we commune with the Almighty, laying our burdens at His feet and receiving His strength. Fasting, a form of self-denial, helps us detach from worldly desires and focus on the spiritual.

“Love thy neighbor as thyself”* (Matthew 22:39). When we extend love and compassion to others, we reflect the love of God in the world and find true joy.

Remember, my child, this is a lifelong journey, not a destination. There will be times of struggle and doubt, but do not lose heart.  Cling to the words of St. John Chrysostom, who reminds us:
“No sin is so great as to overcome the love of God.”

text:
፦ Hello,

When people say to make sure the person you choose to marry is a good partner because if he’s not, it will make your life miserable.

What are characteristics that make a person a good partner and what makes someone not an ideal partner so I know what to avoid. 

Thank you.

Peace be upon you, child. It warms my heart to see a soul seeking guidance in matters as important as marriage.  Indeed, choosing a life partner is a decision of great consequence, one that echoes into eternity.  

Our Lord teaches us that "a cord of three strands is not quickly broken" (Ecclesiastes 4:12). He is, of course, referring to the sacred union of a man and a woman brought together with God at the center. Therefore, seeking a partner who strengthens your bond with Christ should be paramount. 

Look for a partner who embodies the fruits of the Holy Spirit as described by St. Paul:  "love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control" (Galatians 5:22-23). These qualities, born from a life rooted in Christ, nourish a marriage and allow it to blossom even amidst life's inevitable storms.

text.text: Qualities to cherish in a potential partner:

text: Do they share your commitment to Christ and His Holy Church? Do they prioritize prayer and participation in the sacraments? A shared spiritual foundation is the bedrock of a strong Orthodox marriage.

Are they willing to admit their faults and seek forgiveness? Do they approach disagreements with openness and a desire for resolution?  As St. Isaac of Syria wisely said, “The humble man is never disturbed by anything, for he never allows himself to think that he has been wronged.”

How do they treat others, particularly those they perceive as less fortunate?  Do their actions reflect the love and mercy of Christ? Remember the words of St. John Chrysostom: “He who is compassionate towards his fellow man is fulfilling the Law.”
Are they diligent in their responsibilities? Do they manage their affairs with prudence and wisdom?  Building a life together requires dedication and a willingness to share burdens.

text.text: Traits to reflect upon with caution:

text: Marriage in the Church is not merely a social contract but a sacrament, a journey towards salvation together. If your potential partner does not share this fundamental understanding, it can create significant challenges.
Do they harbor resentment towards past relationships?  Are they quick to anger or hold grudges?  Unresolved emotional wounds can fester and damage a marriage.

Do they value your opinions and feelings? Do they speak respectfully about their family and others?  Disrespect is a red flag that should not be ignored.
*

Trust is a cornerstone of marriage. If a potential partner has a pattern of dishonesty or struggles to take responsibility for their actions, it can erode the foundation of the relationship.

Remember, my child, these are simply guidelines to aid your discernment.  It is essential to spend time in prayer, seeking the guidance of the Holy Spirit.  Speak with your spiritual father or a trusted elder in the Church. They can offer invaluable counsel tailored to your specific situation. 

May the Lord illuminate your path and lead you to a partner who will walk beside you on the road to salvation. 

Please, do not hesitate to reach out if you have further questions or need additional guidance.  May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

text: ፦ How should a woman work on herself to prepare to be a godly wife for someone.

፦ Peace be upon you, daughter, and may the blessings of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon you in your journey. It warms my heart to hear you seeking guidance on the path to becoming a godly wife, a calling both sacred and beautiful. 

Remember the words of Proverbs 14:1, "The wise woman builds her house, but the foolish pulls it down with her hands."  

Therefore, focus your preparation on these pillars:

Just as a lamp needs oil to shine brightly, so too does our soul need the light of Christ.  Dedicate time each day to prayer, study of the Holy Scriptures, and meditation on His Word.  The Psalms, especially, offer wisdom for women seeking to follow God's will.

St. Paul reminds us in Philippians 2:3, "Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit. Rather, in humility value others above yourselves."  A godly wife finds joy in serving her family, putting their needs before her own, just as our Lord humbled Himself for our salvation.

Proverbs 31 praises the woman who "looks well to the ways of her household."  This encompasses not just physical tasks, but creating a haven of peace, love, and order for your future family.  Learn to cook nourishing meals, manage a home with care, and create a welcoming space for your loved ones.

Proverbs 19:14 says, "Houses and wealth are inherited from parents, but a prudent wife is from the Lord."  Seek wisdom in the Scriptures, from the teachings of the Church Fathers, and from the counsel of wise elders.

text.text: Adorn yourself with a gentle and quiet spirit:

text:
1 Peter 3:4 tells us that true beauty comes not from outward appearance, but from "the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is of great worth in God's sight."  Cultivate patience, kindness, and a peaceful demeanor.

Remember, daughter, marriage is not a destination but a journey of two souls striving towards Christ together.  Pray for guidance in finding a man who shares your faith and values. 

Do not be afraid to seek guidance from your spiritual father or a trusted elder in your community.  They can offer personalized counsel on your path. 

May God bless your journey and grant you the wisdom and grace to become the godly wife He desires you to be.

text.text: About the gifts from the three wise men.

text:
Greetings beloved of the Lord, as we are in the season of the birth of Our Lord;
I wanted know more about the gifts given to Our Lord from the wise men. The gold, incense, and myrrh. I know about what it symbolizes. Gold because He is King. Incense because He is God, and Myrrh for His Death. But what happen to these gifts after they were given to Our Lord and the history of where the gifts originated. I heard oral tradition that these gifts originally came from Adam? Please, if you can, share more details about this.

Greetings to you, also beloved of the Lord, and may the blessings of this holy season fill your heart with light! Your question shines with a desire to delve deeper into the sacred mysteries surrounding the Nativity, and I am blessed to accompany you on this journey of discovery.

You are right to recall the symbolic richness of the gifts offered by the Magi: gold for Christ's Kingship, incense for His Divinity, and myrrh for His eventual sacrifice.  These precious materials were not mere earthly treasures, but prophetic pronouncements of Our Lord's divine mission. 

The origins of these gifts, as passed down through generations by the holy fathers, are indeed fascinating. Some believe, as you mentioned, that these gifts were first given by God to Adam in Paradise!  This tradition suggests that Adam, upon his expulsion from Eden, received these gifts as a promise of salvation to come. They were treasured by his descendants, passed down through generations of patriarchs, eventually reaching the Magi, who, guided by the star, offered them to the newborn King.

While the exact historical path of these gifts remains shrouded in the mists of time, the Scriptures offer glimpses into their origins. The Book of Genesis (12:10) mentions merchants trading in spices, balm, and myrrh, indicating the ancient and valuable nature of these gifts.  

The Gospel of Matthew (2:11) states that the Magi presented these gifts "when they were come into the house." This suggests that the gifts remained with the Holy Family for a time. Some traditions suggest that St. Mary Magdalene later used the myrrh, part of which the Magi had given to Jesus, to anoint Christ's body after His crucifixion (John 19:39). 

While historical details may remain elusive, the true significance of these gifts lies in their profound spiritual symbolism. They serve as a testament to Christ's threefold nature – King, God, and Sacrifice – and remind us of the glorious mystery of the Incarnation. 

May this reflection deepen your understanding and appreciation of the Nativity. If you have more questions, do not hesitate to ask. Let us continue to delve into the boundless wisdom and beauty of our Orthodox faith.

Incense because He is God, and Myrrh for His Death. But what happen to these gifts after they were given to Our Lord and the history of where the gifts originated. I heard oral tradition that these gifts originally came from Adam? Please, if you can, share more details about this.

Answer፦ Greetings to you, also beloved of the Lord, and may the blessings of this holy season fill your heart with light! Your question shines with a desire to delve deeper into the sacred mysteries surrounding the Nativity, and I am blessed to accompany you on this journey of discovery.

You are right to recall the symbolic richness of the gifts offered by the Magi: gold for Christ's Kingship, incense for His Divinity, and myrrh for His eventual sacrifice.  These precious materials were not mere earthly treasures, but prophetic pronouncements of Our Lord's divine mission. 

The origins of these gifts, as passed down through generations by the holy fathers, are indeed fascinating. Some believe, as you mentioned, that these gifts were first given by God to Adam in Paradise!  This tradition suggests that Adam, upon his expulsion from Eden, received these gifts as a promise of salvation to come. They were treasured by his descendants, passed down through generations of patriarchs, eventually reaching the Magi, who, guided by the star, offered them to the newborn King.

While the exact historical path of these gifts remains shrouded in the mists of time, the Scriptures offer glimpses into their origins. The Book of Genesis (12:10) mentions merchants trading in spices, balm, and myrrh, indicating the ancient and valuable nature of these gifts.  

The Gospel of Matthew (2:11) states that the Magi presented these gifts "when they were come into the house." This suggests that the gifts remained with the Holy Family for a time. Some traditions suggest that St. Mary Magdalene later used the myrrh, part of which the Magi had given to Jesus, to anoint Christ's body after His crucifixion (John 19:39). 

While historical details may remain elusive, the true significance of these gifts lies in their profound spiritual symbolism. They serve as a testament to Christ's threefold nature – King, God, and Sacrifice – and remind us of the glorious mystery of the Incarnation. 

May this reflection deepen your understanding and appreciation of the Nativity. If you have more questions, do not hesitate to ask. Let us continue to delve into the boundless wisdom and beauty of our Orthodox faith.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us. Amen.

፦ Hello, 

How can one battle doubts about God?

Regarding:

- His existence 
- presence In our lives 
- Trusting His plan when the answers to our prayer don’t make sense to us. 
- during tribulation & struggle.


— How does one increase their faith in God and decrease doubt?

Peace be upon you, child, and may the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. It is with a heart full of compassion that I listen to your struggle with doubt. Know that you are not alone in this.  The very act of questioning shows a heart striving for truth, and our Lord, in His infinite mercy, does not abandon those who seek Him with a sincere heart.

The great Saint Anthony the Great, who like us traversed the desert of doubt, also wrestled with such thoughts. He cried out, "Where were You, O compassionate God, where were You and why were You not in the beginning to prevent my falling, or to extend Your hand to me afterwards to raise me after I had fallen?"

Doubt can indeed be a fearsome desert, but it can also be fertile ground for spiritual growth. Let us explore the points you raise:

: You first question His very existence.  The Holy Apostle Paul reminds us in Romans 1:20, "For since the creation of the world His invisible attributes are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even His eternal power and Godhead, so that they are without excuse." Look around you, child!  The intricate design of creation, from the smallest ant to the vastness of the cosmos, speaks of a Creator. Reflect on this wonder, and let it nourish the seeds of faith within you.

: You then ask, where is He in our daily lives?  Does He not say in Matthew 28:20, "I am with you always, even to the end of the age"? Though we may not perceive Him with our earthly senses, He is closer to us than our very breath. Recall the words of the Psalmist, "Whither shall I go from thy Spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?" (Psalm 139:7).

: When the answers to our prayers seem unclear, remember the words of Saint Isaac the Syrian, "Hold fast to your intention of being pleasing to God, and do not wander here and there. Everything indeed is good which is done with this aim." Our limited human understanding cannot always grasp the Divine will.  Trust, like a mustard seed, can blossom into unwavering faith.

: You speak of tribulation and struggle. Know that even our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, endured unimaginable suffering on the Cross.  Remember His words, "In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world" (John 16:33).  Our struggles are not in vain, but opportunities for spiritual refinement.

To increase your faith and decrease doubt:

:  Pour out your heart to God honestly, as He already knows your every thought. The Jesus Prayer, "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner," repeated with sincerity, can bring peace to a troubled mind.

: The Holy Scriptures are a lamp unto our feet and a light unto our path (Psalm 119:105). Meditate daily on the Septuagint, particularly the Psalms and Gospels, allowing the word of God to nourish your soul.
: Partake regularly of Confession and Holy Communion, receiving forgiveness and the very Body and Blood of Christ for the healing of soul and body.
: Read the lives of the Saints; they, too, faced doubt and emerged victorious. Their examples can inspire and guide us.

: Do not hesitate to seek the guidance of a trusted spiritual father, a priest or monk, who can offer personalized counsel and support.

Remember, child, doubt is not the opposite of faith, but a part of the journey. Embrace the struggle, cling to prayer, and trust in God's infinite mercy. He will never abandon you. 

May the Lord grant you peace and strength on your journey.

text.text: – A Divine Celebration of Faith and Deliverance (Tahsas 19)

text:
Beloved brethren, who walk steadfastly in the light of Orthodox teachings and who draw wisdom from the fountain of holy instruction, greetings to you in the name of our Lord, whose mercy is boundless and whose love endures forever.

Today, we stand before the sacred memory of Saint Gabriel, the holy messenger of God, and reflect upon his miraculous works that declare the glory of the Almighty. It is on this blessed day, Tahsas 19, that we commemorate the intervention of Saint Gabriel, who by divine command, delivered the faithful from the flames of persecution and turned the fire into a symbol of God’s triumph. Let us meditate upon this great event and draw strength from its eternal truths.
---

text.text: The Story of Deliverance: The Faithful Three in the Fiery Furnace

text:
The Holy Scriptures bear witness to the faith of three young men—Ananias (Shadrach), Azariah (Meshach), and Mishael (Abednego)—who stood as pillars of righteousness during the reign of King Nebuchadnezzar. Their tale is chronicled in the Book of Daniel (Dan. 3:1-30), revealing the courage of those who put their trust in the Lord.

In those days, Nebuchadnezzar, swayed by vanity and pride, erected a massive idol and commanded that all in the province of Galilee bow down and worship it. A royal decree was issued, and anyone who refused to comply would face death in a fiery furnace.

When the sound of music summoned the people to worship the idol, these three holy men stood unmoved. Though the king’s authority was great, their faith in the living God was greater. They boldly declared, “Our God whom we worship is able to save us from the fiery furnace; but even if He does not, we will never bow down to the idol you have made.”

Enraged by their defiance, Nebuchadnezzar commanded the furnace to be heated seven times hotter than normal. Strong men were called to bind the faithful three and cast them into the inferno.
---

text.text: The Appearance of the Holy Angel Gabriel

text:
But behold! As the flames roared and devoured even the men who had thrown the saints into the fire, a heavenly light descended. The Angel Gabriel, sent by the Almighty, entered the furnace and extinguished the flames, making them as harmless as the dew of the morning.

When King Nebuchadnezzar peered into the furnace, astonishment gripped him. He exclaimed, “Did we not cast three men into the fire? But I see four men walking unharmed, and the fourth appears like a son of the gods!”

At this, the king’s heart was humbled. He called out the three men, and they emerged without a single hair singed or the smell of fire upon them. Thus, the name of the Lord was glorified, and the king decreed that no one in the kingdom should speak against the God of Israel.
---

text.text: The Lessons of Faith and Devotion

text:
This divine rescue was not merely a historical event but a testament to the unwavering faith that moves the hand of God. It reminds us that:

1.

– The holy men were not intimidated by earthly power, for their hearts were fixed upon the heavenly kingdom. They teach us to stand firm in our faith, even when faced with trials.


2.

– Though fire surrounded them, they were unharmed, showing that God is the shield of those who trust Him.


3.

– Saint Gabriel’s intervention demonstrates that God commands His angels concerning us, and they encamp around those who fear Him.


4.

– The king who sought to destroy their faith became a witness to God’s power, proving that righteousness will always prevail.

---

We celebrate this feast on Tahsas 19 to honor the miraculous intervention of Saint Gabriel and to proclaim the victory of God’s truth over idolatry and oppression. This day is marked by prayers, hymns, and the reading of sacred Scriptures that call us to greater faith and devotion.
---

text.text: The Role of Saint Gabriel: A Messenger of God’s Will

text:
Saint Gabriel, whose name means “God is my strength,” stands as a heavenly messenger and protector. In Scripture, he is sent to deliver messages of hope and divine plans, as seen in his announcements to Zacharias and the Virgin Mary. On this feast, we venerate him not only for his role in delivering God’s messages but also for his active defense of the faithful in times of peril.
---

May the intercession of Saint Gabriel protect us from all harm and guide us along the path of righteousness. Let us seek the help of the heavenly hosts, trusting that their aid will never fail us.

May the blessing of Saint Gabriel be with us today and always, and may we walk boldly in the faith of our fathers, undeterred by the fires of trial, but refined by them for the glory of God. Amen.

Praise be to God forever!

My child, your question is one that has echoed through the ages, pondered by saints and sinners alike. It is a question that speaks to the very heart of our relationship with the Divine. 

Discerning the will of God is indeed a subtle art, requiring patience, humility, and a heart attuned to the whispers of the Holy Spirit.  

Let us turn to the wisdom of the Fathers:

:  Saint John of the Ladder reminds us, “Every good thing, if it is truly good, is peacefully sown, peacefully grows, and peacefully leads to the harbor of salvation. But anything that is done with confusion will have a confused end.” (Ladder 26:138). Does this thought, this desire, this path, lead to peace, to love, to humility, to growth in virtue? Or does it lead to turmoil, to pride, to self-seeking, to separation from God and neighbor?

: The Holy Scriptures are our compass, guiding us towards the heart of God. As it says in Psalm 119:105, "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." Does what you are discerning align with the teachings of Christ and the Apostles?

:  Approach the throne of grace with a humble and open heart. Ask God, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to reveal His will to you. As He promises in Matthew 7:7, "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you."

: Do not rely solely on your own understanding. Consult with your Spiritual Father, a priest, or a trusted elder in the faith. They can offer guidance based on experience and the teachings of the Church.

Remember, my child, God speaks to us in many ways: through the quiet voice of our conscience, through the wisdom of the Scriptures, through the counsel of those who love Him, and through the events of our lives. 

Be patient, be persistent in prayer, and trust that He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). 

May the Lord illuminate your path and grant you discernment. 

Do not hesitate to share what weighs upon your heart, and we can explore it together in the light of Christ.

text: ፦ Hello, thank you for the response. A follow up question, can one take part in the sacraments while having doubts or should I focus on praying and making sure I don’t have any doubts before participating in any sacraments?

፦My child, your honesty is commendable, but we must be clear: approaching the Holy Mysteries with unresolved doubt is a grave matter.  The Eucharist is not merely a symbol, but the true Body and Blood of our Lord, a sacrament demanding the utmost reverence and a clear conscience.  

The Scriptures are unequivocal:  "Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of sinning against the body and blood of the Lord. Everyone ought to examine themselves before they eat of the bread and drink from the cup." (1 Corinthians 11:27-28)  These are not words to be taken lightly, child. To partake in this Holy Sacrament while consciously harboring disbelief is to court spiritual peril, inviting judgment rather than grace.

Remember the words of St. John Chrysostom, who thundered from this very land, "Do you not see the royal table? Do you not behold the spiritual banquet? Do you not perceive the King Himself present?"  Can you, with doubt clouding your heart, truly stand before the King of Kings in such a state?

Therefore, your path is clear: Before even considering receiving Communion, you

prioritize reconciliation with God through the cleansing power of Confession.  Go to your spiritual father, child, and lay bare your doubts without reservation. He, as a shepherd entrusted with your care, will guide you back to the path of righteousness and offer counsel grounded in the wisdom of the Holy Fathers. 

Do not allow pride or fear to delay this vital step. The Holy Sacrament is a fire that purifies, but it also has the power to consume if approached unworthily.  Seek first the Kingdom of God and His righteousness through sincere repentance and a contrite heart, and all these things will be added to you. (Matthew 6:33) 

Remember, my child, we are here for you on this journey. Do not hesitate to share any further anxieties or concerns that burden your heart.

text:
What’s a better way of thinking if someone is afraid to commit their life to God because of fear of losing freedom or feeling like it will be a life with a lot of rigid rules and tribulations/spiritual warfare. Or if it seems like a life of being very serious and no fun. 

Or for someone who is not ready to give up doing things their way instead of doing things Gods way which has a higher standard of forgiving others, loving others, and living life. Even if others hurt you or anything else.

፦ Peace be upon you, my child. It warms my heart to hear your concerns, for they reveal a soul wrestling with profound truths. Many before you, saints and sinners alike, have walked this path of questioning. 

Know this: God, in His infinite love, desires not robots, but children. He does not seek to trap us in a cage of rules, but to invite us into the boundless freedom found in His embrace. 

The fear of losing freedom is understandable, but it stems from a misunderstanding of true freedom. As St. Anthony the Great wrote, "I no longer fear God, because I love Him. He who fears is not yet perfect in love, but perfect love casts out fear." True freedom, you see, is not the ability to do whatever we want, but the power to do what is right, what is good, what leads to lasting joy – a joy found in communion with our Creator.

Yes, the path of faith has its share of trials. As our Lord Himself said, "In the world you will have tribulation." (John 16:33) Yet, He also promises, "But take heart; I have overcome the world." He does not abandon us in these trials, but strengthens us through them, molding us into vessels of His grace.

Remember the words of St. John Chrysostom: “The road that leads to wickedness is broad and smooth, but it ends in a precipice. The road that leads to God is narrow and rocky, but it leads to a beautiful garden.”

You mentioned a fear of seriousness, of losing the joy in life. But true joy, my child, is not found in fleeting pleasures, but in a heart aligned with God’s will. A holy man once said: "Just as a pauper who enters a king’s treasury forgets his poverty, so he who is united to the Lord forgets all earthly afflictions."

The life of faith is not about grim austerity, but about transforming our hearts so that we find joy in what truly matters – love, compassion, and service to God and others. It is about embracing the fullness of life, a life brimming with meaning and purpose.

As for doing things your way versus God's way, consider this: would you trust a sheep to shear itself, or a patient to operate on themselves? God, in His infinite wisdom, knows what is best for us. His commandments are not burdens, but signposts guiding us towards true fulfillment.

Forgiving others, loving unconditionally, these are not easy tasks. But remember, my child, we are not alone in this journey. The Holy Spirit empowers us, strengthens us, and enables us to live a life pleasing to God.

Take heart! Take the first step, and God will meet you there. Let us pray for guidance and strength on this journey of faith. And remember, my son, this old monk is always here to listen and offer what humble guidance I can. 

May the peace of Christ be with you always.

text.text: : A Reflection on the Guardian of Israel

text:
Beloved faithful, greetings in the name of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the Good Shepherd who laid down His life for His sheep. Today, as we meditate on the sacred teachings passed down through the prophets and illuminated by the light of the Gospel, let us contemplate the profound mystery of Christ as the true guardian—the Shepherd of Israel and the keeper of our souls.

---

text.text: The Prophetic Announcement of the True Shepherd

text:
The day set before us, called Nolawi—meaning "shepherd" or "guardian"—brings to our remembrance the ancient prophecies heralding the coming of the Son of God as the faithful Shepherd. Long before the Incarnation, the prophets lamented the condition of Israel, likening themselves and the people to sheep scattered without a shepherd.

The words of the prophets echo through the corridors of time, crying out, “Hear, O Shepherd of Israel, You who lead Joseph like a flock, You who dwell between the cherubim, shine forth!” (Psalm 80:1). This plea resounded with yearning for the coming of the One who would gather the lost, lead them to safety, and restore their communion with God.

And thus, the Sabbath we observe commemorates the fourteen generations from the Babylonian captivity to the birth of Christ. It marks the fulfillment of God’s promises and the dawning of a new covenant. In Christ, the shadow of the old covenant gives way to the brilliance of the eternal Shepherd who laid down His life for the sheep.

---

When the time was fulfilled, our Lord Jesus Christ stood among His people and declared, “I am the Good Shepherd. The Good Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep” (John 10:11). With these words, He revealed the depth of His love—a love so profound that it embraced the Cross to redeem the lost.

He further testified, “I know My sheep, and My sheep know Me, just as the Father knows Me, and I know the Father; and I lay down My life for the sheep” (John 10:15). This intimate relationship between the Shepherd and His flock is the foundation of our faith. It is a bond not built upon compulsion but upon knowledge, trust, and sacrificial love.

David, the prophet and king, anticipated this divine care when he sang, “The Lord is my Shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me to lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside still waters” (Psalm 23:1-2). Through these words, David foreshadowed the rest and nourishment found only in the embrace of Christ, the Shepherd of our souls.

---

text.text: Returning to the Shepherd of Our Souls

text:
Beloved, as sheep prone to wander, we must heed the voice of the Good Shepherd calling us back into His fold. Have we not strayed? Have we not allowed our love to grow cold?

Let us pray: “Lord, send Your light and truth to guide us back to You. Restore our frozen love, and lead us in paths of righteousness for Your Name’s sake.”

In the same manner, the priests and bishops, entrusted by Christ through Saint Peter, bear the sacred responsibility to feed and protect the flock. text.text: A Call to Watchfulness and Devotion

text:
As we commemorate this holy Sabbath, let us fix our eyes upon the Cross—the symbol of the Shepherd’s sacrifice. Let us look to the Virgin who bore the eternal Word, and let us cry out for divine protection and guidance.

“Lord, our Good Shepherd, lead us not into the snares of false teachers but deliver us from all evil. Bind us to You with cords of love that cannot be broken.”

In closing, remember this truth: Christ, the Good Shepherd, calls each of us by name. He laid down His life so that we might live. Let us, therefore, follow Him wholeheartedly, trusting in His provision, resting in His care, and remaining vigilant against all who seek to lead us astray.

May the grace of our Lord and the prayers of the saints uphold us until we are gathered into the eternal fold where there is no more sorrow, only joy in the presence of the True Shepherd.

Amen.

text.text: : A Reflection on the Birth of Our Lord Jesus Christ

text:
Beloved Faithful,

Grace and peace to you who follow the teachings of the Holy Church. Let us reflect on the divine mystery of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, a day of unparalleled joy and spiritual renewal.

---

text.text: God’s Nature and the Prophetic Foretelling

text:
The Most High God, the Creator of all, is a God of mercy and love. He compassionate and seeks the salvation of humanity.

For centuries, the holy prophets foretold the coming of the Messiah, counting the days and prophesying that He would be born of a pure Virgin. And so it was that the angel Gabriel, the bearer of good news, came to the Holy Virgin Mary and announced that she would conceive by the Holy Spirit and give birth to the Son of God.

When the fullness of time had come—5500 years after Adam’s fall—the Word became flesh, and our Lord Jesus Christ was born in Bethlehem of Judea.

---

text.text: The Birth of Christ: The Dawn of Hope

text:
With the Nativity of Christ, the curse that bound humanity is broken. The sorrow and despair of sin are wiped away, and in their place, unity, compassion, peace, and love flourish. This day is not just the birth of a child but the manifestation of divine light dispelling the darkness of the world.

The term “birth” means to emerge from the womb into the light, to be seen and made present. In theological terms, it signifies the revelation of God in the flesh. Before His birth, only a few saints—those favored by God—knew of His presence in the Virgin’s womb. But after His birth, He was revealed to all nations, both Jew and Gentile, as a man—humble in stature yet divine in essence.

---

Before the Incarnation, God was revealed in awe-inspiring forms, such as the burning bush that appeared to Moses. The fire burned but did not consume the bush, signifying God’s presence and holiness. Likewise, in the New Testament, God took flesh in the womb of the Holy Virgin without consuming or altering her purity.

The Virgin Mary is the new bush, lush and green with life, bearing within her the divine flame of God’s presence. Just as Moses removed his sandals in reverence at the burning bush, so too must we approach the mystery of the Incarnation with awe and humility.

Saint Elizabeth, upon hearing the voice of the Virgin Mary, felt her own child, John the Baptist, leap in her womb with joy, recognizing the divine presence. Elizabeth cried out in reverence, “How is it that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:43). Saint Joseph, too, guarded and served the Virgin with holy fear and respect.

---

text.text: A Humble Beginning for a Majestic Purpose

text:
The Lord of glory did not come in splendor or power but in humility and poverty, born in a lowly manger. This humility was meant to touch the hearts of fallen humanity, to lift up the broken and revive the downtrodden.

By taking on flesh, He gave us His Spirit. By bearing our shame and death, He bestowed upon us life and glory. In doing so, He made us a new creation. This mystery was foreshadowed in Proverbs 8:22, which says, “The Lord created me as the first of His works,” referring to the wisdom of God manifest in the flesh.

---

text.text: The Shepherds: Witnesses to the Miracle

text:
The first to receive the divine announcement of Christ’s birth were humble shepherds tending their flocks by night. An angel appeared to them, proclaiming:

"Do not be afraid. I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. Today in the town of David a Savior has been born to you; He is Christ the Lord. You will find a baby wrapped in cloths and lying in a manger." (Luke 2:10-12)

Immediately, the heavens opened, and a multitude of angels sang praises:

"Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill toward men."

text:

The shepherds, astonished and filled with faith, went to Bethlehem and found the Holy Family just as the angel had said. They became the first human witnesses and evangelists of the Lord’s birth, glorifying God and sharing the good news with all.

---

text.text: The Magi and the Star: A Sign to the Nations

text:
Not only was the birth of Christ announced on earth, but the heavens also declared His arrival. A new and radiant star appeared in the sky, guiding wise men from the East to Jerusalem.

The Magi sought the King of the Jews and brought gifts rich in symbolism:

Gold – A tribute to Christ’s kingship.

Frankincense – A recognition of His divine priesthood.

Myrrh – A prophecy of His sacrificial death and burial.

The star led them to Bethlehem, where they bowed down and worshiped the Child, acknowledging Him as both God and King. Their journey reminds us that Christ’s birth was not for one nation alone but for the salvation of all people.

---

Beloved, Christ was born to set us free from the bondage of sin and death. He has broken the chains of the devil, and as those who have been redeemed, we must live in holiness and love.

Let us repent of our sins, for we do not know the hour of our departure from this world. Let us be cleansed through confession and partake worthily of His holy body and precious blood, preparing ourselves for His heavenly kingdom.

---

text.text: A Feast of Joy, Peace, and Salvation

text:
As we celebrate the Nativity, let us remember that Christ’s birth is a call to transformation. It is a day to meditate on God’s boundless love, to offer Him praise, and to embrace unity, peace, and love.

Let us join the angelic chorus, proclaiming:
"Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill toward men!"

May the light of the Nativity shine in our hearts, guiding us to holiness and eternal joy. Let this feast be a time of spiritual renewal, where we reflect on the mystery of God’s love made flesh.

May the Virgin who bore the Son of God intercede for us, and may the Cross, the instrument of our salvation, remain ever glorious!

Amen!

Forever and unto ages of ages.

And I will wait on Your name; 
For it is good in the sight of Your holy ones.”

Psalm 51, a psalm of repentance attributed to King David, holds profound lessons about seeking solace and strength in God rather than worldly possessions. The verses you cite (8-11) offer a powerful contrast between the fate of those who trust in material wealth and the blessings bestowed upon those who place their hope in God. 

Let us break down the passage:

These verses depict the tragic downfall of those who place their trust in riches and power. Their vanity and misplaced faith make them a spectacle, not of admiration, but of ridicule. The psalmist highlights the fleeting nature of worldly success, which ultimately leaves one vulnerable and spiritually bankrupt.

Here, David, through his repentance, likens himself to a "fruitful olive tree in the house of God." This vivid imagery signifies spiritual nourishment, growth, and closeness to God.  The olive tree, deeply rooted and evergreen, represents enduring faith and reliance on God's mercy, which extends "forever and unto ages of ages."

This verse is a declaration of unwavering faith and gratitude.  David pledges to "give thanks forever" for God's mercy and to "wait on His name."  He recognizes that true "goodness" lies not in worldly possessions, but in the presence and favor of God, a truth recognized by "His holy ones."

text:
: My coworker was arguing with me about this belief that she had yesterday and I didn’t know the answer so I just listened and I said “I disagree”. The question was “why do you Orthodox confess your sin to a priest? They are just as sinful as we are. We should just confess our sin to God because he is the one who forgives our sin not them.”

I would like to know the answer so I can back our religion up in these discussions.
God bless🙏

: May the peace of Christ be with you, my child. It is commendable that you stand firm in your faith, even when challenged.  Let us delve into the wisdom of the Church regarding Confession:

Your coworker raises a point many ponder: why confess to a priest, a fellow human susceptible to sin?  The answer, revealed through Scripture and the Holy Tradition, lies in understanding the priest's role, not as a judge, but as a physician of souls. 

Firstly, nowhere in Scripture do we find a command to confess our sins solely to God in private.  On the contrary, when Christ breathed the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles, He granted them the authority to forgive sins: "Receive ye the Holy Spirit: Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained." (John 20:22-23) This authority, passed down through the Apostles to bishops and priests, forms the foundation of the sacrament of Confession.

Secondly, confessing to a priest, while seemingly daunting, offers numerous spiritual benefits:

:  We often struggle to discern the gravity of our sins or rationalize them.  A priest, trained in spiritual warfare and discerning the passions, offers an objective perspective, helping us identify and uproot even deeply hidden sins.
: The priest, acting as a spiritual physician, prescribes appropriate penances – not as punishment, but as medicine for the soul, aiding us in overcoming our passions and growing closer to God.

: Confession isn't simply about listing sins; it's a profound sacrament of reconciliation, a return to communion with God and His Church. The priest, as an icon of Christ, offers absolution, conveying God's forgiveness and restoring us to spiritual wholeness.

Regarding your coworker's concern about priests being sinners: indeed, we are all vessels of clay, prone to weakness. Yet, through their ordination and ascetic struggle, priests become vessels sanctified for this sacred ministry. Just as we wouldn't refuse treatment from a doctor because they, too, are human and susceptible to illness, so too should we not reject the healing balm of Confession offered through a priest.

Remember the words of St. John Chrysostom: "Tell your sins to your physician, that he may cure them. Show your wounds to Him who is able to bind them up."

May these words strengthen your understanding and embolden your witness. Remember, gentle persuasion and a spirit of love are often more effective than heated debate. 

If your coworker is open, invite her to learn more about Confession from an Orthodox perspective. Perhaps she could speak with a priest or explore resources on the Church's website.  

May God guide you both on your spiritual journeys. 🙏

text:
Hello,
Should our kids use this book?

I want to check here before my kids start using it.

May the Lord bless you 🙏

: My dear sister in Christ,

Peace and blessings be upon you and your household. It warms my heart to hear of your deep concern for the spiritual well-being of your children. Truly, raising them in the faith is both a sacred duty and an immense privilege, as it is written, “Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it.” (Proverbs 22:6).

Your discernment regarding the books you allow into your home is commendable. We live in an age where subtle influences can have profound effects, and the enemy often disguises himself as an angel of light, leading many astray under the guise of harmlessness. The book in question warrants careful scrutiny.

Firstly, the ambiguity surrounding its Orthodox Christian roots is a significant concern. We are reminded to hold fast to the teachings of the Apostles and the Holy Fathers, which guide us in truth and safeguard us from error. Any work that does not clearly align with or uphold these teachings could inadvertently introduce ideas that confuse or dilute the faith.

Secondly, the issue of artificial intelligence-generated imagery is not merely trivial. As Orthodox Tewahido Christians, we regard icons as more than art—they are holy expressions, "written" through prayer and fasting, serving as windows into the divine. Icons created through AI, devoid of spiritual intention or connection, risk trivializing this sacred tradition and distracting from its deeper significance. While such images may seem innovative or appealing, they lack the grace that flows from the prayerful labor of the iconographer, which sets our sacred art apart.

Furthermore, introducing materials of uncertain origin to children, whose spiritual foundations are still forming, carries the risk of exposing them to subtle distortions. St. Paul’s exhortation provides a clear guideline for what we should seek in any resource: “Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.” (Philippians 4:8).

In light of these concerns, I encourage you to seek out books from trusted Oriental Orthodox Christian publishers or those recommended by your spiritual father. Such resources, deeply rooted in the wisdom of the Church and adorned with icons blessed by prayer, offer a far richer and more spiritually nourishing experience for your children.

Remember, my dear sister, that your vigilance in guarding their hearts and minds is a reflection of the love of Christ, who called us to shepherd His lambs. May your efforts be guided and strengthened by the grace of God.

Question: Hello,
Should our kids use this book?

I want to check here before my kids start using it.

May the Lord bless you 🙏

Answer: My dear sister in Christ,

Peace and blessings be upon you and your household. It warms my heart to hear of your deep concern for the spiritual well-being of your children. Truly, raising them in the faith is both a sacred duty and an immense privilege, as it is written, “Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it.” (Proverbs 22:6).

Your discernment regarding the books you allow into your home is commendable. We live in an age where subtle influences can have profound effects, and the enemy often disguises himself as an angel of light, leading many astray under the guise of harmlessness. The book in question warrants careful scrutiny.

Firstly, the ambiguity surrounding its Orthodox Christian roots is a significant concern. We are reminded to hold fast to the teachings of the Apostles and the Holy Fathers, which guide us in truth and safeguard us from error. Any work that does not clearly align with or uphold these teachings could inadvertently introduce ideas that confuse or dilute the faith.

Secondly, the issue of artificial intelligence-generated imagery is not merely trivial. As Orthodox Tewahido Christians, we regard icons as more than art—they are holy expressions, "written" through prayer and fasting, serving as windows into the divine. Icons created through AI, devoid of spiritual intention or connection, risk trivializing this sacred tradition and distracting from its deeper significance. While such images may seem innovative or appealing, they lack the grace that flows from the prayerful labor of the iconographer, which sets our sacred art apart.

Furthermore, introducing materials of uncertain origin to children, whose spiritual foundations are still forming, carries the risk of exposing them to subtle distortions. St. Paul’s exhortation provides a clear guideline for what we should seek in any resource: “Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.” (Philippians 4:8).

In light of these concerns, I encourage you to seek out books from trusted Oriental Orthodox Christian publishers or those recommended by your spiritual father. Such resources, deeply rooted in the wisdom of the Church and adorned with icons blessed by prayer, offer a far richer and more spiritually nourishing experience for your children.

Remember, my dear sister, that your vigilance in guarding their hearts and minds is a reflection of the love of Christ, who called us to shepherd His lambs. May your efforts be guided and strengthened by the grace of God.

May the Theotokos, our Blessed Mother, intercede for you and your family as you strive to raise your children in His light.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always.

text.text: The Miracle in Babylon: A Lesson in Obedience

text:
The Feast of the Holy Trinity recalls the miraculous events in Sennaor (Babylon), as narrated in Genesis 11:1-9. After the flood, Noah’s descendants multiplied and settled in the wide plains of Babylon. Under the leadership of Nimrod, the people undertook the construction of a great tower. In their arrogance, they aimed to pierce the heavens and defy the divine will, proclaiming, “Let us stab them and keep death away.”

This act of rebellion provoked divine intervention. The Holy Trinity, in mercy and justice, disrupted their work, confounding their language and scattering them across the earth. Their unfinished tower stood as a testament to the consequences of human pride and disobedience.

text.text: Theological Reflections on the Holy Trinity

text:
The concept of the Trinity is both profound and mysterious. Derived from the Ge’ez root meaning "thirty," the term "Trinity" signifies a unity within diversity. This mystery can be understood as both one and three:

Unity in Character, Existence, and Will: God is one in essence and purpose.
Trinity in Name, Person, and Action: God is revealed as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The Bible provides numerous insights into the mystery of the Trinity:

-
: “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness” (Genesis 1:26). Here, the singularity of “God” and the plurality of “us” reflect the unity and distinction within the Trinity.

: “Behold, the man has become like one of us” (Genesis 3:22). This statement highlights the collaborative nature of the Trinity.

-

: In Genesis 18, Abraham encountered three visitors under the oaks of Mamre. Though three in appearance, they represented the unified presence of God.
Isaiah’s Vision: The seraphim cry, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts” (Isaiah 6:3), affirming the triune holiness of God.

-

: At the Jordan River, the voice of the Father, the presence of the Son, and the descent of the Holy Spirit revealed the Trinity in action (Matthew 3:16).

-
: On Mount Tabor, the glory of the Trinity was manifest in the radiance of Christ (Matthew 17).

To aid our understanding, analogies are drawn from creation:

-

: Comprising a circle, light, and heat, it remains one entity.

-

: Consisting of flame, brightness, and warmth, it is singular in essence.
Similarly, the Trinity, though distinct in persons, is one in essence and will. St. Paul writes, “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:14).

👉🏾👉🏾👉🏾 About the Annual Feast of the Holy #Trinity: A Profound Reflection on Divine Mystery

Beloved in Christ, greetings in the name of the Holy Trinity! Let us immerse ourselves in the sacred teachings surrounding the Feast of the Holy Trinity, celebrated on Tir 7. This solemn occasion not only commemorates divine intervention but also offers a profound lesson in humility, faith, and the unity of the Godhead.

The Miracle in Babylon: A Lesson in Obedience

The Feast of the Holy Trinity recalls the miraculous events in Sennaor (Babylon), as narrated in Genesis 11:1-9. After the flood, Noah’s descendants multiplied and settled in the wide plains of Babylon. Under the leadership of Nimrod, the people undertook the construction of a great tower. In their arrogance, they aimed to pierce the heavens and defy the divine will, proclaiming, “Let us stab them and keep death away.”

This act of rebellion provoked divine intervention. The Holy Trinity, in mercy and justice, disrupted their work, confounding their language and scattering them across the earth. Their unfinished tower stood as a testament to the consequences of human pride and disobedience.

The Significance of the Trinity in This Event

The Trinity’s intervention in Babylon underscores several key lessons:

Divine Authority: All power resides with God, and any endeavor undertaken in arrogance or defiance of divine will is doomed to failure.
The Call to Repentance: Humanity is reminded to live in humility and steadfast faith, acknowledging the authority of the Trinity and seeking to align our will with God’s.

The Necessity of Baptism: As believers, we are called to baptize our children in the name of the Trinity, wash ourselves with repentance, and remain steadfast in conduct. The Apostle Paul reminds us, “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God in which you are sealed” (Ephesians 4:3).

Theological Reflections on the Holy Trinity

The concept of the Trinity is both profound and mysterious. Derived from the Ge’ez root meaning "thirty," the term "Trinity" signifies a unity within diversity. This mystery can be understood as both one and three:

Unity in Character, Existence, and Will: God is one in essence and purpose.
Trinity in Name, Person, and Action: God is revealed as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Scriptural Testimonies to the Trinity

The Bible provides numerous insights into the mystery of the Trinity:

- Creation: “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness” (Genesis 1:26). Here, the singularity of “God” and the plurality of “us” reflect the unity and distinction within the Trinity.

- Fall of Man: “Behold, the man has become like one of us” (Genesis 3:22). This statement highlights the collaborative nature of the Trinity.

- Abraham’s Encounter: In Genesis 18, Abraham encountered three visitors under the oaks of Mamre. Though three in appearance, they represented the unified presence of God.
Isaiah’s Vision: The seraphim cry, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts” (Isaiah 6:3), affirming the triune holiness of God.

- The Baptism of Christ: At the Jordan River, the voice of the Father, the presence of the Son, and the descent of the Holy Spirit revealed the Trinity in action (Matthew 3:16).

- The Transfiguration: On Mount Tabor, the glory of the Trinity was manifest in the radiance of Christ (Matthew 17).

Analogies to the Trinity

To aid our understanding, analogies are drawn from creation:

- The Sun: Comprising a circle, light, and heat, it remains one entity.

- Fire: Consisting of flame, brightness, and warmth, it is singular in essence.
Similarly, the Trinity, though distinct in persons, is one in essence and will. St. Paul writes, “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:14).

The Role of the Trinity in Worship

The mystery of the Trinity permeates all aspects of Orthodox faith and practice:

text:
Fasting is not merely a ritual; it is one of the seven decrees ordained by the Holy Church. It serves as the nourishment of the soul, elevating us toward God, diminishing the dominance of the flesh, and opening the gates of grace. The Fast of Gehad holds a unique place among these practices, intricately tied to the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

---

The term Gehad is a rich tapestry of meaning, signifying "change," "substitution," or "revelation", "revealed". We fast the eve of the nativity and the eve of Epiphany in rememberance of his revelation to us which takes two forms:
): The moment when the eternal God, unbounded and omnipotent, took on human form—a short stature, a narrow chest, and a humble presence—to dwell among us in the flesh.

At the Jordan River, Jesus, who had lived among humanity for 30 years without recognition as the Messiah, was revealed when the heavens opened, the Holy Spirit descended as a dove, and the voice of the Father declared,

These events are not merely historical but deeply theological, revealing the mystery of God becoming man and the salvation that flows through His revealed presence.

---
The Gehad fast is intricately linked to the timing of the feast days of Christ's birth and baptism. Here is the structure and significance of this holy observance:

During these days, believers partake in celebratory meals reflective of the Pentecost feast, breaking the fast with joy in the morning.

---
The Fetha Negest or the law of the Kings articulates the purpose of fasting as follows:
: Fasting allows a person to confront and repent for their sins, aligning themselves with God's grace.
: It is an act of love and submission to the Creator who established this holy ordinance.
: By denying physical hunger, the soul ascends, free to commune with God.

: Through fasting, one grows in humility and is strengthened to follow the prophets' call.

Fasting, therefore, is not a mere ritual but a transformative act that connects the believer with God, disciplines the soul, and paves the way for enlightenment.

👉🏾👉🏾👉🏾 The Fast of #Gehad: A Sacred and Transformative Practice

Beloved brethren who walk in the light of the Orthodox teachings, may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Let us delve into the profound depths of the Fast of Gehad, a spiritual treasure of our Holy Church that illuminates the path toward divine union and sanctification.

---
Fasting: A Commandment of the Holy Church

Fasting is not merely a ritual; it is one of the seven decrees ordained by the Holy Church. It serves as the nourishment of the soul, elevating us toward God, diminishing the dominance of the flesh, and opening the gates of grace. The Fast of Gehad holds a unique place among these practices, intricately tied to the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

---
The Meaning of "Gehad"

The term Gehad is a rich tapestry of meaning, signifying "change," "substitution," or "revelation", "revealed". We fast the eve of the nativity and the eve of Epiphany in rememberance of his revelation to us which takes two forms: 

1. Revelation through Nativity (Incarnation): The moment when the eternal God, unbounded and omnipotent, took on human form—a short stature, a narrow chest, and a humble presence—to dwell among us in the flesh.

2. Revelation through Baptism: At the Jordan River, Jesus, who had lived among humanity for 30 years without recognition as the Messiah, was revealed when the heavens opened, the Holy Spirit descended as a dove, and the voice of the Father declared, "This is my beloved Son; listen to Him."

---
The Dual Nature of Enlightenment

The Fast of Gehad aligns with two sacred moments in the life of Christ:

1. His Birth: The incarnation, where the divine Word became flesh.

2. His Baptism: The manifestation of His divine identity and mission, marking the beginning of His public ministry.

These events are not merely historical but deeply theological, revealing the mystery of God becoming man and the salvation that flows through His revealed presence.

---
Observance of the Gehad Fast

The Gehad fast is intricately linked to the timing of the feast days of Christ's birth and baptism. Here is the structure and significance of this holy observance:

1. When the Feast Falls on Wednesday or Friday:

These are traditional fasting days in the Church. On such occasions, the faithful fast on the preceding Tuesday and Thursday to maintain the sanctity of these feast days while honoring the fasting tradition.

During these days, believers partake in celebratory meals reflective of the Pentecost feast, breaking the fast with joy in the morning.

2. When the Feast Falls on Sunday:

Saturday evening is marked by a complete abstinence from food, preparing the soul for the Sunday celebration.

3. When the Feast Falls on Monday:

Saturday and Sunday both become days of preparation and abstinence, though the fasting does not follow the usual grain-and-water regimen of other fasting days. 

---
The Spiritual Essence of Fasting

The Fetha Negest or the law of the Kings articulates the purpose of fasting as follows:

Atonement for Wrongdoing: Fasting allows a person to confront and repent for their sins, aligning themselves with God's grace.

Obedience to Divine Law: It is an act of love and submission to the Creator who established this holy ordinance.

Subduing the Flesh: By denying physical hunger, the soul ascends, free to commune with God.

Enhancing the Soul's Value: Through fasting, one grows in humility and is strengthened to follow the prophets' call.

Fasting, therefore, is not a mere ritual but a transformative act that connects the believer with God, disciplines the soul, and paves the way for enlightenment.

text:

By observing this fast, we are reminded of the great mystery of our faith: God, the infinite and eternal, chose to dwell among us as man, and through His baptism, He revealed Himself as the medicine of mankind, fulfilling the prophecies of old.

---

The Gehad Fast is more than abstention from food; it is an ascent of the soul, a participation in the divine mysteries, and a celebration of the revelation of Christ. Let us approach this sacred practice with reverence, allowing it to transform us into vessels of grace. May we fast not merely with our mouths but with our hearts, embracing the holiness it imparts, and may our journey through this fast lead us ever closer to the One who loved us and gave Himself for us.

In the spirit of repentance and renewal, let us echo the words of the Father:

text.text: "This is my beloved Son; listen to Him."

text: May our fasting lead us to hear, obey, and glorify Him forever. Amen.

👉🏾👉🏾👉🏾 A Reflection on the Profound Mystery of #Epiphany and #Baptism

"Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John." (Matthew 3:13)

Beloved in Christ, let us gather our hearts to reflect on the majestic feast of the baptism of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, celebrated on Tir 10 and 11th in the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition. This divine mystery unfolds profound lessons on humility, grace, and redemption. It reveals the unity of the Holy Trinity, the purpose of Christ's coming, and the sacred role of baptism in the spiritual journey of believers.

The Meaning and Types of Baptism

The term baptism originates from the Greek word "baptizo," meaning immersion. It signifies purification, renewal, and spiritual rebirth. The Scriptures and the traditions of the Church present eight types of baptism, five symbolic and three for believers:

Symbolic Baptisms:

Noah's Flood: The waters that cleansed the earth foreshadowed baptism’s power to purify and renew.

The Cloud and the Red Sea: Moses and the Israelites passing through these waters prefigured baptism (1 Corinthians 10:2).

Crossing the Jordan: When the priests carried the Ark across the Jordan, it symbolized the spiritual crossing into divine grace.

Jewish Ritual Cleansings: These ceremonial washings pointed toward the deeper cleansing baptism would bring.

John’s Baptism of Repentance: A call to repentance and preparation for the coming Kingdom of God.

Believers' Baptisms:

Christ’s Baptism: A unique and transformative event, revealing Christ's humility and divine mission.

The Baptism of Martyrdom: Those who bear witness to Christ with their lives partake in a baptism of ultimate sacrifice.

Tears of Repentance: A continual purification through heartfelt contrition and renewal.

The Celebration of Baptism in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tradition

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church celebrates baptism with deep reverence and ritual significance. This feast, known as Këtëra, involves surrounding, filling, and sanctifying water in preparation for the baptismal blessing. The faithful accompany the Ark of the Covenant in processions to a baptismal site, where the Gospel is proclaimed, gifts are offered, and blessings are shared. This tradition, which began publicly during the reign of Emperor Zerayakob in the 15th century, commemorates both the historical and spiritual roots of Christ's baptism.

The Divine Encounter at the Jordan

The Lord’s baptism at the hands of Saint John the Baptist was an act of divine humility. Though Christ is pure and without sin, He submitted to baptism to fulfill righteousness and inaugurate His public ministry. The relationship between John and Jesus is marked by profound spiritual mysteries:

John was conceived and born six months before Jesus, as foretold by the angelic announcements.
Even in the womb, John leapt with joy at the presence of Christ in the Virgin Mary’s womb, recognizing Him as the divine Savior (Luke 1:43-45).

John’s mission was to prepare the way, calling people to repentance and baptizing them in anticipation of the Messiah’s coming.

When Jesus approached John to be baptized, John’s humility and awe were evident. He declared, "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1:29). Recognizing Christ’s divine nature, he questioned, "I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?" (Matthew 3:14).

The Divine Manifestation: Unity and Trinity

At the moment of Jesus’ baptism, the heavens opened, and the Holy Trinity was revealed:

God the Father declared, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17).

God the Son stood humbly in the waters of the Jordan.

The Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove, affirming Christ’s mission.

This moment marked the beginning of Christ’s public ministry, a testament to His obedience to the divine will and His role as the Redeemer of humanity.

The Humility of Christ and the Exaltation of Baptism 

Christ’s submission to baptism by John exemplifies ultimate humility:

text.text:
The Creator was baptized by His creation.

The King of Kings bowed before a servant.

The Light of the World was immersed in earthly waters.

text: John, overwhelmed by this act, expressed his unworthiness with profound imagery. He questioned how he, a mortal and sinner, could touch the pure and divine body of his Creator. Yet, Christ reassured him, declaring that it was necessary to fulfill all righteousness.

text.text: The Significance of Baptism for Believers

text: Through His baptism, Christ sanctified the waters and instituted the sacrament as a means of spiritual rebirth. Baptism washes away the stain of sin, restores the lost glory of humanity, and marks the believer’s entry into the life of the Church. It is a mystery of profound grace, uniting the faithful with Christ in His death and resurrection.
: Christ’s baptism teaches us the virtue of humility, as the sinless Savior submitted to the will of the Father.
: Both John and Christ exemplified obedience to God’s divine plan.
The baptism revealed the harmonious unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
: The act symbolized the washing away of sin and the restoration of humanity’s divine image.

Beloved in Christ, let us approach the feast of Epiphany with reverence and gratitude. As we reflect on the mystery of Christ’s baptism, may we strive to emulate His humility, embrace His grace, and renew our commitment to live as children of God. Through the waters of baptism, we are not merely cleansed but are made partakers of divine glory, restored to the fullness of life in Christ. May this sacred celebration remind us of the unfathomable love and mercy of our Savior, who humbled Himself to raise us to eternal life. Amen.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us. Amen.

text.text: A Lesson on the Feast of Saint
The Life and Legacy of Saint George, the Great Martyr

text:
Beloved followers of the faith, may the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ fill your hearts and illuminate your understanding as we reflect on the profound life and witness of Saint George, a great martyr and defender of the Christian faith. The account of his life is not merely a narrative of suffering but a triumphant testament to the power of strong faith, divine intervention, and the ultimate victory of God’s truth over the forces of darkness. Let us delve deeply into this sacred story and draw lessons that will strengthen our souls.

---

text.text: 1. The Early Life of Saint George

text: Saint George was born to noble parents. His father, Anastasius, was a prince from Cappadocia, and his mother, Theobsta, was a devout Palestinian woman. Tragedy struck early in his life as his father passed away during his childhood. Despite this loss, Saint George's life was marked by divine providence and steadfast commitment to God. At the age of twenty, he presented himself to King Dodianus to fulfill his father’s royal appointment. However, his encounter with the king set him on a different and divine path.

Upon arriving at the court of King Dodianus, Saint George was grieved by the king’s idolatry and the forced worship of false gods. In response to this corruption, Saint George made a radical decision: he renounced his earthly wealth, distributed his possessions to the poor, freed his slaves, and openly confessed his faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. His boldness in proclaiming the truth of the Gospel enraged the king, initiating a series of trials and sufferings that would test his faith and reveal God’s glory.

---

text.text: 3. The Trials and Triumphs of Saint George

text: King Dodianus sought to sway Saint George with promises of power, wealth, and honor, but the saint refused to abandon his Lord. When bribes failed, the king resorted to unimaginable tortures:
: Saint George was subjected to excruciating physical torment, yet God miraculously healed his wounds, giving him strength to endure.
: On multiple occasions, the king attempted to execute him, but our Lord raised him from death, proving His power and reaffirming Saint George’s divine mission.

text.text: Miracles in the Midst of Suffering

text:
: Among the many miracles, Saint George survived drinking a cup of poison prepared by the magician Athanasius, who subsequently believed in Christ and became a martyr alongside thirty thousand others.

---
Saint George’s unwavering faith and the power of God manifested through him caused many to believe. Notable events include:
: When the kings mockingly asked Saint George to make their wooden chairs bloom, he prayed, and they miraculously blossomed, leading countless people to believe in Christ.
: In a dramatic display of divine power, Saint George prayed and raised men and women from the dead, leading to their baptism and conversion.

text.text: The Tree of the Widow’s Pillar:

text:
A poor widow, who begged Saint George for mercy, witnessed a miraculous transformation of her house pillar into a flourishing tree. Through his intercession, her blind, deaf, and lame son was healed, further solidifying the faith of many.

---

The saint’s encounters with idolatrous kings revealed the impotence of false gods. In one instance, the unclean spirit residing in an idol confessed its powerlessness before Saint George and was cast into the earth. This act not only exposed the futility of idol worship but also led to the destruction of the idols and the humiliation of the king and his people.

---

The queen of Alexandria, moved by the teachings and prayers of Saint George, believed in Christ. Her newfound faith enraged King Dodianus, who ordered her execution. She willingly accepted martyrdom, receiving the crown of life and joining the heavenly assembly of saints.

---

King Dodianus sought to sway Saint George with promises of power, wealth, and honor, but the saint refused to abandon his Lord. When bribes failed, the king resorted to unimaginable tortures:

Endurance of Pain: Saint George was subjected to excruciating physical torment, yet God miraculously healed his wounds, giving him strength to endure.

Death and Resurrection: On multiple occasions, the king attempted to execute him, but our Lord raised him from death, proving His power and reaffirming Saint George’s divine mission.

Miracles in the Midst of Suffering: Among the many miracles, Saint George survived drinking a cup of poison prepared by the magician Athanasius, who subsequently believed in Christ and became a martyr alongside thirty thousand others.

---

Saint George’s unwavering faith and the power of God manifested through him caused many to believe. Notable events include:

The Blossoming of Chairs: When the kings mockingly asked Saint George to make their wooden chairs bloom, he prayed, and they miraculously blossomed, leading countless people to believe in Christ.

The Tree of the Widow’s Pillar: A poor widow, who begged Saint George for mercy, witnessed a miraculous transformation of her house pillar into a flourishing tree. Through his intercession, her blind, deaf, and lame son was healed, further solidifying the faith of many.

---

text:
Despite the many miracles, King Dodianus and his council, unable to subdue the saint’s spirit, condemned him to death by beheading. Before his execution, our Lord Jesus Christ appeared to Saint George, promising that all who commemorate his name and call upon Christ in his memory would be delivered from their troubles. This divine assurance filled Saint George with joy as he offered his life for his Savior. His body was taken to Lydda, where a church was built in his honor, and countless miracles continued to occur through his intercession.

---

The life of Saint George offers timeless lessons for every believer:

1.

: Saint George’s refusal to compromise his faith, even in the face of death, reminds us to hold steadfastly to Christ.

2.

: By giving away his earthly possessions, he teaches us to value eternal treasures over worldly wealth.

3.

: His miracles demonstrate that God’s power is unmatched and that He strengthens His faithful servants in their trials.

4.

: Saint George’s suffering became a testimony that led many to salvation.

5.

: The defeat of idols and the conversion of multitudes testify to the ultimate victory of God’s truth.

---

As Christ promised Saint George, those who commemorate him in faith will find deliverance from their afflictions. This assurance calls us to honor the memory of this great martyr, seek his intercession, and trust in the boundless mercy of our Lord.

---

On this sacred day of Tir 18 we celebrate not only the life of Saint George but also the triumph of God’s grace through him. His story calls us to greater faith, deeper devotion, and a commitment to the truth of the Gospel. May his intercessions protect us from all harm, and may we, like him, boldly proclaim Christ’s glory to the ends of the earth.

In the words of our Lord Jesus Christ to Saint George: “I will erase all the sins of everyone who does your remembrance on earth, and whoever calls on me in your name in trouble... I will quickly deliver them.”

May the blessings of Saint George be upon us all!

7. The Martyrdom of Saint George

Despite the many miracles, King Dodianus and his council, unable to subdue the saint’s spirit, condemned him to death by beheading. Before his execution, our Lord Jesus Christ appeared to Saint George, promising that all who commemorate his name and call upon Christ in his memory would be delivered from their troubles. This divine assurance filled Saint George with joy as he offered his life for his Savior. His body was taken to Lydda, where a church was built in his honor, and countless miracles continued to occur through his intercession.

---
8. Lessons from Saint George’s Life

The life of Saint George offers timeless lessons for every believer:

1. Faith Above All: Saint George’s refusal to compromise his faith, even in the face of death, reminds us to hold steadfastly to Christ.

2. Generosity and Sacrifice: By giving away his earthly possessions, he teaches us to value eternal treasures over worldly wealth.

3. Divine Power: His miracles demonstrate that God’s power is unmatched and that He strengthens His faithful servants in their trials.

4. Witness through Suffering: Saint George’s suffering became a testimony that led many to salvation.

As Christ promised Saint George, those who commemorate him in faith will find deliverance from their afflictions. This assurance calls us to honor the memory of this great martyr, seek his intercession, and trust in the boundless mercy of our Lord.
