text.text:
: A Holy Meditation on the Unity of the True Faith
part 1

text: Brethren beloved in the Lord, I write not with idle words but with the incense of truth drawn from the bosom of Holy Scripture and the unbroken tradition of the Apostles, to illuminate your minds concerning faith and religion, and to call your hearts to unity in the Spirit, as once the prophets proclaimed and the apostles upheld.

What, then, is faith? It is not the conclusion of a philosopher nor the observation of the scientist, but—as the apostle Paul hath written—“the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). Faith is the eye of the soul, the organ by which we perceive what lies beyond the veil of the visible world. The visible is temporal, but the invisible is eternal.

Behold the kingdom of heaven, which no eye hath seen and no ear hath heard, yet we press toward it with hope. What confirms this hope? Faith alone. Faith is not subject to the inquiry of microscopes nor does it rest upon the theories of men. It transcends. It rests in absolute truth, not relative or fluctuating like the truth sought by science. Science alters with age, but faith stands unmoved.

Faith, while inward and spiritual, does not remain idle or formless. Religion is the outward expression, the sacred form that binds faith with worship. Just as the soul is clothed in the body, faith is clothed in religion. Religion is that holy order by which we believe rightly in God and worship Him as He has ordained. This includes what we believe of Him, how we adore Him, and how we perform the sacred rites in His name.

Therefore, religion is the manifestation of faith—the flower which springs from the root of belief, and it is not fashioned by human opinion, but revealed and preserved by divine ordinance.

text.text: One Faith, One Lord, One Baptism

text:
Hearken to the voice of the Apostle Paul: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism.” (Ephesians 4:5). Not many lords, not divided faiths, not manifold baptisms, but one—a sacred unity that befits the majesty of the one God. The purpose of this divine teaching is to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, that schisms and heresies may not defile the holy body of Christ.

This oneness has many aspects, each like a jewel reflecting the light of the one True Faith:

The God of Adam is the God of Abraham, and the God of Abraham is the God of Moses, of David, of Peter, and of us all. He changeth not. His essence is eternal, His character unaltered. To believe in Him as Peter did, and to worship Him as Peter worshipped, is to be one in faith with the Apostles.

This unbroken belief links us across time, generation to generation. When our children worship the Lord as the prophets and apostles did, then is one religion preserved. Christianity is not a new religion, but the fulfillment and continuation of the divine covenant from the beginning.

Baptism is no empty ritual, but the sacred gate through which one enters into the life of Christ. By it, we are born of water and the Spirit, and joined to the family of God. The baptism we receive is not repeated, for there is but one spiritual birth—just as there is one natural birth.

Through baptism, we are made sons and daughters of God, co-heirs with Christ, partakers in His death and resurrection. This sonship is not partial or divided; it is one grace, one inheritance. Therefore, the true religion is that which guards this one baptism and teaches rightly its meaning and power.

text: If our God is one and our baptism one, then our hope is one: the kingdom of heaven. Eternal life is not promised differently to Jew and Gentile, nor to one people over another. Peter preached it to the circumcised, and Paul to the Gentiles, but the substance of their message was the same. Their hope was one, and their faith was one.Thus, we must not divide what God has joined. We must not seek other paths, for salvation lies in the one true hope held forth by the apostolic Church.

The Church is not a collection of independent factions, but one mystical body, with Christ as the Head and all believers as members. Paul, inspired by the Spirit, likens us to a body with many members—hands, feet, eyes—yet all forming a single organism.

We are branches of the one Vine, which is Christ (John 15:5). Though we differ in gifts, in functions, and even in language, we are united in essence. To divide into separate religions is to sever the body, and to do violence to the unity which Christ Himself ordained.

Finally, the Church is led not by many spirits, but by One—the Holy Spirit, who descended at Pentecost (Acts 2:1), and who continues to guide the Church through the Holy Synod and the apostolic succession.

As Paul wrote, “We have all been given one Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:27). If we follow different spirits, we cannot remain in the one Church. If we listen to conflicting voices, we fall into confusion. But where the Holy Spirit speaks, there is harmony, truth, and peace.

Therefore, we confess with boldness and humility: There is only one true religion, led by one Holy Spirit, preaching one hope, grounded in one baptism, centered on one Lord, and rooted in the faith once delivered to the saints.

Let us not be deceived by the multitude of opinions that blow like the winds. Let us stand firm upon the rock of apostolic truth. Let us hand down to our children not novelty, but the ancient faith, and let us worship with the saints as they worshipped: in spirit and in truth, in unity and in holiness.

For what greater inheritance can we pass down, than to say: “I have kept the faith,” the one faith that saves, the one religion that sanctifies, and the one Spirit that seals us for the day of redemption?

text.text:
: A Holy Meditation on the Unity of the True Faith

Part 2

text: Brethren beloved of God, faithful adherents to the Orthodox tradition preserved and proclaimed through the Yohannes Pensa teachings, grace and peace be unto you from God our Father and from our Lord Jesus Christ. Today, let us give ear to a teaching most solemn and true—concerning faith, and concerning religion. Let us not approach this lightly, but with reverence and trembling, as those who seek to understand the mysteries of divine revelation.

text.text: One Religion Given Once for All

text:
Let it be known, O faithful, that religion is one, and it is given once for all. It is not scattered like the seeds of the wind nor repeated like the cycles of the moon. It is not a garment that must be tailored anew for each generation, but a robe woven without seam, handed down from the Apostles to the saints of every age.

Hear now the words of Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, who testifies:

“Beloved, while I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I felt compelled to write to you, urging you to contend earnestly for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints.” (Jude 1:3)

This faith, brethren, was not delivered to be updated or modified. It is not like the inventions of men that improve with time. No! It was founded on the rock, as our Lord declared to Peter:

“You are Peter, and on this rock I will build My Church” (Matthew 16:18).

Religion, then, is not a thing maintained by human tradition, nor can it be enriched by modern thought. It is divinely bestowed, pure and eternal. It is the life of the Church, flowing from the pierced side of Christ, and given without shadow of turning. It is unchanging, because its foundation is the unchangeable One.

text.text: One Religion Means Imitating One Christ

text: But what does this true religion demand of us? It demands imitation—not of many, but of One. It is not a system of ideas, but the life of Christ made manifest in His people. For we have been united to Him not only in word but in very being.

“Do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death? … If we have been united with Him in a death like His, we shall certainly also be united with Him in a resurrection like His.” (Romans 6:3-5)


And again, the Lord commands:

“Learn from Me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29).


What greater religion is there than this—to be united to the death of Christ, that we might also live His resurrection? Religion, therefore, is not ritual alone, nor mere belief, but the imitation of Christ, who is our Lord, our Shepherd, and our Teacher (Matthew 23:8).

Even Paul, the Apostle to the nations, declared:

“Imitate me, as I also imitate Christ.” (1 Corinthians 11:1)


And Peter exhorts us in the words of the Lord:

“Be holy, for I am holy.” (1 Peter 1:16)


Thus, if to live by faith means to imitate the One Christ, then faith is one and religion is one, for they are the reflection of the One whom we follow.

Now some, in their cleverness, attempt to separate the inseparable. They say: “Is it not true that the Amharic Bible says ‘one religion’, but other tongues say ‘one faith’? Then perhaps we may have many religions, all springing from one faith.”

Let us answer not with the words of speculation, but with the truth delivered to the saints. For what is faith, if not the substance of religion? What is religion, if not the outward expression of faith? If we are one in faith, we must be one also in religion—in our belief, in our worship, in our baptism, in our hope, and in our life.

text:
“There is one body and one Spirit just as you were called to one hope when you were called—one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.” (Ephesians 4:4–6)

Therefore, to believe what Saint Peter believed, to worship as he worshipped, and to live as he lived that is the mark of the one true religion. Any deviation from this is not a new expression of the same faith, but a departure from the apostolic way.

To say “many religions, one faith” is to speak as one who divides Christ. For Christ is not divided. His Body, the Church, is not a body with many heads or many minds, but one holy  and apostolic. Thus, the manifestation of one faith is one religion, and different religions—rooted in different beliefs and different practices—cannot be the offspring of the same faith.

Yet it was revealed even in the time of the holy Apostles that there would arise other faiths, other gospels, other spirits. But these are not of God.

 “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God. For many false prophets have gone out into the world.” (1 John 4:1)

Thus, the Church stands as a lighthouse in the storm, holding forth the faith that was once delivered. Let not the winds of modern confusion, nor the voices of false unity, lead us astray. Hold fast to the one religion, the one faith, and the one Lord.

May the God of truth preserve you in steadfastness. May you never forsake the one religion, nor wander from the one faith. Do not look to the left or to the right, but let your eyes be fixed upon Jesus Christ, the author and perfecter of our faith.

text:
Brethren beloved in Christ, greetings in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has called us from darkness into the marvelous light of His truth. Let us incline our hearts, not as those who hear and forget, but as those who plant the seed of the Word deeply into the soil of our soul, that it may bring forth the fruit of righteousness. Today, we consider the awe-filled and life-bestowing words of our Savior:

 "I am the Way, and the Truth, and the Life." John 14:6


In these words lies the whole gospel condensed, the entire mystery of the Incarnation expressed, and the map of salvation drawn out before our eyes. Let us walk reverently through the depth of this holy saying, not skimming its surface but descending into its depths as into a sacred wellspring.

text.text: 1. The Way of Salvation is Christ Himself

text:
When our Lord declared, “I am the Way,” He did not mean merely that He shows the way or teaches the way, but that He Himself is the very path by which we approach the Father. Just as no one can reach the summit of a mountain without walking the path that leads there, so no one can come to God without Christ. There is no alternate road, no secret shortcut; all other paths, though they may seem pleasant and broad, are false and lead only to destruction.

Indeed, there exists a false path that masquerades as truth, a broad road that leads to perdition. But Christ is the true and narrow way, and only those who walk it daily through suffering, through trial, through temptation will reach the kingdom of heaven.

He who follows this Way must be prepared, as our Lord was, to be born without honor, to be exiled for truth’s sake, to be tempted, scorned, and falsely accused. Did they not call Him a demon? Did they not scourge Him and crucify Him as a criminal? And shall we, who bear His name, expect a smoother road?

text.text: 2. The Truth That Guides the Soul

text:
Our Lord continues, “I am the Truth.” He is not merely a bearer of truth or a speaker of wise sayings; He is Truth itself—uncreated, eternal, incorruptible. To follow Christ is not only to walk a path, but to live in truth. Those who walk in lies, in deceit, in self-justification or error, are not walking with Him. The devil tempts us with many falsehoods, enticing us with the appearance of wisdom, as he tempted our Lord in the wilderness. But as Christ repelled every lie with the word of truth, so must we be armed with that same sword.

To live in Christ is to dwell in reality. It is to confess the truth about God, about ourselves, and about the world. The truth is this: that salvation is not ease, but struggle; not riches, but sacrifice; not praise, but persecution. If you are reviled for Christ’s sake, do not be surprised. Rather, rejoice. For it is written: 

“Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” (Matt. 5:10)

“I am the Life.” Just as He is the Way by which we journey, and the Truth which illuminates the path, so also is He the very Life we receive when we walk that road in truth. Apart from Christ, man is dead—even if he lives in the body. The death of Adam brought spiritual death into the world, but Christ, by His death, conquered death.

He has taken our suffering, that we might find rest. He has died our death, that we might live His life. What glory is this, that the Immortal One would embrace mortality, that we the unworthy might be made partakers of divine life!

Do not fear death in the body, dear faithful. If you suffer for Christ, you are blessed. If you lose your possessions, your homeland, even your flesh, but keep your faith, you have lost nothing. For as the Apostle Paul says:

“We carry about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our body.” (2 Cor. 4:10)

This is not mere philosophy, but the essence of our hope: we die daily with Christ, so that we may also rise with Him in glory.

text.text: 4. The Path of Purity and Holiness

text:
Isaiah calls this the “pure path,” the “holy way.” It is not for the profane or careless. It is for the righteous, for those who follow Christ with a pure heart, guided not by ambition or pride, but by humility, love, and perseverance.

Let no one say, “This way is too narrow.” Did not the Lord Himself say:

 “Narrow is the gate and difficult is the way that leads to life, and there are few who find it”? (Matt. 7:14)


Do not expect the world to applaud your journey. They begged our Lord to leave their country; they accused Him, insulted Him, condemned Him. If they did this to the Master, will they treat the servant better?

Yet, brethren, let us not be shaken. For just as Christ was raised from the dead and ascended in glory, so too shall we who walk in His steps. The destination is sure: eternal life, eternal joy, eternal communion with God.

text.text: 5. The Example of the Wise Serpent and the Innocent Dove

text:
Our Lord, in His divine wisdom, counseled us:

“Be wise as serpents and harmless as doves.” (Matt. 10:16)


The serpent, to preserve its head, exposes its body to danger. In the same way, let us be willing to sacrifice all temporal things—wealth, health, even life itself—for the sake of preserving the treasure of our faith. This is not foolishness, but the highest wisdom. For what is a man profited if he gains the whole world and loses his soul?

If we give all, even our very bodies, for Christ, He will restore it all to us in glory. For the Lord is no debtor. He rewards those who lose for His sake with riches eternal, incorruptible, and divine.

text.text: Conclusion: Let Us Walk Without Doubt

text:
Beloved, let us walk this path without doubt. It is a path well-trodden by the prophets, apostles, martyrs, and saints. It is the path of Christ, who went before us, blazing the trail through suffering into victory. Let us not falter when we suffer for His name. Let us not grow weary when the journey is long. For the journey is Christ, the truth is Christ, and the reward is Christ.

Let all glory, dominion, and power be to our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the image of the invisible God, the life of the world, and the path of salvation. May He guide us by His Spirit along this holy way, until we enter into the mansions He has prepared in the house of His Father.


“May our Lord Jesus Christ… lead us on the path of righteousness so that we may enter into the many mansions in His Father’s house in His goodness and love for mankind.”

Isaiah calls this the “pure path,” the “holy way.” It is not for the profane or careless. It is for the righteous, for those who follow Christ with a pure heart, guided not by ambition or pride, but by humility, love, and perseverance.

messages.full_text:
👉🏾👉🏾👉🏾 The Use of #Kebero in Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church Worship

✍️ The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, a revered ancient, apostolic, catholic, national, and global church, stands as one of the world's oldest and foremost faith traditions. Our teachings affirm that drums (specifically the kebero) were not introduced into Christian worship in the 16th century. Instead, their use in spiritual service is deeply rooted in the Old Testament era, predating Christianity, and has continued seamlessly into the New Testament period and remains an integral part of our worship to this day.

✍️ Our Church's rich history, sacred scriptures, historical accounts, and ancient artifacts all bear witness to its observance of the Old Testament system even before the advent of Christianity. This historical continuity is one of the reasons Ethiopia is reverently referred to as a "land of antiquity."

Enduring Legacy and Official Recognition

✍️ The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church has actively worked to legally register its ancient heritage, which has been in continuous use for over a millennium. This includes holy books, sacred artifacts, melodies, and musical instruments used for hymns, along with other properties essential for its spiritual services. We are pleased to share that the Ethiopian Intellectual Property Authority (EIPA) has recognized and affirmed the Church's rightful ownership of these intellectual properties.

✍️ Specifically, the EIPA has officially registered the kebero (drum), tsenatsel (sistrum), mekuamiya (prayer staff), and over ten sacred books as the intellectual property of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, effective April 11, 2024 (Miazia 3, 2017 Ethiopian Calendar). This governmental recognition further solidifies the long-standing and inherent place of these instruments in our tradition.

The Kebero's Deep Scriptural and Liturgical Roots

✍️ The kebero has served as an instrument for spiritual worship since the time of the Old Testament and continues its use in the New Testament. This is strongly supported by the Holy Scriptures, particularly in the Psalms:

👉 Old Testament Witness: The kebero is a sacred instrument of praise to God in both the Old and New Testaments. A powerful example is found when the Israelites were delivered from Egyptian bondage. After God parted the Red Sea, the prophetess Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, took a drum in her hand to lead the people in praise and song to the Lord. As recorded in Exodus 15:20 (NKJV): "Then Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took the timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances."

👉 King David's Directives: David, the beloved King and Psalmist, repeatedly instructs believers to praise God with the kebero (timbrel):

      -> Psalm 149:3 (NKJV): "Let them praise His name with the dance; Let them sing praises to Him with the timbrel and harp."

     -> Psalm 150:4 (NKJV): "Praise Him with the timbrel and dance; Praise Him with stringed instruments and flutes!"

👉 Liturgical Practice: Within the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, the kebero is a fundamental instrument used during Mahlet (the nocturnal praise service) and Zemare (hymns). Along with the tsenatsel and mekuamiya, these are the primary sacred instruments recorded in the Bible and sanctioned by God for hymns and praise. During the Mahlet service, these instruments accompany singing, dancing (shibsheba), ululation (ellelta), and clapping. It's important to note that while other instruments like the masenko, begena, trumpet, krar, washint, enzira, and enbilta are used by congregants for general praise, they are not typically employed during the formal Mahlet service. Furthermore, in our sacred Qidase (Anaphora) service, before the reading of the Gospel, the tradition states, "Take up a psalm, and give the drum."

(Continues) 👇🏾

Profound Theological Symbolism of the Kebero

✍️ Our revered Church fathers have passed down through both written and oral tradition the deep mysteries and symbolism of the kebero. It is far more than a musical instrument; it is a profound theological symbol:

👉 Derivation and Meaning: The word "kebero" itself originates from the Ge'ez word "keberew," meaning "to beat," "to strike," "to hammer," "to tap," or "to hit."

👉 A Symbol of Christ: Most significantly, the kebero is a direct symbol of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

♦️ Striking the Drum: When the kebero is struck from side to side, it vividly reminds us of our Lord being slapped and beaten by the Jews during His Passion. Matthew 26:67-68 (NKJV) recounts: "Then they spit in His face and beat Him; and others struck Him with the palms of their hands, saying, 'Prophesy to us, Christ! Who is the one who struck You?'"

♦️ The Wide Mouth: The wide opening of the kebero symbolizes the divine nature of our Lord. It reminds us of His inherent Godhead, His boundless and infinite authority as God, omnipotent and omnipresent. When we behold its wide expanse, we contemplate Jesus Christ, who, though manifest in a confined stature and narrow chest, is in essence, in His divine nature and existence, equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit, holding and ruling all things.

♦️ The Narrow Mouth: Conversely, the narrow opening of the kebero symbolizes Christ's humanity (Tsebe'at). This narrow opening, which produces sound when beaten, represents God the Son's manifestation in a confined human form, in a short stature and narrow chest. Though He governs all creation, and His authority is without end and His divinity without decay, He united with flesh and was revealed. When we observe this narrow opening, we remember Him, who rules all, yet was confined to a short stature and narrow chest. This echoes John 1:1-14 (NKJV), which states: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God... And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth."

♦️ The Fabric Covering: The cloth that adorns the kebero symbolizes the garment, specifically the "scarlet robe," that the Jews placed upon our Lord on Good Friday to mock Him. Matthew 27:28 (NKJV) records: "Then they stripped Him and put a scarlet robe on Him."

♦️ The Manner of Playing: The kebero is not struck directly but is played by the chanters swaying it from left to right. This motion symbolizes the abuse and humiliation our Lord endured as He was taken from Annas to Caiaphas, and then from Caiaphas to Pilate. The drumming begins gently, then accelerates, symbolizing how the Jews initially mocked and beat our Lord slowly, but then hurried to beat Him intensely, even before Pilate could release Him or the Sabbath day arrived. When the kebero is placed on the ground during Mahlet, it prompts us to reflect on our Lord falling to the ground and suffering torment.

♦️ The Two Parts of the Kebero: When placing the kebero, the wide mouth should always be oriented upwards. Placing the smaller part upwards is considered incorrect.

      👉 The wide part again represents the divine nature of Christ, reminding us of His inherent Godhead and His omnipotence, whose authority has no bounds or limits.
      👉 The narrow part symbolizes His humanity (Tisebe’et), reminding us of our Lord's Incarnation, revealed in a confined human body, as echoed in John 1:14 (NKJV): "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us..."

♦️ Other Symbolic Elements: The intricate interwoven straps on the kebero symbolize the marks of scourging that appeared on our Lord's back. The strap used to carry the kebero symbolizes the rope with which the Jews dragged our Lord.

✍️ The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, a "sea of wisdom," teaches through all its rites and structures, from its roof to its foundation. It instructs both explicitly through spoken word and implicitly through its silent traditions.

(Continues) 👇🏾

text:
Beloved brethren in Christ, children of the Light and heirs of the Kingdom, incline your ears and hearts to this holy instruction. For today, we consider not the fleeting desires of men, but the eternal desire of the Almighty God—what He, the Creator of heaven and earth, seeks from us who are but dust and ashes. It is not gold nor silver He requires, not burnt offerings or incense alone, but something far greater, far holier, far more intimate: He wants your heart, your will, and your faith.

Do not mistake God’s desire for your heart as a poetic metaphor. No, it is the very core of the Gospel. God does not dwell in temples made by hands, but in the hearts of the humble and contrite. He who fashioned your heart desires to reign in it. But He does not force entry; He knocks, He waits. He desires love that is freely given, not extracted. Your heart, once surrendered, becomes a throne for the King of Glory.

And what of the will? Here too, many are mistaken. The will God seeks is not the will of brute strength or iron stubbornness. It is the will that says, “Lord, I want to come home. Help my weakness.” This will, even if faint, is precious in His sight. The moment you will to return, even feebly, God meets you on the road. As Saint Paul declares, “It is God who works in you both to will and to do His good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13). He does not merely observe from afar; He acts within, energizing both the desire and the deed in those who turn to Him.

But take heed, brethren! We must not fall into presumption, saying, “Since God will work, I need not struggle.” Far be it! Such thinking is death. Though grace empowers, it does not eliminate effort. Just as a farmer must till the land even while rain comes from heaven, so must we labor in repentance, prayer, and virtue, even while grace descends from above. Our cooperation with God is the proof of our sincerity, the seal of our covenant.

👉🏾👉🏾👉🏾What Does #God #Want from #Us?  

Beloved brethren in Christ, children of the Light and heirs of the Kingdom, incline your ears and hearts to this holy instruction. For today, we consider not the fleeting desires of men, but the eternal desire of the Almighty God—what He, the Creator of heaven and earth, seeks from us who are but dust and ashes. It is not gold nor silver He requires, not burnt offerings or incense alone, but something far greater, far holier, far more intimate: He wants your heart, your will, and your faith.

Do not mistake God’s desire for your heart as a poetic metaphor. No, it is the very core of the Gospel. God does not dwell in temples made by hands, but in the hearts of the humble and contrite. He who fashioned your heart desires to reign in it. But He does not force entry; He knocks, He waits. He desires love that is freely given, not extracted. Your heart, once surrendered, becomes a throne for the King of Glory.

And what of the will? Here too, many are mistaken. The will God seeks is not the will of brute strength or iron stubbornness. It is the will that says, “Lord, I want to come home. Help my weakness.” This will, even if faint, is precious in His sight. The moment you will to return, even feebly, God meets you on the road. As Saint Paul declares, “It is God who works in you both to will and to do His good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13). He does not merely observe from afar; He acts within, energizing both the desire and the deed in those who turn to Him.

But take heed, brethren! We must not fall into presumption, saying, “Since God will work, I need not struggle.” Far be it! Such thinking is death. Though grace empowers, it does not eliminate effort. Just as a farmer must till the land even while rain comes from heaven, so must we labor in repentance, prayer, and virtue, even while grace descends from above. Our cooperation with God is the proof of our sincerity, the seal of our covenant.

continues 👇🏾

text:
Let us then begin our movement 
toward reconciliation not with fanfare, but with prayer. Prayer is the breath of the soul, the ladder between earth and heaven. Prayer is the place where the weak find strength and the sinner finds the Father's embrace. Yet let our prayers not be mechanical or shallow, but full of tears, full of longing. As it is written, “Fasting is the mother of prayer, the sister of repentance, the source of tears, and the ancient foundation of all good deeds.”

Indeed, fasting and prayer must go together. Fasting humbles the flesh; prayer strengthens the spirit. Together, they till the soil of the heart, making it ready for the divine seed. For how can one say he desires God yet never speaks to Him? Or how can one hope to be sanctified, yet feeds constantly the appetites of the flesh? No, my beloved, if we truly desire God, we must cut away all that clings to the old man and embrace the means He has given for our renewal.

And with prayer, let us also guard our speech and our ears. As the wise Basil of Caesarea teaches, “Be slow and foolish to idle talk; but be wise, for salvation is given through the knowledge of the Holy Scriptures.” Do not be quick to speak but swift to listen, especially to the Word of God. As the Apostle James exhorts, “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath” (James 1:19). In silence and humility, the Lord speaks. In stillness, the Spirit descends.

So then, brethren, what does God want from us? Not the sacrifice of bulls, but the heart that trembles at His word. Not the will of pride, but the will that hungers for grace. Not lip service faith, but living faith that moves mountains and kneels in the dust. Let us begin this holy work today now not with fear, but with trust. For He who calls us is faithful, and His mercy has no measure.

text:
O beloved brethren in Christ, hear now with trembling hearts and minds alight with reverence, the mystery which the Lord revealed to His apostles and to us, concerning the Most Holy Virgin Mary and the Church built not by human hands, but by the hands of God Himself. This is no ordinary story, but a sacred event recorded in the Synaxarion, preserved by the Church, and bathed in divine light.

On Sene 20, in the district of Chalcedon in Caesarea Philippi, our Lord Jesus Christ Himself built a church not of wood, nor of clay, nor of water but by three  stones, drawn together by divine command. This church was built in honor of His Holy Mother, the Virgin Mary, the All-Immaculate Theotokos. It stands among the holiest of her feast days, a monument not only of stone, but of heaven's descent upon earth.

In the eighth year of the Lord’s reign, the apostles Paul and Barnabas, having preached the Gospel and baptized many Gentiles in Philippi, desired to build a holy place where the new believers might worship. But they did not act without heavenly guidance. Saint Peter, the Chief of the Apostles, and Saint John the Beloved, were summoned. And then O awe-striking wonder! the Lord, gathering both the living and the dead, brought together all His apostles in a divine convocation.

Christ our God appeared and said, “I have gathered you to teach you the manner in which churches are to be built throughout the earth in the name of My Mother.” He took them eastward and, with divine majesty, moved three stones into one foundation. He measured it: 24 cubits in height and 12 in width, a mystery in number and in spirit. These stones, soft as wax under divine fire, were fashioned into a church by the hands of the apostles, according to the command and guidance of the Lord.

On the following day, Sene 21, the Lord descended again with His Holy Mother, the Virgin Mary. She stood as the new Ark of the Covenant, holier than that of Moses. He ordained the apostles: Saint Peter as priest, Saint Stephen as deacon, and sanctified the Eucharistic mystery, causing the heavenly bread and cup to descend into that first church. And thus, the apostolic priesthood and the mystery of the Eucharist were sealed under the name of the Theotokos.

What then do these sacred elements mean? Why such precise numbers and symbols? The Church built 24 cubits high mirrors the 24 heavenly prophets, who in the time of kings foretold the coming of Christ. The 12 cubits in width mirror the 12 holy apostles, who bore the Gospel to all lands. The three stones are a figure of the All-Holy Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit one essence, undivided, eternal.

But more still is hidden in this holy teaching:

The church, being divided into three parts, reflects the ark across three divine ages:

1. The Ark of Adam—the beginning of humanity, fallen yet destined for glory.

2. The Ark of Moses—the Law, a shadow of the greater things to come.

3. The Ark of Christ—the fulfillment, in whom all is completed.

Likewise, it reflects three worlds:

The Ark of the Serpent (the world of the fall),

The Ark of Ior (the world of renewal),

The Ark of the Universe (the final, eternal world to come).

And even the angelic orders are shown as a divine reflection of the priestly ranks of the Church:

Angels = Singers

Princes = Anagogians

Elders = Deacons

Powers = Priests

Arbab = Commissaries

Cherubim, Seraphim = Bishops

These ranks are not merely symbols, but living realities. Just as the celestial orders do not usurp one another, so also in the Church no lower order may ascend presumptuously to the higher, and no higher may neglect the service to the lower. Yet all serve in harmony, according to grace and rank, in unity and obedience.

text:
And what shall we say of the heavenly vision seen in the Seraph of the Aramaic?
It is the image of the Church itself:

The Throne of Light – the altar of Christ

The Ark of Light – the Theotokos

The Veil of Light – the mystery of the Incarnation

The Four Pillars – the four evangelists and chief bishops

The Twenty-Four Elders – the company of apostolic bishops around the throne of God (cf. Revelation 4:4)

Let the weak in faith be awakened!  For this is no tale of old, but a present reality: the Church is born of heaven, and the Virgin is her crown. She is not honored for her own sake alone, but because in her the fullness of Christ was pleased to dwell, and in her name, He established the visible sign of salvation on earth the One, Holy, Catholic, and Apostolic Church.

Let us therefore honor the feasts of Sene 20 and 21 with awe and devotion, not as a relic of the past, but as a living remembrance that Christ built His Church in the name of His Mother, and through her intercession, continues to build it even now in every land and heart.

text: Dear beloved in Christ, let us ascend the heights of spiritual reflection and descend with holy tears of gratitude, as we contemplate a mystery revealed through Scripture, Tradition, and the radiant witness of the Holy Virgin. This teaching, drawn from the well of ancient truth and illumined by the light of the Orthodox faith, sets before us a vision of our character, our fall, and our restoration through Our Mother the Blessed Virgin Mary.

text.text: The Image of God in Man: A Mystery of Nature and Spirit

text:
The sacred Scripture declares, “And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness” (Genesis 1:26). These divine words are not mere poetry but thunder from the throne of heaven. They reveal that man is not a beast of the field, nor a mere particle of dust, but a creature shaped by the very hand of God, bearing within him the imprint of divinity.

Man is composed of four physical elements:

Water - the symbol of cleansing and life.

Fire - the image of zeal and divine light.

Wind - the breath of the Spirit.

Earth - the foundation of humility and mortality.

And within him dwell three spiritual qualities, divine treasures bestowed from above:

Intelligence (Understanding) – the eye of the soul, able to know God.

Perception (Speaking) – the word-bearing faculty that reflects the eternal Logos.

Life (Living Forever) – the breath of eternity, an immortal essence breathed into clay.

These seven elements four of the body and three of the soul are united into one sublime nature: the human being. This union forms what we call character, for character is not merely behavior, but the outward revelation of an inward composition.

text.text: The Fall of Character: A Wound in the Nature of Man

text:
This nature, though fashioned in beauty, was wounded by sin. Adam and Eve, our first parents, were endowed with free will, a divine gift allowing them to choose good or evil. But through their transgression, they severed human nature from the holiness and purity in which it was created.

Thus,

Became miserable and afflicted.

Lost its childlike innocence.

Surrendered its freedom and vitality.

Fell into the cold grip of death.

As the Apostle Paul writes, “Sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men, for all sinned…But death reigned from Adam to Moses” (Romans 5:12-14). This was the sin of the flesh, an inheritance of corruption that tainted all who came from Adam’s loins.

The character of man became distorted not lost, but marred awaiting redemption, groaning for the restoration of what once was whole.

text.text: The Longing for Restoration: The Cry of the Ancient Fathers

text:
Throughout the ages, Adam and his children lifted their prayers to heaven, yearning for deliverance. They awaited the fulfillment of the divine promise, a promise not made in vain. God, in His mercy, prepared a bridge, a way back from corruption to incorruption, from death to life.

That bridge is the Virgin Mary, the Mother of our salvation, the support of our character.

Why do we call her thus? Because in her was preserved what was lost in Eve:

Holiness instead of defilement,

Purity of mouth, soul, and body instead of corruption,

Obedience instead of rebellion.

She bore within her womb the One through whom human nature is lifted back to its ancient beauty.

And within him dwell three spiritual qualities, divine treasures bestowed from above:

Intelligence (Understanding) – the eye of the soul, able to know God.

Perception (Speaking) – the word-bearing faculty that reflects the eternal Logos.

Life (Living Forever) – the breath of eternity, an immortal essence breathed into clay.

These seven elements four of the body and three of the soul are united into one sublime nature: the human being. This union forms what we call character, for character is not merely behavior, but the outward revelation of an inward composition.

The Fall of Character: A Wound in the Nature of Man

This nature, though fashioned in beauty, was wounded by sin. Adam and Eve, our first parents, were endowed with free will, a divine gift allowing them to choose good or evil. But through their transgression, they severed human nature from the holiness and purity in which it was created.

Thus, the human nature:

Became miserable and afflicted.

Lost its childlike innocence.

Surrendered its freedom and vitality.

Fell into the cold grip of death.

As the Apostle Paul writes, “Sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men, for all sinned…But death reigned from Adam to Moses” (Romans 5:12-14). This was the sin of the flesh, an inheritance of corruption that tainted all who came from Adam’s loins.

The character of man became distorted not lost, but marred awaiting redemption, groaning for the restoration of what once was whole.

The Longing for Restoration: The Cry of the Ancient Fathers

Throughout the ages, Adam and his children lifted their prayers to heaven, yearning for deliverance. They awaited the fulfillment of the divine promise, a promise not made in vain. God, in His mercy, prepared a bridge, a way back from corruption to incorruption, from death to life.

That bridge is the Virgin Mary, the Mother of our salvation, the support of our character.

Why do we call her thus? Because in her was preserved what was lost in Eve:

Holiness instead of defilement,

Purity of mouth, soul, and body instead of corruption,

Obedience instead of rebellion.

She bore within her womb the One through whom human nature is lifted back to its ancient beauty.

Continues👇🏾

text.text: The Prophetic Witness: Our Mother in the Old Testament

text:
Even before her birth, the Virgin was prefigured and prophesied.

Behold the vision of Jacob, our father in the faith. While in exile and in solitude, he saw in a dream a ladder reaching from earth to heaven, with angels ascending and descending, and the Lord standing above it (Genesis 28:12–13). This was not a mere dream but a divine revelation: the ladder is the Virgin Mary, and the Lord who stood above it descended through her into the world.

This was fulfilled in the cave of Bethlehem, when nine months and five days after the Annunciation, the Lord was born, and angels sang with shepherds, proclaiming, “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2:8–14). Heaven and earth were united through Our Mother.

text.text: The Praise of the Church: Our Lady in the Liturgy

text:
Let us hear the voice of the Church, the Bride of Christ, who lifts her hymn of praise through the mouth of Abba Hiriakos of Bhinsau:

 “Oh, this is a wonderful thing!
O bridge through which the ancient fathers passed from death to life,
O ladder that reaches from earth to heaven,
O beginning of all creation,
O hope of Adam when he was exiled from Paradise.”
(Liturgy of the Hours, verse 30)

O wondrous words! She is not only the hope of Adam, but the renewal of our character, the sanctification of our nature, and the Mother of all who live in Christ.

text.text: Conclusion: The Support of Our Character

text:
Beloved, our character is not a mask we wear, but the echo of our creation and the record of our choices. Though once fallen through the sin of the flesh, our character is now restored through Our Lady, the new Eve, the pure ladder, the glorious vessel.

Let us, therefore:

Revere her as the Support of Our Character,Follow her example in purity and holiness,And entrust ourselves to her intercession, that we may be made worthy of the divine image once more.

text.text:
May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

text:
Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ, those who drink from the living springs of the Holy Orthodox faith and walk in the light of the Church that is One, Holy, Apostolic, and true grace and peace be multiplied unto you. From the treasury of sacred teaching handed down by the apostles, guarded by the Fathers, and faithfully echoed by the voice of repentance, we set before you a flame to rekindle the mind and awaken the soul.

Today, we meditate upon the sacred words of our Lord, spoken to those who thought themselves wise but were in fact blind to truth. Our Lord Jesus Christ, when confronted by the Sadducees those who denied the resurrection of the dead and twisted the Scriptures to fit their own hollow reasoning rebuked them, saying:

“You are misled, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God.”(Matthew 22:29)

Oh, what thunder lies in these words! What warning for every generation! They are addressed not only to ancient deniers of the resurrection, but to all who fail to understand the true meaning of the Holy Scriptures and the immeasurable might of the living God.

text.text: The Mystery of Scripture and the Glory of Our Lady

text:
He who does not know the Scriptures is easily misled. And not knowing the Scriptures means more than mere ignorance of words it is blindness to the mystery that lies within them. The sacred text is not a book of knowledge to be dissected, but a garment woven with divine wisdom, revealing God’s plan for the salvation of man.

Among the loftiest of these mysteries is the glory of the Virgin Mary, the Theotokos She who bore God in the flesh. The Scriptures, when rightly understood, reveal her not as a secondary character in the drama of redemption, but as its sacred gate. The Church, in its wisdom, calls her:

The Mother of God

The Faithful One

The Support of Our Nature


What does this mean? It is no poetic flourish. It is theology doctrine of salvation revealed by God. Those who know the Scriptures understand that these titles declare the power of God working through His handmaid, the Virgin. They do not diminish the glory of Christ; they manifest it more perfectly.

text.text: The Obedience That Heals the Fall

text:
In Eve, disobedience. In Mary, obedience.
In Eve, the door to death was opened. In Mary, the path to life was restored.

Those who ignore this truth who belittle the reason for our salvation expose themselves as strangers to the mystery of Scripture. They can easily comprehend how death entered through Eve. But they are blind to how life entered through the Virgin. They are, as the Lord said, misleading, because they do not know the Scriptures, nor the power of God.

The Orthodox Church, preserved from distortion by the grace of the Holy Spirit, constantly teaches this mystery. In every hymn, in every prayer, she raises the name of Mary not as an idol, but as the vessel through which our Lord took flesh, the gateway through which salvation reentered the world. She is remembered as the foundation of our character, the one through whom the broken image of man was lifted once more toward its original glory.

 The Danger of False Teachers and Empty Titles

text:
But now hear this solemn warning.

There are many who, through ignorance and arrogance, have risen as false teachers. Some do so from the remote corners where the fountains of wisdom have dried. But others are more dangerous still those who dwell within the Church’s walls, who walk among the councils, yet teach another gospel, not of the Apostles.

Like the Sadducees and Pharisees of old, they wear titles and garments of honor. They teach not from the depths of the Apostolic tradition but from the shallow wells of foreign seminaries Western and Eastern alike that do not know the power of God.

They have become as the Lord said in Matthew 23, whitewashed tombs beautiful on the outside, but filled with the bones of corruption.

They drape the Church with veils of cheap glory, distracting the faithful from the pearl within.

They teach a simplified gospel, one pleasing to the ears and saleable to the masses.

They choke the holy tradition with external ornaments, forgetting the inner fire.

As a result, the faithful especially the simple and sincere are ensnared in confusion. They are diverted from contemplating the foundation of our character and fall into shallow debates and empty speech concerning intercession, resurrection, and ascension. These mysteries, which should lift the soul, are made objects of contention by those unfit to speak of them.

text.text: Return to the Wellspring of Wisdom

text:
O beloved, let us not be misled. Let us not be deceived by the pomp of men nor confused by the empty applause of popular religion. Let us instead draw near to the living Church, which has kept the mystery intact through fire and flood.

The foundation is Christ. The glory of His work is revealed through His Mother. The true character of man is restored in the obedience of the Virgin. The power of God is seen not only in the parting of seas or raising of the dead but in the lowly handmaid who gave birth to the Savior.

If our people would open their eyes to the full message of the Scriptures, they would return to the faith of their fathers. They would see that the intercession of our Lady, the resurrection of Christ, and the ascension into glory are all parts of one divine drama, one river of salvation.

Let them no longer be tossed by every wind of doctrine, but anchored in the Apostolic Church.

text.text: A Final Admonition from the Fathers

text:
Our Father George once gave a closing admonition that we recall with reverence, a word which seems perfectly shaped for our present generation: Let not your mind be entangled with the cords of false teaching. Let it ascend instead to the contemplation of Christ, the Virgin, and the power of God revealed in the resurrection.

Let the ignorant be taught. Let the proud be humbled. Let the faithful rejoice in the truth.

text:
The Glory of the Cross and the Apostolic Gospel Preserved in the Orthodox Church

Beloved in Christ,

Peace be unto you who seek the truth, and grace to all who strive for the incorruptible crown of faith. Let us now meditate upon the words of the Apostle Paul, not as words of mere memory, but as the breath of the Holy Spirit echoing from the mount of Zion into the ends of the earth:

 “But we preach Christ crucified.” 1Corinthians 1:22

This declaration though short in speech is deep in mystery, high in glory, and terrible to the proud. In these few words, the great Apostle discloses not only the content of his message, but the very nature of the divine purpose of God for the salvation of the world.

text.text: I. The Conflict of the Cross Against the World’s Wisdom

text:
When the apostles were sent forth like lambs among wolves, they encountered not eager hearts but hardened minds and darkened spirits.

The Jews, who had crucified the Lord of Glory, were not satisfied with the preaching of Christ. They demanded signs mighty deeds like the dividing of the sea, the raining down of manna, the guiding cloud. In their hardness, they desired miracles more than truth.

The Greeks, puffed up with worldly wisdom, had adorned their minds with the philosophies of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle. They had made reason their idol and scoffed at the idea of a suffering God. “What folly!” they said. “What madness to proclaim a God who hungered, thirsted, and was crucified like a criminal!”

The Romans, blinded by idolatry, bowed to emperors who exalted themselves as gods and molded golden images for the people to worship. Yet when they heard that this Gospel removed the distinction between slave and free, man and woman, citizen and foreigner that all were one before God they saw it as a threat to their empire and turned their cruelty upon the apostles.


But amidst this rejection, the apostles did not alter their message. They did not bend to the demands for signs, nor dress the gospel in the garments of philosophical speech, nor make peace with Caesar’s idolatry.

They preached Christ crucified a scandal to the Jews, foolishness to the Greeks, a threat to the Romans yet the wisdom of God and the power of God to those who believe.

text.text: II. The Content of Apostolic Preaching: The Whole Christ

text:
Do not think that “Christ crucified” refers only to His death upon the wood of the Cross. The apostles preached the whole Christ:

His descent from heaven

His incarnation in the womb of the Virgin

His baptism in the Jordan

His teachings and miracles

His Passion and Crucifixion

His Resurrection on the third day

His Ascension and Lordship

His divine nature as Son of God

This Christ, the apostles proclaimed, was foretold by the prophets, foreshadowed in the law, and confirmed in the Gospel. And they commanded that all who believe be baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, that they might receive forgiveness of sins, new birth, and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit.

Beloved in Christ,

His Passion and Crucifixion

His Resurrection on the third day

text.text: III. The Fruit of Apostolic Preaching: Holiness of Life

text:
The apostles did not merely proclaim salvation they formed the Church in holiness. Those who received the Gospel were taught to walk in the likeness of Christ. Consider what they instilled in the baptized:

To grow in the likeness of saints, that the heart might reflect the image of the Savior

To flee paganism, cutting off the idols of the mind and hand

To guard the body the temple of the Holy Spirit from fornication, and to sanctify marriage in purity

To ordain righteous priests, faithful shepherds over the flock of Christ

To honor bishops, abbots, and priests, not as men, but as vessels of the divine mystery

To live by fasting and prayer, and engage in the spiritual struggle that purifies the soul

Such was the gospel preached—not just words, but a way of life. Not abstract theology, but Christ formed in the people, a living testimony of grace.

text.text: IV. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church: A Living Apostolic Witness

text:
As the apostles preached and labored, so too has our Holy Orthodox Tewahedo Church continued in their steps. For two thousand years, she has:

Proclaimed the word of Christ with unshaken boldness

Comforted those who were far from God

Baptized multitudes into the heavenly kingdom

Adorned the Church as the Bride of Christ, pure and radiant

Raised up faithful servants priests, scholars, and saints who have carried the apostolic light into every generation

She has not altered the gospel, nor adopted the customs of heresy, nor bent to the winds of modern corruption. Though some scoff, though others slander, saying “She does not preach Christ,” yet she preaches Christ indeed with her lips, her liturgy, her doctrine, and her martyrdom.

text.text: V. The Enemies Within and Without

text:
Yet, beloved, a shadow has fallen in recent times. There are some who arise:

Criticizing the Church, not from love but rebellion

Seeking to change her worship, not by the Spirit, but by the dictates of flesh and blood

Desiring to hand the flock of God to the beast, by sowing lies and confusing the faithful

They are blinded by materialism, dazzled by the world’s treasures, and cry out in arrogance, “Renew the Church! Change Orthodoxy!” But in their cry is no love for truth, only weeds sown among wheat.

Let such ones beware. For the Church is the pillar and ground of the truth, not subject to innovation, not built on human invention, but rooted in the unchanging gospel of Christ crucified.

text.text: VI. What Does It Mean to Preach Christ?

text:
To preach Christ is to reveal His character:

His humility and obedience

His compassion and longsuffering

His purpose in taking flesh not to rule by force, but to save by love

His divine will that none should perish, but all should come to repentance

Thus the Church preaches Christ not only in words, but in sacrament, in life, in tradition, and in holiness.

text.text: Conclusion: Remain Faithful to Christ Crucified

text:
Let us, therefore, not be ashamed of the Cross, nor deceived by vain speech, nor swayed by worldly arguments. Let us proclaim with holy boldness:

 “We preach Christ crucified” the hope of the hopeless, the strength of the weak, the salvation of the lost, the glory of the Church.

Let us honor our Holy Tewahedo Church, remain within her maternal care, and walk in the ancient paths of the apostles and saints.

text.text:
May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

text: Grace and peace to you, beloved brethren in Christ, followers of the Orthodox way, disciples of the Apostles, and children of the ancient Church. Today, we gather not to hear novelty nor idle tales, but to contemplate deeply upon the God-appointed life of King Solomon, son of David, a vessel of wisdom, a prophet, and righteous ruler of Israel. Let us tread reverently upon the memory of this holy man, that we may glean heavenly wisdom and walk in the counsel of the Lord.

text.text: The Birth of a King Foretold by Grace and Repentance

text: Solomon was not born of a union that began in purity, but of one that was redeemed through bitter repentance. His mother, Bathsheba, had been the wife of Uriah, and through David’s grievous sin, her husband was slain. Yet the Lord, who is rich in mercy, chastened His servant David and drew from him a contrite heart. David wept and fasted, his soul crushed by guilt. The Lord, seeing his sincere return, forgave him. It was after this repentance that Solomon was born  not as a sign of wrath, but of divine mercy. The name "Solomon," which means peace, is a testament to the peace that follows repentance, and the promise of a covenant renewed.

text.text: The Anointing of the Young King

text:
At just twelve years old, Solomon was not yet girded with the wisdom for which he would become known, but he was chosen by God through his father. In those days, Adonijah, David’s other son, sought to usurp the throne. With Joab and Abiathar, he planned a false coronation. But the Lord, who does not forget His promises, moved the heart of Bathsheba and Nathan the prophet, and they reminded David of his oath. David, though frail in body, stood firm in the spirit and proclaimed: "As the Lord lives... Solomon shall reign after me."

Solomon was anointed at Gihon, not in secret but before the nation. Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet poured sacred oil upon his head. A trumpet sounded, and the people cried, "May Solomon reign a thousand years!" Joy filled the land, and David, from his bed, gave thanks to the God of Israel who allowed his eyes to see his successor crowned.

text.text: A Prayer for Wisdom - Not Riches or Revenge

text:
Let us marvel now at Solomon’s prayer at Gibeon, for it reveals the soul of a true king. In a dream the Lord appeared to him and said, "Ask what I shall give thee." How many today would cry out for riches, vengeance, or immortality? But Solomon, humbled before the multitude of God’s people, asked only this: “Give your servant an understanding heart to judge your people, to discern between good and evil.”

The Lord, who searches the hearts of men, was well pleased. And He said, "Because you did not ask for long life, nor riches, nor the death of your enemies, I have granted you a wise and discerning heart - and also riches and honor such as no king before or after shall possess."

Oh what a reward for humility! Let every ruler, priest, and parent learn from Solomon: the heart that seeks wisdom above power shall receive both wisdom and honor.

text.text: A Judgment that Echoed Through Israel

text:
Soon after, the Lord confirmed His gift with a matter of justice. Two women came before Solomon, both claiming the same child. No witness could be found. But Solomon, discerning the hearts, called for a sword   not to harm, but to reveal. “Divide the child,” he said. One mother remained silent, the other cried out, “Give her the child, but do not kill him!” Then Solomon said, “She is the mother.”

All Israel feared and revered him, for they saw not a mere man judging, but the wisdom of God manifest in his rule. Brethren, how often are we blind in judgment, swayed by passion or pride? Let us pray for the spirit of discernment as given to Solomon, that we too may judge rightly in our homes, our churches, our hearts.

text.text: The House of the Lord and the Glory of His Presence

text:
In the fourth year of his reign, Solomon began to build the Temple of the Lord not for his own name, but that God might dwell among His people. For seven years, with unmatched skill and dedication, the king adorned this sanctuary with gold and cedar, cherubim and fine stones. And when the ark of the covenant was brought in, the glory of the Lord descended as a cloud so thick, the priests could not stand.

Solomon prayed, “I have indeed built You a house in which You may dwell forever.” Then he stretched out his hands before the altar and offered a mighty sacrifice: 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep not out of extravagance, but deep reverence. Let us ask ourselves: What offerings do we bring? Is it a sacrifice of the lips, or of the heart?

text.text: The Covenant Renewed and the Lord’s Response

text:
The Lord appeared again to Solomon, as He had in Gibeon. “I have heard your prayer,” He said, “and have sanctified this house. My Name shall be there forever; My eyes and My heart shall always be there.” Yet He added a solemn warning: “If you or your children turn away, I will cut off Israel from the land I gave them, and this house shall become a byword.”

This, beloved, is the mystery of covenant: blessing is maintained through obedience, not simply by name or inheritance. Just as David exhorted Solomon on his deathbed  “Be strong. Keep the law. Walk in His statutes.”  so the Church exhorts her faithful children today.

text.text: A Peaceful End- A Wisdom Remembered

text:
Solomon reigned forty years in Israel, a time of unmatched prosperity and peace. He ruled with a heart anchored in God, and though later years would see trials, his early reign remains a beacon of divine wisdom.

When his course was complete, he died in peace, at the age of fifty-two. Yet his voice still speaks, for he wrote proverbs, songs, and wisdom literature treasures that guide the Church and instruct the soul.

Therefore, dear brethren, let us honor King Solomon, not only for his throne but for his discernment, not for his gold but for his prayer, not for his power but for his obedience. Let rulers learn justice, let children learn reverence, let the Church never cease to pray for wisdom from above.

May the Lord, who crowned Solomon with glory, also crown us with understanding and lead us into His eternal temple, where His presence shines brighter than all earthly gold.

My Name shall be there forever; My eyes and My heart shall always be there.” Yet He added a solemn warning: “If you or your children turn away, I will cut off Israel from the land I gave them, and this house shall become a byword.”

text:
Our father Moses was born among idolaters, worshipping sun, moon, fire, and wind, instructed by pagan parents who raised him in superstition. Such is the power of sin that, though they feared divine retribution in their youth, they grew hardened becoming thieves and “Gefeji,” mighty in sins of violence and gluttony. Our Moses, like an untamed beast, roamed in banditry until his arms grew heavy with blood and robbery.

2.

text.text: Encounter with Grace through a Christian Girl

text: By God’s inscrutable mercy, a captive Christian maiden kindled in him the first spark of repentance. Her words struck him like a hammer upon the rock of his heart, breaking through years of brutal darkness. She taught him that the true God transcends the created sun and moon that their glory fades, but His mercy endures. Moved by her firm faith, Moses began to question the idols and plunged into his own soul’s depths, asking: If the sun were God, why did it fail to save me?

In a moment thick with divine revelation, a voice from heaven summoned him to a monastic life. With trembling heart, Moses and his parents set out for the monastery of Asceticism under Abba Asdros. They entered not as conquerors, but as beggars before holy men yet found themselves among monks whose day was spent with weapons of war, as though the desert was still their battleground.

4

Mercifully, Moses shed his former pride. Obeying even the youngest monk, he served humbly: fetching water at midnight, tilling the earth, lighting the lamps hidden acts of love he performed while others slept, that no one would glory in his deeds. Day after day he bore their burdens, and the desert itself wept with the rain his prayers wrought.

After forty years of seclusion, Moses was elevated to abbot over five hundred souls. His authority stemmed not from ambition, but from meekness; he led new brothers to Christ, healed the wounded hearts around him, and fed those who came to him broken and weary. Thus the Lord confirmed his labors with signs rain and heavenly favor followed his prayers.

In his final hour, Moses visited Abba Mekars, who revealed that a martyr stood among his disciples. Moses responded, “That man is me,” recalling holy scripture: “They who take the sword shall perish by the sword.” With the courage of one who had once wielded death in his hands, he planted himself before the invaders. He cried, “My youth bathed in blood; now my blood I bring to the Lord.”

Thus, on Sene 24, he fell by the sword of the Berbers his body counted among the honored in Asketus. Six slaughtered alongside him, they bore witness that repentance transforms a robber into a martyr.

O children of repentance, hear this: Moses’s life reveals that:

1. No one is beyond grace. From idol worship and violence, salvation springs eternal.

2. Humility is the ladder of ascent. Moses fell prostrate before monks, not arrogantly ruling but serving.

3. Prayer and obedience weld the spirit. By tears, fasting, solitude and labor, true transformation was wrought.

4. Martyrdom crowns the path of repentance. The robber’s sword surrendered, replaced by the sword of Christ.

May the voice of Abune Moses thunder in our souls: "My sins have fled behind me; I judge none who stand today." On this holy day, let us embrace his spirit turning from idols to service from darkness to light.

text: Dearly beloved in Christ, grace and peace from our Lord be multiplied unto you. Today we meditate upon the central proclamation of our faith: Christ crucified. Let our hearts open as we journey into the mysteries entrusted to us.

Our Lord confronted doubt in Caesarea Philippi: “Who do men say that I, the Son of Man, am?” (Matt. 16:13). This question compels us to confess His true nature as revealed in Scripture.

Why is this essential?

To avoid stumbling in our walk with Him.

To know whether our salvation rests upon a mere creature or the Creator Himself.

As He declared, “Blessed is he who does not stumble in Me.” (Luke 7:23) He who walked among us, drank, ate, and grew as a man, yet remained without sin, unshaken in His divine sonship and divine nature.

Our Holy Tewahedo Church, upholding 81 canonical books, proclaims:

We believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, by whom all things visible and invisible were made… Light of Light, true God, begotten, not made, of one essence with the Father.

This doctrine stands upon the Gospel of St. John:

“In the beginning was the Word… and the Word was God… All things were made through Him… The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”(John 1:1–14)

Thus, the incarnate Word divine yet truly united to our flesh bore two natures without confusion, without division, without alteration, and without separation. He is one Christ, one hypostasis, one person.

We reject Nestorian division, Eutychian fusion, and any error that divides or dissolves His true union. We acknowledge that after His resurrection and ascension, Christ remains true God and true Man priest, king, and intercessor.

Our Savior was not a distant redeemer sending angels, but the Lord Himself compassionate, merciful, and personally redeeming.

Isaiah declared:

“Not by a messenger or angel, but by Himself… He redeemed them.

John 3:16 echoes: “For God so loved the world that He gave His only Begotten Son...”

Christ assumed our weakness born in humility, crucified, died to save us from the eternal death that sin brought through Adam and Eve.

Thus stands the mystery we preach: Christ crucified.

He did not come in glory to avoid death, but in humility to embrace it willingly.

He was crucified on a scandalous tree, shameful to human glory, yet powerful for our salvation (“excruciating” indeed means “out of the cross”) .

In that tree, He destroyed the bonds of sin, defeated the devil’s hold, and became a trophy of victory over death and corruption  .

Chrysostom knew well that the Cross is not weak but the power of God (1 Cor. 1:18). It is our shield, our weapon, our baptism's seal, and our ultimate example  .
We are called to take up our cross daily. Living comfortably, in luxury or ease, is contrary to the Cross. Chrysostom lamented those who claim Christ yet avoid hardship (Phil. 3:18–19) .

Embracing humility and willingness to suffer,

Recognizing the Cross as the source of our Transformation,

Seeing that in our suffering, we are united to Him.

Remember that when Christ hung upon the Cross, darkness fell from the sixth to the ninth hour signifying not defeat, but divine judgment, revelation, and the inauguration of a new covenant.

From the Cross flowed transformation for all creation:

It lifted fallen human nature from corruption into deification  .

It broke every tyranny sin, death, demonic powers declaring Christ’s triumph  .

Thus we preach: Christ crucified not a mere concept, but our living Lord: Creator and Redeemer, teacher of humility, conqueror of death.

Beloved, let the Cross not be a relic of history, but the center of your life:

Confess His divinity,

Embrace His humility,

Endure suffering with purpose,

Look for your glorification.

text.text: 5. Preaching Christ in All Forms and Seasons

text:
The Church, our Mother, catechizes her children through feasts, icons, chants, and books each a vessel of divine truth. The nine major and nine minor feasts of our Lord His conception, birth, baptism, crucifixion, resurrection, and more are not mere rituals but proclamations of the gospel.

Even the icons, painted in silence, speak to those who cannot read; they are Scripture in color. The beating drum, the golden cross, the faithful rosary these are the sacred instruments of the Church’s song of Christ crucified. The apocryphal texts, too, bear witness to the love of saints who bore torture for Christ’s sake, whose blood mingled with His in the cup of suffering.

text.text: 6. Rejecting the False Gospels of Signs and Philosophy

text:
Unlike the Jews who sought signs, or the Greeks who sought wisdom, the Orthodox Church seeks Christ crucified. She does not confuse Him with philosophers or prophets, nor treat Him as a mere intercessor or teacher. She rejects the modern blasphemies which attempt to reduce Christ to a voice of morality, or worse, to a tool of political agenda.

No, He is the God of nature, the King of kings, the Lord of lords, our Redeemer and our Hope. We do not follow a philosophy or a movement we follow a Person, the Living Christ, whom we call “my Lord and my God.”

text.text: 7. Let Us Hold Firm to the True Gospel

text:
Let not the blasphemies of heretics or slanderers unsettle your hearts. The Orthodox Tewahedo Church has always preached Christ, not in word only, but in sacrament, icon, feast, and martyrdom. To say otherwise is to echo the voice of the serpent who blasphemes with a forked tongue.

Therefore, beloved, let us be steadfast in the faith. Let us listen to the voice of our holy Church, rooted in the apostles, nourished by the saints, and crowned by the Cross. Let no storm shake your trust, for Christ crucified is the wisdom of God and the power of God (1 Cor. 1:24).

text:
Beloved children of the Church,
Let us now incline our ears to the sacred instruction of our Holy Mother, the Orthodox Church, regarding the saints those shining stars in the firmament of God’s grace. For many, this teaching is a stumbling stone, but to the faithful it is a fountain of wisdom, reverence, and consolation, rooted in Scripture, witnessed in tradition, and confirmed by the grace of the Spirit. Let us then speak plainly and devoutly, not in the speech of man’s philosophy, but in the voice of divine truth.

text.text: 1. The Saints Are Honored, Not Worshiped And God Is Glorified Through Them

text:
It is falsely said by some that the Church offends God by honoring His saints, naming churches after them or commemorating their lives in feast days. Yet, what foolishness is this? For Scripture itself testifies that God is not diminished when He exalts His servants. He created man in His own image, and when He glorifies man, He glorifies His own handiwork. When we honor the saints, we do not rob God; we magnify His grace in them.

The saints are not self-made. They are what they are by the mercy and power of God. In honoring them, we honor what God has done through them, and by this we also honor human nature redeemed, sanctified, and glorified through the Cross of Christ. Therefore, the glory of the saints is nothing less than the reflection of the glory of God Himself.

text.text: 2. Why Are Some Honored More Than Others?

text:
Another complaint is made: “Why do we honor some more than others? Are we not all saints?” Ah, but my beloved, although God’s love is the same for all, not all return that love in equal measure. The saints are those who responded to divine mercy with total devotion. They loved without reserve, they followed Christ without hesitation, and they endured the suffering of the cross even in the valley of the shadow of death.

Some gave up house, name, and reputation; they wandered as strangers in the world, yet God called them His own. And how did God reward them? He said:

 “I will give them in My house and within My walls a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters… an everlasting name” (Isaiah 56:5-7).

Let the scoffer now be silent! If God Himself builds their memorial, shall we not honor what God honors? The Church only proclaims what the Lord has already confirmed in His Word.

Some accuse the Church of worshiping saints. But let us be clear: worship belongs to God alone, and the Church knows this well. The gestures of bowing or kissing an icon, the lighting of candles, or calling upon a saint these are not acts of divine worship, but of deep respect, just as Scripture testifies.

When Cornelius bowed to Peter (Acts 10), or when others bowed in reverence, did they mean to replace God? Certainly not! And even John, overwhelmed by the glory of heaven, fell before an angel. But the angel reminded him of the order of worship directed to God alone.

Let the wise understand: the measure of worship is the heart’s intention, not the body’s posture. No Orthodox bows to the saints as to God, but with reverence and gratitude for their witness, intercession, and example.

text.text: . The Saints Lead Us to Christ They Do Not Replace Him

text:
The intercession of the saints is no competition to Christ’s unique role as Mediator. Far from replacing Him, they bring us nearer to Him, as friends of the Bridegroom who rejoice at His voice. God Himself established this pattern, calling Abraham to intercede (Gen. 20:7), Job to pray for his friends (Job 42:8), and urging us to pray for one another (James 5:16).

Intercession is the fruit of love. When saints pray for us, they reveal their union with Christ and love for His Church. Their prayers are not a detour from Christ, but the work of Christ’s own body the Church united in heaven and on earth.

“God is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matt. 22:32).

Indeed, death does not silence the prayers of the saints. Their love endures; their prayer continues. And if we ask our brethren on earth to pray for us, how much more shall we ask those who behold the face of God?

text.text: 5. The Church’s Unity: In Heaven and On Earth

text:
The Church is one body in Christ those on earth and those in heaven. Hebrews speaks of our being “surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses” (Heb. 12:1). Revelation shows the martyrs crying out to God on behalf of the suffering (Rev. 6:10). And even Abraham, seated in heaven, receives the poor Lazarus into his bosom (Luke 16:22).

Thus, the Church does not invent this mystery but receives it from the living witness of Scripture. Those who have departed in the flesh are not severed from us. Their works follow them (Rev. 14:13), their prayers ascend, and their love remains. The Church in heaven prays with and for the Church on earth.

text.text: 6. Sacred Tradition Upholds What Scripture Declares

text:
From the earliest centuries, the faithful honored the saints. In 155 A.D., the Church of Samaria already showed special love for the martyrs. The bones of saints were regarded with reverence, their lives preserved in memory, and their prayers sought by believers. Tradition is not the invention of man it is the living memory of the Spirit moving through the generations of the faithful.

The Church builds altars in their name, celebrates feast days, and instructs the faithful in their virtues, not as an addition to the gospel but as a mirror of it. The saints are the gospel lived, the Word made fruitful in the soil of men and women like us.

text.text: 7. Conclusion: Let Us Imitate the Saints, Not Revile Them

text:
O soul who questions the saints, do not tear down what God has built. Rather, ask yourself: Do I walk in their footsteps? Do I love Christ as they did? Do I pray, fast, forgive, and serve with such zeal? Let us then strive not to be critics but imitators.

As St. Paul said: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Cor. 11:1). The saints are our elder siblings in the family of God. They do not block the light of Christ they reflect it. And the Church, in her wisdom, teaches us to walk in their light until we, too, become bright lamps in the kingdom of the Lamb.
