text:
Beloved brethren, children of the Light and inheritors of the apostolic faith, grace and peace be multiplied unto you from God our Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ. Today, let us ascend with spiritual minds to consider the sacred purpose and profound symbolism of the bell that voice of metal which resounds in our holy temples and calls both priest and people to divine contemplation.

Let not your ears be dulled by familiarity, nor your hearts forgetful of the wisdom of the fathers. For the ringing of the bell is no mere tradition nor an ornament of ritual, but it is a voice a trumpet of the Church which, like the prophets of old, prepares the hearts of the faithful to meet their God.

text.text: The Bell: Its Origin and Composition

text:
The origin of the bell is not modern. The fathers teach that its beginnings reach back to the days of the righteous Noah. In those ancient days, a sound was needed to summon the chosen ones of God the priests to their service. From that need was born the bell, a herald of duty, a caller to righteousness.

The bell may be made of silver, bronze, iron, or any material that can proclaim a clear sound. Its house differs according to the architecture of the church. In round churches, it stands separate, but in cross-shaped churches, it is attached to the temple, as if the voice of the bell proceeds directly from the heart of the sanctuary.

text.text: I. The Wedding Bell – A Call to Awakening

text:
The Wedding Bell is rung before the doors of the church are opened. It calls the priests and the faithful to prepare their hearts for the holy Mysteries.

It is called the “Wedding Bell” because it reflects the mission of the prophets, who, like bridal friends, prepared the people for the coming of the heavenly Bridegroom. These prophets, turning the people from idols to the living God, were the first voices that stirred Israel to expectation.

So also does this bell stir us from the slumber of sin. Like a trumpet, it awakens our souls, saying: “Come, let us go up to the house of the Lord!” It is the voice of Isaiah, the echo of Malachi, the weeping of Jeremiah all calling us to return to the covenant.

text.text: II. The Entrance Bell of the Liturgy  A Herald of Sacrifice

text:
After the priests have honored the sacrifice in Bethlehem (the Holy Table), they return to the temple, and at this sacred moment, the Entrance Bell is rung. The faithful, moved by reverence, bow their heads and hearts.

This bell rings five times, a mystery signifying the five pillars of the Church. But it also reflects the heavenly declaration of Saint Gabriel to the Virgin:

“Rejoice, full of grace! The Lord is with you!” (Luke 1:26)

The bell, like the voice of the Archangel, announces to us that Christ is present in our midst, that the Holy One has come to dwell in Bethlehem, the House of Bread.

It also echoes the cry of Saint John the Baptist, who, beholding the Lamb, cried:

“Behold, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29)

Thus, this bell is not merely a signalit is a sermon in sound, proclaiming the presence of Christ and calling the people to offer Him the sacrifice of praise.

text.text: III. The Gospel Bell – A Cry of the Apostolic Voice

text:
After the Gospel is read and the deacon proclaims, “Hail, O Christ!”, the Gospel Bell rings three times.

Three times for the mystery of the Holy Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Three times for the threefold proclamation of salvation: by the voice of the prophets, the cry of John the Baptist, and the preaching of the apostles.

This bell symbolizes the ministry of Saint John, the apostles, and the beginning of mankind’s salvation. Before the Lord Himself taught, Saint John prepared the way, preaching repentance that hearts might be made ready for the Gospel. This bell continues that same ministry, stirring souls to hear the Word of God with trembling and joy.

I. The Wedding Bell – A Call to Awakening

The Wedding Bell is rung before the doors of the church are opened. It calls the priests and the faithful to prepare their hearts for the holy Mysteries.

It is called the “Wedding Bell” because it reflects the mission of the prophets, who, like bridal friends, prepared the people for the coming of the heavenly Bridegroom. These prophets, turning the people from idols to the living God, were the first voices that stirred Israel to expectation.

So also does this bell stir us from the slumber of sin. Like a trumpet, it awakens our souls, saying: “Come, let us go up to the house of the Lord!” It is the voice of Isaiah, the echo of Malachi, the weeping of Jeremiah all calling us to return to the covenant.

II. The Entrance Bell of the Liturgy  A Herald of Sacrifice

After the priests have honored the sacrifice in Bethlehem (the Holy Table), they return to the temple, and at this sacred moment, the Entrance Bell is rung. The faithful, moved by reverence, bow their heads and hearts.

This bell rings five times, a mystery signifying the five pillars of the Church. But it also reflects the heavenly declaration of Saint Gabriel to the Virgin:

“Rejoice, full of grace! The Lord is with you!” (Luke 1:26)

The bell, like the voice of the Archangel, announces to us that Christ is present in our midst, that the Holy One has come to dwell in Bethlehem, the House of Bread.

It also echoes the cry of Saint John the Baptist, who, beholding the Lamb, cried:

“Behold, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29)

Thus, this bell is not merely a signalit is a sermon in sound, proclaiming the presence of Christ and calling the people to offer Him the sacrifice of praise.

III. The Gospel Bell – A Cry of the Apostolic Voice

After the Gospel is read and the deacon proclaims, “Hail, O Christ!”, the Gospel Bell rings three times.

Three times for the mystery of the Holy Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Three times for the threefold proclamation of salvation: by the voice of the prophets, the cry of John the Baptist, and the preaching of the apostles.

This bell symbolizes the ministry of Saint John, the apostles, and the beginning of mankind’s salvation. Before the Lord Himself taught, Saint John prepared the way, preaching repentance that hearts might be made ready for the Gospel. This bell continues that same ministry, stirring souls to hear the Word of God with trembling and joy.

Continues 👇🏾

IV. The Bell of the lord - Mourning at the Foot of the Cross

text:
During the sacred moment of the Liturgy, when the priest and people cry out “Lord, have mercy on us” forty-one times, the Bell of the Lord is rung twelve times.

Why twelve? It is the number of the apostles, the foundation stones of the heavenly Jerusalem.

But listen deeper this bell is a cry of sorrow, echoing the weeping of Our Lady, the Holy Virgin Mary, and Saint John the Beloved, who stood beneath the Cross (John 19:25).

As this bell tolls, we are reminded of the Passion, of the grief that filled the heavens and earth when the Son of God was crucified. It beckons us to join in their holy sorrow, to remember that the Cross was borne not only by Christ but also by those who loved Him.

Let the bell pierce your heart, O faithful one, and awaken in you the sacred mourning that leads to eternal joy.

text.text: V. The Bell of the Cross – The Descent of the Divine Gifts

text:
When the priests depart from the sanctuary bearing the Holy Body and Precious Blood, the Bell of the Cross is rung.

This bell is a symbol of the holy acts of Saint Joseph of Arimathea and Saint Nicodemus, who took down the Lord’s Body from the Cross and laid it in the tomb with reverence and sorrow.

It also represents the teaching of the apostles and the descent of the Holy Spirit. For just as Christ gave His Body and Blood for the life of the world, so now, through the apostles’ successors, He gives it still.

At this bell, bow deeply. For the Lamb once slain is now offered to you. The Cross, once lifted high on Golgotha, is lifted once more upon the altar of grace.

O brethren, every bell in the Church is a voice of heaven. Let us not treat it lightly nor hear it with deaf hearts. It is the trumpet of the Spirit, the cry of the prophets, the call of the apostles, the lament of the Virgin, the voice of John in the wilderness.

Each ring is a reminder that time is sacred, that we are called, gathered, instructed, and fed by the Lord who desires not the death of sinners but their return to Him.

Let us thank God for these sacred instruments. Let us not grow weary of their sound, but let them lead us from sleep to prayer, from sorrow to hope, from sin to grace, from earth to heaven.

text: Beloved brethren, heirs of the apostolic faith, children nourished at the breast of the Holy Church, grace and peace be unto you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Today we turn our hearts to reflect upon a sacred practice in our Holy Tradition the giving and bearing of a Christian name. This is not a mere custom, as the careless suppose, but a spiritual inheritance and a divine ordinance. Let us, therefore, with reverent minds and open hearts, consider why a Christian name is not only necessary but a source of divine blessing.

text.text: 1. The Christian Name: A Sacred Gift, Not a Casual Label

text:
There are many who do not recall the Christian name conferred upon them at baptism a sign of the spiritual forgetfulness that plagues this age. Yet the Christian name is not given at random. It is neither cultural decor nor familial tradition. It is bestowed by the priest the hand of the Church as one who acts in the name of the Lord, upon the soul being baptized. It is a holy naming, authorized and sanctified in the waters of rebirth.

The Church, our mother and teacher, receives her children at the font of new life not in mere ceremony, but in mystery and truth. There, the soul is born anew of the Holy Spirit, sealed with myrrh, nourished by the Word of the Cross, and welcomed to partake of the Body and Blood of Christ. In this spiritual birth, the name given is no less than a banner raised above the heart a name not just remembered in time, but recorded in heaven.

text.text: 2. Biblical Roots: God Himself Bestows New Names

text:
From the very foundations of sacred Scripture, we see that God changes names as a sign of covenant, mission, and transformation:

Abram becomes Abraham – the father of many nations.

Jacob becomes Israel – the one who wrestled with God.

Simon becomes Peter – the rock upon which Christ built His Church.

Saul becomes Paul – from persecutor to apostle.

Shall we not understand this divine pattern? God does not do so lightly. He marks those who are His with a name that reflects His purpose in them. So too, in baptism, we are given not just a name, but a destiny, a remembrance, and a spiritual inheritance.

text.text: 3. Why Take the Name of a Saint? Three Divine Reasons
a. A Memorial to the Righteous – Isaiah 56:5

text:
“To them I will give in My house and within My walls a memorial and a name better than sons and daughters…”

The saints are living stones in the heavenly Jerusalem. Their names are not forgotten, for they are engraved upon the mind of the Church and on the lips of the faithful. To bear their name is to place oneself under their intercession and to strive toward their likeness. The Church, like a mother, clothes her children with the names of saints that they may be clothed in their virtues also.

text.text: b. A Channel of Blessing – Proverbs 10:6

text:
“Blessings crown the head of the righteous…”

The name of the righteous is not merely remembered it bestows a blessing. When one is named after a saint, one shares in the overflow of grace that still radiates from their sanctified life. The name is not only a remembrance it is a participation in the saint’s legacy and prayer.

text.text: c. Continuity of Christian Identity in Times of Trial

text: In the days before the terror of Gragn Muhammad, Christians were proudly called by their Christian names. Yet, under persecution, they began to use alternative names to preserve their lives and heritage. Though understandable, this became so widespread that the true names of Christian identity began to fade.

a. A Memorial to the Righteous – Isaiah 56:5

c. Continuity of Christian Identity in Times of Trial

In the days before the terror of Gragn Muhammad, Christians were proudly called by their Christian names. text.text: 4. On the Reverence of Names: What Should Not Be Used

text:
Some names, though biblical or divine in origin, are too holy for human use. Names such as:

Emmanuel (God with us),

El Shaddai (God Almighty),

Jesus - the name above every name,

These are reserved in sanctity. They are not fit for our bearing, lest we profane what is ineffable. Instead, let us adopt names that bear witness to God without equating ourselves to Him:

Gebre Egziabher (Servant of God)

Sahle Selassie (Grace of the Trinity)

Fekrete Christos (Love of Christ)

ZeAmmanuel (Belonging to Immanuel)

These names confess truth while preserving humility.

The names of the saints may be taken directly or reflected indirectly. Examples include:

Zemariam – one who is “of Mary”

Zemikael – one who is “of Michael”

Atsede Mariam – one consecrated to Mary

Tekle Haymanot – the great Ethiopian pillar of faith


Such names root us in the communion of saints. They are bridges between our earthly pilgrimage and the heavenly homeland. When a soul is named after a saint, it walks not alone, but under the guardianship of that holy one.

text.text: Conclusion: Let the Name Be a Blessing

text:
Let us not be careless with the names we bear or the names we give. The Christian name is a treasure  a memory of holiness, a vessel of blessing, and a testimony of our heritage in Christ. Let it be chosen wisely, remembered fervently, and borne with reverence. Let the names of the saints, the servants of God, and the confessors of the truth be ever upon our lips and in our hearts.

May God make us worthy to receive the blessings that flow from this holy tradition.

text:
My dear child, becoming a Christian is not something that is done to you, but rather a journey of the heart, a turning towards God. It is a calling, a gift freely offered by our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and one that we must freely accept.  Think of the parable of the sower in the Gospel of Matthew (13:1-23). The seed of faith must fall on fertile ground and be nurtured to grow.

It is a lifelong process of learning, growing, and deepening your relationship with Christ.  This journey involves repentance, which is a turning away from sin and towards God.  It is not simply regretting our mistakes, but actively choosing a different path, a path illuminated by the light of Christ.

Perhaps you can tell me what draws you to Christianity at this moment? What questions or longings stir within your heart?  Sharing these thoughts can help us explore this path together.

I can offer you resources to learn more about the tenets of the Orthodox Christian faith: the Holy Scriptures, especially the Gospels, which tell the story of Christ’s life, death, and resurrection; the writings of the Church Fathers, like St. John Chrysostom, whose eloquence illuminated the path to God for generations; and the rich traditions of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, a vibrant tapestry woven with centuries of faith.

We can also discuss the importance of prayer, fasting, and almsgiving – spiritual practices that help us draw closer to God and purify our hearts.

Ultimately, my child, the decision to embrace Christ rests with you.  I can guide you, offer support, and share the wisdom of our faith, but it is through your own free will, guided by the Holy Spirit, that you will find your way.

Remember the words of St. Augustine, "Our hearts are restless until they rest in Thee, O Lord."  Perhaps that restlessness is what brings you here today. Let us explore it together in prayer and reflection.  Would you like to share what is on your heart?

Perhaps you can tell me what draws you to Christianity at this moment? What questions or longings stir within your heart?  Sharing these thoughts can help us explore this path together.

I can offer you resources to learn more about the tenets of the Orthodox Christian faith: the Holy Scriptures, especially the Gospels, which tell the story of Christ’s life, death, and resurrection; the writings of the Church Fathers, like St. John Chrysostom, whose eloquence illuminated the path to God for generations; and the rich traditions of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, a vibrant tapestry woven with centuries of faith.

We can also discuss the importance of prayer, fasting, and almsgiving – spiritual practices that help us draw closer to God and purify our hearts.

Ultimately, my child, the decision to embrace Christ rests with you.  I can guide you, offer support, and share the wisdom of our faith, but it is through your own free will, guided by the Holy Spirit, that you will find your way.

Remember the words of St. Augustine, "Our hearts are restless until they rest in Thee, O Lord."  Perhaps that restlessness is what brings you here today. Let us explore it together in prayer and reflection.  Would you like to share what is on your heart?

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us. Amen.

text: Beloved children of the Church, sanctified by the apostolic word and the grace of the Holy Spirit, lend your hearts to this sacred instruction: how the Holy Church received, preserved, and continues to live by the teaching of the Apostles. This is no trivial matter it is the very marrow and foundation of the Church’s faith, life, and salvation. Let us approach this doctrine with reverence, for it is as a flame drawn from the lamp of divine truth.

text.text: The Source of Apostolic Teaching: Christ Himself

text:
The Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior of the world, who is the Way, the Truth, and the Life, entrusted to His chosen Apostles the fullness of divine revelation. The Holy Church, as a sacred vessel, received its life and doctrine not from speculation, nor from human invention, but from the pure hands of those who walked with Christ.

“That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the Word of life...” (1 John 1:1)

The Apostles did not proclaim cleverly devised myths. They bore witness to what their eyes beheld, what their ears heard, what their hands touched, and what their hearts were illuminated to understand through the descent of the Holy Spirit. It is by this divine encounter that their message was authenticated and became the living faith of the Church.

text.text: The Mandate: “Go and Teach All Nations”

text:
The Lord did not merely reveal divine truths to His Apostles He commanded them, saying:

“Go therefore and teach all nations...” (Matthew 28:19)

This divine commission, rooted in heavenly authority, was fulfilled not in isolation but in communion with the Holy Spirit. The teaching they bore was not their own it was Christ's. And this is the teaching that has been handed down to us in two sacred forms:

The Apostolic Tradition is the life-blood of the Church. The holy Apostle Paul declared:

“The things which ye have learned, and received, and heard, and seen in me, do: and the God of peace shall be with you.” (Philippians 4:9)

The Church does not merely echo the words of the Apostles; she lives their very life. Their conduct, their acts, and their holy legacy became the pattern for the faithful. The Tradition of the Apostles is:

Their way of life

Their deeds of righteousness

Their sacrificial ministry

Their unwritten practices received by the Church through communion, worship, and holy discipline

This Apostolic Tradition is not stagnant. It is living transmitted through the liturgical life, the creeds, the priesthood, the sacraments, and the unbroken spiritual lineage of the Church.

Alongside Tradition stands the Holy Bible, especially the New Testament, which is the written form of apostolic truth. The Apostles, guided by the Holy Spirit, inscribed their teachings in the Gospels, Acts, and Epistles. These writings were not meant to stand apart from the Church but to dwell within her, as a treasure entrusted to her bosom.

The Church, not any private individual, is the rightful guardian and interpreter of the Scriptures. For the Bible was written within the Church and for the Church. The Holy Church is the owner of the Bible, not merely its reader. She alone, through the Holy Spirit, preserves its true meaning.

“No prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation...” (2 Peter 1:20)

Thus, Scripture and Tradition together form the two lungs through which the Church breathes.

text.text: The Apostolic Synod – Decisions Sealed by the Spirit

text:
Let us now consider the Apostolic Synod, a model for conciliar decision-making in the Church. The word “synod” comes from the Greek, meaning a gathering or council a holy assembly of shepherds united in the Holy Spirit.

The First Apostolic Synod - Jerusalem, ~50 A.D.

In the city of Jerusalem, the Apostles convened to address a pressing matter: the dispute in Antioch between Jews and Gentiles regarding circumcision and the Mosaic Law. The matter was no small controversy it threatened to divide the fledgling Church.

But the Apostles, led by the Holy Spirit, discerned together and issued this divine declaration:

“It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us…” (Acts 15:28)

This was not merely human judgment it was divine synergy. The decrees of that synod, and others that followed, gave order to:

The doctrine of the Church

The administration of the clergy

The role of the faithful

The discipline and worship of the Church

The Apostolic Synod, therefore, is a continuation of Christ’s teaching through the Spirit-led decisions of His Apostles.

Even today, in apostolic continuity, the Synod of Bishops gathers within the Holy Church, twice each year, to preserve, apply, and proclaim the same doctrine first declared by the Apostles.

O beloved, let us lift our hearts in gratitude. The faith we hold, the Gospel we proclaim, the sacraments we receive, the worship we offer—they are not inventions of men. They are the legacy of holy men who walked with God, whose hands bore the wounds of persecution, whose lips spoke fire from heaven, and whose teachings continue to breathe life into the Body of Christ.

May we cling, not to the passing winds of novel ideas, but to the unshakable rock of Apostolic Teaching.

text: Dear brethren beloved of God, peace be upon you. Let us now consider, in reverence and depth, the sacred and glorious ministry of the blessed Apostle Saint Peter. Let our souls be set aflame by his example, and our faith be strengthened through the knowledge of his life. For he who was once a simple fisherman became a rock upon which Christ founded His Church; he who once trembled before a maidservant was strengthened to face tyrants and martyrs' death. Let us unfold this holy narrative with godly reverence.

text.text: 1. The Humble Beginnings of a Chosen Vessel

text:
Saint Peter, born by the shores of the Sea of Galilee called also the Sea of Gennesaret and the Sea of Tiberias was of the tribe of Reuben. His father's name was Jonah, and his mother's name was Simon. Thus, according to the custom of the Hebrews, he was named Simon, after his mother.

A child of labor and simplicity, he grew up in Capernaum where he was taught the Torah in the synagogue. Like his father, a fisherman by trade, he labored with nets and boats. He married a woman named Concordia (Perpetua), settled in his father’s house, and lived the ordinary life of a Galilean tradesman until grace found him.

text.text: 2. His First Encounter with the Messiah

text:
His brother Andrew, a disciple of Saint John the Baptist, first heard the proclamation, “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1). Without delay, Andrew brought Simon to Christ and declared, “We have found the Messiah” (John 1:42).

Upon seeing Simon, our Lord immediately said, *“You are Simon son of Jonah; you shall be called Cephas” which is interpreted Peter, the rock. This was not merely a change of name, but a divine prophecy of what this man would become. From the mouth of God, the destiny of a simple man was sealed.

text.text: 3. The Miraculous Catch and the Call to Apostleship

text:
One morning by the Sea of Gennesaret, the multitudes pressed upon Christ. He stepped into Peter’s boat and taught from it. Afterward, He commanded Peter to lower his nets once more. Though they had toiled all night and caught nothing, Peter obeyed. What followed was a miracle: nets overflowing with fish.

Overwhelmed, Saint Peter fell at the feet of the Lord, crying, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5:8). The Church Fathers saw in this moment Peter’s profound humility. He who saw the mastery of Christ over creation was struck not with pride, but with a contrite spirit.

Yet Christ said to him, “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be a fisher of men.” And immediately, Peter left everything his wife, his trade, his household and followed the Lord (Luke 5:1-11). What worldly man does such a thing except he who has been pierced by divine love?

text.text: 4. The Zeal and Faith of Saint Peter

text: Peter was not only faithful in deed but fervent in spirit. He was bold to ask questions when the others kept silent and quick to answer when the Lord inquired. He stood at the front of the apostolic circle—not because he sought power, but because he loved deeply and earnestly.

When Christ walked upon the sea, Peter still not yet filled with the Holy Spirit said, “Lord, if it is You, command me to come to You on the water.” The Lord said, “Come.” And though he began to sink from fear, the Lord stretched out His hand to save him (Matthew 14:25-34). Here, we see both Peter’s boldness and weakness his readiness to draw near and his need for grace.

At Caesarea Philippi, when the Lord asked, “Who do you say that I am?”, Peter answered with divine clarity: “You are the Christ, the Son of the Living God” (Matthew 16:16). For this, the Lord blessed him, saying, “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but My Father in heaven.” And He declared, “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church.”

Here, the foundation of the Church was not Peter the man, but Peter’s faith the unwavering confession that Jesus is the Son of God. This became the cornerstone of Christian doctrine long before Nicaea.

Peter, with James and John, beheld the glory of the Lord on Mount Tabor. His garments shone as the sun, and Moses and Elijah appeared. Overwhelmed, Peter offered to build three tabernacles. But the voice from the cloud declared: “This is My beloved Son; listen to Him” (Matthew 17:1–5). The vision was a confirmation of Peter’s earlier confession.

text.text: The Temple Tax and the Coin in the Fish’s Mouth

text: When questioned about the temple tax, Peter answered without consulting Christ. Yet the Lord, knowing all, used the occasion to teach him that the Son of God is not bound by temple tribute. Still, to avoid offense, He miraculously provided the coin from the mouth of a fish (Matthew 17:25–27).
Peter’s love was deep, but his human frailty was not absent.

When Christ began to wash the feet of His disciples, Peter, in awe, refused. But when the Lord said, “If I do not wash you, you have no part with Me,” Peter yielded entirely: “Lord, not only my feet, but my hands and head also!” (John 13:1–13). Such was the eagerness of his heart, though slow to understand.

text.text: The Denial and the Rooster's Crow

text: When Christ foretold that Peter would deny Him, Peter declared boldly, “Even if all fall away, I never will.” Yet, when fear seized him in the high priest’s courtyard, he denied his Master three times. But the moment the rooster crowed, he remembered, and he wept bitterly. Those tears were not of shame alone, but of repentance. And thus he was restored (Matthew 26:69–75).

text.text: 6. After the Resurrection: The Strengthened Shepherd

text:
Peter was the first of the apostles to enter the empty tomb. And when Christ appeared by the Sea of Tiberias and asked him three times, “Do you love Me?”, Peter responded, and was charged: “Feed My sheep.” The denials were undone by triple love. Thus the Lord restored him and confirmed his calling.

Filled with the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, Saint Peter became the mighty preacher of Christ. He baptized three thousand souls in a single day, discerned the secret lies of Ananias and Sapphira, and healed the sick. He traveled through Samaria, Lydda, Joppa, and beyond establishing the Church with unwavering zeal.

text:
Grace and Peace be multiplied unto you, beloved in Christ,
As we turn our hearts and minds to the apostolic labors of the great Apostle Saint Paul, let us approach with humility and zeal. For his ministry is not merely a historical journey, but a holy path etched into the soil of the nations by the very feet of one whose tongue was aflame with divine truth. Let us now, with careful attention, receive the sacred teaching preserved from tradition, and walk the footsteps of the Apostle to the Gentiles.

text.text: The First Missionary Journey: The Fire of Beginnings (c. 46 AD)

text:
When the Holy Spirit summoned the Apostles in Antioch, Paul once a fierce persecutor and now aflame with grace was sent forth with Barnabas (Acts 13:1–3). This was no ordinary journey but a labor of divine urgency. They walked over 2,000 kilometers, traversing regions soaked in pagan darkness to proclaim the Gospel of the risen Lord.

From Cilicia to Cyprus, from Salamis to Paphos, and onward to Perga, Galatia, Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe, the Apostle cast the net of the Kingdom into the seas of idolatry. These places, strangers to the covenant of Abraham, now heard the voice of Christ through Paul. And so was fulfilled the prophecy: “I will give you as a light to the Gentiles” (Isaiah 49:6).

text.text: The Second Missionary Journey: The Shepherd Seeks His Flock (c. 50 AD)

text:
Now separated from Barnabas over the matter of Mark, Saint Paul chose Silas as his new companion. With the wisdom of God guiding his steps, he embarked toward Cilicia and Syria, and the Lord extended his influence into Greece, where new lands awaited the sowing of the Gospel.

He passed through Derbe, Lystra (where he met the young Timothy, his spiritual son), Phrygia, Galatia, and Mysia, then by divine vision was called into Macedonia to Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, and down to Athens and Corinth. The philosophical citadels of the Greeks heard words of life that confounded their wisdom. He reached Ephesus, Caesarea, and returned again to Antioch.

Even amid rejection, he did not falter, for his joy was not in men's applause but in Christ crucified.

text.text: The Third Missionary Journey: The Furnace of Sacrifice (c. 54 AD)

text:
Now like a seasoned soldier of Christ, Saint Paul set out once more. He passed through Galatia, Phrygia, Ephesus, and into Macedonia, Corinth, and Troas, bearing not only the Word but alms for the poor in Jerusalem a token of unity and love among the saints.

Yet this journey would not end in peace. When he entered Jerusalem during the Passover, Jewish opponents who had dogged his steps across the empire now found him vulnerable. They accused him falsely of defiling the temple by bringing in a Gentile Trophimus of Ephesus and stirred the whole city (Acts 22:29). Thus began his imprisonment.

text.text: Captivity in Rome and the Unyielding Gospel (c. 58–60 AD)

text: Chained in body but free in spirit, Saint Paul endured beatings and trials, eventually being sent to Rome. There, in the heart of the empire, he proclaimed Christ for two years while imprisoned, writing letters filled with the joy of heaven, though surrounded by the darkness of Roman cells. Even in fetters, the Gospel ran freely.

text.text: The Fourth Missionary Journey: The Silent Mission (Not recorded in Acts)

text:
Though Scripture is silent, the holy tradition of the Church remembers this last evangelical flame. After his release from Nero’s court, he journeyed to Jerusalem, Ephesus, Laodicea, Macedonia, Crete, Troas, Dalmatia, Nicopolis, and Brundisium. His heart burned to finish what was begun, to comfort the sorrowful, and to tend the scattered sheep.

This fourth journey lasted four years, and in it we see the true heart of a shepherd never satisfied until every soul is strengthened in Christ.

text:
When Nero, in his madness, set Rome ablaze, he wickedly blamed the Christians. A persecution unmatched in cruelty began. Saint Paul, teaching in Nicopolis, was arrested once more.

For two years and six months, he languished in a dark prison. But like Joseph in Egypt, the dungeon could not extinguish his wisdom nor his hope. Finally, on Sene 5, 67 AD, at the age of 74, he was led to the Ostian Way and beheaded, a martyr for the Lord whom he had once persecuted. Thus was fulfilled his own words: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7).

text.text: The Character and Virtues of the Apostle

text:
Humility: Though trained under Gamaliel and an expert in the Law, he called himself a “fool” for Christ (1 Cor. 15:8). He bent the lofty pride of his heart to the humble abasement of the Cross.

Labor and Patience: He preached for 42 years, reaching even unto Spain. He was imprisoned, beaten, starved, and yet never ceased rejoicing. His letters, many written from prison, still overflow with consolation and truth.

Wisdom and Tact: He was both the hammer and the father of the Church. Like a smith, he broke the idols of the Gentiles and forged them into the body of Christ. He brought Titus (a Gentile) and Barnabas (a Jew) together to symbolize the unity of the Church.

Pastoral Love: In his epistles, he remembered the names of the faithful one by one. This was not sentimentality, but the shepherd’s mark to know his sheep.

A Writer Inspired by the Spirit: His letters became scripture. When he could not be with his flocks, his pen became his presence. Even in chains, his words traveled further than he ever could in flesh.

A Man of Labor: Though he taught daily, he worked with his own hands a tentmaker by trade (Acts 18:3–4). He refused to be a burden to the Church and taught, “If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat” (2 Thess. 3:10).

text.text: His Appearance According to the Eastern Tradition

text:
He was short in stature, with a bald head, bright blue eyes, joined eyebrows, and a large nose. His shoulders were broad, his feet curved close together. Not handsome in the eyes of the world, but radiant with the glory of Christ.

Beloved brethren,
Let us remember the Apostle Paul not merely as a teacher of doctrine but as a burning torch, a pillar of suffering, a vessel of grace. Let us imitate his humility, his tireless labor, his wisdom in speech, and above all, his unwavering love for Christ and His Church.

text:
Beloved in Christ, grace and peace be multiplied unto you from the Lord Jesus Christ. In contemplating the lives of the great pillars of our faith Saint Peter and Saint Paul, those shining luminaries of the apostolic age we are not merely engaging in historical recollection. We are beholding, with reverent eyes, the craftsmanship of God in two different vessels, molded by the same Spirit, filled with the same flame, and poured out as drink offerings upon the altar of the Lord’s Church.

Though one was a fisherman and the other a Pharisee; though one was simple and unlearned, and the other deeply trained in the Law; though one followed Christ during His earthly ministry and the other after His ascension yet both were called, transformed, and glorified by the same Lord. Let us, then, look upon their likenesses and learn how God works wonders in diverse instruments for one glorious purpose.

text.text: I. They Were Both Jews, Chosen from Among Their Own Brethren

text:
The Lord did not gather foreigners to establish His Church, but He chose from Israel, the people of the covenant, to be the first stones in the new spiritual temple.

Saint Peter was unmistakably a Jew, as Paul testifies in Galatians 2:14, where he refers to Peter's Jewish heritage.

Saint Paul, likewise, bore the signs of Jewish identity: “Circumcised the eighth day, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews” (Philippians 3:5).

In their Jewish identity, we see the wisdom of God fulfilling the Law and the Prophets, making His messengers arise from those who knew the promises of old.

text.text: II. Both Were Called Directly by the Lord Jesus Christ

text:
The call of God came to both men not by human mediation but by divine intervention:

Peter, while fishing by the Sea of Galilee, heard the voice of the Lord: “Come after Me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:18–19).

Paul, on the road to Damascus, encountered the risen Christ in blinding light: “Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou Me?” (Acts 9:4).

Oh, what a mystery that He who walked in flesh called one with His voice from the shore, and He who was ascended called the other with heavenly glory from above!

text.text: III. Both Had Their Names Changed by the Lord

text:
A change of name signified a change of nature and mission:

Simon, son of Jonah, was renamed Peter a Rock upon whose confession the Church would be built (Matthew 16:17–18).

Saul, the persecutor, became Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles, after his divine calling.

text.text: VI. Both Were Crowned with Martyrdom in the Same Year

text:
Let us not forget the supreme testimony of their love martyrdom.

Peter was crucified in Rome under Nero in A.D. 67. Out of humility, he requested to be crucified upside down, deeming himself unworthy to die as his Lord.

Paul, being a Roman citizen, was not crucified but was beheaded, also under Nero’s persecution.

Both drank from the same cup of suffering and were baptized with the same baptism of blood. One the fisherman, one the Pharisee yet both now reign with Christ.

text.text: Conclusion: Unity in Diversity, Harmony in the Spirit

text:
These two apostles Peter, the pillar of the circumcision, and Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles stand together in the iconography of the Church, not as rivals, but as brothers. They are the two olive trees and two lampstands spoken of in Revelation (Rev. 11:4), who pour out oil and shine with light for the Church throughout the ages.

Let us then imitate their faith, their zeal, their humility, and their love for Christ. Let us not measure ourselves by background or knowledge or worldly honor, but by the cross we are willing to bear and the Gospel we are willing to proclaim.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.

text.text: , the Harp of the Holy Spirit

text: Beloved of Christ, blessed flock of the Lord, attend now to the glorious witness of our father, the righteous luminary of Mesopotamia, the fragrant lily of the desert, the golden harp of the Holy Spirit Saint Ephraim the Syrian, whose feast we solemnly keep on the fifteenth day of Sene. Let your hearts be opened, and your ears attentive, for his life is not merely a history to admire, but a ladder set toward heaven for all who would ascend.

text.text: I. The Noble Beginning and Heavenly Instruction

text:
Saint Ephraim was born in the year 306 after the Incarnation of our Lord, in a land called Ntsibyn in Mesopotamia, where the soil was dry but the Spirit rich. It was no accident that he was born in the diocese of Saint Jacob, one of the 318 god-bearing bishops who thundered at the Council of Nicaea and laid low the heretic Arius. Saint Jacob, a man adorned with the crown of martyrdom, apostleship, and wisdom, became a father not of the flesh, but of the soul, to young Ephraim.

As the child listened to his preaching, the divine Word pierced him like a sword. The Spirit, brooding like a dove over his soul, drew him to Saint Jacob. There he was baptized, not only with water but with tears, not only with doctrine but with fire. At ten years of age, he parted from his earthly parents and was raised under the wings of the bishop, learning the mysteries of Christ as bees draw nectar from the flower.

Is this not the beginning of true wisdom? That the child hears the voice of God in the voice of the preacher? That the soul is taught from youth to tremble before holiness?

text.text: II. The Warrior of Truth and Defender of Doctrine

text:
Through many fastings and unceasing prayers, Saint Ephraim was filled with the Holy Spirit. Like a sword forged in the furnace of asceticism, he went forth to contend with the Gentiles—not with violence, but with truth; not with wrath, but with conviction. His words, like arrows, pierced through error. He became a living shield of orthodoxy.

In the year 325, that holy synod was called at Nicaea, where bishops assembled like stars in the firmament to rebuke the pride of Arius. Ephraim, still young but inflamed with zeal, stood at the side of Abba Jacob. When the heretic was cast down and truth triumphed, Ephraim beheld that night a vision a pillar of light, stretching from earth to heaven, testifying to the glory of the truth preserved.

Can you not see, O brethren, what God bestows upon His friends? That they see what flesh cannot see, that they stand firm when the Church is shaken, and that they are granted the visions of heaven?

text.text: III. Ordained for Glory and Teacher of the Nations

text:
Saint Basil the Great, another pillar of fire, ordained Ephraim a bishop, and shortly thereafter, a priest. His lips became fountains of doctrine, and his mouth a treasury of hymns. His words did not echo in one land, but flowed like the rivers of Eden, refreshing the ends of the earth. His diocese became his pulpit, and the world his audience.

His tongue became the tongue of angels, and his soul the harp of heaven.

text.text: IV. Lover of the Theotokos, the One Who Magnified Her Praise

text:
But what shall we say of his devotion to Our Lady, the Virgin Mother of God? This love was not fleshly, but burning with the fire of the Spirit. While others debated, he adored. While others were content with doctrine, he burst into hymn.

He praised Her not once, nor seven times, but sixty-four times each day. He drew his inspiration from Saint Luke’s Gospel and from her own lips, the Magnificat. He wished her name to be praised like the stars that twinkle without ceasing, like the sands that no man can number, like food that nourishes, and like water that quenches.

Because he poured his heart into her praise, the Theotokos herself appeared to him. Not in silence, not in shadow, but openly and gloriously, clothed in light. She greeted him, saying:

“Peace be upon you, beloved son of Ephraim.”

The ground became a carpet of light, the air a robe of glory. She commanded, “Praise me,” and he, filled with the Holy Spirit, obeyed. He lifted his hands; the angels joined him; the martyrs sang with him.

What mystery is this, O faithful! That a man who praises the Virgin with sincerity will be visited by her in person!

She granted him fourteen thousand hymns and exhortations, and from these the Church still drinks. Most of these were taken by the angels for their own thanksgiving. Others were given to Saint Yared, the golden voice of Ethiopia, who received the seven-day hymns of Our Lady, sung in Axum Zion with Saint Ephraim and Abba Hiriakos, under the light of her presence.

She blessed them with the Cross of Light, and whispered to them her eternal hope. These were not dreams, but mystical realities gifts to those who burn with holy love.

text.text: V. His Blessed End and Everlasting Reward

text:
After seventy years of pleasing God, Saint Ephraim departed this life in peace on Sene 15/ 370 A.D in a holy monastery in Edessa. But he did not die as men die. He was greeted at the veil of eternity by Christ Himself, by the Virgin Theotokos, and by the assembly of saints and martyrs.

He who praised in time now praises eternally. He who sang from the dust now sings from glory. He who was filled with the Spirit now dwells in the bosom of the Holy Trinity.

text.text: Conclusion: A Call to Follow the Harp of the Spirit

text:
Let us not merely admire, but imitate. Let us not be content with applause, but seek communion. For what Saint Ephraim has done, the Church is called to do. Let our lips be like his praising Our Lady, defending the truth, and loving the Word with fire.

O beloved of God, pray today:

“Saint Ephraim, intercede for us! You who saw the Mother of Light, obtain for us purity of heart. You who received the hymns of heaven, teach us how to pray. You who walked with saints and angels, help us walk with God. Amen.”

By the intercessions of Saint Ephraim the Syrian, Abba Hiriakos, Saint Yared, and Abba Giorgis Zegascha, may the Most Holy Virgin grant us wisdom and understanding unto eternal life.

After seventy years of pleasing God, Saint Ephraim departed this life in peace on Sene 15/ 370 A.D in a holy monastery in Edessa. But he did not die as men die. He was greeted at the veil of eternity by Christ Himself, by the Virgin Theotokos, and by the assembly of saints and martyrs.

He who praised in time now praises eternally. He who sang from the dust now sings from glory. He who was filled with the Spirit now dwells in the bosom of the Holy Trinity.

Conclusion: A Call to Follow the Harp of the Spirit

Let us not merely admire, but imitate. Let us not be content with applause, but seek communion. For what Saint Ephraim has done, the Church is called to do. Let our lips be like his praising Our Lady, defending the truth, and loving the Word with fire.

O beloved of God, pray today:

“Saint Ephraim, intercede for us! You who saw the Mother of Light, obtain for us purity of heart. You who received the hymns of heaven, teach us how to pray. You who walked with saints and angels, help us walk with God. Amen.”

By the intercessions of Saint Ephraim the Syrian, Abba Hiriakos, Saint Yared, and Abba Giorgis Zegascha, may the Most Holy Virgin grant us wisdom and understanding unto eternal life.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.

text: Brethren, gathered in the love of Christ, let us now contemplate the radiant example of Saint Kirkos and Saint Eyeluta, whose holy lives blaze like torches in the darkness of this present world. These martyrs, mother and child, shone in the midst of a pagan world, not as those of noble birth in the courts of men, but as citizens of heaven, inheritors of the Kingdom, whose faith triumphed over flame and iron, whose love for Christ outweighed even the pangs of death.

text.text: The Holy Life of Saint Eyeluta and Her Son

text:
Saint Eyeluta, a woman crowned with virtue, lived in Angeben, a region within the Roman Empire. She was a God-fearing Christian, steadfast in both faith and conduct. Her life bore fruit in the form of her son, the blessed child Kirkos, whom she raised in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. They were not merely parent and child, but companions in suffering, fellow pilgrims upon the narrow path that leads to life.

When persecution arose under the tyrant Emperor Alexander, Eyeluta and her son fled Rome to the city of Tarsus, seeking safety not in the mountains nor in the strength of man, but in the providence of God. Yet the shadow of the dragon followed them. The emperor, inflamed by hatred for Christ, entered their land and waged war against the saints of God, hunting them as though they were beasts and not the righteous heirs of eternity.

Soldiers, servants of the king’s cruelty, laid hold of the saints and demanded they deny Christ and worship idols. But their faith was not made of straw to burn in the fire it was tempered steel. Neither fear nor pain could turn their hearts. They confessed Christ boldly, even as swords danced around them and flames kissed their bodies.

They endured trials beyond the capacity of natural strength: their eyes and noses were tormented with salt and mustard; their flesh was torn by red-hot nails and cruel irons. But behold! The fire that was sent to destroy them became as cool water; the iron, as soft clay. God, who preserved the three children in the furnace, also preserved Eyeluta and Kirkos.

Again and again, the tormentors devised new instruments of death. Eyeluta and her son were tied and scourged, their skins flayed and their bodies pierced from shoulder to foot. But the heavens did not remain silent. Saint Gabriel, the archangel of God, descended as a deliverer not to remove them from their struggle, but to sustain them in it, for God’s strength is made perfect in weakness.

Even the blade of the saw and the burning of the iron pan could not claim victory. The Lord, mighty in battle, raised them even from the grip of death and worked wonders before the eyes of the bloodthirsty emperor. These miracles were not merely signs of God’s power, but banners of His love for those who suffer for His Name.

text.text: The Bold Faith of the Child Saint

text:
The child Kirkos, though tender in years, was mighty in spirit. By his prayer, he turned the emperor’s shoe into a living ox a wonder that confounded the tyrant and enflamed his rage. In fury, the emperor severed Kirkos’ tongue, yet God preserved it. For who can silence the voice of those who cry out in faith? The tongue of the child was not for speech alone, but for the praise of the Almighty.

When the moment came for them to be cast into boiling water, and Eyeluta’s motherly heart trembled, the child turned and strengthened her soul:

"O mother, do not be afraid."
Here is a child who became a spiritual father, comforting the one who had borne him. He taught us that courage is not the absence of suffering, but the triumph of hope in the midst of pain.

text:
After every fiery trial, and every torment from men and demons, they received the divine call to eternal rest. At midnight, their holy necks were severed, and they entered the joy of their Lord. It was the 15th of Tir, a day sanctified by their martyrdom and sealed with the crown of life, as promised in the Book of Revelation: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.” (Rev. 2:10)

They despised the vanities of the world and clung to the love of Christ. Their hearts echoed the apostolic cry of Saint Paul:

“For I am convinced that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come... shall separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 8:38)

text.text: A Legacy of Courage and Intercession

text:
Through their steadfastness, not only did they gain salvation for themselves, but 11,004 souls were added to the company of martyrs by the intercession of Saint Gabriel. What man or woman can measure the fruit of one soul’s faithfulness?

Their example compels us: when we are mocked for our faith, when we are rejected for the sake of the Gospel, let us recall the words of Saint Kirkos:

“Take courage! Do not be afraid!”
And let us say to our souls likewise:
“Endure, O my soul, endure for Christ’s sake!”

text.text: The Role of the Angelic Host

text:
Let us not forget the ministry of the holy angels, and especially the vigilant protection of Saint Gabriel, who ministered to the martyrs as he once announced glad tidings to the Virgin. The Scripture affirms:

“The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear Him, and delivers them.” (Psalm 34:7)

So, let us cry out to Saint Gabriel with childlike trust:

“We trust in God, day and night, and hope in your prayers!”
He who protected Eyeluta and Kirkos shall also shield us from the snares of the enemy.

text:
Grace and peace be multiplied to you, beloved of the Lord, seekers of the apostolic truth and keepers of the covenant of Christ. Today we lift the veil from a mystery ancient and yet ever-new, a treasure long hidden in the house of God, now revealed through the teaching of the Orthodox Church the mystery of the Ark in the New Covenant.

Let us now walk reverently into this holy knowledge, not as mere readers of letters, but as beholders of the Spirit, and with fear and trembling approach what the Church has always preserved, though the world has often forgotten.

text.text: I. The Ark: Not an Option but a Mark of the Church

text:
The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, that holy bride adorned in apostolic tradition, teaches this unshakable truth:

A church without the Ark of God is no church at all.

This is not symbolic language. It is canonical and spiritual reality. For the Ark signifies the indwelling presence of God Himself. If the Lord is not present, it is not a temple it is a market, a mere gathering of bodies without the Spirit. Unless a building is consecrated as a church, blessed by the Holy Myron and the prayers of the Archbishop, it is not called a church. It is not made holy by mortar, but by mystery.

This reflects the ancient law: “Where two or three gather in My name, there am I in their midst” (Matt. 18:20). But what is the Lord’s Name if not written upon the Ark, as upon the hearts of His saints?

text.text: II. St. Paul and the Ark: Temple of the Living God

text:
The one who proclaims the necessity of the Ark stands with Saint Paul, that mighty pillar of both Covenants. For Paul declares: “The house of the living God is the temple of the living God.” And what greater adornment has that house than the Ark, which bears the tablets, the Word, the mystery of the covenant?

Paul did not divorce spirit from structure, nor did he abolish the visible for the sake of the invisible. Instead, he recognized that the saints the martyrs, confessors, and those who have finished the race are honored as living temples, and in their name an Ark is consecrated, marked, and honored.

God called them His friends in the flesh; Paul called them the temples of God. But far be it from us to say that because saints are temples, the Ark is now obsolete! Shall we now say the same of Christ whom the Jews crucified because they thought He was unnecessary?

text.text: III. The Ark as Tablet and Altar

text:
In the Old Covenant, the Ark held the tablets of stone, carved by God’s own finger. In the New Covenant, these two Ark and tablet are one. The Ark is now:

The Holy Table 

The Altar on which the body and blood of Christ are mystically offered.

Each Ark is movable, carved not to remain stagnant, but to be brought forth like the tabernacle in the wilderness. Upon it are inscribed:

The Name of the Lord, Alpha and Beta.

The image of the Holy Trinity above.

The Crucifixion of the Lord on the right.

The Virgin Theotokos on the left.

The righteous saint or martyr to whom the church is dedicated, whose name is written.

This is no idle artistry. This is theology in wood and stone, a visible creed, a tabernacle for the mystery of faith.

text.text: IV. The Law Fulfilled, Not Abolished

text:
Let not the ignorant say that the Law is dead. For Christ our Lord declared: “I did not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets, but to fulfill them” (Matt. 5:17). If this were not so, why would Peter and John continue to ascend to the Temple at the hour of prayer? (Acts 3:1)

Saint Paul too affirms this: “What agreement has the temple of God with idols?” (2 Cor. 6:16). Shall we now turn the ark into idolatry by forsaking it altogether? Nay. The temple still stands. The ark still speaks. The Law is fulfilled not discarded.

And if the Old Covenant were only a shadow, then the words of the Lord in Matthew 21:13 “My house shall be called a house of prayer” would have no place in the New. But He spoke them in the Temple, in Jerusalem, under the Gospel. Thus, the continuity is evident. The Old is not abolished but transfigured in the light of the New (2 Cor. 3:7–11; Col. 2:17; Heb. 10:1).

text.text: V. Temple and Ark: Inseparable Mysteries

text:
Let us mark carefully: the Ark is never separated from the Temple, whether in the Law, in the Prophets, or in the Revelation.

The heavens themselves proclaim this:

“The temple of God was opened in heaven, and the Ark of His covenant was seen in His temple” (Rev. 11:19).

How then shall we separate them on earth?

Those who scoff at the Ark, who reject its necessity, are not only irreverent they are ignorant. They betray a shallow understanding of Scripture, for they fail to see the thread that binds worship from Moses to Christ, from David to the apostles.

text.text: VI. Continuity of Ritual: Incense, Praise, and Garments

text:
Let us not despise the rituals ordained by God:

The rising of incense,

The psalms sung with drums and cymbals,

The choir vested in Gothic garments,

These are not distractions but divine links between the two covenants. As it is written in Ezekiel 3:10 and 2 Chronicles 20:21–22, praise and worship are the liturgical chain that unites the Torah and the Gospel.

And this unity is affirmed in the apostolic teaching:

“You are built upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles” (Eph. 2:20).

Our religion is not built upon empty rites or mystical philosophies. It is built upon revelation a divine disclosure, not man’s imagination.

text.text: VII. A Holy Building: The Human Temple

text:
Let none think we speak only of wood and stone. The human body is the building of God, and the conscience is the sanctuary within. Religion is not true unless it sanctifies the soul and brings the heart to moral order.

And yet, just as the heart requires the Word to live, the Church requires the Ark to breathe. The foundation is Christ laid by apostles, preserved by bishops, handed down to us.

Saint Paul too affirms this: “What agreement has the temple of God with idols?” (2 Cor. 6:16). Shall we now turn the ark into idolatry by forsaking it altogether? Nay. The temple still stands. The ark still speaks. The Law is fulfilled not discarded.

And if the Old Covenant were only a shadow, then the words of the Lord in Matthew 21:13 “My house shall be called a house of prayer” would have no place in the New. But He spoke them in the Temple, in Jerusalem, under the Gospel. Thus, the continuity is evident. The Old is not abolished but transfigured in the light of the New (2 Cor. 3:7–11; Col. 2:17; Heb. 10:1).
V. Temple and Ark: Inseparable Mysteries

Let us mark carefully: the Ark is never separated from the Temple, whether in the Law, in the Prophets, or in the Revelation.

The heavens themselves proclaim this:

“The temple of God was opened in heaven, and the Ark of His covenant was seen in His temple” (Rev. 11:19).

How then shall we separate them on earth?

Those who scoff at the Ark, who reject its necessity, are not only irreverent they are ignorant. They betray a shallow understanding of Scripture, for they fail to see the thread that binds worship from Moses to Christ, from David to the apostles.

Let us not despise the rituals ordained by God:

The rising of incense,

The psalms sung with drums and cymbals,

The choir vested in Gothic garments,

“You are built upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles” (Eph. 2:20).

and the Ark that carries the Word of the Covenant.

text:
Dearly beloved brethren,
Grace and peace be multiplied unto you, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit. Let us gather, as the faithful of old around the mountain, to receive the divine teaching not carved in stone this time, but written upon the tablets of the heart by the finger of God Himself. For we are gathered to meditate upon the Ark in the New Testament, that mystery of mysteries, preserved and revealed through the witness of our holy Ethiopian Church.

text.text: I.Prophetic Light Fulfilled in the New Covenant

text:
Let us begin where the prophets left off. The words of Malachi, “From the rising of the sun to its setting, My name will be great among the nations” (Mal. 1:11), are not idle poetry but fire-filled prophecy. He speaks not of the limited worship of the Old Covenant  confined to Jerusalem and the priestly bloodline but of the worship of the nations, which we now see in the Church of Christ.

The Apostle Luke confirms this in Acts 13:49, declaring, “The word of the Lord spread throughout the whole region.” These are not mere historical notes but the unfolding of the divine plan that the covenant would pass to the Gentiles, not because God has abandoned Israel, but because He has fulfilled what He began.

Thus the Ark, which once was hidden in the Holy of Holies, now manifests itself in every altar where Christ’s body and blood are offered. The wise men of the nations began this offering in Bethlehem (Matt. 2:11), bringing incense to the infant King. That same incense is now lifted daily in every Christian temple, a holy fragrance to Christ.

text.text: II. The True Sacrifice: His Body and His Blood

text:
Christ Himself, in the Upper Room, instituted a new sacrifice. “This is My Body, broken for you... this is My Blood, shed for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt. 26:26–28). The old sacrifices are no more. The blood of bulls and goats is silenced. In its place shines the Lamb of God.

What is this but the true fulfillment of the Ark’s purpose? In the Old Testament, it housed the Law and the manna now it houses the Giver of the Law and the Living Bread. The Ark in the New Testament is the altar where the Lord's own flesh and blood are offered, not symbolically but truly and mystically.

And who are they that resist this truth? Are they not like the sons of Judah who, though they hold the Scriptures, do not believe them? (cf. Matt. 26:16, John 12:1). Are they not those torn between two opinions unsure whether to worship in truth or in self-made religion?

Let the question of Elijah ring again: “How long will you be torn between two opinions?” If the Lord is God, follow Him. If the Ark is the throne of the Living God, then let us worship before it with holy fear and trembling.

Now behold, O faithful ones, the distinction given to Ethiopia! For while many nations turned from paganism to Christianity, few preserved the Ark with the reverence and knowledge given to our fathers.

In Egypt, it is called the tablet an object without which the Eucharist is not celebrated. Among the Greeks, Russians, and other Eastern Orthodox, the Andiminsion, a cloth bearing the crucifixion image, is revered in place of the Ark it remains stationary and sacred. Without it, they do not partake of the mysteries.

In the Roman Church, it is called Mensa, meaning “table.” These churches have adapted symbols, and while worthy of reverence, they do not possess the Ark as the Ethiopian Church does. Ethiopia alone that land of prophecy, of ancient faith, of holy Zion guards and honors the Ark not as a relic, but as a living throne.

And why is this important? Because the Ark, in both covenants, is the meeting place between God and man. In the Old, it was where God spoke from the cloud to Moses and Aaron. In the New, it is where the Word-made-Flesh is offered, where divine mercy is poured out in blood.

text.text: IV. Canon and Custom: Wisdom in Simplicity

text:
The Church, in her wisdom, does not bind the faithful to golden boxes and acacia wood alone. For it is written, “God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good” (Gen. 1:31). Therefore, the Ark of the New Covenant may be fashioned from other materials, depending on the ability of the local church.

If gold is available, it may be overlaid.

If acacia wood is not present, another wood may be used.

If precious stones or marble can be carved for the tablets, let it be done; if not, wood suffices.

If two tablets cannot be placed in one Ark, let one be used.

And if even the Ark cannot be made, the tablets themselves may be reverently used as the Ark. This is not a compromise, but a canon a sacred provision given by the Church.

text.text: V. Flesh and Blood: The Mercy Seat of the New Covenant

text:
“He who eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life” (John 6:54). This is not poetry. This is not metaphor. It is the very foundation of the New Covenant. The altar where His Precious Blood is poured is the Ark of Mercy. The priest who approaches it must do so with trembling, and the faithful must receive with awe.

Yet know this also: he who walks in righteousness shall be hated. Not only the wicked are criticized even the good are slandered. But let him not shrink back. As it is said, “A man who does not speak his heart is like one who is ill.” Speak the truth. Bear the reproach of righteousness. Guard the Ark.

text.text: VI. The Ethiopian Church: Faithful to Moses and Christ

text:
Let none dare say the Ethiopian Church pits Moses against Christ. She holds both in honor.

In Moses and in Christ,

In the Old and the New,

In parable and in faith,


She explains the unity of the covenant to all who inquire. As the History of the Ethiopian Church (p. 93) attests, she is not ignorant nor naive. She is ancient, apostolic, and full of wisdom.

And so, when we ask, “Why do we call the altar where His Precious Blood is poured an Ark?” the answer is simple: because it is. It is the throne of the Lamb. It is the new mercy seat. It is the holy place where God meets man.

text.text: , Where the Holy Flesh and Precious

text:
Brethren beloved in the Lord, grace and peace be multiplied unto you in the name of the Only Begotten, our Lord Jesus Christ, who was crucified, is risen, and shall come again in glory. Today, we consider a most sacred mystery, one which joins the threads of the old with the new, the shadow with the fulfillment, and the type with the true essence: Why do we call the holy altar, where the divine flesh and precious blood are consecrated, the Ark?

This is no idle naming. It is not poetry nor mere tradition. It is the inheritance of divine wisdom, rooted in history, sealed by prophecy, and confirmed by apostolic faith.

text.text: I. The Journey from Old to New: Ethiopia’s Holy Continuity

text:
Among the nations of the earth, one land shines forth uniquely in its witness: Ethiopia. Like the Gentiles, she did not cling to the shadows of the Old Testament; nor, like the Jews, did she wait in vain for a messiah to come. Ethiopia alone crossed the Jordan of faith not by abandoning the Old, but by allowing it to be fulfilled in the New.

Before she confessed the name of Christ, Ethiopia already embraced the temple ordinances. The Queen of Sheba journeyed to behold the wisdom of Solomon (1 Kings 10; 2 Chronicles 9), and her seed carried the fear of the Lord in their bones. They offered sacrifices, made pilgrimage to Jerusalem, and upheld the law. But in the fullness of time, she accepted the true Ark Jesus Christ, the Lamb of God. And thus, she calls the altar where He is offered not only altar but Ark.

Yet, brethren, do not confuse the Ark of the Covenant of Moses with this sacred Table. They are not alike in form, nor in size, nor in function. Rather, as the moon fades before the rising sun, so the old Ark yields its glory to the altar of the Lamb.

text.text: II. Contrast Between the Two Arks: The Shadow and the Fulfillment

text:
Let us look with spiritual eyes and discern:

The Old Testament Ark was a golden box, overlaid with gold within and without, carried by four priests, holding the tablets of the Law, and placed behind the veil.

The New Testament Ark our altar is simple in form, often wood or marble, borne by a single deacon with trembling hands, for on it lies the true Word made flesh, not on stone, but living and broken for our salvation.

The old Ark was a seat of divine speech God spoke to prophets from between the cherubim.

The altar, the new Ark, speaks not in thunder and cloud, but by the quiet descent of the Holy Spirit who transforms bread into Body, and wine into Blood.

On the old Ark was written the Law that condemned sin.

On the altar is written the name of mercy Himself: Jesus Christ, the Alpha and the Omega, who bore our sins.

text.text: III. A Universal Mystery Among the Churches

text:
Beloved, the name “Ark” is not confined to Ethiopia. Wherever the faith is preserved, wherever the Eucharist is celebrated as true flesh and true blood not as symbol, but as reality there you will find this mystery guarded:

In Egypt, the Copts call it Luh.

Among the Eastern Orthodox, it is the Antimension a holy cloth upon which no Divine Liturgy may be celebrated unless it bears the relics of the saints.

In Rome, they name it Mensa, the Holy Table.

In Armenia, Syria, India, Greece, Russia, Ukraine, and beyond, this sacred Table is known and revered.

text.text: IV. Why Do We Bow Before the Ark?

text:
We bow not to marble, nor to wood. We bow to Him who sits at the right hand of Majesty (Heb. 8:1), the One through whom all things exist (1 Cor. 8:6), who wears the title King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev. 19:16). He is the One whom angels veil their faces before, whom the cherubim serve, and the seraphim praise.

Thus we kneel before the altar because it holds Him who was nailed to the Cross on Good Friday, Him who said at the Last Supper: “This is my body… this is my blood.” The Ark now is not a relic of memory, but the place of the sacrifice of Calvary, re-presented in every Divine Liturgy.

When the Ark is lifted during baptism, no one bows to the mere church building. All worship is directed to Christ, the faithful and true Ark, who is both the High Priest and the Offering.

text.text: V. “At the Name of Jesus Every Knee Shall Bow”

text:
It is written (Phil. 2:10): “At the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth.” This is not mere figure. It is our instruction. The Ark, inscribed with His name, is like a silent preacher, crying out to us:
“What do you wait for, O man? Bow your knee!”

And we, with all things in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth, bow to Him who is enthroned at the right hand of God. The saints in glory, the angels in light, and the faithful on earth join in reverent worship before this mystery.

O faithful soul, do not gaze upon the altar with casual eyes. There stands the Ark of the New Covenant, wherein is not the Law, but the Lawgiver; not tablets of stone, but the Bread of Life. Let us then approach with awe and trembling, with reverence and love, for the One who gave Himself once upon the Cross, now gives Himself again upon the altar.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.

text.text: of Rama and the Martyrdom of Saint

text: Grace and peace be unto you, beloved brethren in Christ, children of the Apostolic and Orthodox faith, lovers of truth, and inheritors of the covenant. Today, we behold with awe and reverence the great deliverance wrought by the Archangel Saint Gabriel of Rama, whose glorious work is remembered on Hamle 19. Let us enter into this sacred mystery, not with idle ears, but with hearts awakened to marvel at the power of God displayed through His angels and saints.

text.text: The Burning Furnace and the Courage of a Child

text:
It was on this day Hamle 19 that the mighty Archangel Gabriel descended from heaven like lightning to save two humble but heroic souls: the child martyr Saint Kirkos and his mother Saint Eyeluta. These were not noble by birth nor mighty in flesh, but they were crowned with heaven’s glory by their steadfast faith. Behold the mercy of the Lord, who shows His strength through the weak and His majesty through the mouths of babes.

This child, Saint Kirkos, was not yet three years old only two years and nine months and yet he became a defender of the faith, an unshakable pillar against the idolatry of King Alexander. When his mother was pressured to bow to idols, she called upon her son to testify. And lo, the child spoke with divine wisdom: “We do not worship idols, for there is one eternal, unchangeable God, whom we worship.”

The tongue of the child became the trumpet of the Holy Spirit, silencing kings and terrifying demons. Just as the dumb ass rebuked the madness of Balaam, and the stones of Bethany cried out in worship, so too did this infant tongue preach the majesty of the Uncreated Light.

text.text: The Fury of the Tyrant and the Fire of Faith

text:
The cruel king, enraged by the boldness of the child, commanded that a vat of iron forty gallons in size be filled with boiling oil, tar, slag, and poisons, ignited with salt, wax, glue, and lead, until it rose with flames fourteen cubits high. The sound of it was like thunder, the light like the noonday sun. Into this were thrown the mother and her child, and thousands gathered to witness what was thought to be their end.

Yet Saint Kirkos, seeing his mother hesitate at the dreadful sight, became her teacher and comforter:

✤ “Do not fear the splendor of the fire, mother.”

✤ “The God who rescued Ananias, Azariah, and Mishael will also deliver us.”

✤ “He who saved Daniel from lions and Sosanna from evil men will not abandon us now.”

✤ “We must have the patience of Job, who lost all but praised the Lord still.”

This child rebuked his mother not with shame but with tenderness, teaching her to fix her eyes not on the passing fire but on the eternal reward. Then, lifting his eyes to heaven, he prayed with fierce intercession: “O Lord, do not let the enemy boast… strengthen my mother, and glorify Your name among the nations.”

text.text: The Descent of Saint Gabriel of Rama

text:
In the twinkling of an eye, the Archangel Gabriel, who stands before God, descended with heavenly might. The iron cauldron, filled with flame and destruction, was extinguished as dew from heaven. Not even a hair of the saints was touched, for the angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear Him (Psalm 34:7).

The king, astonished but hardened in heart, continued his cruelty: poisoning the child, blinding him with salt and pepper, and finally piercing both mother and child with fourteen sharp irons seven each. Yet Gabriel returned, healing the wounds and reviving the child again and again. When they tried to hang him, the angel loosed the ropes. When they beheaded him, heaven opened.

text:
On Tir 7 , Saint Kirkos completed his race. From his severed neck came not only blood and water, but milk and three crowns symbols of purity, divine favor, and the triple victory over the world, the flesh, and the devil. Our Lord appeared to him in glory, saying:

✤ “Peace be unto you, O virtuous Kirkos. I relieve you of your labor.”

✤ “In every place your name is called, no child will be slaughtered, no cattle diseased, no famine or plague shall remain.”

His body was not buried in the earth, but carried by the chariot of Elijah. His mother followed him the next day in martyrdom Tir 8 joining him in the heavenly joy.

text.text: The Theology of Suffering and Angelic Help

text:
These saints young Kirkos and holy Eyeluta demonstrated that Christianity is not merely a creed, but a calling to suffer, to die, and to rise. As the Apostle said, “Neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities… shall separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:38–39). They chose eternal life over the comforts of the world.

And through it all, Saint Gabriel did not depart from them. As the messenger of God, the protector of souls, and the comforter of the faithful, he appeared again and again until the saints had finished their course.

text.text: The Legacy of Saint Gabriel of Rama

text:
The miracles of Saint Gabriel continue in monasteries and churches where his name is invoked. He heals the sick, defends the suffering, and strengthens the believers. The same angel who stood with Daniel, who announced to Mary, who guided Tobit, now works among us.

Let us not forget his intercession, nor the lesson of Saint Kirkos:

“Take courage! Do not be afraid!”

We who suffer today for our faith must endure, knowing that this path leads to the eternal Kingdom. Let us pray continually to Saint Gabriel, that he might intercede for us, protect us from visible and invisible enemies, and lead us into the company of the saints.

text:
Another question that was asked. 

1. When was God born / when did He began to exist? (Not when Jesus Christ was born). 

2. How does heaven look like? 

Thank you!
፦ These are profound questions, my child, reaching into the very heart of our faith and the mysteries of God.  Let us explore them with reverence and humility.

text.text: 1. When was God born / when did He begin to exist?

text: The very notion of God being "born" is incompatible with our Orthodox understanding of His divine nature. God is eternal, without beginning or end. He is the Uncreated Creator, the Alpha and Omega, as revealed in the Holy Scriptures (Revelation 1:8, 21:6). He is existence itself, the source of all being.  Time, as we perceive it, is a creation of God, existing within His eternal embrace.  Therefore, to ask when God began is akin to asking what lies outside of existence itself - a question that transcends human comprehension.  The Church Fathers, like St. Gregory of Nyssa, explored this concept of God's timeless eternity, emphasizing His transcendence beyond the limitations of our created understanding.  We can only approach this mystery with awe and reverence, acknowledging the limitations of our finite minds in grasping the infinite nature of God.

The nature of Heaven, the Kingdom of God, is another profound mystery.  The Scriptures offer glimpses, describing it as a place of unimaginable beauty, joy, and communion with God.  St. Paul speaks of things "eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, the things which God has prepared for those who love Him” (1 Corinthians 2:9).  The Book of Revelation speaks of a new heaven and a new earth, a city of gold, and the presence of God illuminating all things.

However, these are symbolic representations, attempts to convey the inexpressible reality of dwelling in God's presence.  We should be cautious about interpreting these descriptions literally. The essence of Heaven lies not in its physical characteristics, but in the perfect union with God, the source of all love, joy, and peace.  It is a state of being, a transformation of our very selves into the likeness of Christ, free from the limitations of sin and death.  The Church Fathers often emphasized this transformative aspect of salvation, describing Heaven as a process of theosis, becoming partakers of the divine nature.

Therefore, rather than focusing on what Heaven looks like, we should concentrate on what it means to be in communion with God.  Through prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and participation in the sacraments of the Church, we begin to experience a foretaste of this heavenly Kingdom here on earth.  This journey of spiritual growth, guided by the wisdom of the Church and the grace of the Holy Spirit, prepares us for the ultimate joy of eternal life in the presence of God.  

May these reflections illuminate your understanding, my child. Do not hesitate to ask further questions.  May God guide you on your spiritual journey.

text.text:
May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.
