text.text: In the Footsteps of Glory: Why Are the Names of the Saints Written on the Altar Ark?

text: Brethren in the household of faith, you who walk in the radiant path of the apostles and martyrs, receive the peace of God which surpasses all understanding. Today, we are invited to contemplate a most profound mystery of our Orthodox tradition why the names of the saints are inscribed upon the Ark, that sacred table upon which the Body and Blood of the Lord are mystically offered. This teaching, drawn directly from Holy Scripture and the witness of the Church Fathers, is a wellspring of deep reverence and theological truth.

text.text: The Altar Ark and the Names of the Saints: Witnesses of His Name
Heaven’s Gates Bear Names—So Does the Altar

text:
In the final vision of glory, the heavenly Jerusalem reveals its twelve gates each one named after the twelve apostles (Rev. 21:24). These names shine eternally on the entrance to paradise. If heaven itself bears their names, shall not the earthly Ark, which participates in heavenly mysteries, also bear them?

Thus, the altar ark becomes the visible image of heaven itself, a dwelling where saints are not only remembered but joined to us. It is a declaration that they are not dead, but alive in Christ, surrounding us as a cloud of witnesses.

text.text: Christ, the True Ark of the New Testament

text:
Saint Ephraim the Syrian, in his luminous wisdom, unveils that Christ Himself is the Ark:

“The Ark, carved from indestructible wood and covered with gold inside and out, represents the Word of God, who is indestructible and unchanging.”

The indestructible wood is the humanity of Christ, taken from the Virgin’s flesh.

The gold inside and out is His divinity uncreated, eternal.

The union of wood and gold without mixture or confusion is a perfect image of the union of God and man in the one Person of Christ.

This Ark Jesus Christ entered into the Holy of Holies not made with hands. He bore our griefs, paid our ransom, and shed His blood. At Calvary, He stood between God and man, reconciling both through His cross (Isaiah 53:12, Luke 23:34).

Now, in the Eucharistic mystery, this same Ark Christ offers Himself to those who repent, confess, and receive Him. On this Ark, the saints’ names are written, for they have partaken of His suffering and now reign with Him in glory.

(Part 4)

In the Footsteps of Glory: Why Are the Names of the Saints Written on the Altar Ark?

Brethren in the household of faith, you who walk in the radiant path of the apostles and martyrs, receive the peace of God which surpasses all understanding. Today, we are invited to contemplate a most profound mystery of our Orthodox tradition why the names of the saints are inscribed upon the Ark, that sacred table upon which the Body and Blood of the Lord are mystically offered. This teaching, drawn directly from Holy Scripture and the witness of the Church Fathers, is a wellspring of deep reverence and theological truth.

The Altar Ark and the Names of the Saints: Witnesses of His Name

The altar ark is not merely a table but a mystical throne, a heavenly place upon the earth, a symbol of the New Covenant where divine and human nature are united in the Eucharist. On this holy ark, the names of the saints are inscribed—not arbitrarily, but as a visible sign of the invisible communion between Christ and His faithful ones.

“Those who were faithful to His name until death…”

These are they:

The beheaded, like Saint John the Baptist (Luke 9:9), whose neck bore the blade for the truth;

The stoned, like Saint Stephen, the protomartyr, who cried out for mercy even as the rocks flew (Acts 7:54–60);

The suffering, those who bore shame, imprisonment, and torture for the name of Christ (Acts 4:22);

The co-sufferers, who shared in the passion of the Lord, being made like Him in death (Rom. 8:17);

The faithful finishers, like Saint Paul, who declared, “I have kept the faith, I have finished the race” (2 Tim. 4:7).

These names are not written on the altar as a mere ritualistic gesture. No! They are written as an eternal confession of honor a love that does not forget those whom the Father Himself has honored. For did not the Lord say:

“If anyone serves Me, the Father will honor him” (John 12:26)?

What greater honor than to be remembered in the very place where Christ, the slain Lamb, is made present? What greater intimacy than to be inscribed on the very table of sacrifice?

Heaven’s Gates Bear Names—So Does the Altar

In the final vision of glory, the heavenly Jerusalem reveals its twelve gates each one named after the twelve apostles (Rev. 21:24). These names shine eternally on the entrance to paradise. If heaven itself bears their names, shall not the earthly Ark, which participates in heavenly mysteries, also bear them?

Thus, the altar ark becomes the visible image of heaven itself, a dwelling where saints are not only remembered but joined to us. It is a declaration that they are not dead, but alive in Christ, surrounding us as a cloud of witnesses.

Christ, the True Ark of the New Testament

Saint Ephraim the Syrian, in his luminous wisdom, unveils that Christ Himself is the Ark:

The indestructible wood is the humanity of Christ, taken from the Virgin’s flesh.

The gold inside and out is His divinity uncreated, eternal.

The union of wood and gold without mixture or confusion is a perfect image of the union of God and man in the one Person of Christ.

This Ark Jesus Christ entered into the Holy of Holies not made with hands. He bore our griefs, paid our ransom, and shed His blood. At Calvary, He stood between God and man, reconciling both through His cross (Isaiah 53:12, Luke 23:34).

Now, in the Eucharistic mystery, this same Ark Christ offers Himself to those who repent, confess, and receive Him. On this Ark, the saints’ names are written, for they have partaken of His suffering and now reign with Him in glory.

Continues 👇🏾

text.text: The Mother of God: The Golden Ark

text:
Saint Yared, that holy tongue of Ethiopia, proclaimed:

“You are purer than the pure, like an ark made of unblemished wood adorned with gold... the chosen Virgin.”

If Christ is the Ark, then Mary is the Ark’s Ark, the dwelling of the Incarnate Word. She is golden both within and without, sanctified in body and soul by the Holy Spirit. Her womb bore the living Word as once the Ark bore the tablets of stone. To honor her is to honor Him who dwelled within her. To ignore her is to wound the One she bore.

Let no man say he honors the King while despising His throne.

text.text: All Believers: Living Arks of the Spirit

text:
Saint Paul, that pillar of fire, reminds us that we too are arks temples of the Holy Spirit:

“Do you not know that you are the temple of God?” (1 Cor. 3:16–17)

Each Christian, baptized into Christ, becomes a dwelling of the divine. As the Ark carried the presence of God in the wilderness, so too do we carry His presence in our very bodies. This is no metaphor—it is a mystery and a responsibility.

text.text: In Conclusion: A Communion of Names

text:
To write the names of the saints upon the altar ark is not an innovation it is a theological act. It testifies to:

Their faithfulness,

Their union with Christ the Ark,

Their presence among us,

And their eternal glory written also in the Book of Life (Rev. 13:8).

Let this be our joy: that in honoring them, we honor the One who called them, crowned them, and made them partakers of His eternal liturgy. May their memory be eternal, and may their names written on the altar be written also upon our hearts.

text: By the grace of God and with the wisdom of the Holy Fathers, let us now enter into the divine mystery that surrounds the Ark and the Name of God, as taught in the Scriptures and illuminated by the holy teachings of the Church. Let the reader not approach this teaching with worldly reason, but with the reverent mind of faith, for the truths here are not carnal, but spiritual hidden in symbols, revealed through obedience.

text.text: The Ark Is Not a Mere Sculpture

text:
Many today, in their ignorance or contempt, refer to the Holy Ark as a mere “sculpture”a lifeless form made by human hands. But they err gravely, for they fail to recognize the mystery God has woven into its form. The Ark of the Covenant, as commanded by God Himself, was to be fashioned not for artistic display, but to carry His divine name and presence. It was not man who devised this, but God who commanded Moses:

“Make it like the first”  an instruction not born of Moses’ imagination but from the voice of the Lord (cf. Exodus 25:10, 26:33-34).

Indeed, the Ark bore the very name of God. A sculpture does not bear such a weight. A sculpture is mute and common. But the Ark is sanctified by the inscribed and indwelling Name. Thus, St. Paul never once diminished it by calling it a “sculpture,” but always revered it as the Ark of God.

text.text: The Name of God and His Angel

text:
In the book of Exodus, the Lord speaks plainly:

“Behold, I send an angel before you... Do not provoke him, for he will not pardon your transgressions, for My Name is in him.” (Exodus 23:20–22)

The angel who led the Israelites bore the Name of God. He did not merely carry a mission but embodied the authority of the Lord. To rebel against him was to rebel against God Himself.
So too with the Ark. If the angel bore the Name, how much more could the Ark upon which the glory of God rested? For this reason, to disrespect the Ark was not a small thing it was to profane the Name of the Lord.

text.text: The Ark as a Witness to Worship

text:
The inscription of the Name upon the Ark is a divine testimony:

It is not a man-made form we bow to, but the indwelling Name of the Lord.

Even as we kneel before the Ark in the New Covenant, we are not idolaters. We are those who, like Moses and the prophets, worship in spirit and in truth. We bow not to wood or gold, but to the mystery of God’s presence, as made manifest in His Name.

Just as the Israelites bowed before the Ark in the Tabernacle, so too do we today only now in the full light of the Gospel.

Our forefathers in the faith, instructed by the wisdom of the Holy Spirit, discovered divine names inscribed in sacred places even upon the wings of angels. Among these were names such as:

Alpha and Beta (symbols of beginning and word)

Yehuda, Yod, Ahia, Sherahia, El Shaddai names that carry rich theological weight


These names are not random utterances; they are divine titles, potent against demons, as referenced in the writings of Exodus 2:14 and Revelation 21.
To misunderstand or ignore them is to pray in vain. For how can one call upon a Name they do not know?

Thus, our prayers are only true when we recognize that these names are not of men or angels, but are of God Himself.

👉🏾👉🏾👉🏾The #Ark and the #Name of #God
  
(Part 5)

By the grace of God and with the wisdom of the Holy Fathers, let us now enter into the divine mystery that surrounds the Ark and the Name of God, as taught in the Scriptures and illuminated by the holy teachings of the Church. Let the reader not approach this teaching with worldly reason, but with the reverent mind of faith, for the truths here are not carnal, but spiritual hidden in symbols, revealed through obedience.

The Ark Is Not a Mere Sculpture

Many today, in their ignorance or contempt, refer to the Holy Ark as a mere “sculpture”a lifeless form made by human hands. But they err gravely, for they fail to recognize the mystery God has woven into its form. The Ark of the Covenant, as commanded by God Himself, was to be fashioned not for artistic display, but to carry His divine name and presence. It was not man who devised this, but God who commanded Moses:

“Make it like the first”  an instruction not born of Moses’ imagination but from the voice of the Lord (cf. Exodus 25:10, 26:33-34).

Indeed, the Ark bore the very name of God. A sculpture does not bear such a weight. A sculpture is mute and common. But the Ark is sanctified by the inscribed and indwelling Name. Thus, St. Paul never once diminished it by calling it a “sculpture,” but always revered it as the Ark of God.

The Name of God and His Angel

In the book of Exodus, the Lord speaks plainly:

“Behold, I send an angel before you... Do not provoke him, for he will not pardon your transgressions, for My Name is in him.” (Exodus 23:20–22)

The angel who led the Israelites bore the Name of God. He did not merely carry a mission but embodied the authority of the Lord. To rebel against him was to rebel against God Himself.
So too with the Ark. If the angel bore the Name, how much more could the Ark upon which the glory of God rested? For this reason, to disrespect the Ark was not a small thing it was to profane the Name of the Lord.

The Ark as a Witness to Worship

The inscription of the Name upon the Ark is a divine testimony:

It is not a man-made form we bow to, but the indwelling Name of the Lord.

Even as we kneel before the Ark in the New Covenant, we are not idolaters. We are those who, like Moses and the prophets, worship in spirit and in truth. We bow not to wood or gold, but to the mystery of God’s presence, as made manifest in His Name.

Just as the Israelites bowed before the Ark in the Tabernacle, so too do we today only now in the full light of the Gospel.

The Hidden Names and Mysteries

Our forefathers in the faith, instructed by the wisdom of the Holy Spirit, discovered divine names inscribed in sacred places even upon the wings of angels. Among these were names such as:

Alpha and Beta (symbols of beginning and word)

Yehuda, Yod, Ahia, Sherahia, El Shaddai names that carry rich theological weight


These names are not random utterances; they are divine titles, potent against demons, as referenced in the writings of Exodus 2:14 and Revelation 21.
To misunderstand or ignore them is to pray in vain. For how can one call upon a Name they do not know?

Thus, our prayers are only true when we recognize that these names are not of men or angels, but are of God Himself.

Continues 👇🏾

text.text: The Coming of the False Messiah and the True

text:
The Apocalypse warns of a counterfeit Messiah who shall command, “Write my name on your foreheads”and his number is 666 (Revelation 13:18).

This false Christ mimics the true yet his name is deception.

Contrast this with the Lord who wrote His Name upon the Ark, the angel’s wings, and now upon our hearts through baptism and the Eucharist.
Let us be wise, then, to discern between the authentic inscription of God’s Name and the false imitations of the devil.

text.text: In the New Testament: Ark and Worship

text:
St. Paul affirmed the existence and holiness of the Ark. He did not say “we are the Ark,” as modern confusion suggests. He upheld the reverence due to the Ark because God’s Name was upon it.

The 318 Holy Fathers of the Council (Nicea) determined that the Ark should be both movable and immovable capable of being borne like the original, but fixed in sanctity. Wherever it stands, there we bow (Psalm 131:7):

“We worship at His footstool; we worship where He is.”

This is not idolatry it is obedience to God’s pattern of revealed worship.

The Name of God is unchanging from the Torah to the Gospel, from yesterday to today. What was sacred in the days of Moses remains sacred in Christ, for:

“At the name of Jesus, every knee shall bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.” (Philippians 2:10)

This Name is not a mere label. It is power, it is presence, it is person.

Let no one come to rule over us with foreign doctrines, saying the Ark is no longer needed, or that its reverence is idolatrous. Such people neither understand the mystery nor fear the Name.

We worship the Ark not because it is an object, but because it carries the Name.
We worship at the footstool of our Lord, not because it is material, but because He stands there.
We worship not in ignorance, but according to the wisdom passed down from the Fathers.

text:
Grace and peace be multiplied to you, O beloved in Christ, children of grace and heirs of the promise! Today we reflect with trembling reverence upon the sacred words our risen Lord spoke to Mary Magdalene:

“I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God” (John 20:17).

These divine words, uttered by the Word made flesh, are not simple utterances they are thunders of heaven echoing the mystery of the Incarnation, the unity of divine and human nature in the person of Jesus Christ. Let us open this mystery with care, not with the boldness of flesh but with the meekness of faith.

text.text: 1. The Context of the Word: Resurrection and Revelation

text:
Mary Magdalene stood weeping at the tomb, and the Lord Jesus, having risen from the dead by His own authority, appeared to her and declared this profound saying. Why did He speak in such a manner?

He who is very God of very God, consubstantial with the Father, speaks not out of inferiority, but out of the reality of His incarnation. The flesh He assumed born of the Virgin, taken from creation He now brings into glory. It is as man that He says, “I ascend to my God.” It is as the Incarnate Word, the Theanthropos (Θεάνθρωπος), God-man, that He acknowledges the Father as His God.

The Lord Jesus Christ, in His divine nature, is co-equal, co-eternal with the Father. “I and the Father are one,” He declares (John 10:30). But in His human nature, in the form of a servant, He bows in obedience and humility, not because He is less than God, but because He has truly united Himself to our nature.

He does not say “our God” lest He be counted among the creatures. Rather, He distinguishes between His eternal sonship and the adoptive sonship of the disciples. The phrase “my God” is the voice of His humanity; “your God” is the declaration of our adoption.

text.text: 3. “My Father and Your Father” The Twofold Sonship

text:
“I ascend to my Father and your Father.”

Here the distinction is yet clearer. The Father is the natural Father of Christ, and the gracious Father of the disciples. Christ is the Son by nature, eternally begotten of the Father “Today I have begotten You” (Psalm 2:7) while we are sons by adoption, drawn near through grace. He is the Only-Begotten, we are the many brethren (Romans 8:29).

He did not say “I ascend to our Father,” lest He obscure this essential distinction. His is the eternal generation; ours is the gracious gift. His filiation is from the essence of the Father; ours is by the will of the Father and the work of the Son.

text.text: 4. The Eternal Generation of the Son

text:
Before the foundation of the world, before the stars were set in their place, before time began, the Son was begotten of the Father. Not made. Not created. Begotten.

“Before the morning star, I have begotten You.” (Ps. 110:3)

“You are My Son, today I have begotten You.” (Ps. 2:7)

Here the mystery of divine begetting reveals itself. Just as human parents beget children of their nature, so the Father begets the Son of His own divine nature. The Son is of the same essence (homoousios) with the Father, Light from Light, True God from True God. This is the faith of the Church, confessed in the Creed: Begotten, not made.

text.text: 5. Not a Creature, but the Creator

text: Jesus Christ is not a creature, for no creature can create. The Son is called Creator, because He shares the nature of the Father who creates. “All that the Father has is Mine” (John 16:15). He created the very flesh He assumed from the Virgin. Thus, He is not created, even in His humanity, but born in the flesh, without sin, and without the will of man.

text.text: 6. The Analogy of the Heart, the Word, and the Breath

text:
Let us employ a humble image, though all images fall short of divine mystery.

The Father is like the heart.

The Son is like the Word spoken from the heart.
The Holy Spirit is like the breath that proceeds from the heart and carries the Word.

This analogy does not explain the Trinity, but gives a simple entry into understanding unity in distinction. Just as the heart gives rise to the word and breath without division, so God is one in essence, three in persons.

When the Lord says, “I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God,” He speaks as the one mediator between God and man Jesus Christ, who took on flesh and glorified it.

He brings our humanity into the heavens. He ascends not as a disembodied spirit, but as the crucified and risen Lord, bearing in His glorified body the marks of His Passion. And He declares that the One who is His Father by nature is our Father by grace. The One who is His God according to His humanity is our God both in spirit and body.

We are not children of God by nature. We are dust, clay molded by the hand of the Creator.

“O Lord, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter” (Isaiah 64:8).

But now, by the will of the Father and the blood of the Son, we are called children. “See what love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God and so we are” (1 John 3:1). The apostles are children of grace, not by natural begetting, but by the gift of adoption.

text:

He, the natural Son, speaks of His flesh: “My God”. He, the divine Word, speaks of His eternal origin: “My Father”. We, who are redeemed, call God our Father not by nature but by mercy.

He is our shepherd, our keeper, our helper. He is the eternal Son who made us sons by grace.

Let us honor His divine humility and glorify His saving Ascension. Let us, like Mary Magdalene, hear His voice and cling to Him not in the flesh, but in spirit and truth.

text: Grace and peace to you all in the Name of our Lord and God, Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of the Father, who by His passion and resurrection restored what was lost in Adam, and granted sonship to the forsaken. Today we reflect deeply on the mystery of His promise: “I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you” (John 14:18). This word, uttered on the eve of His passion, is not a mere comfort but a revelation of the divine plan of redemption, of resurrection, and of the restoration of true life in Christ. Let us now delve with awe into the treasure that is hidden in this sacred teaching.

The Lord’s words “I have not left you to be children of the dead” pierce the veil that covers the true condition of fallen man. Who are the children of the dead, if not all those who live apart from the resurrection, who abide in sin and the dominion of death, who know not the power of the Cross?

When Christ was arrested, His disciples fled. Even Peter, the boldest among them, denied Him. And why? Because they still bore the fear of death, and they had not yet become partakers of the resurrection. In this state, they were as orphans bereft of the Father’s Spirit, scattered like sheep, their courage buried with their hope. As it is written: “Then all the disciples forsook Him and fled” (Matt. 26:56).

text.text: 2. Christ Promises to Come Again Not Only at the End, But in the Resurrection

text:
Our Lord did not say merely that He will return at the end of time. No. He assured them, “I am coming to you” that is, even within days. His return was fulfilled not merely at Pentecost or in His second coming, but in His resurrection from the dead. He came again in glory, but veiled in humility. Not with flaming chariots, but through locked doors, bearing wounds in His hands and feet.

He who had died appeared alive, not as a spirit, but in a body glorified no longer subject to hunger or fatigue or decay. “A little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live” (John 14:19). This is not poetry it is power. The disciples did live, not merely with biological breath, but with the Spirit of the living Christ breathed into them (John 20:22). He made them partakers of divine life.

text.text: 3. The Apostles' Baptism Came After the Resurrection

text:
Some think the apostles were already baptized before Christ’s death, perhaps when He washed their feet. But what says the Scripture? A child cannot be born without a father. The Spirit of adoption, the gift of divine sonship, was not yet given for the atonement had not yet been made.

Only after Christ had crushed the gates of hell and offered His blood upon the altar of the Cross did He give His apostles new birth through the Holy Spirit. This was their true baptism not a ceremonial washing, but a spiritual resurrection.

As written in the Book of the Covenant, “Thomas, Matthew, and John were baptized [after the resurrection]... and the Lord said to them, ‘You are the children of God by the Holy Spirit.’” The Church, therefore, rightly teaches that the apostles’ baptism was completed on the day of resurrection, for “Who would have said?” who could dare claim that the Spirit was given before Christ’s blood was poured out for the remission of sins?

7. Scriptural Confirmation of the New Baptism by Christ’s Blood

Let no soul be deceived the power of this baptism is in the blood of Christ, not in water alone. The apostles became children of God not at the Jordan, but at Calvary and the empty tomb. Hear now the Scriptures:

“He purchased the Church with His own blood” (Acts 20:28)

“We have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Heb. 10:10)

“Redeemed… with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Pet. 1:18-19)

“He washed us from our sins in His own blood” (Rev. 1:5)

“You were slain and have redeemed us to God by Your blood” (Rev. 5:9)

These are not poetic verses but divine testimony. The blood is the seal of the covenant, the door of adoption, and the fountain of life.

Conclusion: “You Will See Me… and You Will Live Also” (John 14:19)

Let the world scoff; let unbelievers doubt the resurrection. But for those who see with eyes of faith, Christ has not left us as orphans. He has come again, and again, and again at every altar, in every baptism, in every outpouring of the Spirit.

He who once said “I will not leave you as children of the dead” has fulfilled His word in full. The apostles saw, believed, and lived. And through them, the Church lives, the saints live, and we, too, are made sons and daughters of the resurrection.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.

To bend the knee is to confess the majesty of God. To fall on our face is to declare, with our body, the smallness of man. Prostration is not only outward but inward a bowing of the soul.

“You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve.” (Matt. 4:10)

“God is Spirit, and those who worship Him must worship in spirit and in truth.” (John 4:24)

It is fitting that the faithful prostrate once or thrice before prayer, and many of the fathers prescribe 36 prostrations daily except on the Sabbath, Pentecost, and the major feasts, when joy eclipses mourning.

“Ethiopia has stretched out her hands to God.” (Ps. 67:31)

The uplifted hands are more than gesture they are testimony. They are the sign of power (Ex. 9:29), of supplication (1 Kings 8:22), of justice (Isa. 25:11), of humility (Jer. 4:31), and of creation itself (Isa. 45:12).

To lift the hand is to say, "I have nothing, Lord, but Thee. I surrender. I wait. I hunger."

Let the prayerful soul:

Give glory to God in the highest,

Honor the Ever-Virgin who bore Him,

Revere the life-giving Cross on which our salvation was accomplished.

Prayer must be mingled with repentance, dressed in humility, offered in faith, and guarded with perseverance.

O brethren, what dignity is ours, that we are permitted to speak to the One before whom angels veil their faces! Let us not squander such grace. Let us not approach casually what prophets and patriarchs longed for with tears.

Let your homes be altars. Let your tongues be censors. Let your hearts burn continually like incense before the Lord.

As it is written:

“Pray without ceasing.” (1 Thess. 5:17)

For he who prays never perishes. He who prays draws near to the fire and is not consumed but is made flame.

👉 Question፦ In 1 Corinthians 11:14 it says"14 Doth not even nature itself teach you, that, if a man have long hair, it is a shame unto him?"  Does this mean that it is a sin for men to have long hair?

Answer፦ Beloved child in Christ, peace be unto you. Your question is wise and sincere, and it shows a heart that longs to understand the will of God. Let us walk together in the light of the Scriptures.

The verse you asked about - “Doth not even nature itself teach you, that, if a man have long hair, it is a shame unto him?” (1 Corinthians 11:14) - is not a random comment by the Apostle Paul. It is part of a greater teaching about order, distinction, and honor in how we present ourselves before God and before others.

In Corinth, there was confusion among new believers - many of whom had just come out of pagan religions - about the proper appearance and behavior of men and women. Paul is not merely talking about fashion, but about preserving the God-given distinction between male and female, a distinction rooted in creation itself: “male and female created He them” (Genesis 1:27).

So, does this mean that it is always a sin for a man to have long hair? The answer depends on the reason. In general, yes, the Apostle is warning that men should not take on a feminine appearance, because doing so confuses the natural and spiritual order God has established. In most cases, growing long hair without cause reflects vanity, pride, or rebellion, and this is what the Apostle condemns.

Now, you may ask, what about the Nazarites - men like Samson, who never cut their hair? (Numbers 6:5). This was not a personal choice for fashion or identity. It was a special, divine calling under the Old Covenant. The long hair of a Nazarite was not about appearance - it was a symbol of separation from the world and total devotion to God. It was rare, specific, and done with the blessing of God.

Today, under the New Covenant and the fullness of life in the Church, such vows are no longer practiced in the same way. A man cannot simply declare himself a "Nazarite" to justify long hair. True spiritual devotion today is expressed not by growing hair, but by growing in repentance, obedience, and humility - under the care of the Church and the guidance of a spiritual father.

So, the teaching remains: a man should appear as a man, honoring the image God gave him. Let us not follow the confusion of the world, which seeks to erase the beauty of that difference. Let every part of our life - our dress, our behavior, our hair - glorify God and reflect who He made us to be.

“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40).

Now, my beloved, as you reflect on this truth, how will you begin today to bring your outward appearance into harmony with the inner life Christ is calling you to live?

Beloved in Christ,
May the grace of the Lord be with you, and may your souls be lifted by the truth that prayer is not merely a cry from the lips, but a fire from the heart an ascent to the throne of the Most High. Let us now, with reverent minds and attentive spirits, meditate upon the holy requirements of prayer, that we may not offer incense in vain, but as fragrant oblations received in the heavenly courts.

Prayer, dearly beloved, is not merely the recitation of words or the performance of ritual. It is the elevation of the heart, the pouring out of the soul, and the intimate discourse between the creature and his Creator. It arises not from a narrow heart but from a broad mind, a mind that embraces both the temporal and the eternal, the needs of the body and the cry of the spirit.

Indeed, prayer is the breath of the soul, and its very life. Just as the body cannot live without air, so the soul cannot survive without communion with God. In this light, we begin to see that prayer is not optional; it is essential.

text.text: II. The Example of Hannah (1 Samuel 1:20)

text:
Consider the blessed Hannah, whose soul was heavy with sorrow and whose womb was barren. Yet she did not waver in faith. Continued 👇🏾

VI. The Fourth Requirement: Forgiveness and Mercy

text:
Hear this well, O Christian soul: he who does not forgive, shall not be forgiven. How dare we, stained with many offenses, approach the throne of grace while holding grudges in our heart?

“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” (Matthew 5:7)

To pray is to enter the presence of the One who forgave His murderers. Can we come to such a Lord with hatred in our hearts? Never!

Forgiveness opens the gate of heaven; bitterness shuts it. Let us remember always: if we refuse to hear the cry of the poor, God will refuse to hear our own (Proverbs 21:13).

text.text: VII. The Fifth Requirement: Persistence and Patience in Prayer

text:
It is not enough to pray once and walk away. The Lord teaches us to pray without ceasing, to knock continually, and not to lose heart.

“If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you.” (John 15:7)

God delays not to frustrate, but to refine. He waits not because He is indifferent, but because He desires our persistence to purify our desires. The prayer of the impatient is like a spark in the wind—it flickers and dies.

text.text: VIII. The Sixth Requirement: Tears of Contrition

text:
What does it mean to pray with tears? It is the prayer of the soul that has truly encountered its own poverty and God's immeasurable mercy. Tears are not weakness; they are the overflowing of divine sorrow and love. Saint Ephrem wept so much in prayer that his tears became his theology. Tears cleanse where words fail.

Let us then not be ashamed to cry before our Father for the proud heart remains dry, but the humble heart is watered with tears, and those tears ascend like incense to the throne of God.

Prayer is no light matter. It is the highest work of the soul. It requires faith, purity, love, forgiveness, persistence, and often, tears. These are not burdens, but graces. They are not obstacles, but wings by which prayer ascends to heaven.

Let us not rush to speak before preparing our hearts. Let us not dare to approach with unclean lips and divided souls. But let us walk the narrow way, embracing the sacred requirements, and there at the mercy seat of God we shall find not silence, but answer.

The Assumption and Resurrection of the Holy Virgin Mary
(Part 1)

text: Grace to you, beloved of God, who cling with reverence to the traditions of the Apostles and who call blessed she who bore the Incarnate Word, the Virgin Mary. Today we unfold, as one would a scroll of gold and pearl, the divine mystery of Filseta the Dormition, Resurrection, and Assumption of the Most Blessed Virgin Mary, the Mother of God. Let every soul approach with trembling awe, for we speak not of earthly matters but of the hidden glory God has revealed through His chosen vessel.

The word Filseta (ፍልሰታ) arises from the Gë`ëz root felese, meaning to be born but not an ordinary birth. This is a spiritual rebirth, a passage not from womb to world, but from earth to the heavenly Jerusalem. In the context of Our Lady, it signifies the resurrection and glorious assumption of the Virgin Mary into heaven, body and soul a divine migration from Gethsemane to Paradise, from the grave to the Tree of Life.

Her Filseta is not myth or fable, but the triumphant exodus of the Queen of Heaven, who, having completed her earthly course in holiness, was not left to decay in the tomb, but was raised and glorified by her Son, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

text.text: Her Earthly Journey: A Life Crowned with Grace

text:
O you who ponder the majesty of God, consider how He prepared a dwelling fit for His own coming!

The Virgin Mary spent three years in the house of her parents, Joachim and Anna.

Twelve years she dwelt in the Temple, living in purity and prayer.

For nine months, the Word became flesh within her, in the house of Joseph.

She walked with her divine Son for thirty-three years and three months, serving not only as His Mother, but as His first and most faithful disciple.

After His ascension, she lived fourteen years under the care of the Apostle John the Theologian.

She reposed on Tir 21, in the 49th year of our Lord, at the age of sixty-four having fulfilled her ministry, not with noise or sword, but with meekness, humility, and glory unmatched.

At her death, the Apostles, moved by love and duty, bore her body to Gethsemane. Yet the enemies of Christ, blind with envy and hardened of heart, rose again in hatred. “Let us burn her body,” they cried, “so that none may claim she has risen, as they say of her Son.”

Among them was a Jew named Taufania, who dared lay hands upon her sacred bier. But behold the judgment of God! An angel struck him, and his hands were made lifeless. Thus did heaven proclaim: “Touch not the Ark of God!”

Then the Lord, descending with Saint John, took His Mother on a cloud of glory, placing her beneath the Tree of Life in Paradise. But the Apostles, not knowing this mystery, continued to pray and fast, from Tir 21 until Nehase.

text.text: The Apostles' Fast and the Revelation of Glory

text:
From Nehase 1, the Holy Apostles entered into a profound fast, setting themselves apart, weeping and entreating the Lord with tears. Could they remain silent while she who gave birth to the Savior lay hidden from their eyes? No! Their love compelled them to call upon the God who hears.

After fourteen days, on Nehase 14, the Lord, who forgets not the cries of His saints, answered. He revealed to them the body of the Virgin, full of light and free from decay. With hymns and incense they buried her again, not in sorrow, but in wonder.

text:
And on the third day, Nehase 16, a miracle beyond speech occurred:
By the authority of her Son, the Virgin Mary rose from the dead, as He had on the third day.
As Christ is the firstborn from the dead, the firstfruits of them that sleep, so too His Mother was raised not merely as a token of her holiness, but as a prophecy of the Church’s future glory.

Saint Ephrem bears witness:

“The Virgin Mary, the Mother of God, was resurrected from the dead, like her Son, the Son of God.”
Her resurrection is not like that of Lazarus, to die again. No! Hers is a resurrection of glory and immortality a bodily glorification that does not wait for the general resurrection at the end of time.

text.text: Saint Thomas and the Vision of Her Ascension

text:
As with the Lord’s resurrection, so too with His Mother, the Apostle Thomas arrived late. Yet he was blessed beyond the rest, for he saw what others did not.

The Virgin, ascending in heavenly light, turned to him and said:

“Do not be sad! Do not be sad, for you have seen my resurrection, which your fellow apostles did not see, but rejoice!”

This was not rebuke but divine favor. For through Thomas, we too have seen.

text.text: The Witness of the Prophets and the Church

text:
A thousand years before this glory, her ancestor David foresaw and declared:

“The Queen stands at Your right hand, arrayed in gold” (Ps. 44:9 LXX).

And Saint Yared, the harp of Ethiopia, lifted his voice in praise:

“Our Lady Virgin Mary ascended from earth to heaven, and in heaven she sat with her Son at the right hand of the Father and the Holy Spirit.”

What the prophets saw afar, what the Apostles testified, what the Church preserves, we proclaim today with joy and trembling.

text.text: The Fast of Felseta: A Time of Sacred Devotion

text:
The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, in her apostolic wisdom, has appointed one of the Seven Great Fasts to commemorate this mystery: the Fast of Felseta. From Nehase 1 to Nehase 15 , the faithful old and young alike offer prayers, fasting, and tears, uniting with the Apostles in their longing and with the Virgin in her triumph.

This is not mere custom, but a sacred invitation to contemplate heavenly things.

O faithful soul, ponder the lesson hidden in this mystery:

If the Mother has risen, the children shall not be left behind.

If she who bore Christ was not left to rot, then we, who are members of His Body, shall likewise be glorified.

Let us therefore live in holiness. Let us keep this fast with zeal, not in pretense but in true repentance. Let us venerate the Virgin not with idle lips but with hearts aflame with reverence.

Is there anything else they say  besides the other ones already mentioned in the previous answer?

You ask a good and important question regarding the Kidase, the Divine Liturgy of our Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.  "Leyu Hasab" literally translates to "different idea" or "different intent" or "difference in purpose" It refers to a state of being

to receive the Holy Mysteries of Christ's Body and Blood.

This unworthiness can stem from various reasons, including:

If one harbors unconfessed sin in their heart, they approach the Holy Eucharist without having reconciled with God and His Church. This is akin to the Apostle Paul's warning in 1 Corinthians 11:27-29, where he speaks of partaking in an unworthy manner, bringing judgment upon oneself.

: If one is in a state of anger, resentment, or unforgiveness towards another,  their heart is not properly disposed to receive the Eucharist, which is a sacrament of unity and love. Christ himself teaches us to reconcile with our brother before offering our gift at the altar (Matthew 5:23-24).

: This could include neglecting prayer, fasting, and spiritual reflection in the days leading up to Communion. The Eucharist is not a casual meal, but a holy mystery demanding reverence and preparation.

: Receiving Holy Communion requires complete attention and devotion.  If one's mind is wandering or their heart is preoccupied with worldly matters, they are not fully present to receive the Lord.

The priest's admonition regarding "leyu hasab" serves as a reminder for self-examination and a call to approach the Holy Eucharist with reverence and fear of God.

Beyond the specific mention of "leyu hasab," the priest also exhorts those who are:
: Those who have been formally separated from the Church through disciplinary measures are not permitted to receive Communion until they have been reconciled.

text.text:
A Holy Offering of the Penitent Heart

(Part 3)

text:
Beloved children of the Most High,
Grace and peace be multiplied unto you, who seek the face of the Lord in truth and in brokenness of heart. Today, we are summoned to contemplate a holy mystery the offering of tears in prayer. This mystery is not new, nor is it foreign to the soul that longs for God. It is ancient, eternal, and full of heavenly fire. Let us incline our ears and hearts to the wisdom of our fathers, the testimony of Scripture, and the life of saints, that we may understand what it means to pray with tears.

text.text: I. The Divine Gift of Tears

text:
Saint John the Theologian illumined with the fire of divine lovetaught that tears are both the mother and daughter of prayer. They are the fruit of love and the root of repentance, given by God Himself as a sacred gift to fallen man. For what was man’s first response after his fall? Tears. When Adam and Eve lost paradise, they wept not because of the thorns of the earth, but because they were banished from the face of the Lord.

Thus, tears became the first ladder by which man sought to return to God. The saints teach that the soul’s road home begins not with argument, but with weeping.

text.text: II. David: The Prophet of Tears

text:
King David, a man after God’s own heart, did not weep once and move on. No. He drenched his bed with tears night after night. His sorrow was not momentary, but lifelong. He cried with groans that shook his bones. He wept in psalms that have become the hymns of every penitent heart.

“Weeping may last for the night,” says the Psalmist,

“but joy comes in the morning.” (Psalm 30:5)

This is not the joy of this world, but the joy of the Holy Spirit the joy that comes after true mourning, the joy born from sincere repentance.

Who can forget the bitter weeping of Saint Peter?

“He went out and wept bitterly.” (Luke 22:62)

He had denied the Master. But in his tears, he returned. He did not merely mourn what he had done his tears carried him back to the feet of Christ. It was after this weeping that Christ entrusted him with the care of His flock. This teaches us a great mystery: through tears, the fallen are restored, the weak are entrusted, and mysteries are revealed.

text.text: IV. Tears: The Path of Repentance and the Fruit of Love

text:
Tears are not just a reaction; they are a revelation.

They are the visible sign of the soul’s invisible fire.

They are the outward manifestation of perfect love for God a love that groans over sin, mourns over distance, and clings to God with all its strength.

“The fire of sin is fierce, but a few tears extinguish its flame and purify the soul.”

O, what a divine exchange! A river of tears for an ocean of mercy!

And Saint John Zeswesaw confirms:

“We shall not be judged for failing to work miracles, but for not weeping over our sins.”

Weep, therefore, not as those who despair, but as those who long to be made whole.

text.text: V. Tears in This World vs. Tears in the Next

text:
Mark this with holy trembling:

“If we do not shed tears in this world, we will groan in the next.”

Tears in this world are like the dew of dawn they nourish, soften, and bring life. But in the world to come, tears are tears of shame, of torment, of final regret. Blessed, therefore, are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted (Matt. 5:4). There is no greater wisdom than to weep now, that we may rejoice forever.

text.text: VI. The Meaning of Prayer and Its Heavenly Ascent

text:
Prayer is not mere speech it is a holy mystery. It is:

The earthly man revealing his heavenly nature.

The connection between man and the heavenly God.

A conversation with the Most High, as the Just King wrote.

The praying soul rises like an angel, entering the heavenly court, laying itself upon the altar not with blood, but with tears. This is the true burnt offering a heart crushed, a soul humbled, and a mouth trembling with holy love.

text.text: VII. The Conditions of Acceptable Prayer

text:
Let not the one who prays let his eyes wander or his mind stray. Let him ascend in thought, depart from earth, and draw near to God. Let his mouth and heart be one, and his faith and love be steadfast.

The one who prays rightly:

Prays with humility

Prays with a pure conscience

Prays with sincerity of heart

Prays as a child to his Father

Such a soul shall never be turned away. For the Lord, who searches hearts and sees every tear, will say to such a one: “You are My son. Ask, and you shall receive.”

text.text: VIII. Thanksgiving in Prayer and the Confession of Sin

text:
Saint Paul teaches:

“In everything, by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.” (Phil. 4:6)

Yes even when our requests are not answered as we wish, we are called to thank God. Why? Because He knows better than we do. Because He is just, even when we are judged. The ancient prayer confesses:

“We have sinned… we have gone astray… yet You have done justly.”

The one who confesses his sin and praises God for His justice, even in chastisement, is more grateful than the one who boasts in comfort.

text.text: Conclusion: A Call to Holy Mourning

text:
O you who long for God, weep!
Weep as David wept.
Weep as Peter wept.
Weep as the saints wept.

For such tears are pearls in the hand of the Lord. They are received as offerings, stored as treasures, and answered with joy. Do not be ashamed to cry before the God who wept for you. Let your prayer be not cold and dry, but wet with tears, rich with love, and aflame with repentance.

“I waited patiently for the Lord; He heard my cry. He lifted me from the pit and set my feet upon a rock.” (Psalm 40:1–2)

May your tears be the ink with which your name is written in the Book of Life.

Such a soul shall never be turned away. For the Lord, who searches hearts and sees every tear, will say to such a one: “You are My son. Ask, and you shall receive.”

VIII. Thanksgiving in Prayer and the Confession of Sin

Saint Paul teaches:

“In everything, by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.” (Phil. 4:6)

Yes even when our requests are not answered as we wish, we are called to thank God. Why? Because He knows better than we do. Because He is just, even when we are judged. The ancient prayer confesses:

“We have sinned… we have gone astray… yet You have done justly.”

The one who confesses his sin and praises God for His justice, even in chastisement, is more grateful than the one who boasts in comfort.

Conclusion: A Call to Holy Mourning

O you who long for God, weep!
Weep as David wept.
Weep as Peter wept.
Weep as the saints wept.

For such tears are pearls in the hand of the Lord. They are received as offerings, stored as treasures, and answered with joy. Do not be ashamed to cry before the God who wept for you. Let your prayer be not cold and dry, but wet with tears, rich with love, and aflame with repentance.

“I waited patiently for the Lord; He heard my cry. He lifted me from the pit and set my feet upon a rock.” (Psalm 40:1–2)

May your tears be the ink with which your name is written in the Book of Life.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

text: Beloved children of the Holy Orthodox Church, grace and peace be multiplied unto you from the Lord Jesus Christ, Who was born of the Ever-Virgin Mary, and Who has given to His Church treasures both seen and unseen. Today we speak of the holy Fast that precedes the great Feast of the Assumption of our Lady, the Theotokos, a Fast observed from the first to the fourteenth day of Nehase. Let us hear, not as those who seek mere custom, but as those who long to enter the mystery hidden from ages yet revealed to the saints.

text.text: The Apostolic Origin of the Fast

text:
This Fast is not a tradition born of men’s imagination, nor a mere ordinance added in later times; rather, it is apostolic in its very root. In the days when the holy apostles still walked upon the earth, they themselves set this Fast as a sacred preparation for the remembrance of the Dormition and glorious Assumption of the Mother of God.

When the time came for the all-pure Mother of our Lord to depart this earthly life, the apostles, by divine summons, gathered from the corners of the world to be present at her repose. For two weeks from the first day of the month of Nehase they prepared themselves in prayer, fasting, and thanksgiving, awaiting that solemn hour when they would commit her most holy body to the tomb.

Yet one of them, Thomas, was absent, being at that time far away in apostolic labor. Thus it was that when the Virgin was laid in the tomb, Thomas was not among those who carried her in honor to her rest.

text.text: The Mystery of Thomas and the Resurrection of the Virgin

text:
On the third day after the burial, a wondrous event occurred: the prophecy was fulfilled, and the Mother of Life rose again, even as her Son had triumphed over death. As Thomas journeyed to Jerusalem, a divine cloud bore her toward him. Seeing this, the apostles marveled, yet Thomas’s heart was pierced with sorrow.

Once before, he had missed the manifestation of the Lord’s resurrection, and now, it seemed, he was again denied the vision of so great a mystery. He lamented, saying:

"I did not behold my Lord’s rising with my own eyes, and now I have not seen His Mother’s resurrection. Am I forever to be the last and least in belief?"

But the holy Virgin, with maternal gentleness, comforted him, saying that this vision was granted to him alone. As a testimony, she placed in his hands the burial cloth that had wrapped her body.

Thomas came to the apostles bearing the sacred cloth. They questioned him, saying, "What has befallen our Lady?" Thomas answered with holy boldness, declaring that she had risen and that he had seen her in glory. Yet they, remembering his earlier doubt in the case of the Lord, hesitated to believe.

Thomas led them to her tomb. They opened it and beheld no body within, only the fragrance of paradise filling the air. Then the apostles, struck with awe, confessed: "Truly, she has been taken up into the glory of her Son."

From that time forth, the apostles themselves established a yearly remembrance of these events. They fasted from the first day of Nehase until the fourteenth, and on that day they received again her most pure body, preserved incorrupt, and laid it once more in the tomb. On the third day thereafter the sixteenth of Nehase she was taken up into the heavenly realm, accompanied by her Son, the King of Glory, the angels, and the saints.

This is why the Church, following the example of the apostles, keeps the Fast with reverence: that we may share in the blessing they received, and that the intercession of the Theotokos may never depart from us.

text.text: The Spiritual Purpose of the Fast

text:
The Fast is not an empty ritual. The prophets themselves foresaw and practiced such seasons of abstinence. The holy Daniel, speaking of his own fasting, said:

"In those days I, Daniel, was mourning three full weeks. I ate no pleasant bread, neither came flesh nor wine into my mouth, neither did I anoint myself at all, till three whole weeks were fulfilled" (Dan. 10:2–3).

Thus the faithful abstain from all meat, dairy, and rich foods, devoting themselves instead to prayer, attending the divine services, and works of repentance. This abstinence purifies the body, subdues the passions, and opens the soul to receive heavenly grace.

Therefore, let us not approach this Fast as a burden, but as a ladder to the blessings of heaven. By imitating the faith of the apostles, we honor the Mother of God; by humbling the flesh, we awaken the spirit; by guarding the days of fasting, we prepare for the joy of the Feast.

May the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the never-failing intercession of His holy Mother, preserve us from every evil, keep us steadfast in the Faith, and bring us at last to the eternal feast in the kingdom of God.

: 
The Mystery of the Virgin and the Light of Our Salvation

text:
Beloved in Christ,

On this blessed Saturday, the day on which the Church gathers in luminous praise of the Holy Theotokos, we lift our minds to the heavens and contemplate the mystery of the Virgin Mary, the Mother of our Lord, the pure tabernacle of the Most High. This is not a mere poetic remembrance, but an unveiling of divine truth, truth that angels once announced, prophets foresaw, and the Church continues to proclaim until the end of the ages.

Today, we stand in awe before her, for in her the atmosphere of light is spread, and the throne of light is lifted high. From this throne rises the hymn of thanksgiving, beginning not on earth, but in the eternal counsel of God.

text.text: 1. The Purity of the Mother of God

text:
The saintly Ephrem the Syrian, in his commentary on the Diatesaron, bears witness to her unparalleled holiness:

“The body of Mary is a temple on earth, in which the angel Gabriel sowed the seed of blessing instead of sin, death, and barrenness. You and your mother alone are pure in every way.”

Here we learn that her purity is not merely an outward chastity, but the inward radiance of a soul untainted by corruption. If God Himself chose her as His dwelling, how shall we not, with trembling voices, call her “blessed among women” (Luke 1:28)?

text.text: 2. The One Who Held the Creator

text:
O astonishing mystery! The One who contains the universe was held in the hands of a humble maiden. From her flesh and soul, the eternal Word took human nature, uniting heaven and earth in her womb. The angel’s message, “You shall call His name Jesus” (Luke 1:31), was not mere naming it was the proclamation of His mission: to save His people from their sins (Matthew 1:21).

The name Jesus Yeshua means Savior. In her, the Savior entered the world, and through her, reconciliation with the Father was accomplished.

Abba Hiriakos teaches that the Father looked across all the earth and found none like her. Her fragrance of holiness drew down the Beloved Son. The Holy Spirit overshadowed her; the Almighty clothed Himself in her flesh. Thus she became the living Ark, bearing the Word who abides forever.

text.text: 4. The Daughter of David, Mother of the Eternal Word

text:
She is of the royal lineage, the descendant of David, yet she bore the One who existed before David, the Word who is one in essence with the Father. When the Apostle says that Christ “emptied Himself” (Philippians 2:7), he does not mean that the Word ceased to be God, but that He took upon Himself our weakness to fill us with His grace.

He descended into our poverty, that we might be lifted into His glory He became man so that man might become god by grace.

text.text: 5. The Second Heaven, the Sun of Righteousness

text: From her shone forth the Sun of Righteousness, Christ the Lord, who warmed a world frozen by sin. St. Cyril of Ethiopia rightly calls her “the second heaven above the earth,” for just as the first heaven contains the sun that lights creation, so she bore the true Sun who lights the souls of the saints.

Scripture and the Fathers call her the Tabernacle of the Covenant, the dwelling of the great High Priest. Abba Giorgis Zegescha proclaimed her the “Tabernacle of Light,” for in her the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). She is holier than the gold of Solomon’s temple, for she herself became the temple of the living God a temple that can never be destroyed.

After giving birth, she remained ever-virgin. St. Yohannes Afewerk teaches that her motherhood and virginity were united in a mystery given to no other woman: she bore God, yet the seal of her virginity remained untouched. This is the great sign of the new faith, for in her we see both the humility of man and the changelessness of God.

Again and again, the Fathers plead: “Pray for us, O Lady, that the grace and glory of your Son may not be taken away from us.” For if the Lord was pleased to dwell in her, how much more will He hear the prayers she offers for His people?

Conclusion

Therefore, beloved, on this Saturday, let our praise of Mary not be with lips alone but with purified hearts. She is the ladder, the temple, the tabernacle, the heaven, and the mother yet in all these titles she points not to herself, but to the Son she bore. To honor her is to glorify Him.

Let us then cry with the angels and the saints:

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

text: ፦ What’s the best way to prepare for confession so we don’t forget some sins that we need confess & prepare adequately. Also, best way to prepare for confession to approach it having properly repented.

፦ My child, your desire to thoroughly prepare for the Holy Mystery of Confession is commendable, a true sign of a heart seeking reconciliation with God.  The devil, our adversary, often tries to cloud our minds, making us forget our sins or minimizing their gravity. But with prayer and self-examination, we can overcome these obstacles.

Here are some ways to prepare, drawing upon the wisdom of our Holy Fathers:

: Begin by beseeching the Holy Spirit to illuminate the darkened corners of your heart.  Pray with humility, like the Publican in the Gospel, saying "God, be merciful to me a sinner!" (Luke 18:13).  St. Isaac the Syrian beautifully reminds us, "Enter eagerly into the treasure house that is within you, and you will see the things that are in heaven. For there is but one single entry into this treasure house, and that is humility."  Humility opens the door to honest self-reflection.

: Dedicate time for quiet contemplation. Use the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20) and the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3-12) as mirrors to reflect upon your thoughts, words, and deeds.  Have I loved God with all my heart and my neighbor as myself?  Have I been truthful, humble, and charitable?  Have I indulged in anger, envy, or gluttony?  Consider also the Seven Deadly Sins: pride, envy, wrath, sloth, greed, gluttony, and lust.  Ask yourself how these have manifested in your life.
:  Writing down your sins can be a powerful tool. This act of putting them on paper can help you to concretely confront them and avoid forgetting them in the confessional.

: Fasting helps to subdue the passions and clear the mind. Incorporate fasting, as is appropriate for your health and with the blessing of your spiritual father, leading up to your confession.  Abba Moses, one of the desert fathers, said, "Fasting subdues the body and cleanses the soul."

text.text: Reading Scripture and the Holy Fathers:

text: Immerse yourself in the Word of God and the writings of our Holy Fathers.  Their words can pierce our hearts and reveal areas where we need to repent.  The Psalms especially offer powerful prayers of repentance, such as Psalm 51.

: Some find a confession guide helpful, particularly those new to the sacrament or returning after a long absence. These guides, available from your church or online, can prompt reflection on different areas of sin.

Regarding true repentance, remember that it is not simply remorse for being caught but a genuine sorrow for having offended God and a sincere desire to change. St. John Chrysostom reminds us that “true repentance is not simply to bewail one’s sins, but to change one’s life.”

Finally, my child, remember that the priest acts as an icon of Christ in the confessional, offering absolution through the power bestowed upon him by God. Approach him with humility and trust.  

I will pray for you, my child, as you prepare for this holy sacrament.  Please let me know if you have any further questions.

text: Beloved in Christ, children of the Holy Church, Grace and peace be to you from God, who out of His boundless mercy has not left us in darkness, but has shone upon us the light of salvation through His Only-Begotten Son, born of the Most Holy Virgin Mary. Today, on this blessed Monday, let us unfold the mystery hidden from ages how the mercy of God was revealed to Adam, how the glory of His love was made manifest in the Virgin, and how our salvation was accomplished in the flesh of Christ.

text.text: I. The Mercy of God Toward Fallen Adam

text:
Brethren, consider the boundless compassion of our God! When Adam, the first-formed man, fell through transgression, he was cast out from Paradise, stripped of his glory, and made subject to death. For five thousand and five hundred years, he languished in bondage to the devil, groaning under the weight of his condemnation: "Dust you are, and to dust you shall return" (Gen. 3:19). Yet, the Lord, who is rich in mercy, did not abandon him to eternal ruin.  

Behold the patience of God! He did not immediately pass judgment upon Adam and Eve, but rather, like a loving father seeking his lost child, He called out, "Where are you?" (Gen. 3:9). As St. Ephrem the Syrian teaches, this was not a voice of wrath, but of tender solicitude a divine summons to repentance. Yet, Adam, shrouded in shame, hid himself. Still, the Lord did not cease calling, just as He sends forth His prophets, and finally, His only-begotten Son, to seek and to save that which was lost (Luke 19:10).  

O the depth of God’s love! As St. John Chrysostom proclaims, He who once pronounced judgment upon Adam later restored him, saying through the thief on the cross, "Today you shall be with Me in Paradise" (Luke 23:43). What was lost through disobedience is regained through the obedience of the Second Adam—Christ our Lord.

text.text: II. The All-Holy Theotokos: The Pure Vessel of the Incarnation

text:
But how was this redemption accomplished? Through the womb of the Ever-Virgin Mary, the Mother of God!  

Hearken, O faithful, to the marvel of her purity! Other women are purified in due season, but she was preserved from all defilement from the moment of her conception. As St. Theodotus proclaims, she remained "unchanged in mind and body, pure in soul and virginity."* Other women bear children in the way of nature, but she O wondrous mystery! conceived without seed, bore without corruption, and remained virgin after childbirth.  

What honor can we give her that is sufficient? Other women are praised for bearing righteous men, martyrs, or teachers, but she bore God incarnate! She is the one who united in her person motherhood with virginity, servitude with divine dignity, nourishing with her milk the very One who sustains the sun and moon. The Cherubim tremble before Him, yet He deigned to dwell in her womb for nine months and five days!  

And why was Christ born of a virgin?  

1. To fulfill prophecy: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a Son" (Isa. 7:14). 
 
2. To manifest divine power: Had He been born of seed, men might have doubted His divinity, as St. Gregory the Theologian warns.  

3. To restore the likeness of Adam: As Adam was formed from the virgin earth, so Christ was formed from the Virgin’s womb. As Eve came from Adam’s side, so the Church flows from Christ’s pierced side.  

Thus, the Virgin Mary is the new Eve, through whom life is restored to the world.

As St. Theodotus proclaims, she remained "unchanged in mind and body, pure in soul and virginity."* Other women bear children in the way of nature, but she O wondrous mystery! conceived without seed, bore without corruption, and remained virgin after childbirth.  

What honor can we give her that is sufficient? Other women are praised for bearing righteous men, martyrs, or teachers, but she bore God incarnate! She is the one who united in her person motherhood with virginity, servitude with divine dignity, nourishing with her milk the very One who sustains the sun and moon. The Cherubim tremble before Him, yet He deigned to dwell in her womb for nine months and five days!  

And why was Christ born of a virgin?  

1. To fulfill prophecy: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a Son" (Isa. 7:14). 
 
2. To manifest divine power: Had He been born of seed, men might have doubted His divinity, as St. Gregory the Theologian warns.  

3. To restore the likeness of Adam: As Adam was formed from the virgin earth, so Christ was formed from the Virgin’s womb. As Eve came from Adam’s side, so the Church flows from Christ’s pierced side.  

Thus, the Virgin Mary is the new Eve, through whom life is restored to the world.

Beloved in Christ, children of the Holy Church, Grace and peace be to you from God, who out of His boundless mercy has not left us in darkness, but has shone upon us the light of salvation through His Only-Begotten Son, born of the Most Holy Virgin Mary. Today, on this blessed Monday, let us unfold the mystery hidden from ages how the mercy of God was revealed to Adam, how the glory of His love was made manifest in the Virgin, and how our salvation was accomplished in the flesh of Christ.

I. The Mercy of God Toward Fallen Adam  

Brethren, consider the boundless compassion of our God! When Adam, the first-formed man, fell through transgression, he was cast out from Paradise, stripped of his glory, and made subject to death. For five thousand and five hundred years, he languished in bondage to the devil, groaning under the weight of his condemnation: "Dust you are, and to dust you shall return" (Gen. 3:19). Yet, the Lord, who is rich in mercy, did not abandon him to eternal ruin.  

Behold the patience of God! He did not immediately pass judgment upon Adam and Eve, but rather, like a loving father seeking his lost child, He called out, "Where are you?" (Gen. 3:9). As St. Ephrem the Syrian teaches, this was not a voice of wrath, but of tender solicitude a divine summons to repentance. Yet, Adam, shrouded in shame, hid himself. Still, the Lord did not cease calling, just as He sends forth His prophets, and finally, His only-begotten Son, to seek and to save that which was lost (Luke 19:10).  

O the depth of God’s love! As St. John Chrysostom proclaims, He who once pronounced judgment upon Adam later restored him, saying through the thief on the cross, "Today you shall be with Me in Paradise" (Luke 23:43). What was lost through disobedience is regained through the obedience of the Second Adam—Christ our Lord.  

II. The All-Holy Theotokos: The Pure Vessel of the Incarnation  

But how was this redemption accomplished? Through the womb of the Ever-Virgin Mary, the Mother of God!  

Hearken, O faithful, to the marvel of her purity! Other women are purified in due season, but she was preserved from all defilement from the moment of her conception. As St. Theodotus proclaims, she remained "unchanged in mind and body, pure in soul and virginity."* Other women bear children in the way of nature, but she O wondrous mystery! conceived without seed, bore without corruption, and remained virgin after childbirth.

She is the one who united in her person motherhood with virginity, servitude with divine dignity, nourishing with her milk the very One who sustains the sun and moon. The Cherubim tremble before Him, yet He deigned to dwell in her womb for nine months and five days!

1. To fulfill prophecy: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a Son" (Isa. 7:14). 
 
2. To manifest divine power: Had He been born of seed, men might have doubted His divinity, as St. Gregory the Theologian warns.  

3. To restore the likeness of Adam: As Adam was formed from the virgin earth, so Christ was formed from the Virgin’s womb. As Eve came from Adam’s side, so the Church flows from Christ’s pierced side.  

Thus, the Virgin Mary is the new Eve, through whom life is restored to the world.  

Continues 👇🏾

text.text: III. The Divine Condescension: The Word Made Flesh

text:
Beloved, the Son of God, who is co-eternal with the Father, "emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant" (Phil. 2:7). He did not cease to be God, yet He became perfect man, uniting two natures in one person without confusion.  

St. Cyril teaches us: "The Word became flesh, not by changing His divinity into flesh, but by assuming humanity into His divine person." He who fashioned Adam from the dust now takes Adam’s nature upon Himself to redeem him.  

Why did He do this?  

- To pay the debt of sin, as St. Athanasius declares.  

- To destroy death by death, trampling down the devil’s power.  

- To open Paradise again, as He
promised the thief.

Behold the mystery! The Second Adam undoes the curse of the first. 

 "Through one man, Adam, death entered the world; through one Man, Christ, life is restored!" (Rom. 5:12-21).

text.text: IV. The Song of the Angels and the Triumph Over Hell

text:
When Christ was born, the angels sang, "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace!" (Luke 2:14). Why? Because:  

- Sin was destroyed—the devil’s tyranny was broken.  

- The debt was canceled—the handwriting of our transgressions nailed to the Cross (Col. 2:14). 
 
- Hell was plundered—for Christ descended and led captivity captive (Eph. 4:8).  

The devil, who once deceived Adam with a fruit, is now crushed by the wood of the Cross. The stone of the tomb could not hold the Author of Life!

text.text: V. Let Us Give Thanks and Imitate the Theotokos

text:
Therefore, brethren, let us:  

1. Repent like Adam, who wept for his sins.
  
2. Embrace purity like the Virgin Mary, keeping ourselves unspotted from the world.
  
3. Rejoice in redemption, for where sin abounded, grace abounded much more (Rom. 5:20).  

O Most Holy Theotokos, pray for us, that we may not lose the grace of your Son, who freed Adam from bondage!

text.text:
May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

- Became the living Throne of the Cherubim  

- The Bridal Chamber of the King of kings

- The spiritual Paradise containing the Tree of Life

This is not a small thing, nor a passing commemoration, but a moment in which heaven and earth are joined in the counsel of God, preparing the vessel of our salvation.

text.text: The Righteous Parents, Joachim and Hannah

text:
In the fullness of time, there lived a righteous man, Joachim, noble and steadfast in faith, and his equally virtuous wife, Hannah, adorned with purity but weighed down by a grievous sorrow. For though they were rich in righteousness, they were poor in the blessing of children. And in those days, barrenness was thought by the children of Israel to be a sign of God’s disfavor. The people would whisper that the blessing of Abraham was far from them. Yet they bore the reproach with patience, turning not away from God but toward Him with ceaseless prayer.

In the temple, they wept, pouring out their hearts to the Lord, making a solemn vow: “If You grant us a son, he shall be trained in the service of Your holy house; and if You grant us a daughter, she shall be Your handmaiden, a drawer of water, a weaver of gold for the holy place, a maker of the temple curtains, and consecrated in purity to You.”

text.text: The Appearance of the Archangel Gabriel

text:
One day, as Joachim prayed alone upon a mountain, his heart lifted to the heavens, slumber overtook him. In that quiet, the mighty Archangel Gabriel descended, clothed in light, and spoke with a voice that carried both the peace of heaven and the authority of the Most High:

“Your wife Hannah shall conceive and bear you a daughter, the joy of the whole world, the light of the eyes of many, and through her you shall find salvation.”

At the same time, in another place, Hannah too was praying, her words mingled with tears: “O Lord, God of my fathers, hear Thy servant; give me a blessed daughter, the fruit of my womb, the hope of my heart and the joy of my eyes.” She looked upon a dove playing with its young and lamented: “O Lord, Thou who hast given a child even to this lowly creature, why hast Thou withheld one from me?”

text.text: The Blessing of Zechariah the Priest

text:
Joachim and Hannah went to the priest Zechariah he who would later father John the Baptist and renewed their vow before him. Zechariah, filled with the Spirit, blessed them, saying: “May the Lord hear your prayers, accept your petitions, and fulfill the desires of your hearts.”

That night, God sealed His promise with heavenly visions.

: He beheld the seven heavens opened like a curtain, and from the highest descended a white dove, which rested upon Hannah’s head, entered her ear, and came to rest in her womb a sign of the pure and spiritual conception ordained by God.

: And Hannah saw that the rod of Joachim brought forth fruit in its season, and all creation was nourished by it.

They shared these visions with one another and understood that God had appointed them for a mystery beyond the understanding of men.

👉🏾👉🏾👉🏾On the #Conception of the Most Holy #Virgin #Mary (#Nehase 7)

Beloved in Christ, children of the One, Holy, Apostolic, and Orthodox Faith, let us incline our hearts and ears to this divine mystery, which the Church in her wisdom holds forth to us on the blessed day of Nehase 7 the day of the conception of the Theotokos, the Most Pure and Ever-Blessed Virgin Mary. This is not a small thing, nor a passing commemoration, but a moment in which heaven and earth are joined in the counsel of God, preparing the vessel of our salvation.

The Righteous Parents, Joachim and Hannah

In the fullness of time, there lived a righteous man, Joachim, noble and steadfast in faith, and his equally virtuous wife, Hannah, adorned with purity but weighed down by a grievous sorrow. For though they were rich in righteousness, they were poor in the blessing of children. And in those days, barrenness was thought by the children of Israel to be a sign of God’s disfavor. The people would whisper that the blessing of Abraham was far from them. Yet they bore the reproach with patience, turning not away from God but toward Him with ceaseless prayer.

In the temple, they wept, pouring out their hearts to the Lord, making a solemn vow: “If You grant us a son, he shall be trained in the service of Your holy house; and if You grant us a daughter, she shall be Your handmaiden, a drawer of water, a weaver of gold for the holy place, a maker of the temple curtains, and consecrated in purity to You.”

The Appearance of the Archangel Gabriel

One day, as Joachim prayed alone upon a mountain, his heart lifted to the heavens, slumber overtook him. In that quiet, the mighty Archangel Gabriel descended, clothed in light, and spoke with a voice that carried both the peace of heaven and the authority of the Most High:

“Your wife Hannah shall conceive and bear you a daughter, the joy of the whole world, the light of the eyes of many, and through her you shall find salvation.”

At the same time, in another place, Hannah too was praying, her words mingled with tears: “O Lord, God of my fathers, hear Thy servant; give me a blessed daughter, the fruit of my womb, the hope of my heart and the joy of my eyes.” She looked upon a dove playing with its young and lamented: “O Lord, Thou who hast given a child even to this lowly creature, why hast Thou withheld one from me?”

The Blessing of Zechariah the Priest

Joachim and Hannah went to the priest Zechariah he who would later father John the Baptist and renewed their vow before him. Zechariah, filled with the Spirit, blessed them, saying: “May the Lord hear your prayers, accept your petitions, and fulfill the desires of your hearts.”

That night, God sealed His promise with heavenly visions.

Joachim’s Vision: He beheld the seven heavens opened like a curtain, and from the highest descended a white dove, which rested upon Hannah’s head, entered her ear, and came to rest in her womb a sign of the pure and spiritual conception ordained by God.

Hannah’s Vision: And Hannah saw that the rod of Joachim brought forth fruit in its season, and all creation was nourished by it.

They shared these visions with one another and understood that God had appointed them for a mystery beyond the understanding of men.

Continues 👇🏾

“You will give birth to a beautiful creature, more glorious than men, more glorious even than the angels.”

By God’s will, through the word of the angel, the Most Pure Virgin was conceived not as other children are, but in a manner sanctified from the beginning for the mystery of the Incarnation.

, that holy singer of Ethiopia, declared: “Mary, who is of the seed of Adam, shines like a white pearl in the nature of Adam from the beginning.” In her, God laid the foundation of salvation for Adam and all his children, preparing her with His unsearchable wisdom to be the living temple of His Only-Begotten Son.
, in the divine liturgy, lifted his voice in praise: “O Virgin, you were not conceived by the lust of sin, but were born under the holy vow of Hannah and Joachim.”

For in the womb of Hannah was planted the root from which the Tree of Life would spring, whose fruit is Christ, the Savior of the world.

May the intercession and blessing of the Holy Virgin Mary, conceived this day by the promise of God, be upon us, guide us, and preserve us unto the end.
