text:
Beloved brethren, peace be to you in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Many ask: Can prayer be delivered to our home? Must the prayer of the faithful only be lifted in the temple, or does it also ascend when uttered in the quiet of the household?

The answer is found in the Scriptures and in the life of the Church: prayer is not bound by walls or doors, for wherever the faithful heart is lifted to God, there heaven opens and the angels bear it before the throne of the Almighty. The saints of old and the holy apostles have shown us the hours of prayer, each hour rich with divine mystery. Let us consider them carefully, and learn how prayer sanctifies not only the temple, but also our homes.

At the ninth hour what we call (9 a.m) in the afternoon the angels of God receive the prayers, supplications, and incense of mankind. This is not an invention of man, but witnessed in the Scriptures:

“Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour.” (Acts 3:1)

Cornelius, the centurion, prayed at this hour with earnest heart, and the heavens answered him. (Acts 10:3, 9)

But more than this, the ninth hour is sanctified forever, for it was at this very hour that our Lord Jesus Christ bowed His head upon the cross and delivered His holy soul into the hands of the Father. At this time, therefore, we remember His suffering, His death, His immeasurable poverty for our sake.

Thus, beloved, whether you are in the temple or in your home, sanctify the ninth hour with prayer. Call to mind the crucifixion of Christ. Let your heart be broken in remembrance of His sacrifice, and pray that as Cornelius received mercy, so also your prayer may be accepted by the holy angels and reconciled before God.

The time of the evening prayer is as a Sabbath hour, for just as laborers receive their wages, so too the faithful receive reward for their works. Christ Himself likened the kingdom to laborers in the vineyard, each receiving from the Master his just due. (Matthew 20:1–16)

David declared: “Let my prayer be set forth before Thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice.” (Psalm 140:2) Elijah, at this very hour, offered his sacrifice, and the Holy Trinity accepted it in fire. (1 Kings 18:36) Ezra, likewise, humbled himself in prayer at this hour. (Ezra 9:5)

Most wondrous of all, at this time our Lord descended into the grave according to the flesh, and into hell according to the soul, to bring forth mankind from the shadow of death. (Matthew 27:45–61)

Therefore, when you pray in your home at this hour, remember that Christ entered the depths for your sake, to break open the prison of death and lead you into eternal life.

text.text: The Prayer of the Night (3:00pm)(Before Sleep)

text:
When the day is done and night falls, the faithful commend themselves into the hands of God. We do not know what awaits us in our sleep, but the Shepherd of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps. He guards His flock by day and by night.

Thus, before resting, let every home lift up prayer. Recall the agony of Gethsemane, where the Lord prayed in the night and taught His disciples to watch with Him. (Matthew 26:36) Entrust your household to the Creator with faith, saying, “Peace be upon us, for He watches over us.”

text:
David, the prophet, proclaimed: “At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto you because of your righteous judgments.” (Psalm 118:62) Midnight is no ordinary time; it is crowned with mysteries:

At midnight, Christ was born of the Virgin. (Luke 2:7–8)

At midnight, He was baptized in the Jordan. (Luke 3:21)

At midnight, He rose from the grave in triumph. (John 20:1)

At midnight, He shall come again to judge the living and the dead. (Matthew 25:6; Mark 13:35)

It was also at midnight that Paul and Silas, imprisoned in chains, lifted up songs of praise. (Acts 16:25)

Therefore, when you rise at midnight in your home to pray, recall the mysteries of Christ: His coming down from heaven, His birth of the Virgin Mary, His victory over death, and His second coming in glory. Let your prayer be filled with remembrance and thanksgiving, and ask that you may be counted worthy to stand at His right hand on the Day of Judgment.

These holy hours of prayer are not merely symbols but practices sanctified by the saints. In monasteries, men and women of God endure hardship, silence, even the terrors of the night, so that they might lift prayers without ceasing. They follow the seven hours of prayer, as taught by Abba Giorgis, the Ethiopian Kyrillos, who ordered them with great devotion. Especially during Lent and the season of the Passion, the Church chants these prayers in melodies that pierce the heart and draw the soul heavenward.

👇🏾
 
Prayer is not bound to the temple alone. Just as Cornelius prayed in his house and was heard, so too our homes become holy when we lift our hearts to God at the appointed hours.

text: Beloved children of the Holy Church, peace and grace to you in Christ our Lord. Today we reflect on the meaning of Negere Maryam, which translates as “The Story of Mary”. This story is not simply a biography; it is a divine lesson revealing the secrets God has shared with humanity through the Most Holy Virgin Mary, the Mother of our Savior.
– means “story” or “teaching.”

) – the name of the Holy Virgin.

Thus, Negere Maryam is a sacred lesson teaching us about Mary’s role in God’s plan for salvation.As the rivers of wisdom cannot be fully contained in words, so too is it impossible to exhaust the glory and mystery of Mary in a single narrative.

text.text: “In this lesson, however, let us focus on three key points.”
Three Main Points of the Story

text:
For clarity, we focus on three principal aspects:

1. The Genealogy of the Holy Virgin Mary

2. The Meaning of the Name “Mary”

3. Additional Names by Which She Is Known

text.text: 1. The Genealogy of the Holy Virgin Mary

text: God is holy, and wherever He dwells, that person, place, or object becomes sanctified. Our Lady Mary is called holy because she was prepared as the dwelling place of the Almighty. From her body, Christ took flesh; from her blood, He took life; from her soul, He took the purity fitting for the Incarnation. She is a saint made holy by divine choice, not by human merit, and in her, heaven and earth meet.

The name Mary is derived from the Hebrew word (Mar-yam), meaning “mother of many.” Just as Abraham is called the father of many nations (Gen. 17:5), Mary is rightly the mother of all believers in Christ.

Church scholars further illuminate her name as signifying several profound realities:

a) The Way to the Kingdom of Heaven

Mary is the pathway through which salvation entered the world. By giving birth to Christ, she made eternal life accessible to all Adam’s descendants. All who seek the Kingdom of Heaven rely upon her intercession, for it is through her womb that the Savior of mankind came forth.

b) Grace and Wealth

Though her parents endured reproach for their faith, Mary’s birth became a wellspring of divine grace and wealth for humanity. Through her Adam, who was separated from God’s grace because of sin and crushed under the feet of demons, received grace again and became a partaker of the riches of the Holy Spirit through Our Lady.As Abba Hiriakos extols in the Liturgy : “When Adam was expelled from Paradise, you became his hope.”

c) Perfect in Body and Soul

God, who is perfect in all things, chose Mary to bear His Son. Therefore, she was made perfect in body and soul, prepared to be a pure and holy vessel for the Incarnation.

d) Above Creatures, Below the Creator

Mary is exalted above all angels and saints, not by mere grace alone, but because the Creator Himself took flesh from her. This is why Gabriel proclaimed: “Blessed are you among women” (Luke 1:28). She is above all creation under God, yet remains His servant.

e) Mother of Many

Just as a household has a head and a caretaker, all Christians who are members of Christ’s family find their spiritual mother in Mary, with Christ as the head of their household.

f) Mediator Between God and Man

Mary serves as the bridge between humanity and her Son, God incarnate. She presents human supplications to Him and brings His mercy to mankind. Through her, believers receive the blessing of body and soul, salvation and grace.

Beloved children of the Holy Church, peace and grace to you in Christ our Lord. Today we reflect on the meaning of Negere Maryam, which translates as “The Story of Mary”. This story is not simply a biography; it is a divine lesson revealing the secrets God has shared with humanity through the Most Holy Virgin Mary, the Mother of our Savior.

The Meaning of the Phrase

Negere – means “story” or “teaching.”

Maryam (Mary) – the name of the Holy Virgin.

Thus, Negere Maryam is a sacred lesson teaching us about Mary’s role in God’s plan for salvation.As the rivers of wisdom cannot be fully contained in words, so too is it impossible to exhaust the glory and mystery of Mary in a single narrative.

“In this lesson, however, let us focus on three key points.”

Three Main Points of the Story

For clarity, we focus on three principal aspects:

1. The Genealogy of the Holy Virgin Mary

2. The Meaning of the Name “Mary”

3. Additional Names by Which She Is Known

1. The Genealogy of the Holy Virgin Mary

God is holy, and wherever He dwells, that person, place, or object becomes sanctified. Our Lady Mary is called holy because she was prepared as the dwelling place of the Almighty. From her body, Christ took flesh; from her blood, He took life; from her soul, He took the purity fitting for the Incarnation. She is a saint made holy by divine choice, not by human merit, and in her, heaven and earth meet.

2. The Meaning of the Name “Mary”

The name Mary is derived from the Hebrew word (Mar-yam), meaning “mother of many.” Just as Abraham is called the father of many nations (Gen. 17:5), Mary is rightly the mother of all believers in Christ.

Church scholars further illuminate her name as signifying several profound realities:

a) The Way to the Kingdom of Heaven

Mary is the pathway through which salvation entered the world. By giving birth to Christ, she made eternal life accessible to all Adam’s descendants. All who seek the Kingdom of Heaven rely upon her intercession, for it is through her womb that the Savior of mankind came forth.

b) Grace and Wealth

Though her parents endured reproach for their faith, Mary’s birth became a wellspring of divine grace and wealth for humanity. Through her Adam, who was separated from God’s grace because of sin and crushed under the feet of demons, received grace again and became a partaker of the riches of the Holy Spirit through Our Lady.As Abba Hiriakos extols in the Liturgy : “When Adam was expelled from Paradise, you became his hope.”

c) Perfect in Body and Soul

God, who is perfect in all things, chose Mary to bear His Son. Therefore, she was made perfect in body and soul, prepared to be a pure and holy vessel for the Incarnation.

d) Above Creatures, Below the Creator

Mary is exalted above all angels and saints, not by mere grace alone, but because the Creator Himself took flesh from her. This is why Gabriel proclaimed: “Blessed are you among women” (Luke 1:28). She is above all creation under God, yet remains His servant.

e) Mother of Many

Just as a household has a head and a caretaker, all Christians who are members of Christ’s family find their spiritual mother in Mary, with Christ as the head of their household.

f) Mediator Between God and Man

Mary serves as the bridge between humanity and her Son, God incarnate. She presents human supplications to Him and brings His mercy to mankind. Through her, believers receive the blessing of body and soul, salvation and grace.

Beloved brethren in Christ, children of the Holy Church, peace and grace be with you. Today we turn our hearts to a most important matter: What should we pray? For prayer is the breath of the soul, the ladder to heaven, and the key by which the faithful unlock the treasures of God’s mercy.

The Fathers of the Church, guided by the Holy Spirit, have preserved for us the prayers that sanctify each day, prayers that nourish both monks in their solitude and the faithful in their homes. Let us, then, consider these treasures of prayer one by one.

The Psalms are the school of prayer. From the monasteries of the desert to the homes of the faithful, the Psalms are repeated daily. The Fathers ordered that the Psalms be divided according to the days of the week, so that all 150 must be prayed regularly:

The Psalms of David, like all prayers, contain a prayer appointed for each day.Let us now take a closer look at them:

Monday → Psalms 1–30

Tuesday → Psalms 31–60

Wednesday → Psalms 61–80

Thursday → Psalms 81–110

Friday → Psalms 111–130

Saturday → Psalms 131–150

Sunday → The Prayer of the Prophets and the Song of Solomon

If one cannot recite all, the Fathers permitted the recitation of “One King”—that is, ten psalms per day.

For example, Psalms 1–10 on Monday, Psalms 31–40 on Tuesday, and so forth.Those who are unable to recite everything instead choose certain hymns and offer them each day.

No day should pass without the praise of the Holy Virgin. If possible, the Praises of Mary should be recited all the seven days praises ; if not, it is fitting to recite them daily. After completing the regular daily prayers, it is proper to recite the praises of mary for the day and thus partake in the blessings of Our Lady.”

The monks of Waldeba, the teachers and students of the Church, and all faithful souls lift up the “praises of  Mary” daily. The Virgin is the Covenant of Mercy, and through her intercession we are strengthened. Let us, therefore, make it our habit to greet her in prayer, whether at night before sleep or in the morning when we rise.

The daily reading of the Holy Gospel, especially the Gospel of John, Dividing it into chapters and reading it every day is counted as prayer itself. For in these words we hear the voice of Christ.The Fathers pray this prayer diligently each day.

4.

There are also other prayers such as the Praise of God, the remembrance of Golgotha, the appearances of Christ and His Mother, the prayers of the Book of Prayer, the Psalms, and the miracles of God. Each one prays according to their ability. But at the very least, every Christian should pray the Psalms and the Praises of Mary.

text:
When time is short and we cannot read long prayers, the Fathers taught us to pray short and powerful prayers such as:

Abune Zebesemayat
(The Our Father who art in heaven) 

The Prayer of Faith(tselote haymanot)

Psalm 150 (the great hymn of David)

The Hymn of Mary

Even if the prayer is brief, it seals the day with God’s blessing.

The Fathers also taught that when we pray Psalm 150, it is as though we have prayed the entire Psalter, and we receive the blessing of David. At the very least, we should never leave our homes without saying the Our Father, just as the Lord Jesus Christ commanded.

In monasteries short prayers are often used ande Short prayer may vary from place to place : nine times ( selam leki ) and twelve times (Abune zebesemayat)

A common order of short prayers is as follows:

1. The Our Father (Abune Zebesemayat)

2. One Psalm of David

3. The Praises of Mary (Wudase Maryam) and other hymns

4. Again the (Abune Zebesemayat), followed by BeEnte Egzi’etne Maryam, the Creed (Tselote Haymanot), and the Abune Zebesemayat with Kyrie Eleison (Lord have mercy) said forty-one times.

But the Fathers also warn: if we use only short prayers every day and neglect the longer prayers, our soul may become weak and fall into temptation.

Prayer is not measured by length alone but by constancy and devotion. The Psalms lift our souls to heaven; the Hail Mary( selam leki) unites us to the Virgin’s intercession;the Gospel fills us with Christ’s voice; and the short prayers keep our hearts awake to God in every place and time.

Let us, therefore, not allow a single day to pass without lifting our voices in prayer. For he who prays stands in the company of angels, partakes of the blessings of the saints, and draws down upon himself the mercy of the Holy Trinity.

Beloved children of the holy Orthodox faith, I greet you with the peace of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Today we consider an essential matter for the life of the soul: What should we pray? This question is not small, for prayer is the very breath of the Christian. As the body dies when it ceases to breathe, so the soul grows faint and falls when it ceases to pray. Therefore, let us open the Scriptures, the wisdom of the Fathers, and the tradition of our Church, and learn with zeal what our Lord requires of us in prayer.

text.text: 1. Short Prayers – When They Are Right, and When They Are Wrong

text:
Sometimes, short prayers are necessary:

When we are in deep trouble, like Peter crying, “Lord, save me!”

When time does not allow us to pray long.

These are good and acceptable. New Christians may also begin with short prayers, like infants who first drink milk. but As we mature in faith, we must also grow stronger in prayer.

If we always give God only a few hurried words, and then excuse ourselves saying, “He is merciful, He will understand”, we are misusing His kindness. That is not true devotion but laziness.

The Church gives us prayers to strengthen us:

The Psalms of David,

The Hail Mary,

The liturgical prayers in the services.

These are not only for monks or priests but for all: youth, deacons, clergy, evangelists, singers, and every believer. Whoever neglects them becomes weak and easily falls into temptation.

The center of all prayer is the one Christ Himself taught us: “Our Father who art in heaven” (Abune Zebe-Semayat).

Whenever we pray, we should begin with this. If we are interrupted in the middle of prayer, we should seal that pause with “Our Father,” handle the matter, and then return to prayer, again beginning with “Our Father.”

This way, our prayers are never left unfinished or empty, but always held together by the words of Christ.

text.text: 3. The Power of Prayer in the Church

text:
Do not limit prayer to your home. The Church is the house of God, and prayers offered there are greater and more powerful than any other.

God Himself said:

“My eyes will be open and My ears attentive to the prayer made in this place. I have chosen this house; My eyes and My heart will always be there.” (2 Chronicles 7:15–16)

When the faithful gather together, led by priests, their prayer has great strength because it is united. Therefore, we should be present in church, lifting up our voices with the assembly.

Our greatest duty is to honor the holy Sabbath and to celebrate the Liturgy .

The ancient Fathers Abba Michael and Abba Gabriel warned against those who would celebrate the Liturgy carelessly or without reverence.

We must not only come for the Eucharist itself, but also take part in the hours of prayer, psalms, and hymns before it. These are the spiritual banquet of the Church. To neglect them is to treat ourselves as strangers in our own Mother’s house.

Those who join in these prayers grow in love for the faith of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Those who neglect them risk becoming outsiders to their own inheritance.

We must not only come for the Eucharist itself, but also take part in the hours of prayer, psalms, and hymns before it. These are the spiritual banquet of the Church. To neglect them is to treat ourselves as strangers in our own Mother’s house.

Those who join in these prayers grow in love for the faith of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Those who neglect them risk becoming outsiders to their own inheritance.

text: Beloved brothers and sisters, Jesus   Christ Himself taught us how to pray. The Our Father is short in words, but full of meaning. Every part shows us how to live as God’s children. Let us walk through it clearly.

When you say “Our Father,” you are calling the Creator of all things our Father. That is a great honor. But if you continue to live in sin, how can you truly call Him our Father? To speak these words, your life must reflect them.

We add, “in heaven,” not because God is locked in heaven, but to show that He is above everything and unlike earthly fathers. Earthly fathers give us life in the flesh; the heavenly Father gives us eternal life in the spirit.

The Scripture says: “To all who received Him, He gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12). So when you pray, live as a true son or daughter of heaven.

God’s name is already holy. Nothing we do can make it more holy. But people dishonor His name through sin, while others honor it through obedience.

When you pray, “May Your name be holy,” you are asking that your life and your actions shine so that people see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven (Matthew 5:16).

text.text: 3. “May Your Kingdom Come. May Your Will Be Done on Earth as in Heaven”

text:
God’s kingdom is present wherever His will is obeyed. In heaven the angels do His will completely—quickly and joyfully.

When you pray this, you are asking that God’s will be done in your life and in the world, just as it is in heaven. It means surrendering your desires to Him, fighting against sin, and living as a true citizen of His kingdom.

This prayer is not about wealth or luxury. It is about what we need to live each day. God provides food, clothing, shelter, and strength. Jesus already told us: “Seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well” (Matthew 6:33).

text.text: 5. “Forgive Us Our Sins, as We Forgive Those Who Sin Against Us”

text:
God connects His forgiveness to our forgiveness. If you forgive others, God will forgive you. If you refuse, He will not forgive you (Matthew 6:14–15).

The sinful woman was forgiven because she loved much (Luke 7:47). But the unforgiving servant was punished because he showed no mercy (Matthew 18:23–35).

So when you pray these words, search your heart. If you hold anger or hatred, your prayer condemns you instead of saving you.

text.text: 6. “Do Not Let Us Fall into Temptation, but Rescue Us from Evil”

text:
We ask God not to leave us in trials we cannot endure. Temptations will come, but without His help we are too weak. The flesh is weak, but God makes the spirit strong.

When you pray, “Rescue us from evil,” you are asking for protection from the devil, from sin, and from everything that destroys the soul.

The "Our Father" teaches us everything we need in prayer:

To honor God as Father,

To live so His name is glorified,

To seek His kingdom and His will,

To trust Him for daily needs,

To forgive as He forgives us,

To ask His help against temptation and evil.

Do not just repeat these words with your lips. Let them live in your heart and actions. Then you will not only pray like Christ taught you will live as a true child of the Father.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.

text:
Beloved in Christ, grace and peace to you. Prayer is the breath of the soul, the ladder that unites earth with heaven, the bond that ties the heart of man to the throne of God. If we neglect prayer, we starve the soul; if we cultivate it, we grow in communion with the Lord, with His saints, and with His holy angels.

So then, the question is rightly asked: What should we pray? The holy tradition of the Church has not left us in darkness, but has handed down to us prayers filled with the Holy Spirit—prayers of the righteous, prayers of the saints, prayers from the very mouth of God Himself in the Holy Scriptures.

Let us then look deeply at the treasures that have been placed in our hands.

text.text: 1. The praise of Mary and Daily Prayers

text:
Daily Prayer

Daily Praise of Mary

Anqetse Birhan

The Angels praise her (Ywedswa Melaekt )

Our Father

The Psalms are all prayers. The daily schedule is as follows:

Monday: Psalms 1–30

Tuesday: Psalms 31–60

Wednesday: Psalms 61–80

Thursday: Psalms 81–110

Friday: Psalms 111–130

Saturday: Psalms 131–150; Psalms of Solomon

Sunday: Prophetic Prayers

If it is not possible to pray all the daily psalms:

Pray ten psalms each day.

Special prayer: Psalm 118 (119):1–176.

If even ten psalms are not possible, it is good to at least choose from the following:

Psalm 6, Psalm 12 (13), Psalm 19 (20), Psalm 22 (23), Psalm 24 (25), Psalm 26 (27), Psalm 37 (38), Psalm 50 (51), Psalm 69 (70), Psalm 85 (86), Psalm 90 (91), Psalm 120 (121), Psalm 135 (136), Psalm 140 (141), Psalm 144 (145).

The Praise of the Isrloooaelites (Exodus 15:1–19)

The Prayer of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:1–43)

The Prayer of Hannah, the Mother of Samuel (1 Samuel 1:10)

The Prayer of Manasseh (2 Chronicles 33:12–13)

The Prayer of Isaiah (Isaiah 26:1–21)

The Prayer of King Hezekiah (Isaiah 38:10–20)

The Prayer of Daniel (Daniel 9:4–19)

The Prayer of Jonah (Jonah 2:3–11)

The Prayer of the Three (Prayer Book)

The Song of the Three Children (Prayer Book)

The Prayer of Habakkuk (Habakkuk 3:1–19)

The Prayer of the Virgin Mary (Luke 1:46–55)

The Prayer of Zechariah (Luke 1:68–79)

The Prayer of Simeon (Luke 2:29–32)

✍ Note: The Prayer of Manasseh, the Prayer of the Three, and the Song of the Three Children are found in the prayer books, not in the Bible.

(Wudase amilak)

There is daily praise, and the following psalms of David are prayed at the end of each day:

Psalm 6, Psalm 24 (25), Psalm 37 (38), Psalm 50 (51), Psalm 69 (70), Psalm 85 (86), Psalm 120 (121).

The Gospel of John has 21 chapters.

Three chapters are prayed in three days.

Or one chapter is prayed each day.

Arganon: daily thanksgiving and supplication to Our Lady.

Melkea melk'e: prayers such as Melkea Medhane Alem, Melkea silase , Melkae Eyesus, Melkea Mary, the Holy Angels Melk'e, and finally the Forty-One Kyrie Eleisons with the Lord’s Prayer (with prostrations).

Morning

Daily Prayer

Daily praise of Mary

The Angels praise her (Ywedswa Melaekt )

Praise God of the Day

Forty-One Kyrie Eleisons and the Lord’s Prayer (with prostration)

Our Father

Anqetse Birhan

Gospel of John (one or three chapters)

Psalms of David (one or three psalms)

Our Father


When one prayer ends, it is closed with the Our Father before moving to the next. According to our time and situation, morning and evening prayers may be combined with prostration.

text: Beloved in Christ, today we commemorate the repose of the great Abune Tekle Haymanot of Debre Libanos, the lamp of Ethiopia and the one called Ḥadīs Ḥawārya“the New Apostle.” His memory shines upon us on Nehase 24, together with the repose of other holy fathers and one blessed mother. Their lives, sweeter than honey, are preserved for us as a treasury of faith and endurance.

text.text: The Birth and Divine Election of the Saint

text:
Abune Tekle Haymanot his name meaning “ Plant of the faith ” was conceived by the divine will through the helping of the Archangel Michael, to his father, the priest Tsega Zeab, and to his holy mother egzi harya. His birth took place on Tahisas 24, 1197 A.D., yet even before his coming into the world, he was set apart as a chosen vessel.

On the third day of his infancy, he descended from his mother’s arms and proclaimed: “Holy is the Father, Holy is the Son, Holy is the Holy Spirit.” Thus, from his very lips, God’s praise was perfected, as from the mouth of a nursing babe (Psalm 8:2).

Trained by his father in the sacred liturgy, he was ordained by the Archbishop of Alexandria, Abune Kerlos, and thus consecrated to the service of the Church from his youth. But his destiny was confirmed in the wilderness, where the Archangel Michael appeared and commanded him to abandon the hunting of beasts, and instead to hunt souls for salvation.

Michael announced to him the gifts bestowed by Christ: power to raise the dead, heal the sick, cast out demons, and turn hearts from idols to the true worship of God. The Lord Himself also appeared, blessing him and granting him the apostolic authority first given to the disciples: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.”

“Your name shall no longer be Fisḥa tsyōn (Joy of Zion), but Tekle Haymanot. Its meaning is : the Plant of Father, the Plant of Son, and the Plant of Holy Spirit." and From that day, Tekle Haymanot became the new apostle of Ethiopia. with Michael as his unfailing guardian.

From that hour, Tekle Haymanot devoted his life to the Gospel. He renounced his possessions, giving them to the poor and to the Church, declaring: “O Lord Jesus Christ! I have left open my house on earth, so that You may open the gate of heaven for me.”

Then he began to travel and preach:

Turning people from sin to righteousness.

Turning people from idolatry to the worship of the true God.

Preached in Damot and Wolayta for 12 years, destroying idol worship and planting the faith.and building churches upon the ruins of false worship. Lived in monasteries across Ethiopia, including Debre Damo, Debre Libanos, and Asbo.
In Tigray and Debre Damo, he embraced the monastic life, enduring hardship and performing countless miracles.

Through his labors, monasteries multiplied, disciples were gathered, and entire peoples were illumined with the light of Christ. Truly, Ethiopia received him as her apostle, and his ministry was adorned with wonders beyond number.

text:
The saint’s ascetic feats are awe-inspiring. By divine strength, he was given six radiant wings when the devil sought to destroy him, and he flew as a cherub. He shattered idols, healed the sick, and humbled dragons through the sign of the cross.

Yet his greatest struggle was not against beasts or demons, but against his own flesh. For seven years he stood upon one leg, like a pillar unshaken, fasting without food or water.It was only in the fourth year of the seven years that they tasted a little water. His cane broke beneath him from long vigils, yet he persevered, until the Lord appeared, clothing him with fire and crowning him with seven crowns of life:

For his pure faith,

For his journeys across Ethiopia,

For his sufferings against idolatry,

For his pilgrimages to Jerusalem,

For his fasting and ceaseless prayer,

For his monastic labors,

For his blood shed in the struggle for the faith.

Thus, even before his death, Christ granted him a vision of his heavenly inheritance.

As his repose drew near, he spoke to his disciples with fatherly counsel:

“Not every monk enters the kingdom of heaven, but only those who despise the world. Seek first the righteousness of God. Fast and pray. Love one another. Do not love the fleeting glory of the world, but imitate the fathers of old, who conquered evil through toil and tears. If you share not their sufferings, you will not share their joy.”

He urged them to be free from worldly vanities, to serve the Church without ceasing, and to remain steadfast in prayer and charity. Then, blessing them, he commended his soul to God.

On Nehase 24, 1296 Abune Tekle Haymanot entered into rest. Christ appeared with His Virgin Mother and the holy angels, receiving his pure soul with honor. The angels cried: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His saints” (Psalm 116:15).

He was buried at Debre Asbo, which later became Debre Libanos, and after 57 years his relics were transferred with great solemnity. The Lord promised that no soul invoking the name of Tekle Haymanot whether righteous or sinner would be left without his intercession before the throne of God.

The Church celebrates his holy life in several feasts:

His conception, Megabit 24, 1196

His birth, Tahsas 24, 1197

His ordination, Hidar 24, 1197

The breaking of his leg through prayer, Tir 4, 1289

His repose, Nehase 24, 1296

The translation of his relics, Ginbot 12, 1353

Beloved, the life of Abune Tekle Haymanot is not only history, but prophecy fulfilled in Ethiopia. He is the living witness that God raises up apostles in every generation, and that the Holy Spirit breathes where He wills. His struggle, his counsel, and his intercession remain with us even now.

Let us, therefore, honor his memory with fasting, prayer, and charity, that through his prayers we may also be made worthy of that incorruptible crown prepared for all who love the Lord.

Through the prayers of Abune Tekle Haymanot, may Ethiopia and all who call upon him be preserved in the true faith, now and forevermore. Amen.

text: Beloved in Christ, today we turn our hearts to the luminous memory of Holy Mother Kristos Semra, the fragrant flower of Shewa, the glory of Zion, and the chosen staff of the Holy Virgin Mary. Her story is not merely history; it is a divine testimony, a mirror of faith, a torch of endurance, and a ladder leading heavenward.

Holy Kristos Semra was born in Geye, Shewa Bulga Province, from faithful parents her father Deresani and her mother Eleni. Like the righteous of old, they nurtured their daughter in the fear of God, raising her in the holy order of the Church, and instructing her in the books of both the Old and New Testaments.

When she came of age, they gave her in marriage to Semre Giorgis, son of Eyesus Moa. The Lord blessed their union with twelve children ten sons and two daughters. Yet, unlike many who are distracted by worldly care, Kristos Semra raised her children in discipline and in the law of God, sowing in them the seed of eternal life.

text.text: The King’s Praise and the Vision of St. Michael

text:
In those days reigned the merciful Emperor Gebre Meskel. Hearing of her beauty, her kindness, and her renown, he counted her among the 174 most admirable women of his kingdom. In his favor, he sent 272 young servants to attend to her.

But Kristos Semra, fearing the vanity of earthly praise, turned her heart to God in prayer. And lo! the Archangel Michael appeared to her in vision, greeting her with the heavenly salutation:

“Peace be with you, beloved Kristos Semra. Eat of the bread of heaven, which is the goodness of God.and he fed her”

Filled with the Holy Spirit, she gave thanks to her Creator. With the servants sent by the king, she built a church in honor of St. Michael, just as the Archangel had commanded her.

text.text: Her Ministry and the Miracle of Resurrection

text:
She brought the Ark of the Angel into that holy temple and served God with devotion. Yet trials were not far from her path. One day, a servant girl fell under the power of an unclean spirit and resisted her mistress’s counsel. Soon after, the girl died, and Kristos Semra wept bitterly, lamenting:

“This death shall be accounted as my own sin, O Lord!”

In her grief, she prayed to God, and He, the Creator of life, raised the girl from the dead. Overcome with joy, she declared:

“If the Lord works such wonders for me while still in this passing world, how much more glorious will His gifts be in the life to come!”

text.text: Her Renunciation and Life of Asceticism

text:
Strengthened in spirit, she left her husband, her children, and her household, taking with her only her youngest son. She entered the holy monastery of Debre Libanos, where she dedicated herself to fasting and prayer.

Yet even here, her life was marked by sorrow mingled with glory. When her child was taken into Paradise by the Archangel Michael, she was pierced with grief. But the Archangel comforted her with the revelation that her son rejoices eternally in the kingdom of God.

Led thereafter to Lake Tana, she spent twelve years immersed in the waters, standing in prayer until her body became swollen and even the fish passed through her. Yet Christ appeared to her, granting her ten crowns from heaven and surrounding her with the guardianship of the Archangels Michael, Gabriel, Raphael and above all, His holy Mother, the Virgin Mary.

Burning with divine charity, Kristos Semra prayed even for the enemy of mankind:

“O my Creator, have mercy on the devil, for You have preserved me from his snares. I ask this for the sake of Adam and his children, that he may not deceive them, for their flesh is my flesh.”

The Lord, marveling at her supplication, commanded St. Michael to take her even to Hell. There she spoke with Satan himself, who mocked her attempt at reconciliation and cast her into the flames. But Michael struck Hell with his sword, opening a path of deliverance. And behold! 10,000 souls clung to the radiance of her spirit and were brought forth with her into freedom.

text:
The Lord Jesus Christ promised her a place of rest at the right hand of the Holy Virgin Mary, and He gave her the name:

“The Staff of Mary.”

The Holy Virgin appeared to her and blessed her with words of praise:

“Blessed is the womb that bore you, and blessed the breasts that nursed you. Blessed are the eyes that beheld you, and blessed are those who celebrate your struggle.”

At last, she prepared for her departure. Digging a pit equal to her height, she set spears around her and endured twelve years in this manner of worship, pierced and suffering, yet unwavering. Then, on Nehase 24, her soul was received by the angels, and her body was laid to rest in Geye Monastery, where her holy relics remain for the blessing of the faithful.

The Lord Himself declared to her:

“I will bless twelve generations of those who love you, who call upon your name, who honor your memory, and who celebrate your feast.”

Thus, her name is glorified, her prayers intercede for us, and her memory remains a fountain of blessing until the end of the age.

O beloved faithful, let us imitate the steadfastness of Holy Kristos Semra—her courage in trial, her compassion even for her enemies, her ceaseless prayer, and her trust in the Lord who crowned her.

May her prayers, her intercession, and her unfailing aid be with us all, now and forever.

The Holy Virgin appeared to her and blessed her with words of praise:

“Blessed is the womb that bore you, and blessed the breasts that nursed you. Blessed are the eyes that beheld you, and blessed are those who celebrate your struggle.”

The Lord’s Promise

The Lord Himself declared to her:

“I will bless twelve generations of those who love you, who call upon your name, who honor your memory, and who celebrate your feast.”

Conclusion

O beloved faithful, let us imitate the steadfastness of Holy Kristos Semra—her courage in trial, her compassion even for her enemies, her ceaseless prayer, and her trust in the Lord who crowned her.

text: Beloved in Christ, children of the holy Orthodox Church, grace and peace be unto you. Today let us meditate upon the sacred mystery of prostration, that ancient gesture of worship which the Holy Scriptures commend, and which the Fathers of the Church have faithfully preserved. For the body bows in humility, yet the soul soars in exaltation; the knees bend low, yet the heart rises to heaven. What, then, is the purpose of prostration?

text.text: 1. Prostration of Worship - to God Alone

text:
The first type is the prostration of worship. This is given only to God, because only He is divine by nature.

When we bow to God, we bow to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

This is why our prayer says: “I prostrate for the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one prostrate .”

The word “one worship,” we do not count the number of prostrations, but rather affirm that the act is directed to the one God ( for The Father, The Son, The Holy Sprite ), and to no other. Neither angel nor man, nor any created thing, may receive such adoration. To offer it elsewhere would be idolatry, a theft of the glory due to God.

This kind of prostration must never be given to any creature not to people, angels, or things made by human hands. God warned His people:

“You shall not worship any other gods before me” (Exodus 20:3).

“For I, the Lord your God, am a jealous God” (Exodus 20:5).

To give worship to anyone else is to provoke God’s anger. Worship belongs to Him alone, for He is our Creator, Redeemer, and the source of all life.

The second type is the prostration of honor,or the prostration of grace. This is not prostration of God’s divine nature, but honor shown to the saints, to the Virgin Mary, and even to the Holy Cross.

After we confess “I worship the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit,” our prayers continue with words of honor:

“I bow to our Lady, the Virgin Mary, who gave birth to God, and to the Cross on which Christ was crucified for the life of the world.”

This shows the difference:

Worship is only for God.

Honor is given to those whom God has sanctified and filled with His grace.

When we bow before Mary, we do not worship her as God. We honor her because she bore God in the flesh.When we bow before the Cross, we do not worship the wood, but honor it because it carried Christ and became the instrument of our salvation.

The Bible itself supports this kind of honor. Isaac blessed Jacob with these words:

“Let nations serve you, and princes bow down to you; be lord over your brothers, and let your father’s sons bow down to you. Cursed be he who curses you, and blessed be he who blesses you” (Genesis 27:29).

Though Esau was the firstborn, God gave Jacob the blessing. From that moment, God was called the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The act of bowing before Jacob was not worship of him as God, but honor for the grace God placed upon him.

Prostration has a deep spiritual meaning.

Bowing down shows humility, that we are dust before God.

Touching the ground reminds us of our weakness and mortality.

Rising again points to our hope of resurrection in Christ.

Thus, every prostration becomes a silent sermon. It teaches us humility, reminds us of God’s holiness, and strengthens our faith in eternal life.
So then, we must keep these two truths in our hearts:
- belongs to God alone: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

- belongs to the saints, to the Virgin Mary, and to the Cross, because God’s grace shines through them.

When we worship God, we confess His majesty.When we honor His saints, we glorify the God who sanctified them.

text: Beloved brothers and sisters, today we continue our meditation on the holy mystery of prostration. This act of bowing down is not a human invention, but a sacred gesture found throughout the Scriptures. Both in the Old and New Testaments, we see prophets, kings, and apostles bowing before God and His chosen servants. The Church, guided by the Holy Spirit, has preserved this tradition and ordered it with wisdom.

text.text: 1. The Witness of the Old Testament

text:
When Moses longed to know the name of his God, the Lord revealed Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob - the God who blessed Jacob through Isaac and gave him the inheritance. In this revelation, we see blessing and covenant.

Obadiah, the commander of King Ahab’s army, bowed before Elijah, saying, “My lord” (1 Kings 18:8).

The captain of fifty, sent by King Ahaziah with his soldiers, bowed down before Elijah and pleaded, “O man of God, let my life and the lives of these fifty servants of yours be precious in your sight” (2 Kings 1:13). Because he bowed and honored the prophet, his prayer was heard, and he and his men were spared from the fire of heaven.

The men of Jericho bowed before Elisha when they saw that the spirit of Elijah rested upon him (2 Kings 2:15).

The Shunammite woman bowed before Elisha in her sorrow when her child died, and again in her joy when the child was restored to life (2 Kings 4:27–37).

text.text: 2. The Witness of the New Testament

text:
The New Testament also shows us the same reverence:

The jailer at Philippi, trembling with fear, bowed down before Paul and Silas after the earthquake shook the prison and their chains fell away (Acts 16:29).

These examples show that bowing is not only fitting but also powerful, for God accepts humility and honors reverence.

The Holy Church teaches us that prostration is not all of one kind. There are three orders of prostration:

(a) Full Prostration - Wediq

This is to fall completely to the ground, with forehead, fingers, and knees touching the earth.

“He bowed his face to the ground” (Gen. 19:1).

“He bowed down and worshiped” (Num. 22:31; John 5:15).

“He fell at his feet and worshiped him” (Acts 10:25).

“I fell at his feet to worship him” (Rev. 19:10).

This is the most complete form of surrender and humility before God.

B) Kneeling Prostration(astebrko)

This is done by bending the knees and lowering the body. It is what St. Paul meant when he wrote: “…that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Phil. 2:10).

The hymn of the Church proclaims: “Standing on our knees, by the will of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, we bow down and worship Christ who raised us up to salvation.”

(c) Bowing of the Head - (Adnon)

This is a gentler form of reverence, where the head, forehead, and neck are inclined. At the close of the Divine Liturgy the deacon prays: “Save “‘Humble yourselves before the Lord our God…’ - this is what He is saying.”

text.text: 4. Times When We Do Not Bow

text:
The Church, in her wisdom, has also set aside holy times when bowing is not practiced. These include:

On Sundays, the day of the Resurrection.

On Saturdays, the first day of the week.

On the feast of Pentecost and during its season.

On the feasts of the Lord.

On the feast of the Virgin Mary.

On the feast of Saint Michael.

After we accept Eucharist 

But if these feasts fall on the Day of the Passion or on the Feast of the Cross, then prostration is performed, for those days recall the Lord’s suffering and His victory through the Cross.

text: Beloved in Christ, peace and blessing to you from the Lord who governs heaven and earth, who establishes the boundaries of the seas, who gathers the waters, and who clothes the skies with clouds. Today let us reflect on the divine mystery of the cloud what it is, how it was created, and what hidden message it contains for us who believe.

In the beginning, when God made the heavens and the earth, He arranged the waters in wondrous fashion. The Scriptures bear witness that He separated them and appointed their places.

One part He raised up, calling it the expanse, the firmament stretched out between earth and heaven.

Another portion of the waters, which He placed above the expanse, He called the sea.

The last portion He divided into seven parts, and the last seventh part, he called ocean, the great deep which surrounds the earth.

The solid part beneath He called the earth, which He adorned with fruitfulness and gave as a dwelling place for mankind.

Behold how our God, with wisdom, arranged even the waters in order and harmony, so that the creation might reflect His majesty.

After this ordering, the Lord brought forth yet another wonder: He caused dry vapor to rise from the dry land and moist vapor to rise from the sea. From their mingling, He formed the cloud, that light and smoke-like creation which floats above the green earth.

The Psalmist declares: “He causes the vapors to ascend from the ends of the earth” (Psalm 134:7). Thus, the cloud is not of heavy substance, but of delicate and unseen particles, gathered together by the word of the Lord.

text.text: The Nature and Work of the Cloud

text:
What is a cloud? It is a subtle, smoke-like body, invisible to touch, yet powerful in purpose. It is the chosen vessel that bears rain.

Through the mystery of evaporation, the waters of the seas and rivers are lifted upward. They are gathered into the cloud, and when the Lord commands, they are poured forth again upon the earth. But notice, brethren, how wisely God has ordered it: the waters do not descend in confusion or destruction, but in measure and in season, “filtered,” as it were, through the very body of the cloud, so that they fall gently and fruitfully.

This is why Saint Epiphanius, in his holy liturgy, testifies: “He causes the rain to fall in the wilderness where there is no man.” Mark the wonder! Even where no man dwells, where no eye beholds, the Lord waters the desert. Why? To show that His goodness is not limited to human need, but extends over all creation.

He sends the snow upon the desolate places, and pours water where men dwell. Each has its appointed place: the wilderness clothed in snow, the city refreshed with rain. Behind this, the Fathers discern a greater mystery.

Yet this is not all. The cloud bears within it a spiritual mystery. Just as rain is poured forth from heaven through the hidden work of God, so also did our Lord Jesus Christ come down to us.

By the unfathomable wisdom of the Father, the eternal Son was conceived without seed in the womb of the Holy Virgin Mary, overshadowed by the Holy Spirit, as a hidden cloud bearing the water of life. He came down upon the barren desert of this world, and made the wilderness of our hearts fruitful by His grace.

And when He had accomplished His saving work teaching, healing, suffering, dying, and rising again He sent forth His holy apostles, as streams of living water, to carry His Gospel to all nations. For He Himself commanded them: “Go and teach” (Matthew 28:19).

Thus, the mystery of the cloud points us to the Incarnation, the life-giving descent of Christ, and the apostolic mission which continues to water the whole earth with the teaching of truth.

text: Beloved brethren in Christ, peace and grace be multiplied unto you. Today we turn to a sacred question: When is prostration offered? How much is required of us? And what does the Church call this holy act? Let us attend carefully, for in these mysteries we are taught how to humble the body so that the soul may ascend to God.

God, who is infinite and uncontained, is not bound by any place. He is higher than the heavens, deeper than the abyss, and His presence stretches from horizon to horizon. Yet we, being finite creatures bound by space and time, are in need of holy places to direct our prayer.

Therefore, we gather in the temple of God the Church. Church means both the dwelling of Christ in His people, and the gathering place of the faithful. When we call the Church the dwelling of Christ, we mean His presence in the souls of the righteous, in the individual believer, and in the community. When we call the Church the house of Christ, we speak of the consecrated building where His people assemble.

Thus, the Church is the house of God Himself. It is the place where His name is called, His glory proclaimed, and the sacrifice of thanksgiving is continually offered. Wherever the faithful gather, there is the Church; for He has promised: “Where two or three are gathered in My name, there am I in their midst” (Matthew 18:20).

The first reason we worship in the Church is because it is His house, and where the King is, there His servants the holy angels and the righteous saints also dwell. We bow with reverence before God and honor those who serve Him.

We bend our hips, fall upon our knees, and touch the ground with our hands and forehead. Why? Because though God is everywhere present, He Himself declares: “Heaven is My throne, and the earth is My footstool” (Matthew 5:35). When therefore we touch the earth with our heads, we humble ourselves at His feet, acknowledging His majesty.

In this way, both the worship that belongs to God alone (the prostration of His nature) and the honor shown to His saints (the prostration of grace) are performed outwardly in the same act yet the heart distinguishes their meaning.

When prostration is made in church, we turn to the East, for the Sun of Righteousness rose from the East. If we are not in a church, we set before us a holy sign: a cross, the Gospel, or an icon. Having bowed, we seal our prayer with the words: “O God, have mercy on us, and through the Virgin Mary, have mercy on us.”

In prayers of repentance, our spiritual father appoints how many prostrate and prayers we should perform, guiding us as a physician prescribes medicine. 

Whoever is moved by zeal may increase their prayers; whoever is weak may offer as they can but always remembering the sufferings of Christ. for the prostrations that we offer no strict limit is set.

In this way, both the worship that belongs to God alone (the prostration of His nature) and the honor shown to His saints (the prostration of grace) are performed outwardly in the same act yet the heart distinguishes their meaning.

When prostration is made in church, we turn to the East, for the Sun of Righteousness rose from the East. If we are not in a church, we set before us a holy sign: a cross, the Gospel, or an icon. Having bowed, we seal our prayer with the words: “O God, have mercy on us, and through the Virgin Mary, have mercy on us.”

In prayers of repentance, our spiritual father appoints how many prostrate and prayers we should perform, guiding us as a physician prescribes medicine. 

Whoever is moved by zeal may increase their prayers; whoever is weak may offer as they can but always remembering the sufferings of Christ. for the prostrations that we offer no strict limit is set.

text:
Beloved in Christ, today the Church gathers us into the holy mystery of remembrance. On the twenty-eighth day of Nehase, we celebrate the feast of the righteous patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. These fathers are not merely figures of history, but pillars of faith, roots of the covenant, and living examples of obedience, humility, and trust in the Most High.

Let us, therefore, with reverence, recount their lives, not to glorify men, but to magnify the Lord who worked wonders through them. For as the Scriptures proclaim, “God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared for them a city” (Hebrews 11:16).

The kingdom of heaven itself is adorned with their names, for Christ declared: “Many will come from the east and the west and will sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 8:11). Their righteousness shines more numerous than the stars, and their faith is counted as everlasting treasure. What tongue can fully tell their glory? What pen can describe their holiness? It is enough for us to fall in awe before their Creator and cry, “Glory! Glory! To God who is wondrous in His saints.”

Abraham, the father of faith, began his journey amidst idols, for his father Terah fashioned them. Yet, seeking the true God, Abraham saw the emptiness of wood and stone. He mocked their lifelessness, saying: “Eyes they have, but they see not; ears they have, but they hear not.” He shattered the false gods and set his heart upon the living Lord.

He departed to Canaan, trusting only in the promise of God. He faced famine, sojourned in Egypt and Palestine, yet in all these, the Creator honored him. Kings trembled before him, prophets were healed by his prayer, and strangers were welcomed into his tent. His hospitality was so great that he would not taste food unless it was shared with a guest. And behold, the Lord rewarded him: the Holy Trinity itself came to him in the plains of Mamre. and by his humility washed the feet of the Godhead.

He pleaded before the Lord for Sodom and Gomorrah, showing both mercy and boldness in intercession. And when tested, he did not withhold his beloved son but offered him upon the altar. For this obedience, he is called father of prophets, apostles, kings, and priests the very root of the covenant.

So beloved was he, that the angels proclaimed him:

“Abraham, friend of God”

“Abraham, faithful to God”

“Abraham, beloved of God”

Even in the place of the dead, God granted him a resting place of honor, shielding him from the reach of demons, until the coming of Christ.

Our father Abraham is honored in glory, holiness, and grace from Genesis to the Revelation of John. The saints invoke the Creator in his name. Because of his holiness, even the forces of darkness could not approach him. Abraham rested in peace one thousand nine hundred years before the birth of Christ, having lived one hundred and seventy-five years

Isaac, son of the promise, born by divine intervention, was pure and blameless. In him we behold the image of Christ, for he was the willing sacrifice. When Abraham, in obedience, bound him upon the altar, Isaac did not resist. He said instead, “Bind me, father, lest I move against you; cover my eyes, lest your heart be softened with pity.”

O wondrous obedience! O holy humility! For this reason, we honor him saying: “Peace be upon Isaac, who was faithful to his father.”

God spared his life, revealing the mystery of Christ’s coming sacrifice. Isaac lived one hundred and eighty years, walking in holiness. With his wife Rebecca, he conceived Jacob and Esau. At his passing, a heavenly voice declared:

“I will honor him who honors my friend Isaac.”

“Who bows in his name, who prays in his name, who shows mercy in his name I will reward him in heaven.”

Thus Isaac rests, adorned with blessings and eternal glory.

text:
Jacob, the third patriarch, followed in the footsteps of his fathers. Receiving the blessing of the firstborn, he fled to Syria. Along the way, he lay upon a stone and beheld a wondrous vision: a golden ladder reaching to heaven, with angels ascending and descending. This ladder is the mystery of the Virgin Mary, through whom the Son of God descended to earth.

Jacob proclaimed, “This is the house of God and the gate of heaven.”

He became the father of twelve sons, from whom came prophets, priests, kings, and judges—the holy nation of Israel. After serving his uncle Laban twenty-one years, he returned to Canaan, where he wrestled with God Himself. In that struggle of love, he was renamed Israel, “he who prevails with God.”

Saint Jacob suffered greatly in his old age. His sons sold their brother Joseph and deceived him, saying, ‘He has been devoured by wild beasts.’ Grieving without comfort, Jacob wept until he lost his sight. Later, when famine struck the land, he went down to Egypt with about seventy-five members of his household at the age of one hundred and thirty. There he lived for seventeen years, and at the age of one hundred and forty-seven he died, and his sons buried him with honor.

On Nehase 28, the Church celebrates the feast of our holy fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. They are honored as pillars of faith, and heaven itself is called by their name. Their glory is greater than the stars, and in remembering them we glorify their Creator, saying: “Glory to God who is wondrous in His saints!”

text.text: and When It Is Not Offered

text: Dear brothers and sisters, the Holy Church has given us clear teaching about prostration. She shows us the days and times when it should be offered and the days when it should not. These rules are not given by chance, but are established with wisdom, so that we may worship God in the right way and at the right time.

First, let us understand when it is not permitted to prostrate. For the Church, like a wise mother, teaches that not every day is the same, nor every hour alike.

Saturdays and Sundays are exempt from prostration. For these are the days of joy, the days of rest, the days in which the light of the Resurrection shines. How can one bow in mourning on the day that Christ has triumphed over death?

Likewise, on the great feasts of the Lord His conception, His birth, His baptism, His triumphal entry on Hosanna, His resurrection, His ascension, His descent of the Spirit at Pentecost, and His glory revealed upon Mount Tabor the Church forbids prostration. These are days not of lament but of jubilation, not of abasement but of exaltation, for on these days Christ revealed His power and majesty.

In addition, on the feasts of the holy ones Our Lady on the 21st, Saint Michael on the 12th, and the Fathers on the 29th we do not bow to the ground, for the joy of the saints is shared by the faithful.

Thus, let all understand: there is a difference between the reverence we show when entering the church, bowing before the cross, venerating the holy Gospel, or greeting the holy icons, and the canonical act of prostration that belongs to the ordered life of the Church. The teaching on prostration does not refer to every gesture of adoration, but specifically to the prostration established as a permanent canon of the Church.

text.text: Days and Times When Prostration Is Commanded

text:
Yet the Church, like a skillful physician, also prescribes for us the times when prostration is necessary, when the soul must humble itself before God in body as well as in spirit.

When we are given a special canon of penance, we must prostrate.

When we hear the words of Scripture that call us to worship, we must prostrate.

During the Divine Liturgy, when the Church proclaims, “Worship God with fear,” “Pray,” “Humble yourselves in repentance,” then let every knee bend, for heaven itself bends in awe before the mysteries.

During the time of the Passion, in the holy and great week, the Church orders us to prostrate with fasting, prayer, and tears, for then we walk with Christ in His suffering.

During the holy fasts, we must sanctify the season with prayer, almsgiving, tears, and prostration, so that our fasting may be acceptable to the Lord.

In the life of penance, when the Scriptures declare, “Humble yourselves, you who are in penance,” let us fall to the ground, for the Fathers taught their children that prostration is inseparable from repentance.

Even in our daily prayer, when we say:
“Peace be upon the Holy Church, the image of the heavenly Jerusalem, the dwelling of the Godhead, the model of Him who has set us free from sin,”
the very words call us to bend low, for the soul cannot utter such words without humbling the body before the Lord.

Thus, before the cross, before the holy Scriptures, before the images of the saints, before the Gospel of life, let every Christian prostrate in faith.

Days and Times When Prostration Is Commanded

Yet the Church, like a skillful physician, also prescribes for us the times when prostration is necessary, when the soul must humble itself before God in body as well as in spirit.

When we are given a special canon of penance, we must prostrate.

When we hear the words of Scripture that call us to worship, we must prostrate.

During the Divine Liturgy, when the Church proclaims, “Worship God with fear,” “Pray,” “Humble yourselves in repentance,” then let every knee bend, for heaven itself bends in awe before the mysteries.

During the time of the Passion, in the holy and great week, the Church orders us to prostrate with fasting, prayer, and tears, for then we walk with Christ in His suffering.

During the holy fasts, we must sanctify the season with prayer, almsgiving, tears, and prostration, so that our fasting may be acceptable to the Lord.

In the life of penance, when the Scriptures declare, “Humble yourselves, you who are in penance,” let us fall to the ground, for the Fathers taught their children that prostration is inseparable from repentance.

Even in our daily prayer, when we say:
“Peace be upon the Holy Church, the image of the heavenly Jerusalem, the dwelling of the Godhead, the model of Him who has set us free from sin,”
the very words call us to bend low, for the soul cannot utter such words without humbling the body before the Lord.

Thus, before the cross, before the holy Scriptures, before the images of the saints, before the Gospel of life, let every Christian prostrate in faith.

Continues 👇🏾

text:
But what shall we say as we prostrate? With the tongue we invoke the name of God; with the heart we remember the sufferings of Christ; with the soul we beg for forgiveness of our sins. Let each man say:

“O Lord, forgive us, remember not our iniquities. Have mercy on us, not according to our righteousness, but according to Your abundant kindness. You are our Creator, our King, our Shepherd, our Savior. To You alone we bow in faith and submission.”

This is the voice of true prostration: not empty motion, but the offering of the heart.

And how much shall we bow? The Church teaches that the number of our prostrations is not left to chance or habit but is guided by spiritual fathers. For one hundred prostrations offered in love will receive from God a hundredfold reward. Two hundred, three hundred, or more, each shall be reckoned, for God does not forget even the smallest act of service.

If the prostration is made in penance, then the measure is given by the Fathers according to the weight of sin, and the penitent bows as medicine for the soul. If it is offered freely out of love, then the Lord receives it as an offering of devotion.

Be assured, brethren, that no labor of ours is wasted before God. For He who weighs the hairs of our head and the drops of rain also weighs every prostration, every bow, every tear, and grants to His children the reward of their faithfulness.
Therefore, let us keep the wisdom of the Church with reverence. Let us prostrate when commanded, and in all things glorify Christ who bowed the heavens and came down for our salvation.

text: Beloved in Christ, peace and grace be multiplied to you. Today let us reflect on the mystery of the cloud in Holy Scripture. What does the cloud signify? What does it reveal to us about God, His saints, and His holy Mother, the Virgin Mary? The Church, following the words of the prophets, apostles, and evangelists, teaches us that the cloud is not an only mere natural wonder, but a holy sign of God’s presence, His protection, and His glory.

text.text: 1. The Cloud and the Virgin Mary

text:
St. John the Theologian writes: “And the woman fled into the wilderness, to a place prepared by God, that they should feed her there for one thousand two hundred and sixty days” (Rev. 12:6). This woman is none other than the Virgin Mary, who fled into exile, carrying her Son, the Creator of the worlds. She wandered as a refugee, holding Him who Himself appointed the bounds of creation, yet who, in His humility, allowed Himself to be borne in her arms.

When the dragon was cast down, he pursued the woman, but she was given two wings of a great eagle to fly into the wilderness (Rev. 12:13–15). The Fathers call her a swift cloud, bearing within her the Sun of Righteousness. Isaiah had spoken long before: “Heaven is My throne, and the earth is My footstool” (Isa. 66:1). She carried Him who fills all things, once in her arms, once upon her back, as she journeyed through the deserts of Egypt and into Ethiopia.

Blessed was Ethiopia, for she received the Virgin and her Child. Habakkuk foresaw this, saying: “I saw the tents of Ethiopia in affliction, and the curtains of Midian trembled” (Hab. 3:7). Thus Ethiopia rejoiced, offering love and humility in welcoming the Mother and her Son.

text.text: 2. The Cloud as the Glory of God

text:
The cloud in Scripture is a revelation of God’s majesty. In the days of Moses, God appeared in the tabernacle of meeting as a pillar of cloud. “When Moses entered the tabernacle, the pillar of cloud descended and stood at the door, and God spoke with him” (Exod. 33:8–9).

When Solomon completed the great Temple, again the cloud descended: “The house of the Lord was filled with the cloud, so that the priests could not stand to minister, for the glory of the Lord filled the house” (1 Kings 8:10).

In the New Testament, on Mount Tabor, the Lord revealed His divine light to Peter, James, and John. A bright cloud overshadowed them, and from it the voice of the Father was heard (Matt. 17:1–5).

And on the fortieth day after His Resurrection, when Christ ascended from the Mount of Olives, “a cloud received Him out of their sight” (Acts 1:9). The same cloud shall appear again at His Second Coming: “Behold, He is coming with clouds, and every eye shall see Him, even those who pierced Him” (Rev. 1:7).

The cloud is also an image of the saints, in whom the glory of God is revealed across the ages. St. Paul writes: “Since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily ensnares us” (Heb. 12:1).

Why are the saints likened to clouds? Just as the cloud shields us from the burning heat of the sun, so the saints, through their prayers, shield us from the wrath of God. Where there are clouds, there is rain; where there are saints, there is mercy. Their intercession brings refreshment to the Church as rain waters the earth.

text.text: 4. The Virgin Mary as the Highest Cloud

text: Above all, the Virgin Mary is the cloud most glorious. In her, the Creator revealed His glory more profoundly than in any other creature. The prophets foretold her, Moses proclaimed her, and through her God made His dwelling among men. Her womb became His throne for nine months; from her flesh He took flesh, from her soul He took a soul, and at her breast He received nourishment. In her the glory of God was most perfectly revealed, hidden yet shining forth for the salvation of the world.

text: Beloved in Christ, today we learn when the Church commands us to bow down in repentance, and when She tells us to stand in joy. Prostration is holy, but it is not done at all times. For there is a season for sorrow and a season for gladness. Guided by Scripture and the canons of the Fathers, the Church shows us these proper times, so that our worship may be pleasing to God.

text.text: I. The Times When Prostration Is Forbidden

text:
The first and chief among the days on which prostration is set aside is the Lord’s Day, the first day of the week, the day of His Resurrection. On this day we commemorate not mourning but victory, not abasement but triumph. For Christ, who was laid in the tomb, rose again in glory, and on this day He shall come again to judge the living and the dead.

The canons declare: “The known times when prostration to the ground is to be abandoned… are Sundays and the feast of Pentecost” (Fetha Negest, Article 14, No. 537). Again it says: “There is no prostration on Sundays and on the feasts of Pentecost, for these are days of joy” (Fetḥa Negest, Article 19, No. 715).
Thus the whole Church rejoices, standing upright before the Risen One, for the Sabbath of the new covenant is a day of liberty.

Pentecost, the fiftieth day, is the feast of the Spirit, the day when heaven was opened and tongues of fire descended upon the apostles. It is the perfection of Pascha, the crown of fifty days of joy.
On this day, as the Fathers teach, fasting is abolished, and so also prostration. Even if the fiftieth day falls upon a Wednesday or Friday, days usually given to fasting, yet the feast prevails, and we eat and rejoice as on Christmas or Easter.

text.text: 3. On the Great Feasts of Our Lord

text:
The law of the Church likewise forbids prostration on the great feasts of Christ. These are days of triumph, not lamentation. They include: His Conception, Nativity, Baptism, Hosanna, Resurrection, Ascension, Pentecost, and His Transfiguration on Mount Tabor. those are the eight feast of Christ but the Only one feast is excepted . the veneration of the Cross for though the Cross is an instrument of death, it is also the throne of His glory, and prostrate before it is .

4.

text.text: On the Feast of Our Lady, the Theotokos

text: As the feasts of the Lord are days of joy, so also the feast of His holy Mother. The canons declare that on the days of her feast, prostration is not permitted. For she who bore the Word in her womb is honored in joy, not in mourning.

Hear the wisdom of the Fathers: after partaking of the Body and Blood of Christ, we do not cast ourselves to the ground, but rather stand in reverence and thanksgiving, for the King of Glory has entered within us. The Fetha Negest says: “After receiving His body and blood, they refrain from worshipping” (Article 14, Nos. 536–537).

We do not abase ourselves, for He has lifted us up to communion with Himself. Our task in that hour is to glorify His Body and Blood, not to fall prostrate.

text.text: 6. On the 12th, 21st, and 29th Days of Each Month

text:
These days have been set aside by ancient custom.

The 12th is the feast of Saint Michael the Archangel, celebrated monthly in joy, for the Archangel is the defender of God’s people.

The 21st is dedicated to the Theotokos.

The 29th is consecrated to the memory of the Lord’s feasts.
On these days, as on the greater feasts, prostration is forbidden.

text: Beloved in Christ, children of the Holy Church, grace and peace be multiplied to you from the Lord who renews the times and seasons, who gathers the years into His hand, and who makes the sun to rise over the righteous and the wicked alike. Today let us lift our minds to the holy mystery of Pagume, the voluntary fast of Judith, and the spiritual meaning hidden in this blessed season at the threshold of the New Year.

The word Pagume means increase. It comes at the end of the Ethiopian year, and it is appointed for five days, or, once every four years in the leap year, for six days. Thus Ethiopia, in the providence of God, has earned the name: “The Land of Thirteen Months of Sunshine.”

When Pagume extends to six days, it aligns with the reckoning of the ancients, and in that year the fast of the Prophets, also called the fast of the Nativity, is broken on Nehase, with the celebration of the birth of Christ our Savior following thereafter.

Among the two voluntary fasts preserved in the Holy Church, one belongs to this month of Pagume. It is called the Fast of (Yodit). Yet,beloved, many are unaware of this fast.

But let none confuse this holy Yodit with the infamous Yodit Gudit, the one remembered in church history for her destructive deeds. No, the Yodit whom we honor is she whom Scripture praises: a widow of Israel, a woman of courage, chastity, and fasting.

Hear the account, as the Holy Book records it:

When the mighty king Nebuchadnezzar had subdued his enemies, he sent forth his general Holofernes with twelve thousand foot soldiers and twelve thousand horsemen, saying, “Go, enlarge my dominion, receive tribute from the submissive, and crush those who resist” (Judith 2:7). With this command, Holofernes swept through many nations, destroying and subduing them, until he came to the land of Judah. There he inflicted great suffering, and the children of Israel cried out in anguish.

At that time, Judith(Yodit), whose husband had died, lived in holy widowhood. She dwelt apart, clothed herself in sackcloth, humbled her soul with fasting, and wept continually before God on behalf of her people. On the third day, as she entered the temple, the Lord who does not desire the ruin of His creation revealed to her the path of deliverance (Judith 8:2).

she Strengthened by prayer and fasting. Because of her, the Israelites rose up, pursued their enemies, and drove them as far as the Jordan. Thus was shame turned into victory, weakness into strength, mourning into triumph.

Beloved, the Church therefore appoints this fast in the month of Pagume, so that we may imitate Judith’s holy zeal. For just as she conquered by fasting and prayer, so also must we, the children of the New Covenant, overcome our enemies: not flesh and blood, but Satan and the passions of the flesh.

Through voluntary fasting, we humble our bodies that our spirits may be exalted; we discipline our desires that we may receive power from the Creator; we arm ourselves with prayer that we may overcome the adversary.

text:
Pagume also holds another mystery. It is the month of transition. As the year comes to its end, and as winter’s darkness prepares to pass, so Pagume reminds us of the greater passage: the Resurrection.

For just as Pagume turns us from the old year to the new, the Resurrection turns us from what is temporary to what is eternal, from earth to heaven, from death to life.

Every year, in the month of Pagume, Christians gather in the church from nightfall to receive baptism with holy water. Through this, we seek God’s mercy: that He may grant us a blessed new year, forgive the sins of the past, heal us from our infirmities, sanctify our lives, and prepare us for a future filled with His blessing.

text.text: A Prayer for the New Year

text:
Let us then beseech the Lord of times and seasons:

That He grant us a new year of peace and health,

That He turn our hearts to repentance,

That He make us worthy to partake of His holy Body and precious Blood,

That He number us among the heirs of His everlasting Kingdom.
