text: Beloved children of the covenant, heirs of the promise, and followers of the Orthodox faith, grace and peace be multiplied to you from God the Father and from our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Today we set before our hearts a sacred mystery: What is the symbol of the cloud? The Scriptures, the Fathers, and the holy tradition all testify to its meaning, showing us that the cloud is not a mere vapor of the sky but a living sign of God’s mercy, His covenant, and His dwelling among His people.

text.text: 1. The Cloud of Noah – The Rainbow of the Covenant

text:
After the great flood, when the waters had subsided and the ark came to rest, Noah, the righteous man, offered a sacrifice of thanksgiving. God, moved with mercy, blessed Noah and his sons, commanding them: “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth” (Gen. 9:1). Yet Noah, full of sorrow, spoke: “Lord, my children will sin again, and will You not in Your justice destroy them once more?”

Then the Lord, who is good and merciful, established a covenant of peace. He said: “I will set My bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth. Never again shall the waters become a flood to destroy all flesh” (Gen. 9:12–15). Thus, the rainbow appeared in the heavens as the seal of God’s promise.

The rainbow is not only a reminder that God will not flood the earth again it is also a symbol of Christ and His Mother, the Holy Virgin Mary. Just as the rainbow shines with four colors, for it is four-faced, symbolizing the flesh of man made from the four elements, and prefiguring the fullness of Christ revealed through the four holy Gospels. And as the rainbow rests in the cloud, so too the covenant of God rests in His chosen vessel, the Holy Virgin Mary.

Our Lord Jesus, while hanging on the cross, entrusted her to us, saying to the beloved disciple: “Behold your mother” (John 19:27). She is, therefore, the Mother of the Covenant. Just as the rainbow stood as a sign that the flood of wrath would not return, so the Virgin is the sign that salvation has come into the world through her Son.

The holy scholar Abba Giorgis, in his book Enzira Sibhat, praises her: “You are the rainbow of the covenant, the sign that the rain of wrath will no longer fall upon the earth.” Likewise, Abba Tsige and Abba Gebre Mariam in Mahlete Tsige proclaim: “The rainbow of Noah’s covenant is fulfilled in you, O Virgin, for as the heavens are adorned with stars, so the earth is adorned with flowers and fruits through you.” Thus, the cloud that bore the rainbow becomes a symbol of Mary, who bore the Sun of Righteousness, Christ Himself.

text.text: 2. The Cloud of Moses – The Shelter of Mercy

text:
Let us now look to the days of Moses, the great lawgiver. He led Israel out of bondage in Egypt into the wilderness. Yet the people hardened their hearts, grumbling and rebelling, so that the journey of forty days stretched into forty years. Among the rebels were Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. The earth opened and swallowed them, and judgment fell upon their households. Fear and confusion seized the people, and they rose against Moses and Aaron, crying out to stone them.

But what says the Scripture?

Scripture says: “Moses and Aaron went into the tabernacle of the congregation, and the cloud covered it, and the glory of the Lord appeared” (Num. 16:42). The cloud descended, wrapping them in God’s protection and saving them from destruction.

This cloud, too, is a symbol of the Holy Virgin Mary. Just as the cloud shielded Moses and Aaron, so the Virgin protects all who call upon her with faith. She is a refuge and a covering for those who trust in her, guarding them from the attacks of the enemy and interceding before her Son on their behalf.

text: Beloved brothers and sisters, today we continue learning about the mystery of the cloud in the Holy Scriptures. The cloud is not only a natural thing it is a sign chosen by God to reveal His covenant, His mercy, and His salvation. In this part, we look at the cloud of Elijah and the cloud of Isaiah.

text.text: 3. The Cloud of Elijah – The Little Hand that Brought Rain

text:
In the days of King Ahab, Israel was consumed with idolatry. The queen Jezebel slew the prophets of the Lord, raising up hundreds of false priests in their place. The king, instead of defending the worship of the true God, joined her in spreading corruption. Therefore, God’s servant Elijah, aflame with zeal, prayed that the heavens would be shut. And for three years and six months, no rain fell upon the earth; famine spread over the land, and the people suffered hunger.

When at last the time had come, God commanded Elijah to appear before Ahab. The prophet cried out: “How long will you hesitate between two opinions? If the Lord is God, follow Him!” (1 Kings 18:21). On Mount Carmel, before the priests of Baal and all the people, Elijah called upon the Lord, and fire descended from heaven to consume the sacrifice. The false prophets were silenced, and the God of Israel was glorified.

But the work of Elijah was not yet finished. He ascended Mount Carmel once more, bowed himself down, and prayed with his face between his knees. sent his servant to look toward the sea. The servant returned six times with nothing. But on the seventh time he said: “Behold, a little cloud, as small as a man’s hand, rises from the sea.” (1 Kings 18:44).

Then Elijah proclaimed: “Go, say to Ahab, prepare your chariot before the rain stops you!” And immediately, the sky grew black with clouds and wind, and a mighty rain fell, watering the earth and ending the famine (1 Kings 18:45).

Behold the mystery! The cloud was small, no larger than a man’s hand yet from it came a flood of rain that refreshed the land. So too the Holy Virgin Mary: though she appeared as a humble maiden among men, she was chosen to bear the Son of God. Through her, the true rain descended the mercy of Christ, the water of life, the comfort of those who hunger for peace and thirst for righteousness.

St. Ephrem the Syrian, in the hymns of the Church, praised her with these words: “You are the true cloud, O Virgin, from which descended the rain of mercy.”

text.text: 4. The Cloud of Isaiah – The Swift Cloud Bearing the Lord

text:
Seven centuries before the coming of Christ, the prophet Isaiah foresaw the mystery and declared: “Behold, the Lord rides upon a swift cloud, and shall come into Egypt” (Isaiah 19:1). Who is this swift cloud? The Fathers teach with one voice: it is the Holy Virgin Mary.

For when the Lord was born in Bethlehem, Herod sought to kill Him. An angel appeared to Joseph in a dream and commanded: “Take the young Child and His mother, and flee into Egypt” (Matthew 2:13). Thus was the prophecy fulfilled: the Lord indeed came into Egypt riding upon the cloud of His Mother. Through her, He entered into the land of idols and scattered their images, proving Himself to be the one true God.

Beloved, let us understand with fear and joy: the cloud in Scripture always points us to the same mystery. To Noah, the cloud bore the rainbow of the covenant. To Moses, it covered the tabernacle with God’s glory. To Elijah, it appeared as a small hand bringing rain. To Isaiah, it was the swift cloud carrying the Lord into Egypt.

In all these, the cloud reveals the Holy Virgin Mary. She is the cloud who bore the Sun of Righteousness, the hand through which the mercy of God was poured, the vessel chosen to carry the Savior into the world. Through her, the famine of sin is ended, and the drought of mercy is filled with abundant rain.

Therefore, let us cry out with faith: “O Virgin Mary, our covenant and our cloud, remember us before your Son!”

text: Beloved in Christ, today we reflect on the deep meaning of the month of Pagume and the wisdom of the Church in teaching us to fast and to seek baptism during these holy days. May God’s grace, the prayers of the saints, and the protection of His holy angels guide and strengthen us.

Pagume is unlike the other months. In the order of the Ethiopian calendar it stands as the thirteenth month, short in days but great in meaning. It has either five days or, in the years of St. John, six days. Pagume Three , in this time the seven heavens are opened and the prayers of the faithful ascend unhindered before the throne of God.

Though small in number of days, its greatness surpasses many months, for it symbolizes a transition. Just as the year passes from old into new, so Pagume proclaims the mystery of the end of the world: a passage from time to eternity, from the temporal life to the everlasting kingdom, from the darkness of winter to the dawn of unending day. Thus, it becomes for us an image of the Day of Judgment, when Christ shall appear in glory to judge the living and the dead.

text.text: Why Do We Fast in Pagume?

text:
Because Pagume is a remembrance of the last day, the Church teaches us to pass through it with fasting, prayer, and supplication. Monks in monasteries spend these days as in a closed week of devotion, shutting out the noise of the world.

This fasting is not one of compulsion, for Pagume is not counted among the seven great fasts of the Church. Yet the faithful, desiring the blessings of God, willingly embrace it. For if we sanctify the eve of the New Year with prayer and humility, the year to come will be filled with blessings according to the will of God.

Our fathers have shown us the path: with fasting, they prayed for the good of the nation, for the peace of the Church, for the mercy of the Creator. And we, their children, must imitate them. If we spend Pagume not in feasting or drunkenness but in fasting, God will reconcile us, heal our wounds, destroy pestilence, and grant unity and peace to His Holy Church and to our land.

text.text: Why Are We Baptized in Pagume?

text:
Many believers are baptized in Pagume because this month is connected to the Archangel Raphael, whose name means “God heals.”

During Pagume, the waters of the world rivers, seas, lakes, and even rain are blessed by angels.

Because of this, baptism in these waters brings healing from sickness and protection from evil.

Farmers also believe that even their crops are purified during Pagume, especially on Pagume 3rd, which is the feast day of Archangel Raphael.

The Bible confirms this mystery: “For at certain times an angel of the Lord went down into the pool and stirred the water; and whoever stepped in first was healed of whatever disease he had” (John 5:4). In the same way, during Pagume, the Archangel Raphael blesses the waters for healing and salvation.

Rain that falls is collected and kept as holy water.

It is sprinkled in homes, soaked into grain, and given to the sick, because it drives away evil spirits and brings blessing.

Pregnant women may drink from this water, because Raphael is called the opener of the womb, and by God’s mercy he helps them give birth safely.

text: Raphael is one of the seven princes who stand before the throne of God. As he himself declared in the Book of Tobit: “I am Raphael, one of the seven princes of glory” (Tobit 12:15). In the beginning, when God created the angelic hosts, He placed Raphael over many tribes of angels, and in Ramah he established him as leader of the mighty ones. Thus, he is not only a healer of men but a commander of angels, ever ready to serve the will of the Most High.

Finally, Pagume calls to our remembrance the return of Christ. In the hymns of the Church, sung during these days, we proclaim His coming in majesty, His judgment of the nations, and the establishment of the new age. The shortness of this month reminds us that time itself will come to an end, and that eternity will soon begin.

Thus, every day of Pagume is a summons to repentance, a call to purity, a preparation for the Lord who is to come.

Beloved, let us not spend these days in vain indulgence but in sober watchfulness. Let us fast with sincerity, pray with faith, and if possible, partake in the mystery of baptism with holy water blessed by the Archangel Raphael. Then, reconciled to God, we shall receive healing for body and soul, peace for our homes, and blessings for the year ahead.

text.text: ) and the Sage Who Reached It

text:
)

Beloved children of the Orthodox faith, grace and peace be multiplied to you. Today let us reflect on a mystery handed down in the Church, a subject both profound and wondrous: the Sea of Thoughts what it means, and who is the blessed sage that attained its depth. May the Holy Spirit enlighten us as we consider this teaching.

text.text: What Is the Sea of Thoughts?

text:
The Sea of Thoughts is a name given to the ordered measure of time, a numbered era. It is called a sea because of its vastness and depth, just as the waters of the ocean spread out beyond sight. In the same way, the Sea of Thoughts includes not only the simple counting of numbers addition, subtraction, multiplication to fix the days of feasts and fasts, but also the contemplation of the sun, the moon, and the stars.

For time itself is not random, but is arranged by God and entrusted to the stewardship of the Church. Humanity, in obedience to divine wisdom, arranges the divisions of days, months, and years so that both social life and the worship of God may proceed in order.

The Science of Time

This holy science of measuring time is called Bahre ḥasāb. The word is joined from two parts:

Bahir - meaning time or period.

Ḥasābe - meaning counting, reckoning, or measure.


Thus Bahre ḥasāb signifies a numbered period or world-year.

It is likened to the sea because of its vastness: its depths contain secrets upon secrets, hidden meanings and mysteries, just as the ocean has unfathomable paths. In this way, the reckoning of times is not merely practical but spiritual it reveals the order of God’s creation and guides His people in their worship.

text.text: The Sea of Thoughts in the Church’s Library

text:
The wisdom of the Sea of Thoughts is preserved within the treasury of the Church. Our spiritual library is founded upon four councils or pillars:

1. The Old Testament

2. The New Testament

3. The Book of the Monks

4. The Elders (Haymanote Abew)

And beyond these is a Fifth Council, which is divided into two ways: the path of Abu Shakar and the path of the Sea of Thoughts itself.

text.text: The Feast of the Archangel Saint

text: Beloved in Christ, children of the holy Church, peace and grace be multiplied unto you. Today we gather to remember with reverence the annual feast of the Archangel Raphael, which shines forth on the third day of Pagume. Among the many commemorations of this blessed month, this feast holds a special place, for it calls us to contemplate the mercy of God revealed through His angelic minister, Raphael, whose very name proclaims: “Healing from God.”

text.text: The Name and Dignity of Raphael

text:
The name Raphael comes from two words: Rufa, meaning health, medicine, and healing, and El, the holy name of God. Joined together, the name declares his mission: healing given by God to His people. Thus the Lord testified in the Scripture: “Behold, I send My angel before you… Do not resist him, for My name is in him” (Ex. 23:20–22).

This Raphael, the gentle and merciful one, stands among the seven archangels, and in rank is placed after Michael and Gabriel. Of himself he bore witness, saying: “I am Raphael, one of the seven chiefs who bring the prayers of the saints before the throne of glory” (Tobit 12:15).

He is, therefore, both intercessor and guardian, offering our supplications to God, reconciling us to the Creator, and ever praising the Most High with the heavenly hosts.

text.text: 1. The Healer of the Sick "Fewase Duyan"

text:
When our Lord Jesus Christ walked the earth, He healed both body and soul. Likewise, Raphael has been appointed by the Almighty to heal mankind of sickness and of sin. Enoch testifies: “Saint Raphael is appointed over all diseases and wounds of the children of men” (Enoch 10:13).

Thus, as Christ healed the paralytic with the words “Rise, take up your bed, and walk” (Jn. 5:8), so Raphael heals by intercession and prayer, curing wounds both visible and hidden. He is a physician of God, a protector who shields us from the maladies of flesh and the corruption of the soul.

text.text: 2. The Opener of the Womb"Fetahe Mahtsen"

text:
God, who made barren Sarah to laugh with joy, who gave children to Rachel, Hannah, and Elizabeth, has appointed Raphael as minister of this mystery. He comforts mothers in labor, protects children in the womb, and eases the pangs of childbirth.

From the first moment of conception until the hour of delivery, Raphael does not depart, but stands guard as a heavenly midwife, easing pain and safeguarding life. Thus mothers cry his name in prayer, and through his intercession are delivered with joy.

As Christ cast out unclean spirits, so Raphael has received authority to bind the demons. When Sarah, daughter of Raguel, was tormented by the demon Asmodeus, Raphael expelled him with divine power (Tobit 3:8, 17).

Enoch also records: “Bind Azazel hand and foot, and cast him into the darkness” (Enoch 10:4–7). This same Raphael is today sent to drive away from us envy, hatred, deceit, and every whisper of the evil one.

Raphael is not only healer and protector, but also intercessor, who carries the prayers of men before the throne of God. As he declared: “I am Raphael… who brings the prayers of the saints before the glory of the Holy One” (Tobit 12:15).

A wondrous miracle bears witness: when the faithful prayed in a church on an island near Alexandria, the devil sought to destroy them by stirring the waters beneath. Yet when they cried out to God in Raphael’s name, the angel struck the reef with the sign of the Cross, and the danger ceased. Thus he revealed himself as guardian of the faithful and protector of the Church.

text.text: 5. The Guide of the Way (Meraë Fênot)

text:
When young Tobias journeyed to Media, Raphael went with him in the form of a companion, guiding and protecting him from dangers (cf. Ex. 23:20). At the river Tigris, when a great fish sought to swallow him, Raphael delivered him and showed him how its gall and liver would become medicine and weapon against evil.

Thus is Raphael revealed as guide to travelers, protector of pilgrims, and helper to those who face trials along the road. Even now, the Church invokes him as guardian of the way.

Raphael is also called the Angel of the Bridegroom, for he blessed the union of Tobias and Sarah. Though Sarah’s seven husbands had perished by the demon’s hand, Raphael taught Tobias how to overcome the evil one: by prayer, by faith, and by the burning of the fish’s liver.

That night, the demon fled, and Tobias and Sarah prayed together, committing their marriage to God. As Christ blessed the wedding at Cana, so Raphael sanctified theirs, showing that true marriage is preserved not by fleshly desire, but by the fear of God and the intercession of His saints.

Even now, Raphael blesses the marriages of the faithful, making their homes secure in peace.

"

Finally, Raphael restored the sight of Tobit, father of Tobias, by means of the fish’s gall. Just as Christ opened the eyes of the blind with clay and spittle, so Raphael gave light to Tobit’s darkness.

Thus he is the angel who enlightens not only the eyes of the body, but the eyes of the heart. He opens for us the vision of faith, that we may behold the mercy of God and walk in His light.

Beloved, this feast falls in the month of Pagume, which is the bridge between the old year and the new. The Fathers teach us that Pagume signifies the Day of Resurrection: the cleansing of the old age, and the preparation for the Kingdom of God to come.

Thus the feast of Raphael, celebrated on Pagume 3, is the crown of the passing year and the threshold of the new. The waters of this time are believed to be blessed, and the faithful cry out in faith: “Saint Raphael, help us! Protect us!”

Beloved brothers and sisters, let us remember that Saint Raphael is not only a figure of the past, but a living servant of God for us today.

When we are sick, we can call on him, for he is the healer.

When dangers surround us, we can ask for his protection.

When demons tempt us, we can cry out to him with faith.

When our prayers feel weak, he carries them to God’s throne.

When we walk in confusion, he guides our steps.

When families begin in marriage, he blesses them.

When blindness, either of body or soul, covers us, he brings light.

If we honor him with faith and purity of heart, his intercession will guard us, his blessing will guide us, and his prayers will help lead us to the kingdom of God.

Through Saint Raphael’s prayers, may our lives be healed, our journeys safe, and our eyes opened to the glory of the Lord.

text: Beloved in Christ, sons and daughters of the holy Orthodox faith, we greet you with the peace of God. Today we turn our attention to the mystery of time as it is ordered in Ethiopia a land sanctified by the Gospel, whose very measure of days bears witness to the wisdom of the Creator. Let us therefore behold with reverence how the year is divided, how the seasons are appointed, and how the order of months gives glory to God, who is the Lord of times and ages.

text.text: 1. The Ethiopian Year and Its Seasons

text:
The Ethiopian reckoning of time is wondrous and full of meaning. Unlike the systems of other nations, Ethiopia counts a year as consisting of thirteen months, and it is divided into four great seasons. These are not arbitrary, but carefully set in order by divine providence and witnessed to in the writings of Saint Yared.

The four seasons are:

1. Keremt – from Sene 26 to Meskerem 25.

2. Metsew (Tbi) – from Meskerem 26 to Tahisas 25.

3. Bega (Hagay) – from Tahisas 26 to Megabit 25.

4. Tsedey – from Megabit 26 to Sene 25.

Each season has 99 days, except Keremt, which has 95 days.

Saint Yared, the holy hymnographer, spoke of these seasons and showed how each one gives glory to God.

This season, also called Tbi, begins in the fourth week after Keremt. It runs from Meskerem 26 to Tahisas 25, making 90 days in total.

Saint Yared gives it a noble description: “You made the seasons so that we may boast of your wonderful power. You gave the Keremt for rain and the Metsew for flowers” (Digwa Zetsge Kufale 2 Jo.2÷23; cf. Jer. 5:24).

This is the season of harvest. The rains of Keremt water the earth, and in Metsew the earth brings forth fruit in abundance. Flowers bloom across Ethiopia on fields, hills, and mountains alike. Its chief months are Tikimt, Hidar, and Tahisas. It is truly the time of nature’s adornment, when the earth rejoices in her Creator.

Following Metsew comes Bega, also called Hagay, which stretches from Tahisas 26 to Megabit 25, encompassing the months of Tir, Yekatit, and Megabit.

The word Hagay is derived from the Geʿez tongue, meaning “summer” or “time of the sun.” One fourth of the year it occupies, and thus it is called the hand of the seasons. Scripture itself acknowledges this order: “You made Keremt and Bega” (Ps. 75:17; Zech. 14:10; Gen. 10:22).

Bega is the season of brightness, of harvest, of spring and dryness. The grains, ripened by the sun, are gathered into barns. In this time, Ethiopia celebrates the fruit of labor. Yekatit, in particular, is a month when the gathered harvest is safely stored. Because the barns are full, the people turn to feasting, celebrating baptisms, marriages, and annual festivals. This period is known as the Merawi, the season of rejoicing.

2.1 The Season of Metsew (Tbi)

This season, also called Tbi, begins in the fourth week after Keremt. It runs from Meskerem 26 to Tahisas 25, making 90 days in total.

Saint Yared gives it a noble description: “You made the seasons so that we may boast of your wonderful power. You gave the Keremt for rain and the Metsew for flowers” (Digwa Zetsge Kufale 2 Jo.2÷23; cf. Jer. 5:24).

2.2. The Season of Bega (Haggay)

Following Metsew comes Bega, also called Hagay, which stretches from Tahisas 26 to Megabit 25, encompassing the months of Tir, Yekatit, and Megabit.

text:
Next comes Tsedey, a season of transition, stretching from Megabit 26 to Sene 25. It includes the months of Miyaziya, Ginbot, and Sene.

Tsedey contains the qualities of the other seasons. On one hand, it is the time of the Belig harvest—sown, reaped, and threshed. On the other, it is the time when the land is prepared for the coming Keremt rains. Thus, it is both the season of conclusion and of preparation.

Saint Yared in his hymn declares."ይሁብ ዝናመ ተወን"(yihub zname tewen)  the Belg rains are given.” The people labor diligently, sowing where there is fall rain, and where there is none, plowing and preparing the fields. An old proverb says, “One Sene does not replace two Sene that are harvested,” reminding us that diligence today cannot be postponed to tomorrow.

2.

Keremt, from Sene 26 to Meskerem 25, is the season of rain and water. Its months are Hamle, Nehase, Pagume, and Meskerem. Water, in this season, pours forth from heaven, washing the earth, quenching its fire, and blessing it with moisture.

Saint Yared declares:The Lord of the Ages, the Almighty, brings us winter every year, and the clouds hear His word.” The rains of Keremt are not mere waters, but the mercy and blessing of God poured upon His people. It is the season of renewal and life-giving abundance, when the earth, like a servant, listens to the word of its Master.

The years of John, Matthew, and Mark are 365 days and 6 hours (from Meskerem 1 to Pagume 5).

The year of Luke alone is 366 days (from Meskerem 1 to Pagume 6).

Thus, the four Evangelists themselves mark the rhythm of the year, binding time to the Gospel.

The word for month in Geʿez is Werh, which in Amharic is Werh and in plural form Wereh. In the Ethiopian calendar, there are twelve months of thirty days each. At the end, five days are added or six in the leap year of Luke. This differs from the Western system, where months vary in length.

Unlike the European calendar, the months are equal in length, reflecting order and balance.

Thus, beloved, the Ethiopian reckoning of time is no mere human invention but a reflection of divine wisdom. It marks the turning of the seasons with prayer, labor, and thanksgiving. Each season carries its own mystery: Keremt brings rain, Metsew brings flowers, Bega brings harvest and joy, Tsedey brings diligence and preparation.

As Saint Yared and the Scriptures testify, God Himself ordains the times and the seasons, that man may remember His power and give thanks. Truly, time itself becomes a hymn to the Creator: the rains, the sun, the harvest, and the plow all sing the praises of the Lord who gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater.

text.text: 1. The Months and Their Origins in Ge’ez

text:
The year of Ethiopia, preserved in the tongue of the fathers, Ge’ez, is not a mere calendar of convenience, but a mirror of life, labor, and the mysteries of God’s providence. Each month bears a name not chosen at random, but springing from the rhythms of creation and the deeds of man.

Meskerem (1st month) - From Mes’e and Kerem, meaning “the night has passed, the rainy season is over.” Just as Noah beheld the dry land after the flood, so too Meskerem proclaims new beginnings after the darkness of rain.

Tikimt (2nd month) - From "Tekeme", meaning “work, useful time.” This month summons us to diligence, reminding us that man was placed in the garden to labor and keep it.

Hidar (3rd month) - From "Hadere," “to spend the night in the harvest field.” It recalls the toil and vigilance of the farmer, who guards his fruits even through the night.

Tahsas (4th month) - From "Hasese", meaning “searched.” In this month crops are inspected, and the fathers teach that it also signifies the searching of the wise men who sought the newborn Christ. Thus, it binds earthly labor to divine revelation.

Tir (5th month) - From Netere, Teyere, Atreye, meaning “flash, heat, buying season.” The sun burns, and commerce is busy, cattle and grain exchanged. Creation teaches man both need and provision.

Yekatit (6th month) - From Ketete, Ketit, “to nest, to store in the barn.” 

Megabit (7th month) - From "Megebe", “to feed, to eat standing.” A month of strength and nourishment, calling man to rise and be sustained.

Miyazya (8th month) - From "Mehaze", “to be brave, to be strong,” and also remembered as the season of weddings. It binds together courage and joy, the household and the covenant.

Ginbot (9th month) - From "Genebe", “to build, to dig, to prepare the land.” Here we see the farmer clearing fields, just as the soul must prepare its heart for the seed of the Word.

Sene (10th month) - From "Seneye", “beautiful.” Nature itself bursts into glory, creation testifying to the majesty of God.

Hamle (11th month) - From "Hamele", “to harvest, to pick.” The barns are filled, but let us not forget the greater harvest, when the Lord of the vineyard shall return for His fruit.

Nehase (12th month) - From Anahsye, Nehase, “to lighten, to ease.” The heavy rains depart, and the earth breathes relief. 

Pagume (13th month) - From the Greek Epagumenos, “to add.” It is an addition, a reminder that God’s times are not bound by man, but that He adds as He wills.

Thus each month is a sermon in itself, and a chapter of creation.

text.text: 2. The Balance of Day and Night

text:
The year is not only divided by months, but by the measure of day and night. See how the Creato orders the light:

Meskerem: Day length 12 hours Night length 12 hours

👉Tikmt: Day length 11 hours Night length 13 hours

👉Hidar: Day length 10 hours Night length 14 hours

👉Tahsas: Day length 09 hours Night length 15 hours

👉Tir: Day length 10 hours Night length 14 hours

👉Yekatit: Day length 11 hours Night length 13 hours

👉Megabit: Day length 12 hours Night length 12 hours

👉Miyazya: Day length 13 hours Night length 11 hours

👉Ginbot: Day length 14 hours Night length 10 hours

👉Sene: Day length 15 hours Night length 09 hours

👉Hamle: Day length 14 hours Night length 10 hours

👉Nehase: Day length 13 hours, the length of the night is 11 hours.

So the cycle of day and night preaches to us the mysteries of life: there is a time of joy and a time of trial, a time when light seems hidden and a time when it shines in glory. Yet all is measured by the wisdom of Him who “made the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night” (Genesis 1:16).

Time is further bound in the cycle of the week, called Samint, from the Ge’ez word Semene meaning “eight.” For though the week has seven days, the cycle leads us from Sunday back to Sunday, from first to first, thus creating an eighth day that foreshadows eternity - the day beyond time, the Day of the Lord.

Each day bears its meaning from creation itself:

Sunday (Ehud) - From Ahade, “to make one.” It is the first day, the day when God began His creation.

Monday (Segno) - From Saneye, “to make two.” It marks the second day, when God divided the waters above and below.

Tuesday (Maksegno / Selus) - From Selese, “to make three.” The third day, when the earth brought forth vegetation.

Wednesday (E'rob) - From Rebi’a, “to make four.” The day when the heavenly lights were set in their place.

Thursday (Hamus) - From Hamese, “to make five.” The day of the sea creatures and birds, filling the waters and skies.

Friday (Arb )"Arebe" - From Arebe, “to include.” The sixth day, when man himself was created, and all things brought to completion.

Saturday (Kidame )" Kedamit"— Meaning “first,” for it is the first Sabbath, the day of holy rest, when God sanctified the seventh day.

Thus, the very names of the days are a living catechism of creation, teaching us each week to remember the mighty works of God.

Behold then, dearly beloved, how the Ethiopian reckoning of time is no idle system, but a treasury of wisdom. Each month, each day, each hour whispers the voice of God: “Redeem the time, for the days are evil” (Ephesians 5:16). Time passes, but it does not vanish; it carries us as a river carries a boat, either toward salvation if we steer with vigilance, or toward ruin if we drift in neglect.

Therefore, let us not despise the hours, nor treat the days as common. Rather, let us sanctify them with prayer, labor, and thanksgiving. For just as the sun rises and sets according to God’s command, so too our lives are measured by Him who is the Lord of time, the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End.

text_entities.text: 2. The Balance of Day and Night

The year is not only divided by months, but by the measure of day and night. See how the Creato orders the light:

Meskerem: Day length 12 hours Night length 12 hours

👉Tikmt: Day length 11 hours Night length 13 hours

👉Hidar: Day length 10 hours Night length 14 hours

👉Tahsas: Day length 09 hours Night length 15 hours

👉Tir: Day length 10 hours Night length 14 hours

👉Yekatit: Day length 11 hours Night length 13 hours

👉Megabit: Day length 12 hours Night length 12 hours

👉Miyazya: Day length 13 hours Night length 11 hours

👉Ginbot: Day length 14 hours Night length 10 hours

👉Sene: Day length 15 hours Night length 09 hours

👉Hamle: Day length 14 hours Night length 10 hours

👉Nehase: Day length 13 hours, the length of the night is 11 hours.

So the cycle of day and night preaches to us the mysteries of life: there is a time of joy and a time of trial, a time when light seems hidden and a time when it shines in glory. Yet all is measured by the wisdom of Him who “made the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night” (Genesis 1:16).

Time is further bound in the cycle of the week, called Samint, from the Ge’ez word Semene meaning “eight.” For though the week has seven days, the cycle leads us from Sunday back to Sunday, from first to first, thus creating an eighth day that foreshadows eternity - the day beyond time, the Day of the Lord.

Each day bears its meaning from creation itself:

Sunday (Ehud) - From Ahade, “to make one.” It is the first day, the day when God began His creation.

Monday (Segno) - From Saneye, “to make two.” It marks the second day, when God divided the waters above and below.

Tuesday (Maksegno / Selus) - From Selese, “to make three.” The third day, when the earth brought forth vegetation.

Wednesday (E'rob) - From Rebi’a, “to make four.” The day when the heavenly lights were set in their place.

Thursday (Hamus) - From Hamese, “to make five.” The day of the sea creatures and birds, filling the waters and skies.

Friday (Arb )"Arebe" - From Arebe, “to include.” The sixth day, when man himself was created, and all things brought to completion.

Saturday (Kidame )" Kedamit"— Meaning “first,” for it is the first Sabbath, the day of holy rest, when God sanctified the seventh day.

Thus, the very names of the days are a living catechism of creation, teaching us each week to remember the mighty works of God.

Behold then, dearly beloved, how the Ethiopian reckoning of time is no idle system, but a treasury of wisdom. Each month, each day, each hour whispers the voice of God: “Redeem the time, for the days are evil” (Ephesians 5:16). Time passes, but it does not vanish; it carries us as a river carries a boat, either toward salvation if we steer with vigilance, or toward ruin if we drift in neglect.

Therefore, let us not despise the hours, nor treat the days as common. Rather, let us sanctify them with prayer, labor, and thanksgiving. For just as the sun rises and sets according to God’s command, so too our lives are measured by Him who is the Lord of time, the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

Beloved children of the Church, heirs of the ancient faith of the fathers, peace and grace be multiplied unto you. Today we turn to a matter profound and wondrous: the understanding of time itself, and how our Ethiopian tradition preserved through the wisdom of the saints and scholars defines, measures, and sanctifies it.

For time is no mere invention of men, but a gift from God, a framework within which the mystery of salvation unfolds. As the Psalmist testifies: “Of old Thou didst lay the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Thy hands. They shall perish, but Thou shalt endure; yea, all of them shall wax old like a garment, and as a vesture shalt Thou change them, and they shall be changed. But Thou art the same, and Thy years shall have no end” (Ps. 101:24–28).

Thus, while the heavens and the earth pass away, the Lord remains immutable; and man, His creature, moves through the appointed times until he returns to the Maker.

text.text: The Scholar of Time: Abushakhr Wolde Abel Herem

text:
The Scholar of Time: Abushakhr Wolde Abel Herem

Among those who reflected on the divine order of times was Abushakhr Wolde Abel Herem, also remembered as Yohannes Fiqrum. He was a mathematician and philosopher, one who delved into the mystery of chronology and the reckoning of days. His work, published in 1962, builds upon the study of ancient systems of time.

Nine scholars,  examined and commented on his numbers and ideas:

Seid Welde Bettrik

Mahboub Menbegawi

Seidawyan  Jews

Yohannes Afewerk

Qerlos

Epiphanios

Yohannes Zedamasko

Markos Welde Qember

Giorgis Welde Amid (also called Hamid)

Though his book is mathematical, Ethiopians also count it as a poetic book, because it explains time in a way that praises God’s creation.

Abushakhr explains that time, when measured by the conscience, divides itself into three great periods:

1. The time of the present – that which we see and live in.

2. The time of the past – that which has been and is remembered.

3. The time of the prophet (the future) – that which is yet to come and is foretold.

Thus, human thought, word, and action are bound in time. Our life is measured in ages, our deeds unfold in succession, and our salvation is worked out in the history God governs.

Moses himself, speaking in Deuteronomy, bears witness to this mystery: “Since the day that God created man upon the earth, and from one end of heaven unto the other, hath there been any such thing as this great thing is, or hath been heard like it?” (Deut. 4:32).

The Ethiopian system teaches that from Adam to Christ there are 5,500 years. This is called the Year of Judgment (Fda). From the birth of Christ until now, we live in the Year of Mercy, the age of grace brought forth by the Incarnation.

The union of these two gives us the Year of the World (Amete Alem):

Year of the World = Year of Mercy + Year of Judgment

Thus, in the year 2018 A.D., the calculation is:

2018 + 5500 = 7518

Time is also sanctified through the witness of the Four Evangelists. The Year of the World is divided by four, revealing which Gospel governs the age.

2018 + 5500 = 7518

7518 ÷ 4 = 1879 {remainder 2}

7518 - ( 4 × 1879)

         = 7518 -  7516=2

If remainder = 1 → the time of Matthew

If remainder = 2 → the time of Mark

If remainder = 3 → the time of Luke

If remainder = 0 → the time of John

Thus, since the remainder is 2, the year 2018 belongs to Mark, the Evangelist of boldness and action. This is the Time of Mark.

Even if we divide only the Year of Mercy (2018) by four, the result is the same: remainder 2 again, the time of Mark.

text.text: The "Elete Qemer" – The First Day of the Year

text:
The Ethiopian system also discerns the weekday upon which the New Year (Meskerem 1) falls.

Elete Qemer =Year of the World + Month of Rabi’it ÷ 7

= (7518 + 1879) ÷ 7
= 9397 ÷ 7 
= 1342 {remainder is 3}

If remainder = 3, the year begins on a Thursday. Thus, the Ethiopian year 2018 start on a Thursday.

Meskerem 1st is used

If the remainder is 0, it is Monday

If the remainder is 1, it is Tuesday

If the remainder is 2, it is Wednesday

If the remainder is 3, it is Thursday

If the remainder is 4, it is Friday

If the remainder is 5, it is Saturday

If the remainder is 6, it is the beginning of Sunday

text.text: The Sacred Days of the Calendar

text: The Ethiopian reckoning roots itself in the days of creation:
(" Tinte E'let") – the day the world was created, the first day of light.
( " Tinte kemer")– the day plants and living creatures came forth, and the day the calendar itself began.

(" Tinte yon") – the day the sun, moon, and stars were set in the heavens.

These three days form the foundation of Ethiopian time: the dawn of the cosmos, the ordering of life, and the shining of heavenly lights. Thus, the calendar is not arbitrary but woven into the very fabric of Genesis.

Brothers and sisters, the Ethiopian time system is not just a way of counting days. It is a theology of time:

It remembers creation.

It points to Christ’s coming.

It honors the Evangelists who proclaimed salvation.

It orders the year according to God’s works.

Every New Year reminds us that our life is moving within God’s plan. Time began with Adam, was redeemed by Christ, and will be fulfilled when He returns in glory.

As St. Paul says: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever” (Heb. 13:8).

Let us then live our days wisely, offering every year and every moment back to Him.

text.text: , and the Commemoration of Saint John (2018)

text: Beloved in Christ, children of the Holy Church, grace and peace be to you. Let us now meditate on the mystery of the New Year as it is revealed to us in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewaḥedo Church, and let us uncover why the first day of Meskerem is sanctified, why it is adorned with the remembrance of Saint John the Baptist, and how this holy time calls us to repentance and renewal.

text.text: 1. When is the New Year Celebrated?

text:
When the measure of an era is fulfilled and the old cycle comes to its end, the Church marks this turning of time with a holy day. This day is called by many names: the change of the year, the beginning of the year,Enkutatash and in Gëʿëz, the “ርዕሰ አውዳ ዓመት” (Ri-E'se Awdamet ). Each year, on the first day of the month of  (Meskerem 1 by the Ethiopian reckoning), the faithful gather to proclaim the passage from one age into another.

It marks the passing of the old time and the beginning of a new one. The Church teaches us that this day belongs to God, for He is the Lord of time.

text.text: 2,Why is the New Year Celebrated in Meskerem?

text:
The fathers of the Church teach that the reason Ethiopia celebrates the New Year in Meskerem is that the sun, the moon, and the stars complete their yearly cycle in the small month of Pagumē and begin anew in "Meskerem". At this sacred turning, day and night are equal, each being twelve hours, just as in the beginning when God created balance and order.

The year, carefully counted, has 364 days, and thus the transition into Meskerem marks the fullness of creation’s cycle.

“He created the sun, the moon, and the stars to mark the days” (1 Enoch 21:49).

Moreover, the Holy Tradition remembers that in this very month the waters of the great flood receded, and the earth appeared once again after sin had been washed away from the generation of Noah (Gen. 8:13; Kufal 7:1). Thus "Meskerem" is not only the renewal of the stars but also the renewal of the earth.

text.text: 3. The Evangelists and the Order of the Year

text:
The Church divides the times of the year according to the four Evangelists, for all history must be understood in the light of the Gospel:

He was conceived in the time of John and born in the time of Matthew.

He was baptized in the time of Mark.

He was crucified in the time of Luke and freed the world from sin and curse.

The fathers devised a sacred calculation: to determine which Evangelist governs a year, one must take the year of Mercy (the current year since the coming of Christ) and add it to 5500, the years of the Old Testament. Then The sum is divided by four, and the remainder reveals the Evangelist:

If remainder is 1, it is the time of Matthew.

If remainder is 2, it is the time of Mark.

If remainder is 3, it is the time of Luke.

If no remainder, it is the time of John.

In this way, time itself is joined to the preaching of the Gospel, and every year is sanctified under the voice of an Evangelist.

This calculation can be seen with an example:

2017 A.D. + 5500 = 7517.
When 7517 is divided by 4, the remainder is 1, which means the year belongs to Matthew.

2018 A.D. + 5500 = 7518.
When 7518 is divided by 4, the remainder is 2, which means the year belongs to Mark.

The word Enkutatash also carries a deeper story. Tradition tells us that when the Queen of Sheba returned from visiting Solomon, he gifted her a ring of pearls ,saying: “Gold for your finger.” or enku le-tatsh) From this, the New Year in Ethiopia came to be called "Enkutatash," meaning a jewel, a gift, or a crown of time.

In Ethiopia, this is also the season when the land is renewed by rain and filled with blossoms. Children and young girls dress in white, carry green grass and bright yellow flowers, and sing songs of thanksgiving to God for blessing the new year.

This day is called by many names: the change of the year, the beginning of the year,Enkutatash and in Gëʿëz, the “ርዕሰ አውዳ ዓመት” (Ri-E'se Awdamet ). Each year, on the first day of the month of  (Meskerem 1 by the Ethiopian reckoning), the faithful gather to proclaim the passage from one age into another.

It marks the passing of the old time and the beginning of a new one. The Church teaches us that this day belongs to God, for He is the Lord of time.
2,Why is the New Year Celebrated in Meskerem?

The fathers of the Church teach that the reason Ethiopia celebrates the New Year in Meskerem is that the sun, the moon, and the stars complete their yearly cycle in the small month of Pagumē and begin anew in "Meskerem". At this sacred turning, day and night are equal, each being twelve hours, just as in the beginning when God created balance and order.

The year, carefully counted, has 364 days, and thus the transition into Meskerem marks the fullness of creation’s cycle.

“He created the sun, the moon, and the stars to mark the days” (1 Enoch 21:49).

Moreover, the Holy Tradition remembers that in this very month the waters of the great flood receded, and the earth appeared once again after sin had been washed away from the generation of Noah (Gen. 8:13; Kufal 7:1). Thus "Meskerem" is not only the renewal of the stars but also the renewal of the earth.
3. The Evangelists and the Order of the Year

The Church divides the times of the year according to the four Evangelists, for all history must be understood in the light of the Gospel:

He was conceived in the time of John and born in the time of Matthew.

He was baptized in the time of Mark.

He was crucified in the time of Luke and freed the world from sin and curse.

The fathers devised a sacred calculation: to determine which Evangelist governs a year, one must take the year of Mercy (the current year since the coming of Christ) and add it to 5500, the years of the Old Testament. Then The sum is divided by four, and the remainder reveals the Evangelist:

If remainder is 1, it is the time of Matthew.

If remainder is 2, it is the time of Mark.

If remainder is 3, it is the time of Luke.

If no remainder, it is the time of John.

In this way, time itself is joined to the preaching of the Gospel, and every year is sanctified under the voice of an Evangelist.

This calculation can be seen with an example:

2017 A.D. + 5500 = 7517.
When 7517 is divided by 4, the remainder is 1, which means the year belongs to Matthew.

2018 A.D. + 5500 = 7518.
When 7518 is divided by 4, the remainder is 2, which means the year belongs to Mark.

The word Enkutatash also carries a deeper story. Tradition tells us that when the Queen of Sheba returned from visiting Solomon, he gifted her a ring of pearls ,saying: “Gold for your finger.” or enku le-tatsh) From this, the New Year in Ethiopia came to be called "Enkutatash," meaning a jewel, a gift, or a crown of time.

In Ethiopia, this is also the season when the land is renewed by rain and filled with blossoms. Children and young girls dress in white, carry green grass and bright yellow flowers, and sing songs of thanksgiving to God for blessing the new year.

text.text: 5,Why is the New Year Called in the Name of Saint John?

text:
The holy Fathers decreed that the first day of Meskerem should be consecrated in memory of Saint John the Baptist. Why? Because John stands as the bridge between the Old and the New he is the voice crying in the wilderness, the herald of Christ, the one who says, “Prepare the way of the Lord, make His paths straight” (Isa. 40:3; Mark 1:1-4).

John’s ministry was the beginning of the Gospel. As the year begins, so the Gospel began with John, calling the world to repentance. Thus, the Ethiopian New Year bears his name, to remind us that with every cycle of time we are summoned to conversion, to the baptism of tears, and to the renewal of life in Christ.

text.text: 6. Why is the Ethiopian Calendar Different?

text:
The calendars of the nations are many, for each people set their measure of time according to their own history.

The Romans began their reckoning from the year their city of Rome was founded.

The Greeks counted from the time of Alexander the Great.

The Syrians, borrowing from the Romans, counted their year by the course of the sun, dividing it, and first setting their New Year by that measure. Later, in 460 A.D., they moved their New Year to "Meskerem" 1 to honor the martyrs.

The Egyptians, too, held their beginning in Meskerem.

In 46 B.C., Julius Caesar established what is called the Julian Calendar. He divided the year into 365 days and 6 hours, giving some months 30 days, others 31, and  28 days, 29 days with a leap day added every four years. This became the foundation of the European system.

Later, the Roman monk Dionysius Exiguus calculated the years from what he believed to be the birth of Christ, turning the calendar into one marked “Before Christ” and “After Christ.” This historical event became the source of the Western calendar.

But the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewaḥedo Church did not follow the Romans, nor the Greeks, nor the Syrians. Instead, she held fast to the divine measure of the Fathers. Our Church teaches that from Adam to Christ there were 5,500 years, and upon this foundation she adds the years since the Incarnation. This makes our calendar distinct, and it appears seven years “behind” the West, not because of error, but because of fidelity.

As Chief Kidane Weld Kifle bears witness:

“When Ethiopia counts the Old Testament as 5,500 years, the era of Christ becomes unique and does not match the calendars of other nations. For this reason, we are always seven years behind, both East and West, because we have abandoned the historians and taken the translators of the Gospel as our starting point.”

Therefore, the Ethiopian calendar is not man-made history, but a theological witness. It proclaims that time itself is measured not by earthly empires, but by the mystery of salvation from Adam to Christ, and from Christ to the present day.

text.text: 7. How Should We Celebrate the New Year?

text:
Beloved, let us not think of the New Year as mere numbers written in a book. Time is not given to us for vanity, but for repentance. Every New Year is God’s gift, that we may amend the sins of yesterday, reconcile with our enemies, clothe the naked, feed the hungry, and quench the thirst of the poor.

The Apostle Peter warns us:

“The past time of our life may suffice us to have done the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revelings, banqueting, and abominable idolatries” (1 Pet. 4:3).

Therefore, let us not spend the New Year in drunkenness, dancing, or vanity. Rather, let us spend it in prayer, in the Divine Liturgy, in the giving of alms, and in thanksgiving to God.

The parable of the fig tree reminds us that God grants us yet another year as a loan of time (Luke 13:6-9). Let us not squander this grace, but let us bear fruits thirty, sixty, and a hundredfold for the kingdom of heaven.

The Ethiopian New Year, celebrated on Meskerem 1, is more than a date it is the mystery of renewal in creation, in salvation history, and in the life of the soul. It unites the harmony of the stars, the memory of the flood, the witness of the Evangelists, the tradition of the Queen of Sheba, and the call of John the Baptist into a single proclamation: “Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand!”

The name John means “Grace of God.” This is not a small matter, for the grace of God is the fountain of all life, the root of forgiveness, and the power by which sinners are made saints. Just as the Scriptures tell us of John the Baptist he was sent ahead of Christ, proclaiming repentance so the very name testifies that God’s grace is given to humanity through him.

The Church, guided by divine wisdom, commemorates Saint John in the times of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Before the year begins, he is remembered. Why? Because John is the one who stands at the threshold of two covenants: at the end of the Old Testament and at the dawn of the New. He is the lamp shining before the Sun of Righteousness.

Saint Mark, echoing Isaiah, says: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare the way of the Lord, make His paths straight” (Mark 1:1–4; Isaiah 40:3–4). This voice was none other than John the Baptist, son of Zechariah, who baptized in the wilderness, who bore witness to Christ, and who announced salvation by repentance and forgiveness. His ministry was not for himself, but for the Lord whom he proclaimed.

text.text: 5. The Biblical Foundation of the New Year

text:
The Book of Numbers teaches that the beginning of the year in Meskerem is a blessed season. On this day, the hours of day and night are equal twelve and twelve. After this day, the daylight begins to decrease. The change of the seasons, marked by the stars, the sun, and the moon, is not by accident but by divine order. As the book of Enoch declares: “He created the sun and the moon as a sign of the time” (Enoch 21:49).

Even in the time of Noah, it was in the first month that the waters subsided, and the earth appeared again (Genesis 8:13). Thus, the rebirth of the world after the flood coincided with this sacred month. The fathers saw in this the historical and divine root of the New Year: a new creation, a new beginning, a fresh grace.

text.text: 6. The Spiritual Call of the New Year

text:
The feast of Saint John, or R-ʾEse Awdamet, is not only about days and numbers. It is a call to repentance and renewal. As Saint Paul teaches: “Behold, the old things have passed away, and all things are become new in Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:17). On this day, we are urged to leave behind evil deeds, and to clothe ourselves with new good works that please God.

The fathers compare this to:

a student advancing to a higher level,

a farmer planting after the winter,

a worker persevering through rains to see the summer sun.

So too the faithful must embrace spiritual growth as the new year dawns.

text:
This feast is also called Enkutatash, meaning “the gift of jewels.” Two ancient traditions explain this:

In the time of Noah, When Noah first divided the continents among his three sons, Africa was given to Cam.he landed in Ethiopia during Meskerem. Seeing the land blooming with beauty, he cried and said “You have given me a pearl of a pearl!”(Enku Eta wetashlgn  ) Hence, this season was named Enkutatash.

In the time of the Queen of Sheba, when she visited Solomon, she brought rich gifts of gold and spices. Solomon, showing her the treasures of his palace, placed a jewel upon her finger, saying: “Let the pearl be an ornament for you.” This also took place in Meskerem, and from it the name Enkutatash entered our heritage.

Thus, Enkutatash signifies joy, blessing, and the flowering of new life.

text: Brethren, time itself is the servant of God. The sun and the moon were set for seasons, days, and years, and Ethiopia, by divine grace, has preserved a calendar that begins in light, not in darkness. Each year opens on Sunday, the first day of creation, when God said: “Let there be light.” Thus the Ethiopian system is not mere calculation, but a witness to the order of salvation.

In this sacred reckoning, the months of the year are aligned not by chance, but by a divine harmony:

Meskerem 1 is the beginning of Miyazya 1.

Tikimt 1 is the beginning of Ginbot 1.

Hidar 1 is the beginning of Sene 1.

Tahisas 1 is the beginning of Hamle 1.

Tir 1 is the beginning of Nehase 1.

“Thus, the year itself begins where creation began on a Sunday. Yet the presence of Pagume 5 prevents Sunday from always being the first day of the new year.”.

At the close of the year stands the month of Pagumen, which seals the year and prepares the way for the new.

Pagumen 5 is called Mriya—“the chosen day,” the day of medicine, light, and birth. It is not used to alter the year’s order but is set apart as holy. For example, if Meskerem 1 fell on Wednesday in 2017, it fell on Thursday in 2018.

This day is bound to the mystery of the Lord’s Nativity. The 5th of Pagumen always corresponds with the day of the coming Christmas. Thus, if Pagumen 5 was on a Wednesday, then Christmas also fell on Wednesday. For this reason the day is also named the Feast of the Nativity of the Savior.


When the year is a leap year, Pagumen becomes six days, and the sixth day is called the Feast of the Nativity of John, the day of crossing over. Why is this so? Because the fifteen kal’its—fractions of time—accumulate year by year, and in four years they form one day. Hence, every four years a sixth day is added.

But what of the remaining kal’its? For one day is made of 3600 kal’its, requiring 600 years to complete. At that time, Pagumen itself becomes seven days, revealing the fullness of creation, for seven is the number of perfection.

“But in the time of John, the sixth day of Pagumen caused the Feast of the Nativity to be celebrated one day earlier, on Tahisas 28. Some may ask, why then do Baptism, Circumcision, and other feasts remain unchanged? The scholars answer: because generations have always counted the weeks in expectation of the Nativity; and since the other feasts flow from His birth, they follow their order without alteration

text.text: The Difference from the Gregorian Calendar

text: In the Gregorian calendar, the leap year is hidden in February, after their new year has already begun. But in Ethiopia, the extra day is revealed openly at the year’s end, before the dawning of the new year. Thus, our reckoning is not cloaked in secrecy but shines with light, testifying to God’s order.

The Testimony of the Fathers

Saint Demetrius, the twelfth Patriarch of Alexandria, ordered the feasts and fasts with apostolic authority:

Nineveh Fast, the Great Fast, and the Fast of the Apostles begin on Mondays.

The Mount of Olives, Hosanna, Resurrection, and Pentecost begin on Sundays.

The Feast of Priests and the Fast of the Savior begin on Wednesdays.

The Ascension is always on Thursday.

The Crucifixion never departs from Friday.

Thus the rhythm of the week is preserved in holiness. The days are sanctified, and time itself becomes a vessel of grace.

And to guard against confusion, the Fathers also taught what days the great feasts never fall upon:

text:
The Fast of Nineveh cannot fall before the 17th of Terr nor after the 21st of Yekatit. 

The Great Fast(Abiyi) cannot fall before the 1st of Yekatit nor after the 5th of Megabit. 

The Feast of Debre Zeit cannot fall before the 28th of Yekatit nor after the 2nd of Miyazya. 

The Feast of Hosanna cannot fall before the 19th of Megabit nor after the 23rd of Miyazya. 

The Feast of the Crucifixion cannot fall before the 24th of Megabit nor after the 28th of Miyazya.

 The Feast of the Resurrection cannot fall before the 26th of Megabit nor after the 30th of Miyazya.

 The Feast of Rikbe Kahnat(The Ordination of Priests) cannot fall before the 20th of Miyazya nor after the 24th of Ginbot. 

The Feast of the Ascension cannot fall before the 5th of Ginbot nor after the 9th of Sene. 

The Feast of the Paraclete(Pentecost) cannot fall before the 15th of Ginbot nor after the 19th of Sene.

The Fast of the Apostles cannot fall before the 16th of Ginbot nor after the 20th of Sene.

The Fast of Salvation(Nenewe) cannot fall before the 18th of Ginbot nor after the 22nd of Sene.
To know the days with precision, the Fathers gave us the formula of Class(Medeb), Chair, Abeqte, MetiqE', Mebaja Hamer, and Tewsak.
) : We find it by dividing the world year by 19.
: Chair: We get a chair by subtracting one from the class.

: means the remaining year/period .it helps to distinguishes night and moon phases, marking the seasons.

“Metqeʾ (መጥቅዕ) means a bell. When the bell is struck, the people gather and messages are announced. In the same way, festivals and celebrations are arranged through Metqeʾ, for their appointed times can be known by it. Thus, Metqeʾ is joined with the days of the week to form Mebaja Hamer.”

: also called Mebagia Hamer, means ‘summer journey.’ The word Mebaja itself can be translated as ‘storehouse’ or ‘storage,’ while Hamer means ‘ship’ or ‘transportation.’

Mebaja Hamer is formed from the union of Metiqe' and days, and it refers to the appointed day on which festivals and holy days are celebrated. The image of the ship (Hamer) symbolizes the system by which the feasts move and are carried through time.”

Thus, the system of the Ethiopian Church does not merely track days but teaches theology. It shows us that time itself is a vessel, and Christ is its captain.
Beloved, the Ethiopian calendar is a divine gift, not a human invention. Pagume marks the holy feasts, and time itself guides the faithful through God’s sacred plan.

text: Beloved brethren, let us lift our hearts to contemplate the glory of God revealed in His servant, Saint John the Baptist, the harbinger of the Messiah, the bridge between the Old and the New. In the wisdom of the Church, the New Year is marked by the feast of Saint John, for he signifies the end of the old era and the dawn of the new, fulfilling the prophecies of the prophets and the angelic announcements that heralded the coming of our Savior.

From the beginning, God prepared this servant. Zechariah, the righteous priest, and his wife Elizabeth, both blameless in all the commandments, were without children. Yet their fervent prayers were heard. As Zechariah performed his service in the temple, the angel Gabriel appeared, saying:

"Do not be afraid, Zechariah; your prayer is heard. Your wife will bear a son, and you shall name him John. He will be great before the Lord, filled with the Holy Spirit even in his mother’s womb, and he will turn the hearts of the children of Israel back to God." (Luke 1:13-17)

Doubt seized Zechariah, and he questioned, “How shall I know this?” Gabriel replied, “I am Gabriel, sent from the presence of God. You shall be mute until the fulfillment of these words.” And so it came to pass: Zechariah remained speechless, a living sign of God’s word, until the birth of his son.

The righteous Elizabeth conceived, hidden for five months, showing that God alone brings life where there was none, and that the impossible is made possible by divine will.

Saint John was conceived on Meskerem 26, and in the sixth month, the Blessed Virgin Mary visited Elizabeth. The unborn John leapt in Elizabeth’s womb at the presence of the Savior, recognizing in the Spirit the One who was to come. Elizabeth proclaimed:

"Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. Blessed is she who believed that the Lord would fulfill His promise." (Luke 1:42-45)

On the 30th of Sene, John was born. Though relatives wished to name him after his father, Elizabeth declared, “He shall be called John.” Zechariah, regaining his speech, glorified God, saying,

"You, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the Lord to prepare His ways, to give knowledge of salvation to His people by the forgiveness of their sins, to guide our feet into the way of peace." (Luke 1:76-79)

From his earliest days, John was preserved by God from the snares of men. When Herod sought to kill the holy child, Elizabeth fled with John into the wilderness. There he was nourished by heavenly providence, protected from wild beasts, fed with locusts and honey, clothed in camel hair with a leather belt, living as Elijah did in the days of old. Luke testifies: “And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, and was in the wilderness until the day of his appearing to Israel.” (Luke 1:80)

For twenty-three years, John lived in purity, removed from the corruption of the world, guided by angels, and communing with God alone. In his ascetic life, he foreshadowed the ministry of Christ, bridging the Old Covenant with the New, calling all to repentance.

text: Beloved brethren, hear with reverence the wisdom of the fathers, for the times and seasons of the Church are not arranged by men according to their own will, but are preserved by divine tradition. The calendar of Ethiopia is not a mere reckoning of days, but a sacred order by which the mysteries of salvation, the fasts, and the feasts of our Lord and His saints are revealed to us. To neglect this wisdom is to walk in darkness, but to understand it is to walk in the light of God’s appointed times.

The Church has received from the fathers seven fasts. Four of these change their dates each year according to the calculation of Mebaja Hamer, while three are fixed and never change.

The four fasts that vary are:

1. The Great Fast (Abiy tsom),

2. The Fast of the Resurrection,

3. The Fast of Nineveh(Tsome Nenewey),

4. The Fast of the Apostles.

The three fasts that are fixed each year are:

1. The Fast of the Prophets (Christmas Fast),

2. The Fast of ("Gehad")or( "tsome Gehad"),

3. The Fast of the Virgin Mary.

Each of these is bound to its own mystery of salvation.

The Fast of the Prophets begins on the 15th of "Hidar", as a preparation for the Feast of the Nativity of Christ.

The Fast of ("Gehad")or( "tsome Gehad"), is observed as a substitute fast. It always falls on the eve of the Feast of the Lord’s Baptism. If Baptism is on Friday, then Thursday is kept as the fast; if on Saturday, then Friday is kept. The fathers have decreed that this fast must always precede the feast, even if the day itself would not ordinarily be a fast.

The Fast of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary is the remembrance of the apostolic fast, when the holy apostles fasted two weeks in longing to behold the resurrection of the Theotokos. This fast begins on Nehase 1st, and two weeks later the Dormition of our Lady is celebrated.

" is a special number, or code, assigned to a particular fast or holy day. By using this number, the dates of holidays and festivals can be determined. The count of Tewsak begins on Saturday.

Saturday = 8

Monday = 6

Tuesday = 5

Wednesday = 4

Thursday = 3

Friday = 2

By these numbers, the fasts and feasts are aligned with the mysteries of salvation.

At the center of this calculation lies Mebaja Hamer, which is defined as:

Mebaja Hamer = (መጥቅዕ)Metike' + the day of tewsak which also beale metike is performed.

Metike'(መጥቅዕ)= Last Year Metike'+ Tinte Metike' (ጥንተ መጥቅዕ).

Here, Tinte Metike' is always the fixed number 19.

The fathers handed down this rule:

If Metike' is greater than 14, it falls in Meskerem.

If it is less than 14, it falls in Tikimt.
This law never changes.

To understand how this system works, let us consider the year 2018 (E.C.).

First, the “class”(መደብ) (calculation) is found 

{5500} + 2018) ÷ 19

= 7518 ÷ 19 = 395

 { remainder } =13

Thus the class is 13.

The Seat(ወንበር) = Class – 1 = 12.

From this, the Day is calculated:

Metike'= seat ÷ 30

12 × 19 = 228

 228 ÷ 30 = 7 

{ remainder } 18

So Metike' = 18.

Now, Mebaja Hamer is found by adding this number to the Metik E' of the corresponding day of the Tewsak.

Since the 18th falls on a Sunday, and the Tewsak of Sunday is 7:

Mebaja Hamer = 18 + 7 = 25

Thus, the Mebaja Hamer of 2018 is 25, and from this number the fasts and feasts of the year are determined.

The main function of the Mebaja Hamer is to determine the dates of feasts and festivals in conjunction with the Tewsak. Therefore, it is necessary to know the Tewsak assigned to each feast and festival. By using the Mebaja Hamer together with the Tewsak of the festivals, the exact dates of the celebrations can be calculated.

5. The Fast of Nineveh"Tsome Nenewey"

This fast is unique, for it has no Tewsak of its own but depends entirely upon the Mebaja Hamer. 

1. If the Beale Metike'(በዓለ መጥቅዕ) (reference point) falls in Meskerem, the Fast of Nineveh is kept in Tir.

2. If Beale Metike'(በዓለ መጥቅዕ)  falls in Tikimt, the Fast is kept in Yekatit.

3. If Beale Metike'(በዓለ መጥቅዕ) is greater than 14, and when added to the day’s Tewsak exceeds 30, then also the Fast is in Yekatit.

Thus by the wisdom of the fathers, the time of this fast is never in doubt.

Beloved, see how nothing in the Church is by chance. Even the counting of days is sanctified. God, who set the stars in their courses and divided the times and seasons from the beginning, has also ordered the calendar of His Church for the salvation of His people.

Therefore let us keep the fasts and the feasts not as burdens, but as blessings; not as mere reckonings of time, but as holy seasons appointed for repentance, thanksgiving, and joy. For through the discipline of the calendar, the soul is trained in order, obedience, and remembrance of the works of God.

text:
O beloved brethren, what shall we say of this wondrous man? Shall we call him prophet? He is more than a prophet. Shall we name him apostle? He is greater still. Shall we call him martyr? He is crowned with blood. Saint John the Baptist is the burning lamp that shone in the wilderness, the voice that shook the desert, the bridge from the shadow of the Law to the dawn of Grace.

He was the finger pointing to the Sun, the herald crying: “Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight His paths!” He sought no honor for himself, but with every word and deed directed the eyes of men to Christ, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.

text.text: I. The Ministry and Testimony of John

text:
John was sent not to glorify himself, but to point with a burning finger toward the Christ. With humility he declared: “I baptize you with water for repentance, but He who comes after me is mightier than I, the latchet of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.”

Here we behold his humility. Though multitudes came to him, he would not accept their reverence as though he were the Messiah. Rather, he proclaimed, “Behold, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.” This was no common word, but the greatest testimony ever uttered by human lips, for in those words John revealed both the incarnation and the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ.

When the Pharisees questioned him “What do you say about yourself?” he confessed without hesitation: “I am not the Christ. I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Make straight the way of the Lord.” See his faithfulness! He refuses glory for himself, but labors only that Christ may be known.

When the Virgin Mary came to Elizabeth, the mother of John, she exclaimed with holy awe: “How is it that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” Thus, even before his birth, John bore witness to the Lord, leaping in the womb at the sound of Mary’s voice.

When our Lord came to be baptized by him, Saint John humbly acknowledged Christ’s divinity, saying: “I need to be baptized by You, and do You come to me? How can the Lord come to His servant, while the servant goes to his Master?” (Matthew 3:14).

When Saint John said to our Lord, “I baptize others in Your name, but in whose name shall I baptize You?” the Lord answered: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek; You are the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world; You are the Light of God, the Son of the Father. Jesus Christ, have mercy on us.”

In obedience, John did as he was commanded and baptized our Lord on Tir 11.

And when the Lord consented to be baptized, the heavens opened, the Spirit descended like a dove, and the Father’s voice thundered: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” In that moment the mystery of the Holy Trinity was revealed to the world through the ministry of John.

5

John, who had baptized Christ, was not spared the cup of suffering. At thirty years of age, he was called to bear witness with his own blood. Because he reproved Herod for his unlawful union with Herodias, he was cast into prison.

During a feast, Herodias’ daughter danced and pleased the king. Bound by his drunken oath, Herod commanded John’s beheading. O tragic folly! Not out of justice, not out of grief, but for the sake of a banquet, a dance, and a rash promise, the righteous man was slain. text: The name John means “God is grace.” At his birth, his parents, Zechariah and Elizabeth, rejoiced, and the Gospel names him Fissa Wahaset joy and happiness. Filled with the Holy Spirit even in his mother’s womb, he grew in holiness in the wilderness, living as a monk, baptizing unto repentance, and finally baptizing the Lord Himself.

Saint John the Baptist was not given for one time or for one people only. His life, his words, and his martyrdom continue to echo across the ages as a testimony to all generations. Among prophets, among priests, among martyrs, he holds a unique place. For he was chosen above all to touch with his own hands the very head of the Incarnate God.

The fathers teach us that even if Raguel with his zeal, or Job with his righteousness, had desired to baptize the divine Fire, they would not have been granted such honor. Angels themselves tremble before the throne of God, yet John was counted worthy to baptize the Word made flesh in the waters of the Jordan. This single act places him beyond comparison, for he did what no prophet, priest, or righteous man before him had done.

His witness was not only with his lips but with his whole being. He was the voice crying in the wilderness, preparing the way for Christ. He was the prophet pointing to the Lamb of God. He was the teacher calling all men to repentance. And when his time was fulfilled, he became the martyr whose blood sealed his testimony.

Our Lord declared of him: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? … A prophet? Yes, I say to you, and more than a prophet. Behold, I send My messenger before Your face, who will prepare Your way before You.” And again: “Among those born of women there has not risen a greater than John the Baptist.” (Matthew 11:9–11). These words are not spoken of any other man, but of John alone.

text:
👇🏾

Therefore, his life is a lamp for every age. To the humble, he shows humility, for he confessed, “I am not the Christ.” To the courageous, he shows boldness, for he reproved kings without fear. To the pure, he shows holiness, for he lived in the wilderness in fasting and prayer. To the faithful, he shows steadfastness, for he endured imprisonment and death rather than betray the truth.

His witness endures even now in the Church. Each year, the faithful commemorate his birth, his baptism of Christ, his martyrdom, and the transfer of his holy relics. His name is remembered in the liturgy, his call to repentance is proclaimed in every generation, and his example stands as a bridge between the Old Covenant and the New.

Thus, John’s life is not bound to history; it is a living testimony. His voice still cries to us today: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” His lamp still shines to guide us until we come into the full light of the Sun of Righteousness, our Lord Jesus Christ.

Saint John received his covenant on Meskerem His life and teachings, the wonders and miracles he performed, the covenant given to him by God, and his martyrdom are all extensively recorded in his writings.

Beloved in Christ, children of the holy Church, I greet you in the peace of the Lord, who is the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. Today, we shall meditate upon the mystery of time, and how our fathers in Ethiopia, guided by divine wisdom, have preserved a holy order for the reckoning of days, seasons, and years.

For the Scripture says: “You have blessed the year with Your goodness” (Psalm 64:11). Time itself is sanctified, for it is the unfolding of God’s providence, from the creation of Adam until the coming of Christ, and from the Resurrection until the consummation of all things.

text.text: The Order of the Fasts and Feasts

text:
The Ethiopian calendar anchors its holy observances upon the Fast of Nineveh (Tsome Nenewe), for just as the repentance of the people of Nineveh turned away the wrath of God, so this fast becomes the foundation of all others. From this, the classification of the year is set.

For example, in the year 2018 AD, by the calculation of Mebaja Hamer, the number of days from Nineveh fast( tsome nenewe) until the Fast of Salvation (Tsome Dihnet) was 121. Dividing by 30, four full months and one day remain; thus, the fast began on Ginbot 26. From this single anchor point, the entire calendar of fasts and feasts unfolds:

Meskel on Meskerem 17, a Saturday.

The Fast of the Prophets (Gena Fast) beginning Hidar 15, a Monday.

Timqet (Baptism) on Tir 11, Monday.

The Great Fast (Hudade) beginning Yekatit 2.

Debre Zeyt on Megabit 6, Sunday.

Hosae'na on Megabit 27, Sunday.

Crucifixion on Miyazya 2, Friday.

Resurrection on Miyazya 4, Sunday.

Ascension on Ginbot 13, Thursday.

Pentecost (Paraclete) on Ginbot 23, Sunday.

Thus, whoever knows the beginning of Nineveh can trace the steps of the whole liturgical year, past, present, and to come.

Consider, beloved, the story of our forefather Adam. He was created on a Friday, and after forty days was placed in Paradise. There he lived in innocence for seven years, one month, and seventeen days. But in disobedience, eating of the forbidden fruit, he fell. Yet even in his fall, God gave a promise: “From your seed shall come the Savior, after five thousand and five hundred years, to redeem mankind.”

Thus, the children of Adam began to mark time by the sun, the moon, and the stars, awaiting the day of salvation. Time itself became a prophecy, a witness pointing to Christ.

text.text: The Life of Our Lord in Time

text:
He was conceived on Megabit 29, 5500, at 3:00 AM, a Sunday ,during the time of john

He was born on Tahisas 29, 5501, at 10:00 PM, a Tuesday,during the time of Matthew 

He was baptized on Tir 10, at 10:00 PM.during the time of luke

In the year 5533, which corresponds to the 33rd year of Matthew Era, Christ revealed His divine light to the apostles on Mount Tabor. This took place on Sunday, August 13,at noon.

He entered Jerusalem on Megabit 22, 5534, a Sunday, riding on a donkey’s colt,during the time of mark

On Megabit 26, Thursday, He fulfilled the Passover, giving the new covenant of His Body and Blood ,during the time of mark

On Megabit 27, Friday, He was crucified, yielding His soul at the sixth hour ,during the time of mark

On Megabit 29, Sunday, He rose in glory at midnight, during the time of mark

And on Ginbot 8, at 3:00 AM, He ascended to His Father, during the time of mark

Thus, every hour and every date is not empty, but filled with the presence of Christ, who sanctified time by His own life.
