text.text: The Ancient Witness of the Fathers

text:
The holy Fathers also recorded that once in every 600 years, the month of Pagumen contains 7 days. For just as the world is renewed in cycles, so also does the calendar reveal the hidden harmony of creation.

Why is this so? Because in every day of 24 hours, there is an excess of 0.4 seconds. Over centuries, these seconds accumulate, they bring forth the seven-day Pagumen once in six hundred years.

Moreover, there is a mystical reckoning called Rina Maalt and Rina Nacht. In the Ethiopian calendar, the year is counted as 365 days, 15 latitudes, and 6 kal’it that is, 365 days, 6 hours, 2 minutes, and 24 seconds. When 2 minutes and 24 seconds are gathered together, they bring forth the seven-day Pagumen once in six hundred years.for one kal’it equals 24 seconds.

Thus:

In 5 years there are 30 kal’it.

In 10 years there are 60 kal’it.

In 100 years, 240 seconds, which equal 10 latitudes.

In 200 years, 20 latitudes.

In 300 years, 30 latitudes.

In 400 years, 40 latitudes.

In 500 years, 50 latitudes.

And in 600 years, 60 latitudes.

Sixty latitudes are equal to 1,440 minutes, or one complete day. Therefore, after 600 years, the addition of time produces the seven-day Pagumen.

Indeed, the last such month was seen in the year 1700 AD (or 7800 before borth of Christ ). The next will come in 2300 AD, after the span of 283 years.

text.text: The Mystery of Latitude and Longitude

text:
The Fathers also taught:

Latitude is the path of light moving from north to south.

Longitude is the path of light moving from east to west.

Let us, therefore, lift our hearts with the Psalmist, saying:
“you hast blessed the crown of the year with Thy goodness” (Psalm 64:11).

And let us beseech our merciful God, who grants us to see a new year in our lifetime, that He may bless the coming year with peace, with health of body and soul, and with repentance, that we may be made worthy to partake of the Holy Eucharist

The holy Fathers also recorded that once in every 600 years, the month of Pagumen contains 7 days. For just as the world is renewed in cycles, so also does the calendar reveal the hidden harmony of creation.

Why is this so? Because in every day of 24 hours, there is an excess of 0.4 seconds. Over centuries, these seconds accumulate, they bring forth the seven-day Pagumen once in six hundred years.

Moreover, there is a mystical reckoning called Rina Maalt and Rina Nacht. In the Ethiopian calendar, the year is counted as 365 days, 15 latitudes, and 6 kal’it that is, 365 days, 6 hours, 2 minutes, and 24 seconds. When 2 minutes and 24 seconds are gathered together, they bring forth the seven-day Pagumen once in six hundred years.for one kal’it equals 24 seconds.

Thus:

In 5 years there are 30 kal’it.

In 10 years there are 60 kal’it.

In 100 years, 240 seconds, which equal 10 latitudes.

In 200 years, 20 latitudes.

In 300 years, 30 latitudes.

In 400 years, 40 latitudes.

In 500 years, 50 latitudes.

And in 600 years, 60 latitudes.

Sixty latitudes are equal to 1,440 minutes, or one complete day. Therefore, after 600 years, the addition of time produces the seven-day Pagumen.

Indeed, the last such month was seen in the year 1700 AD (or 7800 before borth of Christ ). The next will come in 2300 AD, after the span of 283 years.

The Mystery of Latitude and Longitude

The Fathers also taught:

Latitude is the path of light moving from north to south.

Longitude is the path of light moving from east to west.

Conclusion 

Let us, therefore, lift our hearts with the Psalmist, saying:
“you hast blessed the crown of the year with Thy goodness” (Psalm 64:11).

And let us beseech our merciful God, who grants us to see a new year in our lifetime, that He may bless the coming year with peace, with health of body and soul, and with repentance, that we may be made worthy to partake of the Holy Eucharist

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. .

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

Beloved in Christ, lovers of the truth handed down by the holy Church, today we take up a matter of great importance: the mystery of grace prostration. Let us incline our hearts, that we may understand what it means, and by whose command it was delivered to the saints.

The Meaning of Grace Prostration

Grace prostration is the reverent bow offered not only to God but to all those sanctified in Him, to the vessels of His glory, and to the signs of His salvation. It is not the adoration due to the Holy Trinity, but the honor of grace given to:

The Holy Virgin Mary, the Theotokos,

The Holy Cross of our Lord,

The Holy Angels,

The Martyrs,

The Righteous and Saints,

The Holy Church,

The Holy Places,

The Ark,

text.text: The Holy Relics of the righteous.

text:
The daily prayer of the Church, therefore, does not end only with the words: “I bow down to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.” Rather, it continues: “I bow down to the Virgin Mary, who bore God in the flesh; I bow down to the Cross on which Christ was crucified for the salvation of the world.”

Here we see that the prostration of grace is distinct from the prostration of worship ( to God alone ) or prostration of worship belongs to the Holy Trinity alone, but Grace prostration are rightly given to all that God has sanctified.
It is God Himself who taught us to give this honor. The Scriptures testify to this from the very beginning.

When Isaac blessed Jacob, he spoke the words:
“Let nations serve you, and peoples bow down to you. Be lord over your brothers, and let your mother’s sons bow down to you. Cursed be everyone who curses you, and blessed be everyone who blesses you.” (Gen. 27:29).

Though Esau was the elder son, it was Jacob who received the blessing by divine providence. For God Himself ratified Isaac’s words, so much so that He was thereafter called the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob—and not of Esau. If honoring the saints were contrary to God, would He have permitted Isaac’s blessing? Would He not have rebuked it? Instead, He confirmed it.

Years later, Jacob himself bowed down before Esau (Gen. 33:3), showing that prostration is not idolatry, but an act of humility and respect sanctified by God.

Consider also the righteous Joseph. God gave him a dream:
“Behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and behold, my sheaf stood upright, and your sheaves gathered around and bowed down to my sheaf.” (Gen. 37:7).

His brothers despised him for it, saying: “Shall you indeed reign over us?” Yet the vision came from God. And again the Lord showed Joseph another dream: “Behold, the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me.” (Gen. 37:9).

What happened? His brothers conspired against him, cast him into a pit, and sold him into slavery. Yet when famine struck, those same brothers came to Egypt and fulfilled God’s word: “Joseph’s brothers came and bowed themselves before him with their faces to the ground.” (Gen. 42:6).

So too, those who refuse to honor the saints are like Joseph’s brothers full of envy, resisting God’s revelation. Yet in the time of spiritual famine, they will be compelled to bow, whether in this life or in judgment.

Isaiah proclaimed: “All who despise you shall bow down at the soles of your feet.” (Isa. 60:14).

In Luke’s Gospel, As Lazarus, who was denied alms on earth, was asked in Sheol through Abraham's intercession. Luke 16:20-31

In Acts, the jailer who bound Paul and Silas fell trembling at their feet, crying out after the prison shook by God’s power: “He fell down before Paul and Silas.” (Acts 16:29). Was it Paul who demanded worship? No! It was God who caused His servants to be honored.

Beloved in Christ, children of the Holy Church, peace and grace be with you. Today, we set our hearts upon the mystery of zemen—a word rich with meaning both in Scripture and in the created order.

In the Greek language of the New Testament, the word zemen is translated as kairos, which means a specific time appointed for an action or an opportunity given to us to do something. It is not simply the turning of the clock, but the moment when God calls us to act, to repent, to harvest, to rejoice.

In the Ethiopian tradition, one zemen (year) consists of 13 months and 365¼ days, arranged into four great seasons, each reflecting God’s providence:
The season of ripening, when the sown seed matures, the stars fill the sky, and the earth is clothed with flowers. As Saint Yared sang, “The heavens are adorned and the earth blossoms with delight.”
The time of burning heat, when the earth is parched, the green leaves wither, and dust covers the fields. Rain is withheld.
The gentle season of showers, when the earth drinks small rains, and tender green shoots once again appear.
The season of heavy rains, which itself contains seven holy divisions, :

(በዓተ ክረምት) ( የዘር ወቅት ) (Sene 26 – Hamle 19): The earth receives its first rains, softening the soil for plowing and sowing. As the Psalmist declares, “He who covers the heavens with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth” (Ps. 146:8).

Filling of the Sea (Hamle 20 – Nehase 10): The rains gather in rivers and seas, the clouds thunder, and creation trembles with God’s majesty. Saint Yared proclaimed, “The sea saw Him and fled; the earth bowed before Him.”

): The time of the crow’s chick, born featherless and abandoned by its mother. Yet God feeds it with small creatures carried by the rains, until it grows to fullness. Here we remember the Lord’s care, who “gives food to the young ravens that cry” (Ps. 146:9).

– Light of the Dawn (Nehase. 29 – pagume 5): The clouds disperse, the rains subside, and the earth is clothed in brightness. Saint Yared declared of God, “You are He who brings forth the morning light.”

(Meskerem. 1 – 8): it's beginning of Ethiopian year . This season is dedicated with St. John the Baptist, for he stands as the end of the prophets and the dawn of the Gospel. He was beheaded on Meskerem 2, and thus the beginning of the year is sanctified in his name.

The time of fruit-bearing, when the seeds sown by toil begin to yield thirty, sixty, and a hundredfold. It is the hour of thanksgiving, when the farmer reaps with joy what was sown with tears, echoing the Psalmist: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Ps. 125:5–6).

“The nine days from Meskerem 17 to Meskerem 27 are called Meskel because the church commemorate the time when the Cross of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, which had been buried out of Jewish envy, was later searched for and uncovered by Queen Helena. After the Cross was found and brought forth, the Church celebrated the Divine Liturgy house , and for this reason the feast is called" Meskel.”

text:
Beloved in Christ, faithful followers of the holy Church , we greet you in the peace of God. On this blessed day, the Holy Church commemorates the repose of the righteous and glorious Saint Elizabeth, the mother of Saint John the Baptist, the Forerunner of our Lord. Let us, therefore, recall her life with reverence, and learn from her faith and steadfastness.

✍🏾

Saint Elizabeth was born from the house of Levi, from the priestly line of Aaron. Through Aaron came Tekta and Trika, and from them Hermela was born. Hermela, a woman of virtue, was joined in marriage to a blessed man named Matat, and from their union came three holy daughters.

👉🏾The first was Mary, who bore Saint Salome.

👉🏾The second was Sophia, who bore Saint Elizabeth.

👉🏾The third was Anna, who bore the Virgin Mary, the Queen of Heaven and Earth.

Thus, the Virgin Mary, Saint Elizabeth, and Saint Salome are bound together in one holy family, sanctified by the will of God.

text.text: Her Marriage and Conception of John

text:
✍ Her Marriage and Conception of John
In due time, Elizabeth was given in marriage to the priest Zechariah, a man righteous and blameless before the Lord. Yet, though they walked uprightly, they were barren and without child. But when Zechariah was one  hundred years old and Elizabeth ninety , the mercy of God visited them. By the Annunciation of the Angel, Elizabeth conceived the great prophet, Saint John the Baptist, on Meskerem 26. For six months she hid herself in wonder at the miracle wrought within her.

text.text: The Visitation of the Mother of God

text: When the Virgin Mary heard of Elizabeth’s blessed state, she went to visit her. As the Mother of God greeted her kinswoman, Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit and gave thanks with a loud voice. The child in her womb, Saint John, leapt for joy at the sound of the Virgin’s voice and, though yet unborn, he bowed in worship before the Creator who was being carried in the Virgin’s womb. Thus the Forerunner bore witness to Christ even from the hidden place of his mother’s womb.

text.text: The Trial and the Raising of John

text: When John was but two years and six months old, Herod the cruel king sent forth soldiers to slaughter the innocents in Israel. In those days, Elizabeth took her child and fled, hiding him in the wilderness. Zechariah the priest was slain between the altar and the temple for refusing to betray the child. Alone and widowed, Elizabeth raised John in the wilderness of Ziph. There he grew in purity, sustained by the providence of God, until the day of his ministry.

On this day, Meskerem 7, Elizabeth departed from this earthly life on the monastery of zifata and entered into eternal rest, having fulfilled her role as mother of the Prophet, the Forerunner, 

Let us, therefore, honor her memory, giving glory to God who chose her womb to bring forth the herald of His Christ. May her prayers and intercessions strengthen us to walk in humility and obedience, as she did, until we also come to rest in the eternal Kingdom.

On this blessed day, the Holy Church commemorates the repose of the righteous and glorious Saint Elizabeth, the mother of Saint John the Baptist, the Forerunner of our Lord. Let us, therefore, recall her life with reverence, and learn from her faith and steadfastness.

✍🏾

Saint Elizabeth was born from the house of Levi, from the priestly line of Aaron. Through Aaron came Tekta and Trika, and from them Hermela was born. Hermela, a woman of virtue, was joined in marriage to a blessed man named Matat, and from their union came three holy daughters.

👉🏾The first was Mary, who bore Saint Salome.

👉🏾The second was Sophia, who bore Saint Elizabeth.

👉🏾The third was Anna, who bore the Virgin Mary, the Queen of Heaven and Earth.

Thus, the Virgin Mary, Saint Elizabeth, and Saint Salome are bound together in one holy family, sanctified by the will of God.
Her Marriage and Conception of John

✍ Her Marriage and Conception of John
In due time, Elizabeth was given in marriage to the priest Zechariah, a man righteous and blameless before the Lord. Yet, though they walked uprightly, they were barren and without child. But when Zechariah was one  hundred years old and Elizabeth ninety , the mercy of God visited them. By the Annunciation of the Angel, Elizabeth conceived the great prophet, Saint John the Baptist, on Meskerem 26. For six months she hid herself in wonder at the miracle wrought within her.
The Visitation of the Mother of God

When the Virgin Mary heard of Elizabeth’s blessed state, she went to visit her. As the Mother of God greeted her kinswoman, Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit and gave thanks with a loud voice. The child in her womb, Saint John, leapt for joy at the sound of the Virgin’s voice and, though yet unborn, he bowed in worship before the Creator who was being carried in the Virgin’s womb. Thus the Forerunner bore witness to Christ even from the hidden place of his mother’s womb.
The Trial and the Raising of John

When John was but two years and six months old, Herod the cruel king sent forth soldiers to slaughter the innocents in Israel. In those days, Elizabeth took her child and fled, hiding him in the wilderness. Zechariah the priest was slain between the altar and the temple for refusing to betray the child. Alone and widowed, Elizabeth raised John in the wilderness of Ziph. There he grew in purity, sustained by the providence of God, until the day of his ministry.

On this day, Meskerem 7, Elizabeth departed from this earthly life on the monastery of zifata and entered into eternal rest, having fulfilled her role as mother of the Prophet, the Forerunner, 

Let us, therefore, honor her memory, giving glory to God who chose her womb to bring forth the herald of His Christ. May her prayers and intercessions strengthen us to walk in humility and obedience, as she did, until we also come to rest in the eternal Kingdom.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

text:
Beloved in Christ, children of the Holy Orthodox faith, let us lift up our hearts with thanksgiving to God who orders the times and seasons, who “set the lights in the firmament of heaven to divide the day from the night, and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years” (Gen. 1:14).

It is not by accident, nor by human invention, that Meskerem is for us the beginning of the year. Rather, this beginning has been sanctified by Scripture, confirmed by the lives of the righteous, kept by our holy forefathers, and preserved by our Church to this very day.

text.text: The Meaning of a Year and the Order of Creation

text:
The first of the months in Ethiopia is Meskerem, which falls in September. It is called “the month of the year” because it crowns the cycle of the lights in the heavens. The sun, the moon, and the stars finish their course in Pagume, and a new cycle begins in Meskerem. At this time, day and night are perfectly equal: twelve hours of light, twelve hours of darkness. Thus the year contain 364 days, as is written in the Book of Enoch:

“The night is equal to the day, and if you count the year carefully, it will be three hundred and sixty-four days” (Enoch 26:44).

And the Prophet Jeremiah cries out, “Renew our days as before” (Lam. 5:21), teaching us that each new year is a renewal of life, an opportunity to begin again.

In the days of Noah, after the floodwaters receded, the earth appeared in the “first month” (Kufale 7:1). The Book of Jubilees declares:

“In the beginning of the first month he commanded him to make an ark for himself, and the earth was dry in it” (Kufal 24:7).

Thus, the end of destruction and the beginning of renewed life came in this month. Noah and his family, stepping out of the ark into a cleansed earth, celebrated it as the beginning of a new year. So too, in our own Meskerem, the dark and rainy season passes away, the earth dries, flowers blossom, fruits ripen, and life begins anew.

text.text: The Queen of Sheba and Solomon

text:
Our history also teaches that in this same month the Queen of Sheba went up to Jerusalem. After marveling at the wisdom of Solomon, she returned to Ethiopia laden with precious gifts. For this reason, Meskerem 1 is forever known as the “month of the year of the year, Enkuletatash” a month of wisdom and abundance.

God’s Command to Moses and Israel

It was in this month too that God commanded Moses to make the beginning of the year. In Leviticus we read of the great feasts appointed in the seventh month (Lev. 23:53). Israel departed from Egypt by God’s command in this season, and this time was sanctified as a memorial forever.

And note well, beloved: until the eleventh century, the whole Christian world celebrated the new year in Meskerem. Only in the days off Gregory VII (1073–1085) was the celebration transferred to Tir, to tie it with the Nativity. Yet the Eastern Church, faithful to her inheritance, never forsook Meskerem. Greece, Russia, Romania, Alexandria, and Ethiopia still proclaim Meskerem as the beginning of the year.

Europeans change their seasons in Tir, but we Ethiopians reckon the change in Meskerem, when light and darkness are equal. Herein lies not only a natural wisdom, but a spiritual one: for as the world moves from cloud and gloom into brightness, so too we are called to pass from sin and shadow into the light of Christ.

text:
Our Ethiopian calendar differs from the European by seven years and eight months. When they say it is 2025, we say it is 2018. After four months, they will say 2026, but we will not yet. Many explanations are given: some say we delayed in recognizing Christ’s birth; others speak of Adam’s seven years in Paradise. But these are mere conjectures.

In truth, Ethiopia has never been ignorant of the Lord’s coming. Did not Ethiopian kings bring gifts at His birth? Did not our fathers preserve the knowledge that Adam spent seven years in Paradise? These years are counted within our reckoning, which measures 5500 years from creation until the coming of Christ. Thus the Ethiopian calendar stands correct and true.

Unlike the Western world, whose months vary in length thirty one, thirty, and twenty-eight days we have a perfect order: twelve months of thirty days, and a thirteenth month of five or six days in leap years. For here the balance of day and night, each of twelve hours, is preserved.

The Naming of the Eras

Each era of our calendar is named after one of the four evangelists Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John who, though separated in time and place, spoke with one voice under the inspiration of the Holy  Spirit. The Gospel is “the good news”:? salvation of body and soul, the passing from death to life, the liberation from the tyranny of the devil.

To know which evangelist marks the age, we add 5500 years to the year of Mercy (2018)and divide by four. A remainder of one is Matthew, two is Mark, three is Luke, and zero is John. Thus even in the order of time itself, the voice of the Gospel resounds.

Why do Europeans begin their new year on Meskerem 11 while we begin on Meskerem 1? The answer lies in the calendar reform of Pope Gregory XIII in 1582. He shortened the year from 365 days and 6 hour to 365 days and 5 hours, thereby removing ten days. Tikmt 5 became Tikmt 15, and so the calendars diverged. But the Ethiopian Church rejected this innovation, keeping the fullness of the year as 365 days and 6 hours.

text.text: The Spiritual Meaning of the New Year

text:
And so, dearly beloved, when Meskerem dawns, it is not only the turning of the earth or the changing of the seasons. It is a sign of the renewal of the soul. The clouds depart, the sun shines, the fields grow green, the air is sweet with blossoms. So too must our hearts be renewed: the darkness of sin cast away, the fragrance of virtue springing forth.

Saint Peter exhorts us: “The past is enough for you” (1 Peter 4:3). Enough of sin! Enough of drunkenness, lust, and idolatry! If times change but we remain the same, the change profits us nothing. A new year is a time of repentance: to say, “Forgive us for the past and guard us in the future.”

Therefore, let us embrace Meskerem as a holy beginning. Let us cast off the darkness of the old year, let us shine in the light of Christ, let us renew our minds and our works. Let us plan afresh with diligence, strengthen what is weak, and fill what is lacking.

May this new year be for us a season of peace and prosperity, a time of repentance and renewal, a time of charity and faithfulness. May the intercession of the Virgin Mary, the prayers of the saints, and the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ be with us always.

text.text: I. The Woman of Enmity: Eve and Mary

text:

In Eve we see the mother of corruption, for by her disobedience sin entered, and death reigned.

In Mary, the new Eve, we behold the mother of life, for by her obedience the curse was overturned and the blessing restored.

The serpent triumphed over the first woman, but the second woman crushed his head. This is the warfare St. John saw: “The dragon was enraged with the woman, and went to make war with the rest of her offspring” (Rev. 12:17). Already the Psalmist declared: “You crushed the heads of the dragon” (Ps. 74:14). And the piercing of Christ’s hands and feet (Ps. 22:16) reveals how the serpent sought to wound the Seed of the woman but in striking, he was undone.

text.text: II. The Parable of Noah’s Ark

text:

The ark itself is the Virgin Mary.

Noah himself is a type of Christ, the just man who delivers his household.

Noah’s entrance into the ark signifies the Word’s conception in the Virgin’s womb.

The ark’s three parts reveal the threefold purity of the Virgin:

purity of body,

purity of soul,

purity of heart.

They also signify her perpetual virginity:

before conception,

during conception,

after conception;

before childbirth,

during childbirth,

after childbirth.

As the dove of peace returned to Noah with the olive branch (Gen. 8:8–12), so Mary is the ark of salvation, the dwelling of peace, the vessel chosen by God for our deliverance.

Mark this well: as all who despised the ark perished in the flood, so all who despise the intercession of the Virgin risk shipwreck of their souls. To reject her is to reject the work of God Himself, for she is the faithful vessel He has chosen. And if God has justified her and magnified her, who shall accuse? For indeed, she is “blessed among women” (Luke 1:42).

Finally, let us ascend with Jacob’s vision. He saw a ladder reaching from earth to heaven, upon which angels ascended and descended, and the Lord stood above it (Gen. 28:12–13).

This ladder is the Virgin Mary, by whom heaven was united with earth.

The stone upon which Jacob rested signifies the foundation of the prophets, who foretold her.

The ladder itself reveals the Incarnation: the descent of God to man, the ascent of man to God.

The King upon the ladder is Christ, who reigned nine months in her womb as upon a throne, and who reigns eternally in the heavens without end.

The angels ascending and descending proclaim the mystery: that by her, the Word took flesh; 

On the other hand, the angels ascending and descending upon the ladder clearly reveal that the human flesh, once humbled from its original glory and weakened in nature, was exalted and glorified by the Word of God, and is now united with Him in the one divine nature of the Godhead.

Thus Mary is revealed as the “Mother of God,” the golden ladder joining heaven and earth, the living gate through which the King of glory entered.

Brethren, behold the wonder: from Genesis to Revelation, in prophecy, in parable, in vision, the Virgin is ever present. She is the Woman who conquers the serpent, the Ark that saves from wrath, the Ladder uniting heaven and earth.

Therefore let us not neglect so great a gift, but with reverence and love seek refuge in her intercessions. For through her, the Word became flesh; through her, the curse was lifted; through her, we are invited to life eternal.

text.text: The Mystery of Our Mother, the

text: Beloved in Christ, let us lift our hearts in thanksgiving and praise, for today we meditate upon the mystery of Our Mother, the Holy Virgin Mary the ark of life, the cloud of blessing, and the rainbow of the covenant.

text.text: Mary as the Rainbow of God’s Covenant

text:
When the waters of the flood subsided and Noah, the righteous, came forth from the ark, he offered sacrifice before the Lord. In that moment, God made a covenant with Noah and with all flesh, saying:

“I set My bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth” (Gen. 9:13).

This rainbow was more than the refracted light of heaven—it was a divine mystery, a prophecy hidden for ages and revealed in Christ through His Mother. For as the rainbow shines with many colors, so too the Virgin bore within herself the fullness of grace, adorned with every virtue, and became the sign of peace between heaven and earth.

Noah lamented, fearing the sins of his children would once again provoke the wrath of God. But the Lord, in His mercy, declared that He would not again destroy the earth with water. Instead, He gave the rainbow as a remembrance of His covenant. The Lord revealed this prophecy to Noah, declaring that a creation formed from the four elements would not again destroy mankind with a flood. Instead, the cloud itself was a symbol of the Holy Virgin Mary, through whom the Son would take flesh from His Mother’s body and a human soul from her soul, be born, and bring salvation to mankind. 

Thus, the rainbow was not only a symbol of reprieve from destruction, but a prophecy of salvation through the Incarnation.

text.text: Witness of the Fathers and Scholars

text:
The great Fathers of the Church discerned this mystery with spiritual eyes.

Saint Ephrem the Syrian, with piercing wisdom, declared that the Virgin is the living cloud who bore the Sun of Righteousness.

Abba Giorgis Ze Gasicha, in his Enzira Sibhat holy book, praises her as the covenant itself: “You are the rainbow, the sign of peace, that the rain of wrath shall not fall upon the earth again.”

Abba Tsige Dengel and Abba Gebre Mariam, in their Mahlete Tsige Holy book, testify that the Virgin is the rainbow of salvation, given to Noah as a mystery, fulfilled in the flesh of the Mother of God.

Indeed, Ethiopia, the cherished homeland of the Virgin, has preserved this truth with profound devotion. The faithful call the rainbow “Mary’s Mekenet” the throne of Mary. For just as the rainbow crowns the sky with its brilliance, so the Virgin crowns the earth with her intercession.

Beloved, no matter how great our sins, we are not abandoned. the Virgin Mary, standing beneath the Cross of her Son at Golgotha, received the promise of intercession. She prays unceasingly for her children, entreating her Son to show mercy, to forgive, and to bless us.

She is not only the rainbow of Noah but also the ladder of Jacob, the bush of Moses, the temple of Solomon, and the tabernacle of glyory. Through her, heaven was opened, and through her, the wrath that we deserved was stayed.

Therefore, we cry out:
O Holy Virgin Mary, rainbow of covenant, intercede for us before your Son! Obtain for us forgiveness, and bless us with your maternal love, which never departs from the faithful.
Let us then honor her, not with lips alone, but with lives adorned with purity, humility, and charity. For she who bore God in her womb calls us to bear Him in our hearts.

text:
Beloved brethren in Christ, children of the holy Orthodox faith, let us rejoice and give thanks to God, for today we recall the wondrous miracle of Tsedeniya Maryam, the day sanctified by the appearance of the holy icon of the Mother of God, the Virgin Mary, on the tenth of Meskerem.

This is no ordinary remembrance but a holy testimony of the providence of God and the loving intercession of the Queen of Heaven.

text.text: Martha of Tsedeniya and the Desire for Eternal Riches

text:
In the land called Tsedeniya, there lived a woman named Martha, chosen and honored by God. She was wealthy, but unlike many who cling to riches, she considered the vanity of worldly possessions. In her heart she said:

“What shall it profit a man to gain the whole world, but lose his soul?” (Mark 8:36).

Inspired by this truth, Martha resolved to turn her wealth into a work greater than all earthly works the work of hospitality, which Scripture so often exalts. She remembered how Abraham welcomed the Holy Trinity beneath the oak of Mamre, how Lot received the holy angels, and how Martha of Bethany, the sister of Lazarus, made her home a resting place for Christ Himself.

Following their example, Martha built a great guest-house and prepared a table as for a king’s banquet, daily receiving strangers as though they were the Lord Himself. In doing so, she prepared her heart to be a dwelling place for God.

text.text: Martha’s Desire for the Holy Image

text:
One evening, as she conversed with her guests, she heard of a sacred image of the Holy Virgin Mary, strong in flesh and soul, said to be painted by St. Luke the Evangelist. It was renowned for answering prayers and working miracles through her Son. Hearing this, Martha’s heart burned like fire with love for the Virgin. In tears, she pleaded:

“Is there anyone among you who will go to Jerusalem and bring me this holy image? I will give all that I have for this treasure.”

A holy monk, moved by her devotion, promised to fulfill her request. He traveled to Jerusalem, purchased the holy icon, and began his journey back.

On the way to Tsedeniya, the monk encountered grave dangers.

A lion, fierce and roaring, leapt upon him to devour him. In terror, he fell to the ground. At that moment, the holy icon cried out with a voice seven times louder than the lion’s roar, and the beast fled in fear.

Later, bandits surrounded him with intent to kill. Again, the image resounded with a voice like thunder, and the robbers scattered in confusion, not knowing whence the cry came.

Seeing these wonders, the monk marveled at the power of the image of the Mother of God and thought to himself: “I will take her to Ethiopia, that she may be my helper.” Yet he erred, not knowing that the Virgin herself had chosen to dwell with Martha, who loved her with all her heart.

text.text: The Virgin’s Choice and the Monk’s Struggle

text:
When the monk sought to avoid Martha and sail directly to Ethiopia, the winds of heaven rose against him, driving his ship back to the shores of Tsedeniya. There he entered Martha’s house, lodging with travelers.

Three times he attempted to leave, but a miraculous door open to all others remained shut before him. Martha, seeing his strange affliction, asked what troubled him. In shame, the monk confessed, recounting the miracles of the icon. At last, he surrendered it to her, saying:

text:
Martha, filled with joy, received the image as Queen Helena once received the Holy Cross. With reverence she built a splendid sanctuary, like Solomon for the Ark of Zion. She placed the holy icon in honor, set lamps burning day and night, and she was worshipped with tears and uplifted hands.

Soon, miracles abounded. The wise and faithful who came saw the image as if it had taken on flesh. Tears flowed from her image, and those who were anointed with it were healed of their afflicting diseases. News had spread across the world:

The image of the Mother of God, look like strong in flesh and soul, had come from Jerusalem to Tsedeniya on the tenth of Meskerem.

The bishops, beholding these wonders, established the commemoration of this holy day so that generations might never forget.

Beloved, this feast teaches us:

That true wealth is not in gold or silver, but in charity and devotion.

That the Mother of God hears the cries of her children and comes swiftly to their aid.

That her presence sanctifies homes, heals the sick, and drives away the adversary.

That God Himself directs the steps of those who honor His Mother, making their houses temples of grace.

Therefore, on this holy day, let us cry out with faith:

O Lady Mary, Queen of Heaven and Tsedeniya, Ark of Salvation and Mother of our Lord, intercede for us! As you chose to dwell in the house of Martha, so dwell also in our hearts. Drive far from us the lion of the enemy, scatter the robbers of our souls, and lead us into the eternal kingdom of your Son, Jesus Christ.

text:
Beloved in Christ, heirs of the faith of the apostles, peace and blessing be upon you. Today we reflect on a subject which stirs the tongue of critics and tests the understanding of the faithful: Why do we bow, why do we fall in prostration before the holy icons of the saints?

Let us first establish the foundation: when we prostrate before a holy icon, we do not worship the wood, the paint, or the artist’s craft. No, God forbid! The Church condemns such idolatry. Rather, in bowing we honor the one whom the image represents. To Christ Himself when we kneel before His icon; to His holy saints when we bow before their likenesses asking their intercession, seeking their blessing, and remembering their faith. Thus, our prostration passes through the image to its prototype, just as a kiss upon a royal seal is meant for the king, not for the wax.

Those who know little of Scripture raise the objection: “You shall not make for yourself a carved image” (Exodus 20:4). They point the finger and accuse the Church of violating God’s word. Yet they speak without wisdom. For did not God Himself command Moses, saying, “Make an Ark of acacia wood” (Deuteronomy 10:1–5)? And did He not order that cherubim of gold be placed upon it (Exodus 25:18)?

For honor’s sake, God Himself commanded Moses: “Make an ark of acacia wood” (Deuteronomy 10:1–5). Now, after declaring, “You shall not make for yourself any carved image,” did God then command Moses to make the Ark? Did He mean that Moses should fashion idols to be worshiped? Perish the thought! The commandment was not against holy icons, but against idols, images raised for demons. To call the Ark an idol would be blasphemy, for God Himself declared, “There I will meet with you, and I will speak with you from above the mercy seat” (Exodus 25:22). Thus, the Ark was not an idol, but the dwelling of God’s glory.

Do we, in honoring holy icons, depart from the apostolic faith? By no means! Consider the apostles themselves. In the book of Acts, it is written that the sick were laid upon beds and mats in the streets, “so that even the shadow of Peter might fall upon them” (Acts 5:15). And behold, they were healed! If mere shadows shadows that pass away and leave no form could be channels of divine grace through faith, how much more the image, which clearly bears the likeness of the one depicted?

Therefore, if the faithful were healed by Peter’s shadow, shall we doubt that God, through His saints, will grant blessings when we pray before their icons in faith? But remember: faith is the key. For it is written, “Let not the one who doubts suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord” (James 1:7).

text:
From ancient times the Church was adorning her temples with sacred paintings. The walls of holy churches testifying with color the mysteries of the faith. Tradition tells us that Saint Luke the Evangelist painted the first image of the Most Holy Virgin Theotokos. This is received by others, though rejected by Protestants who cast aside the living tradition.

We also recall the holy tradition of the icon of Christ given to the King . When the king longed to behold the Lord’s face, a painter was sent. Yet Christ’s suffering covered His countenance with blood.. Then the righteous Veronica, moved with compassion, wiped His face with a cloth, and behold! His image was imprinted upon it not by human hand, but by divine power. This became the holy icon known as the Veronica's image.

The ancient Church also used symbols: the rooster, recalling Peter’s tears of repentance; the donkey, symbol of Christ’s humility; and many others.

It is also said that Saint John painted the image of the Crucifixion for Tiberius Caesar, bearing witness in the early Church to the centrality of the holy icons.showing how deep the roots of sacred art extend in our tradition.

But what of the commandment: “You shall not bow down to them or serve them” (Exodus 20:5)? Does our prostration not contradict this?

Understand, beloved: the Church does not bow to idols, nor serve them. Our prostration before the Ark, before the Cross, before the images of Christ and His saints, is not worship of wood or paint, but reverence for God and for those who bore witness to Him. God Himself commanded the making of the Ark, promising to dwell upon it.  God is not man that He should change. The prohibition was against false gods; the commandment to fashion the Ark was holy, and its reverence was commanded.

Thus, when we bow before a holy icon, our reverence ascends to Christ, to His Mother, to His saints. We distinguish holy icons from idols as day from night. For idols belong to demons, but holy icons belong to God. Idols deceive and destroy, but holy icons remind, instruct, and sanctify.

Therefore, dearly beloved, let no one confuse our holy prostrations with idolatry. We worship God alone. But we honor His saints, for they honored Him with their blood. We bow before their icons, not as idols, but as windows to heaven, ladders of remembrance, conduits of blessing.

Let us, then, with boldness of faith and without doubt, bow before the holy icons not to wood, not to color, but to Christ our Lord and to His victorious saints, whose faces shine in them. And may our prostrations be received as prayers rising to heaven.

text: Beloved children of the Orthodox faith, grace and peace be unto you in the name of our Lord. Today we continue our meditation on a question that many raise with confusion and accusation: Is a picture an idol? Let us open the eyes of our understanding, so that we may discern the truth handed down by the Church.

text.text: The Distinction Between Idols and Holy Icons

text:
An idol and a holy icon are not the same. An idol is the false god that men have fashioned in rebellion against the true God. It is the image of Satan, a counterfeit divinity before which the nations bow. But a holy picture is not fashioned for worship; it serves the worship of the living God. It is a witness to His work, and to His saints who have borne witness to His name.

The ignorant claim: “Many people think that when we bow before an image or kiss it, we are worshiping an idol. But this is a misunderstanding. Even among those outside the Church, such as those who venerate trees, it is not the wood itself they call a god, but the spirit they believe dwells within it. How then can the Church, which firmly condemns idolatry, be accused of worshiping idols? When we honor holy icons, we do not adore the wood or paint, but rather show reverence to the holy person whom the image represents.

Consider this: if one bows before an image of the Theotokos, does he say, “Blessed be this wood and paint”? No! He says, “My Lady, intercede for me.” Just as when one kisses the Book of the Gospels, he does not adore parchment and ink, but honors the living Word that dwells therein. So also when we kiss the image, we honor not the lifeless material, but Him whose image is portrayed.

text.text: The Necessity of Icons for the Faithful

text:
And what of those who cannot read?, who cannot hear the Scriptures proclaimed with understanding? Will they be cast aside? No. The Church, like a tender mother, gives them pictures, so that with their eyes they may behold the mysteries of God. text.text: The Proper Placement of Holy Icons

text:
Yet, beloved, do not handle holy things carelessly. Too many treat icons as ornaments, scattering them about their homes without reverence. But icons are sacred and should be kept in clean places. If possible, set aside a space for them; if not, gather them together in dignity, veiling them to protect them from dust.

Do not place them in profane spots, nor cram them into pockets or bags as if they were trinkets. And if an image grows old or damaged, do not cast it aside as refuse. Bring it to the Church, that it may be preserved with honor. For that which once bore the image of Christ or His saints must never be treated with contempt.

Therefore, dearly beloved, let no one deceive you by equating holy pictures with idols. Idols are demons in disguise, but icons are teachers of the faith, companions in prayer, windows into heaven. They gather the wandering mind, instruct the ignorant, and stir the heart to holiness. Handle them with reverence, and may they always lift your gaze from earth to heaven.

text: Beloved in the Lord, children of the holy Church, hear now with understanding the teaching given to us in this sacred season, the Season of Fruit. The days from Meskerem 9 to 15 are known in the Church as the Season of Fruit. It is not by accident that the Fathers of the Church named this time so, for the visible creation itself preaches a hidden mystery. The earth, in these days, adorns herself with harvest: crops ripen, trees bend under their burden, seeds fall to the ground, and beasts of the field feed from them. Yet beneath the veil of plants and fruits lies a lesson for the soul, teaching us how we too are called to bear fruit worthy of eternal life.

The Season of Fruit is the time when plants sprout, blossom, and yield their harvest, when mankind, cattle, and even the wild beasts are nourished by the bounty of the earth. In the same way, the Church in these days feeds the faithful with sermons and teachings that unfold this mystery, showing us that all visible things preach to us the invisible.

The fathers divide plants into three types:

Those peeled by a fingernail, like the lemon, the banana, the taro.

Those reaped with a sickle, such as wheat, teff, barley.

Those cut down with a scythe, like the olive, the warka, the wanza, the cedar.

Their nature, like our own, is composed of the four elements: wind, fire, water, and earth.
 
Because they are created from the wind, they blossom in the wind and bring forth fruit.

Because they are created from fire, some of them give off fire when struck against one another.

Because they are created from water, they produce moisture and sap.

Because they are created from earth, when they are cut down they decay and return to the soil.

In the same way their fruits differ:

Some produce in themselves (wheat, barley, teff).

Some on their sides (sorghum, corn, beans).

Some within their belly (pumpkin, squash).

Some by their toil beneath the soil (onion, radish, carrot, potato).

Thus the Church interprets Genesis 1:6–13, showing that every form of growth is an image of spiritual truth.

For the Scriptures compare man to plants:

The swiftness of man is likened to the speed of the wind.

The anger of man is likened to the fire .

The steadiness of man is likened to the calmness of water.

The end of man is likened to the patience and mortality of the earth.

And as the seed must rot to bring forth fruit, so man must die to be raised incorruptible. Hear the Apostle Paul: “It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body” (1 Cor. 15:42–44).

As not every plant produces equally, so not every believer shines with the same conduct. Some are barren, some produce little, some produce abundantly. Fruit is the image of good works and of eternal reward. Many live carelessly in sin, some struggle toward virtue, and few, like fathers and mothers in holiness, persevere to great excellence.

Saint Paul exhorts: “He who sows sparingly will reap sparingly, and he who sows bountifully will reap bountifully” (2 Cor. 9:6–10). The farmer reaps what he sows; so also each of us shall receive according to our works. The Apostle James adds: “Be patient, brethren, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient until he receives the early and latter rain. You also be patient; establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand” (Jas. 5:7–8).

text:
When David cries, “The earth has yielded her fruit” (Ps. 66:6; 84:12), the fathers interpret:

Earth means Jerusalem, the Church, the faithful, or even our Lady.

Fruit is the Word of God, the worship of God, and most especially our Lord Jesus Christ.

For from the earth meaning the Virgin Mary the Fruit of life, Christ Himself, was brought forth. Therefore daily we echo the angel’s words: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Lk. 1:28).

Christ Himself taught by seeds: some fall by the road and are snatched away; some spring up on rocky ground but wither for lack of roots; some are choked by thorns; and some fall on good soil, yielding thirty, sixty, or a hundredfold. So is every soul that hears the Word. The careless hear but do not understand; the shallow rejoice but fall in trial; the worldly are smothered by riches and cares; but the faithful keep the Word, live it, and abound in every good work. (Matt. 13:1–23).

The hundredfold are martyrs, offering their lives.

The sixtyfold are monks, renouncing the world.

The thirtyfold are lay believers who live righteously in the world.

Each has his measure, yet each is precious, for the Lord crowns not the number but the faithfulness.

But as useless plants are cut down and burned, so every unfruitful Christian faces judgment. “The axe is laid to the root of the trees; every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. 3:10). Let us therefore take heed, for hell awaits the barren soul.

text.text: Growing as the Seed of Christ

text:
The seed grows in stages: in itself, in its sides, in its inner life, and in its labor. So must we:

Grow in fear of God within ourselves.

Support one another in love.

Keep purity inwardly.

Walk in humility outwardly.

Just as plants bring forth fruit in due season, so must we hasten to bring forth righteousness: first in small beginnings, then in greater works, and finally in perfection. The Christian is seed sown by Christ in the good soil of His Church; we must not waste such a gift but grow into heirs of the Kingdom.

The Season of Fruit is not a mere calendar mark, but a summons: to remember that we are seeds, planted in the soil of faith, watered by the Word, nourished by the Spirit, and destined for harvest. Some will be thirtyfold, some sixty, some a hundred but woe to the barren. May God grant that we pass through these stages and, at the end, be gathered as good wheat into His eternal barns.

Continued 👇🏾

The Fruit of the Earth

When David cries, “The earth has yielded her fruit” (Ps. 66:6; 84:12), the fathers interpret:

Earth means Jerusalem, the Church, the faithful, or even our Lady.

Fruit is the Word of God, the worship of God, and most especially our Lord Jesus Christ.

For from the earth meaning the Virgin Mary the Fruit of life, Christ Himself, was brought forth. Therefore daily we echo the angel’s words: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Lk. 1:28).

Christ Himself taught by seeds: some fall by the road and are snatched away; some spring up on rocky ground but wither for lack of roots; some are choked by thorns; and some fall on good soil, yielding thirty, sixty, or a hundredfold. So is every soul that hears the Word. The careless hear but do not understand; the shallow rejoice but fall in trial; the worldly are smothered by riches and cares; but the faithful keep the Word, live it, and abound in every good work. (Matt. 13:1–23).

The Fathers explain the mystery:

The hundredfold are martyrs, offering their lives.

The sixtyfold are monks, renouncing the world.

The thirtyfold are lay believers who live righteously in the world.

Each has his measure, yet each is precious, for the Lord crowns not the number but the faithfulness.

The Warning of Barren Trees

But as useless plants are cut down and burned, so every unfruitful Christian faces judgment. “The axe is laid to the root of the trees; every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. 3:10). Let us therefore take heed, for hell awaits the barren soul.

Growing as the Seed of Christ

The seed grows in stages: in itself, in its sides, in its inner life, and in its labor. So must we:

Grow in fear of God within ourselves.

Support one another in love.

Keep purity inwardly.

Walk in humility outwardly.

Just as plants bring forth fruit in due season, so must we hasten to bring forth righteousness: first in small beginnings, then in greater works, and finally in perfection. The Christian is seed sown by Christ in the good soil of His Church; we must not waste such a gift but grow into heirs of the Kingdom.

Conclusion

The Season of Fruit is not a mere calendar mark, but a summons: to remember that we are seeds, planted in the soil of faith, watered by the Word, nourished by the Spirit, and destined for harvest. Some will be thirtyfold, some sixty, some a hundred but woe to the barren. May God grant that we pass through these stages and, at the end, be gathered as good wheat into His eternal barns.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.

text: Beloved, hear the wisdom of the Scriptures and the tradition of the holy Church. For the matter of sacred images is not a thing invented by man’s imagination, nor the vain carving of wood and stone. It is rooted in the divine command, shown forth in the Law and the Prophets, and confirmed by the Holy Fathers in council.

text.text: The Origin of Sacred Images in Scripture

text:
From the earliest days, the Lord Himself instructed His servants to fashion images for His glory. Did He not say to His prophet Ezekiel: “And you, son of man, take a brick and lay it before you, and draw a picture of the city of Jerusalem, and surround it” (Ezekiel 4:1)? By this command, God Himself set forth the use of representation for instruction and remembrance.

When the Ark of the Covenant was made, God commanded Moses: “And you shall make one cherub on one side of the mercy seat, and another cherub on the other side… and their wings shall overshadow the mercy seat” (Exodus 25). These were not idols, but living witnesses carved in form, proclaiming that the God who cannot be seen nevertheless allows His servants to use images as shadows and signs of heavenly mysteries.

Likewise, in the building of Solomon’s Temple, two mighty cherubim of olive wood, each ten cubits high, were set within the Most Holy Place. Their wings stretched from one wall to another, touching in the midst, covered with gold, and surrounded with palm trees and blossoms (1 Kings 6:23–29).Here we see that even divine worship in ancient times included sacred imagery, not as objects of worship themselves, but as vessels of remembrance and instruction.

text.text: Sacred Images in the Early Church

text:
From the beginning, Christians followed this example. In caves and hidden places, they painted the stories of Scripture, showing forth the lives of the saints, the martyrs, and the mighty works of God. By these images, the faithful were instructed and the memory of the righteous preserved.

By the eighth century, a dispute arose among Christians over the use of holy icons. Two extremes appeared:

Iconolatry: those who revered images excessively, treating them almost as gods.

Iconomachy: those who rejected images entirely, wishing to remove them from worship.

The conflict continued until the Second Council of Nicaea in 787,To heal this wound, the Holy Spirit gathered the Fathers at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787. There it was declared that holy icons are to be kept, honored. The images of Christ, the Theotokos, angels, prophets, apostles, martyrs, and righteous people are to be honored, not worshipped, as they reveal God’s glory (Pillar of Faith, ch. 13).

Holy icons are not made at random, nor according to the vain imaginations of men. They are painted by those called by God, following the canonical order of the Church. Tradition holds that the first image of the Crucifixion of Christ was painted by the holy Evangelist John himself for Emperor Tiberius.

The making of an image begins in prayer. The artist, before laying down even a single line, implores God for wisdom and grace. For it is not mere skill but divine gift that fashions a true holy icon.

Even the colors are chosen not by whim, but by sacred meaning:
symbolizes the blood of martyrdom, the struggle and sacrifice of the saints.
proclaims purity and resurrection, fitting for Christ risen and for the Virgin taken up in glory.

declares the eternal divinity of God, seen in the image of the Holy Trinity.

The size of an icon may vary small for prayer books, grand for the walls of a temple but in every place it must be treated with reverence.

text:
Peace be upon you, my child.  Your question delves into the very heart of Christian life – forgiveness, a virtue often misunderstood and challenging to practice, particularly in the face of deep hurt, like infidelity.  You ask about the balance between forgiveness and consequences, a tension that has wrestled with the faithful for centuries.

The Lord's Prayer itself instructs us to ask God to "forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us" (Matthew 6:12, Luke 11:4).  This suggests a reciprocity, a mirroring of divine forgiveness.  Just as God forgives us, not by eliminating the consequences of sin (sickness, death entered the world through sin), but by offering redemption and healing, so too should we forgive.

Christ's parable of the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:23-35) powerfully illustrates this.  The king forgave an immense debt, yet the servant refused to forgive a much smaller debt owed to him.  This highlights the disproportionate mercy we receive from God and the expectation that we extend similar mercy to others.  The parable does not, however, negate the justice of the king's final punishment.  The unforgiving servant faced consequences for his hard-heartedness.

Forgiveness, in the true Christian sense, is not condoning the sin. It is not forgetting or pretending it didn't happen.  Rather, it is releasing the grip of anger and resentment, a conscious decision to let go of the desire for revenge or retribution.  This is for our own spiritual healing, as much as for the other person.  St. John Chrysostom, in his homilies on Matthew, speaks eloquently about how harboring anger harms us more than the person who wronged us.

Regarding consequences, these are often necessary for growth and repentance.  In the case of infidelity, requesting therapy, setting boundaries, or even choosing separation can be acts of love – both for oneself and the offending spouse.  These actions are not antithetical to forgiveness; they can be part of the healing process.  Think of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11-32). The father embraced his returning son with boundless love (forgiveness), but the son still experienced the consequences of his actions – the loss of his inheritance, the hardship he endured.  This experience ultimately led to his repentance and restoration.

Conditional forgiveness, in the sense of withholding inner forgiveness until certain conditions are met, can be a slippery slope.  It risks becoming a tool of manipulation.  However, setting boundaries and expectations for reconciliation is not inherently wrong. It's an act of wisdom, reflecting a commitment to the health and integrity of the relationship.  Just as a physician prescribes medicine for healing, so too can we encourage steps towards repentance and restoration.

Therefore, my child, strive for genuine forgiveness – releasing the bitterness and anger.  Simultaneously, recognize the wisdom in setting boundaries and seeking appropriate help, such as counseling from a priest or therapist. These are not mutually exclusive; they can work together to bring healing and, God willing, reconciliation.  

Remember the words of St. Isaac the Syrian, "He who has not tasted the sweetness of forgiveness has not tasted the goodness of God."  Pray for the strength to forgive, and for wisdom to discern the path forward.  I will continue to pray for you as well.  Please do not hesitate to return and share your progress.  May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

text: Beloved children of the holy Church, who desire to worship God in spirit and in truth, let us now turn our attention to the question of holy icons. For many have stumbled here, taking into their hands what is foreign to the Orthodox tradition, and in so doing, they dishonor both the faith and the mysteries of God.

text.text: On Images Outside the Orthodox Church

text: In many lands, especially in the West, there have arisen images that do not belong to the order of the Eastern Orthodox Church. These images, though they may appear beautiful to the eyes of men, are in fact alien to the order of the fathers. Among these, we see depictions of Christ our God being sold with the hand raised in a two-fingers. But we, the children of the Church, have received another tradition: the one-fingered image, which confesses the mystery of the unity of the divine and human natures in Christ. For in Him are two natures, yet one Lord; two realities, yet one Person. The holy icons make this known, not by accident, but by the deliberate witness of the Church. Whoever neglects this is careless with the faith, for a false image can breed a false understanding in the heart.

text.text: On the Authority of the First Images

text: Therefore, let us cleave to the images that we have inherited from the beginning, those that the fathers have received and handed down. When questions arise, let us not rely on private imagination, but seek the wisdom of priests and scholars, for they are stewards of the mysteries of God.

text.text: On the Relationship Between Icon and Representation

text: Know also, brethren, that in order to understand any painting, there must be a harmony between the painter and the subject represented. For what is an icon, if not a mirror of its owner? It may bear likeness through movement, appearance, shape, color, or even the message it conveys. But unless we know when it was painted, by whom it was painted, and for whom it was painted, we risk falling into error. Many false judgments arise when men seize an image without first discerning its meaning.

let us take the example of the letter “H.” Though it appears the same in form, its sound differs among peoples: for Ethiopians it bears one sound, for the English another, and for the Russians yet another. Here we see that a single written sign may not always carry the same voice or meaning.

Thus, if an Englishman were to stand before a chart of the holy Geʿez letters and declare, “This is H,” he would fall into error. For the sacred letters of Geʿez are not to be defined merely by outward appearance, nor by foreign naming, but by the true sound and meaning given to them.

Therefore, before we hasten to place a label upon any letter or image, we must understand its meaning. Without meaning, the sign is empty; but with meaning rightly discerned, the sign becomes full of truth and light.

Think also of the rainbow. To us Christians, it is the covenant God made with Noah, and it also signifies the beauty of the Mother of God. But in other places, the rainbow has been claimed for wickedness, as the mark of those who imitate the sins of Sodom. Does this mean that a Christian wearing rainbow colors has abandoned Christ? No. It means only that men interpret signs according to their hearts.

Even the holy Cross itself testifies to this. For Saint Paul declared that to those who believe, it is salvation, but to those who perish, it is foolishness. To us it is life, but to the Romans it was once the instrument of death. Thus it is plain that the same image bears contrary meanings depending on the eyes that behold it.

For in Him are two natures, yet one Lord; two realities, yet one Person. The holy icons make this known, not by accident, but by the deliberate witness of the Church. On the Authority of the First Images

Therefore, let us cleave to the images that we have inherited from the beginning, those that the fathers have received and handed down. When questions arise, let us not rely on private imagination, but seek the wisdom of priests and scholars, for they are stewards of the mysteries of God.
On the Relationship Between Icon and Representation

Know also, brethren, that in order to understand any painting, there must be a harmony between the painter and the subject represented. For what is an icon, if not a mirror of its owner? It may bear likeness through movement, appearance, shape, color, or even the message it conveys. But unless we know when it was painted, by whom it was painted, and for whom it was painted, we risk falling into error. Many false judgments arise when men seize an image without first discerning its meaning.

let us take the example of the letter “H.” Though it appears the same in form, its sound differs among peoples: for Ethiopians it bears one sound, for the English another, and for the Russians yet another. Here we see that a single written sign may not always carry the same voice or meaning.

Thus, if an Englishman were to stand before a chart of the holy Geʿez letters and declare, “This is H,” he would fall into error. For the sacred letters of Geʿez are not to be defined merely by outward appearance, nor by foreign naming, but by the true sound and meaning given to them.

Therefore, before we hasten to place a label upon any letter or image, we must understand its meaning. Without meaning, the sign is empty; but with meaning rightly discerned, the sign becomes full of truth and light.

Think also of the rainbow. To us Christians, it is the covenant God made with Noah, and it also signifies the beauty of the Mother of God. But in other places, the rainbow has been claimed for wickedness, as the mark of those who imitate the sins of Sodom. Does this mean that a Christian wearing rainbow colors has abandoned Christ? To us it is life, but to the Romans it was once the instrument of death. Thus it is plain that the same image bears contrary meanings depending on the eyes that behold it.

text.text: On the Temptations of Holy Pictures

text: The Church has always known the correct way to depict the Mother of God and the saints. Yet in every age temptations arise, and strange pictures enter among the faithful. Without realizing it, some have violated the order of the Church by adopting these alien forms. It caused the faithful, through lack of understanding, to oppose the order of the Church.

Therefore, let us, the children of Tewahedo, approach the Church with humility and use only those pictures that faithfully express her teaching. By doing so, we safeguard the holy tradition, we strengthen the bond of the Church, and we keep for ourselves the blessing of true worship. To bring into the house of God what is foreign is to invite confusion, but to preserve what is ours is to walk in the path of the fathers.

Let us, then, lift up praise: to God who grants wisdom, to the Virgin Mother who intercedes for us, and to the Cross that shines with glory and victory.

Beloved, holy icons are not decorations but confessions of faith. If we follow what the Church has given, we honor Christ and His saints; if we borrow what is foreign, we bring confusion into our souls. Let us keep the icons handed down to us, guard them with reverence, and through them behold the mystery of God.

Misle Fkur Welda"( ምስለ ፍቁር ወልዳ ሥዕል )

text: Beloved in Christ, heirs of the apostolic faith, let us speak of the holy icon of Our Lady, the Virgin Mother of God, as she appears in the paintings treasured by the Orthodox Church, and especially in the tradition of Fiqur Wolda. These images are not idle ornaments, nor are they vain embellishments. They are sermons in color and form, sacraments in paint, which instruct the faithful and remind the soul of divine mysteries.
In many sacred depictions, Our Lady wears a crown. This crown is rich in meaning, encompassing both earthly imagery and heavenly truth:

text.text: 1. The Crown of Martyrdom and Suffering

text: The crown upon her head signifies the suffering she willingly bore for Christ. From christ conception until the end of her earthly life, Mary embraced the trials of this world, enduring them with perfect love and grace. For this reason, she is rightly called Mother of Martyrs, a model of steadfastness and sacrificial devotion for all who suffer for the sake of the Lord.

Beyond this, the crown testifies that she is the Mother of the King of Kings, the Savior of the world. Chosen by God, she is appointed Queen, as prophesied by Saint David: “The queen shall stand at your right hand” (Psalm 44:4). Yet, let it be noted that this queenship is not an earthly or political glory, but the recognition of her holiness, humility, and service in God’s plan.

text.text: The Symbolism of Color and Garments

text:
The garments painted upon the Even the types of clothing we see in her paintings are symbolic, not true representations of what Our Lady actually wore during her life."
Among them, the blue robe is most radiant:

It signifies her humility, the most precious jewel of her soul.
: Blue reflects the serene and humble disposition of Our Lady.
: Just as the Ark carried God’s presence, Mary became the dwelling of God Incarnate (Numbers 4:6–12, Exodus 28:31).
Blue recalls the firmament and the rising sun, symbolic of Christ’s glory appearing in her (Malachi 4:2, Matthew 17:2).
, once a precious and rare dye, became known as Mary’s dress in our tradition not to indicate literal clothing, but to signify her sacred and exalted role.

text.text: Crowns of the Saints and Our Lord

text:
It is important to distinguish between earthly and divine crowns. Our Lord Jesus Christ, eternal King, is not crowned like human kings. The crown of thorns He bore, however, reminds us of His suffering for humankind.

Similarly, the crowns of saints signify their crowns of righteousness and life, granted by God in reward for their struggles and steadfastness in Christ (James 1:12, Revelation 2:10). These crowns, therefore, are spiritual symbols of victory, not earthly adornments.

text.text: The Ethiopian Tradition and the Angels

text: In the tradition of the Ethiopian Church, the holy icon of Our Lady of Fiqur Wolda is only considered complete when the angels stand beside her. Saint Michael and Saint Gabriel, guardians of the mystery, are painted at her left and right. For the Queen of Heaven does not appear in isolation, but is surrounded by the heavenly host, honored by those spirits who never cease to minister before the throne of God.

But take heed, beloved, not every image that bears the Virgin’s likeness follows the canons of the fathers. Some paintings on the market or hanging in temples are borrowed from foreign traditions: Greek, Russian, or Catholic, born not of Ethiopian soil but of other lands. These, though beautiful, do not always reflect the fullness of our own Church’s inheritance. The very reform of art in our history has led to a forgetting of the old ways, and so the Byzantine Nazarene style has sometimes replaced the Ethiopian hand.

Therefore, when you gaze upon the image of Our Lady crowned, do not look with fleshly eyes only. See the martyr’s crown of her suffering, the Queen’s crown of her exaltation. Read in the blue garment her humility, her dwelling as the Ark, her likeness to heaven itself. Remember that her Son wears no royal diadem but the crown of thorns, and that the saints are crowned by His gift. And let the angels, Michael and Gabriel, remind you that she stands not alone but as Queen amidst the heavenly court.

text:
Hello, 

I was wondering why girls aren’t allowed to go inside the church when they are on their periods? A question was asked & I wasn’t sure what the church’s teaching on this is. 

Thank you 🙏🏾

👉

፦ Peace and grace be multiplied unto you, beloved in Christ.

You ask well, for to seek understanding is itself a fragrant offering before God. Many stumble here, imagining that the Church despises womanhood, or that the natural courses of the body are sin. Far be it! He who fashioned Eve from Adam's side and took flesh from the womb of the Virgin would never call His own handiwork defiled. "All that God created is very good," says the Scripture (Genesis 1:31).

Why then this ancient restraint? The fathers teach us that it is not a sentence of guilt, but a hedge of reverence. From of old, the spilling of human blood - whether from a wound or the hidden chamber of nature - has been kept apart from the holy place. For within the sanctuary is poured only the Blood of the Lamb, which alone takes away the sin of the world. The law of Moses foreshadowed this mystery; Christ fulfilled it. Yet the Church, like a wise mother, preserves the sign so that our hearts may never grow careless before the dread and life-giving Mysteries.

Mark this well: the woman in her days is not exiled from God. Let her pray in her chamber, let her lift her heart like incense, let her read the divine Scriptures and call on the Name above every name. Only let her refrain, for a little while, from crossing the threshold where the Blood of Christ speaks more loudly than all earthly blood. This is no reproach but a schooling in awe, that all of us - men and women, whole and wounded - may learn that the House of God is heaven upon earth.

Therefore, my child, receive this ordinance not as a yoke of shame but as a reminder of the majesty of Him who sanctifies both body and soul. When the appointed days are past, enter again with joy, and know that the Lord who fashioned you is never far from those who seek Him in purity of heart.

፦ My dear sister in Christ,

You speak with pain, yet with a searching and discerning heart. Your reference to Scripture reveals a love for truth over appearances, which is good and pleasing to God. However, the Church teaches us to examine our own soul before focusing on others not because your suffering is your fault, but because salvation begins with, “Lord, have mercy on me, the sinner.”

St. John Chrysostom, calls marriage “a little Church” and advises: “Correct yourself first, and then your household will be corrected.” Before addressing your husband’s hypocrisy, quietly reflect:

1. Have I allowed bitterness to take root?

2. Do I pray for his repentance with tears, or do I mostly accuse him in my heart?

3. Do I speak to him to win arguments or to heal?

4. Have I sought my father confessor’s counsel, bringing my wounds to Christ’s light?

This is not to excuse his sins but to protect your soul, ensuring his failings don’t become yours.

You’ve rightly identified questions a deacon or any Christian man must face. Scripture is clear:

1. If he stands at the altar but despises the one flesh God joined to him, his prayers are hindered (1 Peter 3:7).

2. If he offers incense while unreconciled with his wife, the Lord says, “Leave the gift and be reconciled first” (Matt. 5:23-24).

3. St. Chrysostom warns that a man who adorns the Church but neglects his wife “has overturned the very altar of his own house.”

Such service, without humility at home, risks becoming empty ritual.
: Bring your struggle to a trusted confessor. This ensures obedience and protects you from mere complaint.
Pray the Jesus Prayer for yourself and your husband by name, asking Christ to soften both hearts.

In peaceful moments, speak simply, without accusation: “My heart is hurt. I need us to pray and seek forgiveness together.”
Boundaries with Love: If his words become abusive or threatening, know that the Church does not bless silence in the face of harm. Seeking help honors the image of God in you and your children.

1. You cannot save him through arguments; only Christ can pierce the heart.

2. Your salvation is not bound to his hypocrisy. Your humility, prayer, and patience free of self-condemnation are precious to God.

3. A deacon can deceive himself like a Pharisee, but you must not let his blindness draw you into darkness.

Stand before Christ, confess your sins, keep your heart free of hatred, and pray for light to reach your husband. This is the Orthodox way: repentance beginning with oneself and love that neither excuses sin nor assumes judgment, but entrusts it to God.

text: Beloved in Christ, children of the one holy and apostolic Church, let us turn our hearts to the mystery of the Cross and to the great feast which has been delivered to us by the fathers: the Feast of the Finding of the Cross and the Demera celebration. It is not an empty tradition nor a mere spectacle of fire and incense, but a remembrance of the very power by which death was slain and life was given to the world.

Among the nine great feasts of the Lord, the Feast of the Cross shines with peculiar brightness. Every year, on the seventeenth of Meskerem and in the tenth of Megabit , the faithful in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church gather to magnify the triumph of the life-giving cross. This is not a feast limited to the Church alone, but one that has overflowed into the life of nations. From ancient times until today, the Feast of the Cross has been honored by Christians, respected by those of other faiths, and even recognized by governments. In our day, the Demera Festival itself has been inscribed in the annals of UNESCO’s world heritage, so that what the Church has long revered is now declared by the world as a treasure of humanity.

text.text: The History and Mystery of the Cross

text:
The origins of this feast go back to the days of Saint Eleni, mother of the great Emperor Constantine. Though born of Jewish descent and once joined to a pagan king, Eleni received the call of God and became the instrument chosen to restore to the Church the most holy relic of our salvation: the Cross of the Lord.

For that Cross, upon which the Lord of Glory was hung in shame, became the wellspring of miracles. It healed the sick, opened the eyes of the blind, cleansed the lepers, strengthened the lame, and cast out the demons. Through it, Christ displayed His power, so that both Jew and Gentile might behold His mercy. Yet envy darkened the hearts of those who crucified Him, and they sought to bury the Cross in obscurity. They cast it into a place of refuse, heaping upon it filth and earth, disguising its location with the crosses of the two thieves, so that men might not distinguish it. Over years it became covered, hidden beneath a great mountain.

Although no one had the authority or ability to recover the Cross, many Christians and devout believers in the region knew the exact place where it was buried. However, after the birth of our Lord, in the year 70 AD, when King Titos invaded, Jerusalem and the surrounding lands were destroyed, and a great massacre was carried out against the people. As a result, it became impossible to determine the location of the Cross.

For this reason, though many faithful servants of God were grieved over the burial of the Cross, they were powerless to recover it, and it remained hidden in the earth for more than thirty years.

In the year 327, Queen Eleni, aflame with faith and prayer, resolved to recover the Cross. She begged the Lord for the conversion of her son, Constantine, who had been born to a pagan mother, and she prayed  to uncover the Lord’s instrument of salvation.

After Queen Eleni arrived in Jerusalem, she sought to uncover the hill or mountain where she believed the Holy Cross was buried, according to the history she had learned beforehand. Yet her efforts bore no fruit, for she could not find it. She also questioned the Jews living in the area, but none would reveal the truth to her. Therefore, with steadfast faith, she turned continually to God in fervent and special prayer. 

In the end, because the revelation of the Cross was God’s will, an old man named Kirakos, who lived in a cave, saw the queen’s weariness and spoke to her with wisdom: “Do not grow weary in vain. Gather much wood, place incense upon it, and set it aflame. When the smoke rises to heaven and bends down to earth, it will show the place of the Cross.” The queen obeyed his counsel, and by her faith and prayer the mystery was revealed.
