text:
Thus it was done. With prayer and reverence the demera was kindled. The fire blazed, and the smoke rose heavenward like the prayers of the saints. Then, bowing down from the sky, the smoke stretched forth its hand, as it were, and rested upon the place where the Cross was buried. At this, the words of Saint Yared resounded in truth: “The incense rose up; the smoke bowed to the ground; the wooden cross that the Jews buried at Golgotha was found today.”

Queen Eleni began her labor on Meskerem 17, and by God’s providence, on the tenth day of Megabit, the Cross was uncovered. From that moment, the world rejoiced. For this reason, every year on the eve of Meskerem 16, the faithful light torches and pile wood into great pyres, re-enacting that holy revelation. This is the Demera: the fire that marks the path to the Cross, the smoke that witnesses to God’s guidance, the flame that burns away doubt and leads us to the cross of life.

This feast, Demera Beal, is kept in every town and village, with crosses raised .Believers gather in procession, chanting the ancient hymns such as "Eyoha Abebaye Meskerem Tebaye" , their voices mingling with the crackling fire and the fragrance of incense. Even in Addis Ababa, at the great Meskel Square, the celebration fills the eyes of the world with awe. Pilgrims and tourists alike come to witness, though not all understand the mystery. Some celebrate with pure hearts, others in ways estranged from the sacred meaning. Yet the Cross itself endures, drawing friend and foe alike to stand in its shadow.

For the Cross is triumph. Though enemies of the Cross persist, they cannot quench the flame of this feast, nor silence the praise that rises from Ethiopia to the ends of the earth.

Therefore, beloved, when we keep the Feast of the Cross and the Demera, let us not regard it as mere tradition or spectacle, but as a living testimony of God’s power. The Cross once hidden beneath refuse now shines with eternal glory. The fire of Demera reminds us that what was lost has been found, what was buried has been raised, and what was despised has become our boast.

text.text: 1. Scriptural Foundation for the Adoration of the Cross

text: The holy Psalmist David declares: “We bow to the place where His feet stood” (Ps. 131:7). If even the ground upon which the Lord set His feet is worthy of reverence, then the Cross on which His entire body was stretched and His blood poured out is infinitely more deserving of honor.

Our Orthodox Church instructs us in the hymn of the Fasting Dgwa: “We worship Your Cross, O Lord, and we glorify You.” This is not poetry only, but doctrine, for the Cross is the very means of salvation. It is exalted in every prayer, every liturgy, and every divine service. There is no act of worship in the Church where the Cross is absent.

The Cross is revered because it bore the sacred body of Christ. Upon it He was nailed, upon it His blood was shed, and upon it He triumphed over sin and death. Thus, the Cross is not mere wood, but sanctified by His Passion, transformed into the sign of victory, the banner of salvation, and the seal of the faithful.

text.text: 4. The Liturgical Celebration of the Cross

text: The Church celebrates the Cross with two great annual feasts: Megabit 10 and Meskerem 17. Yet beyond these days, the Cross is remembered continually. It is honored every day and every hour, woven into the very life of worship, the rhythm of prayer, and the heart of the faithful.

Saint Yared proclaims: “On this day, the feast of the Cross shines in heaven and on earth, it shines for the nations and for the whole world, bringing peace and joy. Let it always be praised!” The feast is not local but cosmic, celebrated in heaven and on earth alike, declaring Christ’s triumph to all creation.

When we bow to the Cross, we do not adore wood but the mystery it carries the sacrifice of Christ, the triumph of His death, and the power that crushed the devil. To venerate the Cross is to confess the Gospel in its fullest expression: Christ crucified, risen, and glorified.

Beloved, let us remain steadfast in our love for the Cross, honoring it not with lips only but with lives shaped by its power. May God grant us to understand its meaning, to love its mystery, and to inherit the kingdom prepared for those who remain faithful in His house. Amen.

👉🏾👉🏾👉🏾Does the Holy #Cross Deserve #Adoration?

1. Scriptural Foundation for the Adoration of the Cross

The holy Psalmist David declares: “We bow to the place where His feet stood” (Ps. 131:7). If even the ground upon which the Lord set His feet is worthy of reverence, then the Cross on which His entire body was stretched and His blood poured out is infinitely more deserving of honor.

2. The Teaching of the Church

Our Orthodox Church instructs us in the hymn of the Fasting Dgwa: “We worship Your Cross, O Lord, and we glorify You.” This is not poetry only, but doctrine, for the Cross is the very means of salvation. It is exalted in every prayer, every liturgy, and every divine service. There is no act of worship in the Church where the Cross is absent.

3. Why the Cross Is Honored

The Cross is revered because it bore the sacred body of Christ. Upon it He was nailed, upon it His blood was shed, and upon it He triumphed over sin and death. Thus, the Cross is not mere wood, but sanctified by His Passion, transformed into the sign of victory, the banner of salvation, and the seal of the faithful.

4. The Liturgical Celebration of the Cross

The Church celebrates the Cross with two great annual feasts: Megabit 10 and Meskerem 17. Yet beyond these days, the Cross is remembered continually. It is honored every day and every hour, woven into the very life of worship, the rhythm of prayer, and the heart of the faithful.

5. The Testimony of Saint Yared

Saint Yared proclaims: “On this day, the feast of the Cross shines in heaven and on earth, it shines for the nations and for the whole world, bringing peace and joy. Let it always be praised!” The feast is not local but cosmic, celebrated in heaven and on earth alike, declaring Christ’s triumph to all creation.

6. The Meaning of Our Adoration

When we bow to the Cross, we do not adore wood but the mystery it carries the sacrifice of Christ, the triumph of His death, and the power that crushed the devil. To venerate the Cross is to confess the Gospel in its fullest expression: Christ crucified, risen, and glorified.

7. Conclusion and Prayer

Beloved, let us remain steadfast in our love for the Cross, honoring it not with lips only but with lives shaped by its power. May God grant us to understand its meaning, to love its mystery, and to inherit the kingdom prepared for those who remain faithful in His house. Amen.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

text: Beloved in Christ, hear and learn with reverence the mystery handed down concerning the depiction of the Virgin Mother in holy icons. For the icons of the Church are not idle paintings nor lifeless artistry, but symbols of the divine economy of salvation. Through them, truth is preached without words, and the eyes of the faithful are lifted upward to the heavenly realities.

text.text: 1. The Angelic Witnesses in the Icon

text: When the Virgin is painted, she is not alone. When the holy icon portrays the Virgin, there stand also the great archangels. Behold Saint Michael, who holds the spear with which our Lord was pierced and the rod dipped in gall; behold Saint Gabriel, bearing the cross of three sides, a cross known to the Russian Church, though foreign to the ancient custom of Ethiopia. The Greek inscriptions upon these images likewise testify that these forms are not of the Ethiopian tradition.

text.text: 2. The Position of the Virgin: Right or Left?

text: The faithful have long asked: should Our Lady be shown on the right or left of Christ? Both are seen in the holy icons.

text.text: Why Our Lady Is Depicted on the Right

text:
The holy psalmist spoke long before the birth of Christ, declaring: “The queen shall stand at your right hand” (Psalm 44:4). In this prophecy, the Church sees the Virgin Mother, who bore the King of Glory. For this reason, iconographers often place her holding the Lord in her left arm, so that she may stand at His right hand. Since the 17th century, this orientation has become common, spreading so widely that many forgot there were other ways.

Yet some have judged wrongly, saying the other position is an error. But wisdom teaches otherwise. If she is painted holding the Lord on her right arm, then indeed she appears on His left but this does not diminish her honor. For whether right or left in the painting, her place remains the same in the mystery: the Mother beside her Son, the Queen beside her King.

text.text: Why Our Lady Is Depicted on the Left

text:
The holy painters who set the Virgin upon the left do not act without reason, but with wisdom drawn from the life of every mother. For what mother holds her child always on one side only? At times she carries him on her right, at times on her left. And when she nourishes him, she offers both breasts; to deny this would be to deny her very motherhood. Shall we then say that Christ, who grew strong on the miraculous milk of His Mother, was not also fed from her right breast? God forbid! For the milk of both breasts testifies that the Virgin is truly His Mother, and even now that her 2 breast pure milk stands as witness when she intercedes before her Son.

Moreover, the Scripture that speaks of “the queen at your right hand” (Psalm 44) is not bound to the direction of the body. The right hand is not merely a side, but a sign of honor and glory. Therefore, whether painted on the left or on the right, the Virgin’s mystery is unchanged. As the interpreters teach, David’s words also mean this: “She shall stand firm in the honor you have given her.”

text.text: 3. The Meaning of the Hand and the Fingers

text: : By extending two fingers, the Virgin bears witness that she is virgin in both soul and body, a complete virgin in the kingdom.

: When the Lord extends one finger, it proclaims the unity of God, the One to whom alone worship belongs. When two fingers are shown, it speaks of His two births: begotten of the Father before all ages, and born from Virgin Mary without father.

His hand often points toward the star on the Virgin’s shoulder, the same star that guided the wise men.

text.text: 4. The Star and the prophecy Story

text: The star recalls the prophecy fulfilled when the wise came from the East. Their father, the philosopher Jeredshet, had once seen an icon of the Virgin with her Child while studying near the Nek-a may( ነቅዓ ማይ ). He carved it, and at his death instructed them to seek the heavenly King when a star rose. So it was that they found the Child with His Mother, as written in Matthew 2:11, and offered gifts. Thus the Virgin becomes the sign of the New Covenant, given to us as Mother.

Why is she shown holding a mitre? It is the symbol of her royalty and honor. It recalls her blessing at Debre Mittimaq and her witness before Thomas and the fathers who bore the cross. Though artists vary the size and form of the mitre, its meaning endures: majesty and blessing.

text.text: 6. The Veil and the Artist’s Hand

text: The mehareb or veil has its place in the icon, though its full meaning is not always disclosed. In such matters the artist is free to shape the image according to the tradition received, without forcing interpretations where none were intended. The image is a symbol.

Whether with crown or without, the Virgin is shown as Queen beside her Son. She is His throne, His Mother, His intercessor. The icon declares her steadfast glory, her maternal love, and her royal dignity. No detail diminishes the greater truth: that she bore God in her womb, and through her the New Covenant was given to mankind.

text: Beloved in Christ, today we reflect upon the mystery of the Holy Cross, that wood sanctified by the Blood of God Himself, by which heaven was opened, hell was shaken, and death was crushed. The Cross is not mere wood, nor a carved shape, but the throne of love, the altar of sacrifice, and the sign of victory. It is rightly called Negere Meskel the proclamation of the Cross for through it the world heard the news of salvation.

text.text: The Cross as the Teaching of Salvation

text: The Cross is the school where Christ Himself taught mankind the lesson of love and suffering. Upon it, the foundation of hell was torn apart, the wall that divided man and God was destroyed, and death itself was trampled down. The prophets foresaw it, the apostles proclaimed it, the Church Fathers preserved it, and the teachers of today hand it down still. To remember the Cross is to taste joy of spirit, for every feast of the Cross fills the faithful with heavenly gladness.
“You have given a sign to those who fear you, that they may flee from the arrow of the enemy” (Psalm 59:4). The Cross is that sign refuge from the enemy’s arrow.
“The Cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us it is the power of God” (1 Cor. 1:18). The wisdom of heaven is foolishness to the proud, yet salvation to the humble.

named its glories: it is the hope of Christians, the resurrection of the dead, the guide of the blind, the prophecy of the prophets, the preaching of the apostles, the glory of the martyrs, the perseverance of nuns, the purity of virgins, the foundation of the Church, and the peace of the world.

, reflecting on the mystery of the Cross, said: “Think for a moment, O man, and ask yourself whether all the work of the world could be done without the cross. Without this symbol of victory, it is impossible to cross the sea. Without it, the sculptors and the wise men do not make any sculptures. text.text: the Nature of the Holy Cross

text:
The Holy Cross is not only a symbol but the very place where the mystery of salvation was revealed. Upon it, many sick were healed, the dead were raised, and countless miracles were performed.

It is upon the Cross that:

God revealed His love for mankind (Phil. 2:8; 1 Jn. 4:9; Jn. 3:16).

The flesh and blood of Christ were tested (Book of Mysteries, Abba George 5:28).

Man was reconciled with God (2 Cor. 5:19; Eph. 2:14).

Sin was broken (Rom. 6:22).

The power of death was abolished (Heb. 2:14–15; 2 Tim. 1:10).

Salvation was accomplished (1 Pet. 2:24).

Satan was defeated (Col. 1:20).

Peace was given (Col. 1:20).

Believers received strength (1 Cor. 1:18).


Therefore, the Cross is the defeat of demons and the punishment of unclean spirits. It is the perfect medicine for both body and soul. It is the power by which angels serve and priests minister. It is the crown of the Holy Church, the crown of monasteries, and the glory of all Christians.

The Psalmist, speaking with prophetic voice, declared: “We will worship at the foot of the throne of God” (Ps. 131:7). And St. Yared, the heavenly harp of Ethiopia, echoes this by singing: “We will worship at the foot of the throne, O Lord, the Holy One of Israel” (Tsome Diguwa). Therefore, our Holy Church, adorned with hymnody and prayer, bows before the Cross with grace and reverence.

Why? Because the Cross is the very body upon which Christ was crucified, the altar stained with His most precious Blood, the place where His boundless power was revealed. Thus St. Yared proclaims in the Deguwa: “On this day, the feast of the Cross, glorious in heaven and on earth, may it shine upon the nations, may it be praised forever.”

Indeed, the Church has never celebrated a liturgy, sung a hymn, or lifted a prayer without the Cross being named, remembered, and exalted. Twice each year she holds great feasts in its honor on Megabit 10 and Meskerem 17  yet every day, every hour, the Cross is praised upon her lips.

When the Cross of our Lord first revealed its power, raising the dead and shining with light, the envious Jews sought to bury it in shame. They covered it with refuse, and over time a hill rose upon it. As generations passed, the memory of its place faded into silence.

But the Lord, who hides treasures only to reveal them in due season, stirred the heart of Queen Eleni, mother of Constantine the Great. She vowed that if her son embraced Christ, she would journey to Jerusalem and recover the buried Cross. She raised him in the fear of God, and Constantine, strengthened by heavenly power, cast down his enemies and reigned as a Christian king.

True to her vow, Eleni came to Jerusalem. Guided by the wisdom of an old man named Kirakos, she set fire to wood upon the hill of refuse on Meskerem 16. As the smoke of incense ascended, it pointed to the hidden place of the Cross. She dug with zeal, and on Megabit 10, the precious Cross of Christ was revealed.

text.text: St. Yared sings of this miracle

text:
: “The Cross was buried on Golgotha; the Jews who cast it away were buried in their shame. A miracle was performed when the noble Queen Eleni found the Holy Cross  a wonder and a marvel!” (Book of the Cross, p. 26).

Thus, on Meskerem 16, the faithful gather wood for the great fire of Demera, lighting torches and singing with joy: “Eyoha Abebaye Meskerem Tebaye” And on Meskerem 17, the Church consecrates the memory of the Cross, recalling its revelation with splendor and awe.

text.text: The Example of the Cross and the Torch

text:
St. Yared, sings again: “Today the Cross is praised; today it has brought us to our brothers in peace and joy before God” (Book of the Cross, p. 4).

The Cross and the torch are bound together in prayer: the torch recalls Queen Eleni’s process as she searched for the treasure of Christ’s Cross, and the Cross itself shines as the true light of freedom for all the world. When we lift the torch, we confess that we have arrived at the true day of salvation, the light that scatters all darkness.

text.text: The Cross as the Pride of the Church

text:
In general, the Cross holds the highest honor in the life of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. As mentioned above, the Cross is the foundation foretold by the prophets, the example revealed in their prophecies, and the teaching proclaimed by the apostles. In particular, the apostle St. Paul declared: “Far be it from me to boast except in the Cross of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14).

In the same way, the Holy Church shares in the suffering of Christ by exalting the Cross as her crown and glory  placing it upon her domes, encircling her walls, and making Calvary, the place of the Cross, her very heart and center. Moreover, she commemorates the mystery of the Cross not only in the great feasts of the year, but in every prayer, every liturgy, and every day of her worship.

The Cross is the throne of love, the sign of victory, the light of freedom, the staff of the Church, the terror of demons, the crown of the faithful. To it we bow, through it we pray, by it we are saved.

text:
Beloved in Christ,

Grace and peace be with you, from the One who was lifted upon the Cross for our salvation. Let us open our hearts and minds to the wonder of this sacred sign, not as a mere piece of wood, but as the instrument through which the Almighty revealed His infinite love, conquered death, and reconciled humanity to Himself.

When we speak the word “cross,” or when it touches our minds, a spiritual felling awakens within the faithful. The Cross brings to our remembrance that Christ, the Lord of Glory, was crucified upon it. Through it the kingdom of darkness trembled, the wall of enmity between God and man was torn down, and the reign of death was broken, opening to us the way of the resurrection. Thus the Cross is not a mere piece of wood, but a spiritual sanctuary, a holy place sanctified by the blood of the Lamb.

It is upon this Cross that unclean spirits are vanquished, demons flee, and both the sickness of body and the wounds of the soul are healed. The Cross is the altar of angels and the dwelling of priests, where both heavenly hosts and earthly ministers lift up unceasing praise.

The Cross is the diadem of the Holy Church, the crown of monasteries, and the ornament of every Christian soul. As the Psalmist declares: “You have given a sign to those who fear You, that they may flee from the arrow of the enemy” (Ps. 59:4). Indeed, the Cross is that sign - our shield of salvation, our refuge from the darts of the evil one.

St. Paul testifies: “The word of the Cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God” (1 Cor. 1:18). He teaches us that the cross is the power and wisdom of God..

text: “The Cross is the hope of Christians, the resurrection of the dead, the guide of the blind, the hope of the anointed. The Cross is the prophecy of the prophets, the preaching of the apostles, the glory of the martyrs, the righteousness of the just, the perseverance of monks, the purity of virgins, the foundation of the Church, the stability and peace of the world.”

, reflecting on the mystery of the Cross, said: “Think for a moment, O man, and ask yourself whether all the work of the world could be done without the cross?Without this symbol of victory? it is impossible to cross the sea. Without it, the sculptors and the wise men do not make any sculptures. For the form of man is itself a cross; and birds, like crosses, fly in the air.” (First Apology, Ch. 55).

: “We should not be ashamed to confess the Crucified Christ. We should boldly honor the Cross by sealing it on our foreheads, on our hands, and upon all that we wear. We should mark it on the bread we eat and the cup we drink, when we go out and when we return, when we lie down and when we rise, when we journey and when we rest.” (Catechesis XIII, 36).

text: Before the crucifixion of Christ, the Cross was seen as a curse, a symbol of shame, as the Law says: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. 21:23). But by the death of the sinless One upon it, the curse was turned into blessing, the shame into glory, the instrument of death into the fountain of life.

Without it, the sculptors and the wise men do not make any sculptures. For the form of man is itself a cross; and birds, like crosses, fly in the air.” (First Apology, Ch. 55).

Saint Cyril of Jerusalem exhorts us: “We should not be ashamed to confess the Crucified Christ. We should boldly honor the Cross by sealing it on our foreheads, on our hands, and upon all that we wear. We should mark it on the bread we eat and the cup we drink, when we go out and when we return, when we lie down and when we rise, when we journey and when we rest.” (Catechesis XIII, 36).

3. The Cross in Prophecy and Tradition

Before the crucifixion of Christ, the Cross was seen as a curse, a symbol of shame, as the Law says: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. 21:23). But by the death of the sinless One upon it, the curse was turned into blessing, the shame into glory, the instrument of death into the fountain of life.

text.text: Why then do we, as Ethiopians, celebrate the Cross with such great honor, particularly on Meskerem 17?

text:
When the Cross of Christ shone with heavenly light and even raised the dead, the unbelieving Jews sought to conceal it, burying it under heaps of refuse until the place became a mound, guarded and forgotten through generations. Yet the providence of God raised up Queen Eleni, the mother of Constantine. She vowed that if her son embraced Christ, she would seek the buried Cross. Indeed, Constantine was baptized and reigned by the power of the Lord

Queen Eleni began the search. Guided by divine sign, she set fire to wood, and the rising smoke marked the place of the Cross. Thus excavation began on Meskerem 17, and after months of labor, on Megabit 10, the precious Cross was found. St. Yared sang: “A miracle and a wonder happened when the holy Cross was found by the noble Queen Eleni.”

On Meskerem 16, the vigil of the finding, the faithful gather wood both dry and green, pile it high, and set it aflame in joyful commemoration. With torches in their hands they proclaim: “Eyoha Abebaye Meskerem Tebaye !”

Why is the feast kept on Meskerem 17 and not Megabit 10, when the Cross was found? Because Megabit falls within the Great Fast, when feasts of rejoicing cannot be celebrated. Thus the Church, in her wisdom, appointed Meskerem 17 as the solemn commemoration.

The torch of Demera itself carries deep meaning: it recalls the fire that revealed the burial place of the Cross, the lamps that guided those who dug in darkness, and above all, it proclaims that the Cross of Christ is the true light of freedom and salvation to the world.

text.text: How did the Cross come to our land?

text:
in 1334,the 29th year of his second reign, the Patriarch of Alexandria, Abune Michael 47th, endured affliction. For the Pharaoh of Egypt, blinded by arrogance, oppressed the Christians of his land, demanding: “If you do not follow my religion, you will not be able to live in Egypt.” Heavy taxes and bitter threats were laid upon the faithful. The people, wearied by torment, sent their cries across the Nile and desert, to Emperor Dawit of Ethiopia: “We have begged in the name of God to relieve us of the suffering we have suffered, and our Patriarch.”

Hearing this, Emperor Dawit rose with holy zeal, saying, “The army is strong, and the people are strong.” He did not count the cost to himself, but took thought for the suffering flock of Christ. He advanced his forces even unto Khartoum. There, perceiving the strength of Egypt, the Emperor and his council chose a weapon more powerful than sword or spear: they sought to strike fear by closing the Nile itself, the very lifeblood of the land.

When Merwan Elgaden, the ruler of Egypt, heard this, he trembled. Gathering his nobles, he asked, “What is better for us?” Their counsel was wise in its fear: “If the Nile is taken from us, our people shall perish of thirst. Better to yield than to die.” And so they sent forth Abune Michael, freed from prison, carrying with him two thousand pieces of gold to appease the Ethiopian Emperor.

But Emperor Dawit, filled with faith, spurned their bribe. “I do not want silver and gold,” he declared, “I want the Cross on which my Lord Jesus Christ was crucified.” Thus, pressed between death and life, Egypt consented. On Meskerem10, 1395, they delivered to Ethiopia not only the Cross, but also a holy icon of the Virgin Mother, painted by the very hand of Saint Luke.

From this day forth, the Feast of the Emperor’s Cross has been celebrated each year on Meskerem 10, a memorial to God’s mercy and to the steadfastness of our fathers. One week later, on Meskerem 17, while remembering the great Queen Eleni, Emperor Dawit beheld a vision: “My Cross will remain on the Cross.” Astonished, he fell to the ground, and there yielded his soul to the Lord.

text:
👇🏾

His son, Emperor Zera Yacob, was not without sign, for again the vision was repeated to him: “Put My Cross on cross place .” Desiring to fulfill the mystery, he searched through the land until he found a place shaped like the very Cross of Calvary, where Christ’s right hand had rested. There, on Meskerem 21, 1446, he placed the Cross at Geshen Amba, the holy mountain where today stands Debre Kerbe Mariam, the monastery of the Lord.

Geshen, that towering rock in Wollo Province, Ambasel, has but a single entrance, as though heaven itself had sealed it for sanctity. Through the ages it has borne many names:

From the reign of Emperor Dilna-ad (866 AD) until the 11th century, it was called Debre Kerbe.

In the 11th century, when Emperor Lalibela carved a church named "Egziabher ab" upon that mountain it named "Debre Egziabher", after that it was renamed Debre Negesit.

In 1446, when Zer-a Yacob placed the Cross there, the old name returned: Debre Kerbe.

The people, seeing the Emperor “carry his Cross” there, gave it the name Geshen, from the Ge’ez “Gese” or the Amharic “Gesegese,”

Thus the name Geshen endures even to this day, “The book by Merigeta Yemane Birhan Addise, which records the history of the Geshen Debre Kerbe Monastery, explains in detail how the area received its name.”a sign that the Cross has indeed been carried into Ethiopia, not by man’s will alone but by God’s providence.

Therefore, let us not think of the Cross as a distant memory, but as our daily life. It is the power of God for our salvation, the sign of our deliverance, the lamp in our darkness, the staff of our pilgrimage, the crown of the Church, the terror of demons, the consolation of the faithful, and the glory of Christ Himself.

text:
✍🏾Beloved in Christ, sons and daughters of the Holy Church, let us open our eyes not to the shadows of the world but to the blazing light of the Cross, which shines more radiant than the sun. The Cross is not one, simple, poor object. It is the fountain of mysteries, the seal of faith, the throne of the King. Therefore the Church, with her profound wisdom and artistic vision, has adorned the Cross in many forms, that through visible shapes she may reveal to us invisible truths.

✍🏾The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church has long been a treasury of sacred art and holy symbols: her paintings, her vestments, her sacred festivals, even the gestures of joy and mourning all proclaim the faith that was once delivered to the saints. Yet among these, the Cross stands supreme, for it is not mere ornament but the very sign of salvation. When we gaze upon its design, our hearts must not stop at its outward beauty. Rather, the icons must pierce our understanding and awaken in us the memory of Christ crucified. For what is a picture worth, if the mystery is not perceived?

✍🏾Thus the Church, like a wise mother, has given us many kinds of crosses. She names them, fashions them from diverse materials, and sets them in service, so that we may learn from every angle the depth of Christ’s work for us. Just as Scripture speaks in manifold ways of the same Lord, so the Cross is shown in manifold forms, each form unveiling another facet of Christ’s saving work. If we behold these icons with faith and understanding, then Christ is painted upon our hearts; but if we look without discernment, we remain blind like the Galatians, before whom Christ was portrayed as crucified, yet they did not perceive His grace (Galatians 3:1).

If we behold these icons with faith and understanding, then Christ is painted upon our hearts; but if we look without discernment, we remain blind like the Galatians, before whom Christ was portrayed as crucified, yet they did not perceive His grace (Galatians 3:1).

I. The Cross by Material

👉🏾 Wooden Cross: Symbolizes the very wood upon which our Lord was crucified.

👉🏾 Iron Cross: Represents the five iron nails with which our Lord was fastened to the Cross.

👉🏾 Silver Cross: Reminds us of Judas’s betrayal, when he sold our Lord for thirty pieces of silver.

👉🏾 Gold Cross: Signifies the pure and incorruptible nature of our Lord.

👉🏾 Copper Cross: Copper, with its red hue, symbolizes the blood of Christ.

II. The Cross by Design

👉🏾Arwe Birt Cross ( አርዌ ብርት መስቀል): Symbolizes the bronze serpent that Moses lifted up in the wilderness.

👉🏾 Apostle Cross (ሐዋርያ መስቀል): Represents the apostles traveling to every nation, preaching and teaching the Gospel.

👉🏾 Qerne Begi-e Cross (ቀርነ በግዕ መስቀል): Signifies our Lord as the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world.

👉🏾 Awde Alem Cross (አውደ አለም መስቀል): A symbol of the salvation of all people through the Cross of Christ.

👉🏾 Lenginos Cross (ሌንጊኖስ መስቀል): Reminds us of the spear that pierced the side of our Lord.

👉🏾 Keranyo Cross(ቀራንዮ መስቀል): Points directly to the Cross on Calvary, where our Lord was crucified.

👉🏾 Lisane Ke Lebat Cross( ልሳነ ከለባት መስቀል): Symbolizes the saints guarding the Church with their teachings, just as a faithful dog guards the house of its master.

👉🏾Timhrte Ntfit Cross (ትምህርተ ንትፊት መስቀል): Depicts the sufferings of our Lord His side pierced, His head crowned with thorns, and His body wounded for our salvation.

👉🏾 Etse Sabek Cross(እፀ ሳቤቅ መስቀል): Represents Christ as the sacrificial Lamb, foreshadowed in the ram offered in place of Isaac. It is also associated with the Sabeq leaf, a symbol of this sacrifice.

text.text:
About the Holy Cross
Why Do We

text:
✍🏾Beloved in Christ, children of God, let us lift our hearts to behold the mystery that is the boast of the Church and the terror of demons: the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. For to the world it appears as weakness and shame, but to the faithful it is strength, redemption, and the crown of glory.

✍🏾The Apostle cries aloud, “The word of the Cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God” (1 Cor. 1:18). And what greater power has ever been revealed than when the Son of God stretched out His hands, was pierced in the flesh, poured forth His blood, and by death destroyed death?

✍🏾The Cross shines with glory not because of wood or nails, but because upon it the Lord of Glory was hung. Just as the donkey of Hosanna was adorned with honor, not because of itself, but because Christ sat upon it (Matt. 21:8), so too the Cross is exalted because Christ was lifted up upon it. What once was a symbol of shame has become the throne of salvation.

✍🏾It is by the Cross that the ancient word of God was fulfilled: “He shall crush your head” (Gen. 3:15). The Cross is the weapon by which Satan’s head was crushed, his dominion broken, his malice undone. For every believer who clings to the Christ , the Cross is the strength to trample down the enemy.

✍🏾The Scriptures proclaim the power of the Cross even before it was revealed:

👉🏾When Moses lifted up his hands in the form of a cross, Israel prevailed over its enemies. So too do we, the new Israel, conquer the demons by the power of the Cross.

👉🏾When Jacob crossed his hands upon the sons of Joseph, blessing flowed forth (Gen. 48:13–20). In the same way, the Cross is the fountain of blessing for body and soul.

👉🏾The rod of Moses worked wonders (Ex. 4:14), the mantle of Elijah parted the waters (2 Kings 2:7–14), the Jordan healed Naaman (2 Kings 5:1–10), and the oil anointed the sick (Mark 6:13, James 5:14).

👉🏾The waters of Siloam restored sight (John 9:1–12), the garments of Paul healed the afflicted and cast out demons (Acts 19:11–12), and the very shadow of Peter brought health (Acts 5:15–16).

✍🏾If such power was revealed through rod, mantle, water, and cloth, shall not the Cross of Christ, sanctified by His blood, overflow with even greater power?

text.text: The Folly of the World and the Wisdom of God

text:
✍🏾The devil whispers to his slaves, “Why do you bow to wood? Why do you honor the Cross?” Yet such objections are nothing but echoes of hell. For it is not the material that we venerate, but the power of Christ revealed through it. Just as God used ordinary things in ages past to show His might, so He has sanctified the Cross to be the sign of His victory.

✍🏾To despise the Cross is to align oneself with those of whom the Apostle warned: “Many walk as enemies of the Cross of Christ… their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their mind is on earthly things” (Phil. 3:18–19). Such men hate the very sign by which they might have been saved.

text.text: The Refuge and Boast of the Faithful

text:
✍🏾The Cross is the banner given to those who fear God, that they might flee from the arrows of the evil one (Ps. 59:4–5). Therefore, we boast in it, as Paul did: “Far be it from me to glory except in the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world is crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14).

✍🏾This is why the faithful wear the Cross upon their necks, sign themselves with it in prayer, adorn their garments with it, and mark their houses with it. The Cross is our refuge in every place, our shield in every trial, our boast in every generation. To the world it is folly; to us, it is life.

✍🏾St. Paul tells us that we should bow before the Holy Cross: “We will worship at the place where His feet stood” (Ps. 13:7). Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ was crucified on the cross on Friday. He tells us that through the cross we will be saved from Satan. Christ was crucified on the cross so that our curse might be removed, and we might be blessed in both body and soul. Therefore, the cross destroys the curse and grants us life in body and soul.

✍🏾On the Cross, enmity was slain, for the devil who sows hatred between man and God was himself defeated (Eph. 2:16). On the Cross, curse was destroyed, for Christ became Crucified for our curse , that we might receive blessing in body and soul. On the Cross, man and angels were reconciled, heaven and earth united, and the love of God was revealed in fullness.

✍🏾Whenever we see the Cross, we are reminded of how much God loves us for He loved us even to death upon it. Therefore we rejoice, we bless, we worship, we glory in the Cross. It is our redemption, our power, our salvation, our everlasting boast.

✍🏾Let us then embrace the Cross with faith and joy, never separating ourselves from Christ who sanctified it with His blood. Let us hold it as our banner, our strength, and our crown. For the Cross has crushed the devil, destroyed enmity, reconciled creation, and revealed the boundless love of God.

text:
✍🏾Beloved in the Lord, the glory of the Cross is the glory of our faith. For through the Cross the curse was broken, death was destroyed, and the gates of Paradise flung open to the sons of Adam. The Orthodox Church, like a faithful guardian, raises the Cross high, venerates it, sings of it, and engraves it upon her children. For what the world despises, the Church embraces as her crown, and what men once feared as a sign of shame, we proclaim as the very throne of victory.

✍🏾Here lies the difference between the holy Orthodox faith and those who walk in the steps of Protestantism. For they neither trace the sign of the Cross upon themselves, nor bless their homes or garments with it. They do not wear the Cross upon their bodies, nor lift it upon their temples, nor celebrate its feasts, nor rejoice in its praises. But the Orthodox, taught by Christ and the apostles, have been entrusted with the honor due to the Cross, not as an ornament of wood or metal, but as the power and wisdom of God.

text.text: 1. Christ Himself set the Cross at the center of discipleship

text:
✍🏾Our Lord, even before He stretched out His hands upon the wood, proclaimed the mystery of the Cross. He said: “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow after Me is not worthy of Me” (Matt. 10:38). Again He declared: “If anyone would come after Me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me” (Mark 8:34). To the rich young ruler He said: “Take up your cross and follow Me” (Mark 10:21). And once more, “Whoever does not bear his cross and come after Me cannot be My disciple” (Luke 14:27).

✍🏾Behold how He speaks with insistence: not once or twice, but many times He sets the Cross as the mark of true discipleship. Therefore, When we make the sign of the cross with our hand (Mamateb), we remember and honor the teachings and commandments that our Lord has given us.

text.text: 2. The Cross is proclaimed by angels and apostles

text:
✍🏾Even the angels confessed the Lord as the Crucified One. When they announced the resurrection, they said to the women: “I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified” (Matt. 28:5–6). Though He had risen, the angel did not cast aside the name of the Cross, for the Resurrection cannot be separated from the Crucifixion.

So too did the apostles preach. Peter cried to the Jews: “Let all the house of Israel know assuredly that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2:36). Paul declared boldly: “We preach Christ crucified” (1 Cor. 1:23). And again he said: “I determined to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and Him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2).

Thus the Cross is the unshakable foundation of apostolic preaching and angelic proclamation alike.

text.text: 3. The Cross was the apostles’ glory

text: ✍🏾The apostle Paul confesses: “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14). See the paradox: the cross, a thing despised by men, becomes the very boast of the saints. For in it Paul beheld his true freedom: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). The cross stripped him of earthly pride and clothed him with heavenly honor. What greater glory can a man have than to be marked with the cross?

text.text: 4. The Cross reveals divine love and forgiveness

text:
✍🏾Every time we Blessing our bodies by moving our hands in the shape of a cross, we remember the immeasurable love of God. Isaiah foresaw this mystery: “The Lord laid on Him the iniquity of us all” (Isa. 53:6). John the Baptist pointed to Him: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). The apostle John declares: “He is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:2).

The cross, then, is not merely wood it is the place where mercy triumphed over judgment, where sin was blotted out, and where forgiveness gushed forth like an endless spring.

For what the world despises, the Church embraces as her crown, and what men once feared as a sign of shame, we proclaim as the very throne of victory.

✍🏾Here lies the difference between the holy Orthodox faith and those who walk in the steps of Protestantism. For they neither trace the sign of the Cross upon themselves, nor bless their homes or garments with it. They do not wear the Cross upon their bodies, nor lift it upon their temples, nor celebrate its feasts, nor rejoice in its praises. But the Orthodox, taught by Christ and the apostles, have been entrusted with the honor due to the Cross, not as an ornament of wood or metal, but as the power and wisdom of God.

1. Christ Himself set the Cross at the center of discipleship

✍🏾Our Lord, even before He stretched out His hands upon the wood, proclaimed the mystery of the Cross. He said: “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow after Me is not worthy of Me” (Matt. 10:38). Again He declared: “If anyone would come after Me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me” (Mark 8:34). To the rich young ruler He said: “Take up your cross and follow Me” (Mark 10:21). And once more, “Whoever does not bear his cross and come after Me cannot be My disciple” (Luke 14:27).

✍🏾Behold how He speaks with insistence: not once or twice, but many times He sets the Cross as the mark of true discipleship. Therefore, When we make the sign of the cross with our hand (Mamateb), we remember and honor the teachings and commandments that our Lord has given us.

2. The Cross is proclaimed by angels and apostles

✍🏾Even the angels confessed the Lord as the Crucified One. When they announced the resurrection, they said to the women: “I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified” (Matt. 28:5–6). Though He had risen, the angel did not cast aside the name of the Cross, for the Resurrection cannot be separated from the Crucifixion.

So too did the apostles preach. Peter cried to the Jews: “Let all the house of Israel know assuredly that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2:36). Paul declared boldly: “We preach Christ crucified” (1 Cor. 1:23). And again he said: “I determined to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and Him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2).

Thus the Cross is the unshakable foundation of apostolic preaching and angelic proclamation alike.

3. The Cross was the apostles’ glory

✍🏾The apostle Paul confesses: “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14). See the paradox: the cross, a thing despised by men, becomes the very boast of the saints. For in it Paul beheld his true freedom: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). The cross stripped him of earthly pride and clothed him with heavenly honor. What greater glory can a man have than to be marked with the cross?

4. The Cross reveals divine love and forgiveness

✍🏾Every time we Blessing our bodies by moving our hands in the shape of a cross, we remember the immeasurable love of God. Isaiah foresaw this mystery: “The Lord laid on Him the iniquity of us all” (Isa. 53:6). John the Baptist pointed to Him: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). The apostle John declares: “He is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:2).

The cross, then, is not merely wood it is the place where mercy triumphed over judgment, where sin was blotted out, and where forgiveness gushed forth like an endless spring.

Continues 👇🏾

text.text: 5. The Cross is our open confession

text: ✍🏾When we make the sign of the cross ( moving our hand from the forehead to the chest, and from the left shoulder to the right shoulder.), we show that we belong to the cross. By carrying the cross on our necks, designing it in our jewelry, and placing it high in our places of faith, we declare openly that we are the people of Jesus Christ, who was crucified for us. We are not ashamed of the cross before others; instead, we are proud of it and hold firmly to it. Even without words,The sign of the cross becomes a witness of our faith to all who see us.

text.text: 6. Worshiping God with Spirit, Mind, and Body

text:
✍🏾Man is a spirit, mind, and physical being. The cross is understood not only by thought but also through our senses seeing and touching it helps us remember Christ’s crucifixion.

✍🏾We worship God with our spirit, mind, and body. Every time when we sign ourselves with the Cross and say In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit", we express our belief in the Holy Trinity. Making the sign of the cross unites our body, mind, and spirit in devotion, reminding us of Christ’s sacrifice and victory.

✍🏾Behold then, beloved, the glory of the Cross. Angels proclaim it, apostles preach it, prophets foretell it, martyrs embrace it, and the Church raises it high as her boast. Through it we are reconciled, by it we are sealed, in it we are glorified.

Let us therefore venerate the Cross, not as mere wood, but as the throne of the Lamb, the ladder of Jacob, the key to Paradise, and the banner of victory.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.

text:
✍🏾At Geshen, a great temple was built, and the relics were placed with honor:

the red robe worn by Christ on Good Friday,

The cup ,of bitterness that He drank.

the icon of His Holy Head painted by St. John,

the icon of Our Lady painted by St. Luke,

the bones of saints,

and relics from Jerusalem, Rome, Egypt, and beyond.

✍🏾On Meskerem 21, 1440 A.D., the Cross was enthroned at Geshen, and the church was consecrated. Our Lord Himself appeared and declared: “This place shall be Jerusalem, where I was born, Golgotha where I was crucified, and the Tomb where I was buried. My goodness shall visit all who come here, and My mercy shall never depart from them.”

Thus Geshen became for Ethiopia a second Jerusalem, a living witness to the Cross.

✍🏾Emperor Zera Yacob ordered the building of a church in honor of the Holy Virgin Mary beside the church of God the Father. He inscribed in the Book of Tefut blessings for all who dwell near Geshen, promising protection and divine favor. Kings, bishops, and nobles enriched the monastery with gifts of books, vessels, and crosses, so that it became a treasury of faith and culture for all Ethiopia.

✍🏾To this day, on Meskerem 21, the faithful of Ethiopia gathers at Geshen Maryam to honor the enthronement of the Cross and to receive blessing. On that holy mountain the faithful tastes the mercy of Christ who sanctified it with His promise.

✍🏾Beloved, Geshen Maryam is a sign of God’s love for Ethiopia. The Lord who was crucified on Golgotha has set a new Golgotha in our midst, so that we too may draw near to His Cross. The story of Geshen teaches us that God chooses and sanctifies places, for the salvation of His people.

Let us therefore rejoice in the mystery of the Cross enthroned in Geshen, and may the mercy of Christ who appeared there make our hearts also into His Jerusalem, His Calvary, His dwelling place. Amen.

text:
Dear faithful followers of the Orthodox teaching, we greet you with the blessings of our Lord. Today we reflect upon a pivotal moment in the history of the Church, the Holy Council of Nicaea, and we invite you to meditate deeply upon its meaning and significance.

✍🏾 At this time, Emperor Constantine, moved by the guidance of God, commanded that the temples of idols be closed and that the churches of the Lord be opened. He then summoned the scholars and fathers of the Church from every land to assemble in Nicaea to confront the heresy and defend the true faith.

✍🏾 From Miyaziya 21 to Meskerem 21. 2348 scholars and bishops gathered in Nicaea. The city was chosen for its size, central location, and suitability to host the bishops, priests, and the emperor with his retinue. Among these holy men were those who, like the apostles of old, had performed miracles raising the dead, cleansing lepers, giving sight to the blind, healing the sick, and bearing the wounds of their devotion for the faith of Christ.

✍🏾After a week spent in prayer and fasting, the assembly formally began on Hidar 9. Emperor Constantine presided, and Alexander of Alexandria spoke on behalf of the Church. Each bishop recorded his name, his region, and his faith. Among 2,348 attendees, 318 bishops stood united in one voice, confessing clearly:

"the Son is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit in divinity, power, will, and existence.”

✍🏾 These 318 holy scholars, reflecting the example of the 318 sons of Abraham (Gen. 14:14), condemned the heresy of Arius and established the Nicene Creed the firm foundation of our faith. Through their wisdom and guidance, the Church was strengthened, and the true teaching about the divinity of Christ was preserved for all generations.

✍🏾Though the council formally concluded on Hidar 9, the bishops had gathered on Meskerem 21. This day is remembered in the Church as a celebration of  " Bzuhan mariyam" because we remember the holy fathers who defended the faith. It is a day to honor the unity, courage, and devotion of those who preserved the truth of God’s Son against all error.

Dear faithful followers of the Orthodox teaching, we greet you with the blessings of our Lord. Today we reflect upon a pivotal moment in the history of the Church, the Holy Council of Nicaea, and we invite you to meditate deeply upon its meaning and significance.

✍🏾 At this time, Emperor Constantine, moved by the guidance of God, commanded that the temples of idols be closed and that the churches of the Lord be opened. He then summoned the scholars and fathers of the Church from every land to assemble in Nicaea to confront the heresy and defend the true faith.

✍🏾 From Miyaziya 21 to Meskerem 21. 2348 scholars and bishops gathered in Nicaea. The city was chosen for its size, central location, and suitability to host the bishops, priests, and the emperor with his retinue. Among these holy men were those who, like the apostles of old, had performed miracles raising the dead, cleansing lepers, giving sight to the blind, healing the sick, and bearing the wounds of their devotion for the faith of Christ.

✍🏾After a week spent in prayer and fasting, the assembly formally began on Hidar 9. Emperor Constantine presided, and Alexander of Alexandria spoke on behalf of the Church. Each bishop recorded his name, his region, and his faith. Among 2,348 attendees, 318 bishops stood united in one voice, confessing clearly:

"the Son is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit in divinity, power, will, and existence.”

✍🏾 These 318 holy scholars, reflecting the example of the 318 sons of Abraham (Gen. 14:14), condemned the heresy of Arius and established the Nicene Creed the firm foundation of our faith. Through their wisdom and guidance, the Church was strengthened, and the true teaching about the divinity of Christ was preserved for all generations.

✍🏾Though the council formally concluded on Hidar 9, the bishops had gathered on Meskerem 21. This day is remembered in the Church as a celebration of  " Bzuhan mariyam" because we remember the holy fathers who defended the faith. It is a day to honor the unity, courage, and devotion of those who preserved the truth of God’s Son against all error.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

question :-How does a person get spiritual healing from sin / a new heart ?

text:
-My beloved child in Christ,May the peace of our Lord and Savior Eyesus Kristos be with you. Your question is not a small one; it is the very heart of our life in God. You ask how one receives healing from sin and is granted a new heart. This is the question that has echoed in the souls of the faithful since Adam first felt the chill of his separation from the garden. It is the cry of King David, who prayed in his repentance, "Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me" (Psalm 50:10, LXX).

Know this first, dear one: the desire you feel for this healing is itself a gift from God. It is the Holy Spirit calling you back to the Father's house. Our Lord does not desire the death of a sinner, but that he should turn from his way and live.

The Holy Church, in her wisdom given by Christ, does not see sin as merely a legal transgression, a breaking of rules. She sees it as a sickness, a wound upon the soul that separates us from the source of Life, who is God Himself. And for a sickness, one does not need a judge, but a Physician. Our Lord Eyesus Kristos is that Great Physician, and the Holy Church is His hospital, filled with the medicines of salvation.

So, how does this healing, this heart-transplant of the soul, take place? It is a journey, a process of turning back to God, which we call Metanoia repentance. This is not just a feeling of sorrow, but a complete re-orientation of your life, your mind, and your will towards God.

But what is this repentance? It is not simply feeling sorry. It is a profound turning, a re-orientation of your entire life. It is composed of these vital steps:

text.text: 1. The Awakening and Confession (The Cleansing of the Wound)

text:
The first step is to come to yourself, like the Prodigal Son in the far country (Luke 15). You must see the sickness for what it is. Then, with humility and hope, you must come to the spiritual hospital, to the Mystery of Holy Confession. Do not fear the priest (Kahen). He is not there as your accuser, but as a witness to your repentance and a dispenser of God's grace. He is the surgeon's assistant, and Christ is the Surgeon. Through the priest, Christ Himself hears your confession and, by the power given to His apostles when He said, "Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven" (Matthew 18:18), He absolves your sins.

As the great St. John Chrysostom says, "Do not be ashamed to enter again into the Church. Be ashamed when you sin. Do not be ashamed when you repent. Pay attention to what the devil did to you. These are two things: sin and shame. The devil conquered you by the first and now wants to conquer you by the second. But do not be conquered." In confession, you expose the wound to the Physician so that it may be cleansed and healed.

Once the wound is cleansed through confession, it must be filled with life. The ultimate medicine for the soul is the Body and Blood of our Lord Himself in the Holy Eucharist (Qurban). He told us, "Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life... He who eats My flesh and drinks My blood abides in Me, and I in him" (John 6:54, 56). This is the very definition of a new heart—to have Christ abiding within you, and you in Him. St. Ignatius of Antioch called Holy Communion "the medicine of immortality, the antidote to prevent us from dying, and to live forever in Jesus Christ." This divine food purifies us, strengthens us against temptation, and unites us to God in the most intimate way possible.

text.text: Built in the Name of the Holy Virgin
Question :-Where is the Building up of the first church in the name of our Holy Virgin Mariam (ሕንፀተ ቤተ ክርስቲያን)?

text:
My beloved child in Christ,

Your question touches upon a foundation stone of our faith and a day of great joy for all who take refuge in the prayers of the Most Holy Theotokos, our Mother the Virgin Mariam. You ask about the Feast of Hintsete Bete Kristiyan (ሕንፀተ ቤተ ክርስቲያን), the "Building of the Church," a day we celebrate with great reverence on the 21st day of the month of Sene.

You ask "Where?" The answer, according to our Holy Tradition (Tewfit), is that the building of this first and most holy church in the name of the Theotokos took place in the city of Philippi.

The ancient city of Philippi, where the Holy Apostles gathered and where our Lord Himself descended to bless the foundation of the first church in His Mother's name, is located in the modern-day country of Greece. It is in the northern part of that country.

On Sene 20, in the district of Chalcedon in Caesarea Philippi, our Lord Jesus Christ Himself built a church not of wood, nor of clay, nor of water but by three stones, drawn together by divine command. This church was built in honor of His Holy Mother, the Virgin Mary, the All-Immaculate Theotokos. It stands among the holiest of her feast days, a monument not only of stone, but of heaven's descent upon earth.

In the eighth year of the Lord’s reign, the apostles Paul and Barnabas, having preached the Gospel and baptized many Gentiles in Philippi, desired to build a holy place where the new believers might worship. But they did not act without heavenly guidance. Saint Peter, the Chief of the Apostles, and Saint John the Beloved, were summoned. And then O awe-striking wonder! the Lord, gathering both the living and the dead, brought together all His apostles in a divine convocation.

Christ our God appeared and said, “I have gathered you to teach you the manner in which churches are to be built throughout the earth in the name of My Mother.” He took them eastward and, with divine majesty, moved three stones into one foundation. He measured it: 24 cubits in height and 12 in width, a mystery in number and in spirit. These stones, soft as wax under divine fire, were fashioned into a church by the hands of the apostles, according to the command and guidance of the Lord.

On the following day, Sene 21, the Lord descended again with His Holy Mother, the Virgin Mary. She stood as the new Ark of the Covenant, holier than that of Moses. He ordained the apostles: Saint Peter as priest, Saint Stephen as deacon, and sanctified the Eucharistic mystery, causing the heavenly bread and cup to descend into that first church. And thus, the apostolic priesthood and the mystery of the Eucharist were sealed under the name of the Theotokos.

So, when we celebrate Hintsete Bete Kristiyan, we remember that every one of our parish churches, no matter how humble, stands on that same foundation laid in Philippi. Christ is the cornerstone, the Apostles are the foundation, and the prayers of the Theotokos are the unbreakable roof that shelters us all.

May the intercessions of our Holy Mother, the Virgin Mariam, whose first church was built by the hands of the Apostles and consecrated by her Son, protect you and keep you always.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

In the eighth year of the Lord’s reign, the apostles Paul and Barnabas, having preached the Gospel and baptized many Gentiles in Philippi, desired to build a holy place where the new believers might worship. But they did not act without heavenly guidance. Saint Peter, the Chief of the Apostles, and Saint John the Beloved, were summoned. And then O awe-striking wonder! the Lord, gathering both the living and the dead, brought together all His apostles in a divine convocation.

Christ our God appeared and said, “I have gathered you to teach you the manner in which churches are to be built throughout the earth in the name of My Mother.” He took them eastward and, with divine majesty, moved three stones into one foundation. He measured it: 24 cubits in height and 12 in width, a mystery in number and in spirit. These stones, soft as wax under divine fire, were fashioned into a church by the hands of the apostles, according to the command and guidance of the Lord.

On the following day, Sene 21, the Lord descended again with His Holy Mother, the Virgin Mary. She stood as the new Ark of the Covenant, holier than that of Moses. He ordained the apostles: Saint Peter as priest, Saint Stephen as deacon, and sanctified the Eucharistic mystery, causing the heavenly bread and cup to descend into that first church. And thus, the apostolic priesthood and the mystery of the Eucharist were sealed under the name of the Theotokos.

So, when we celebrate Hintsete Bete Kristiyan, we remember that every one of our parish churches, no matter how humble, stands on that same foundation laid in Philippi. Christ is the cornerstone, the Apostles are the foundation, and the prayers of the Theotokos are the unbreakable roof that shelters us all.

May the intercessions of our Holy Mother, the Virgin Mariam, whose first church was built by the hands of the Apostles and consecrated by her Son, protect you and keep you always.

The Orthodox Church lifts it high in glory, for in it we see both the humility of the Lord and the exaltation of mankind. Let us then unfold how the glory of the Cross is revealed among us.

text.text: 7. Making The Sign of the Cross as a Testimony of Faith

text:
When we Make and trace the holy sign of the Cross upon our bodies, we testify to the faith that has saved us. Moving the hand from the forehead to the chest, we confess that the eternal Son descended from the heavens and humbled Himself to dwell among men. Moving from the left shoulder to the right, we proclaim that humanity has been transferred from darkness to light, from death to life, and from the left hand of judgment to the right hand of glory.

Thus, every motion of the hand becomes a sermon. The Cross itself preaches to our souls that Christ “humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Therefore God also has highly exalted Him” (Phil. 2:8–9). Each time we make this holy seal, our earthly body is lifted up into the hope of the heavenly kingdom.

text.text: 8. The Cross as a Lesson for Children and the Faithful

text: making the sign of the Cross is not silent ritual but living instruction. At every moment before prayer, when entering the church, before sleep, or upon rising it reminds us of the sacrifice of Christ. For this reason the Church teaches children from their earliest days to make the sign cross themselves, so that the Cross may become their teacher and guardian. The Cross is both prayer and catechism, guiding the faithful to remember the Lord always.

text.text: 9. making the sign of Cross as a Proclamation of Christ’s Death

text:
✍🏾Each time when we make sign of Cross , we declare the death of the Lord. For it is written: “As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes” (1 Cor. 11:26). Indeed, in the Eucharist we proclaim His sacrifice, yet the Eucharist is not celebrated everywhere and at all times. But making the sign of the Cross can be made anywhere and at any time, were are never without a reminder of our Lord’s death and His saving work. Each time we make the sign of Cross, we proclaim that Christ was crucified for our salvation. By this holy sign, we not only remember His sacrifice but also confess our faith before heaven and earth.

✍🏾 Thus, the sign of the Cross becomes for us both a prayer and a shield, a constant act of worship, uniting our body and soul in the memory of the Lord’s passion and victory.

text.text: 10. The Cross as the Reminder of Sin and Salvation

text:
The Cross teaches us that “the wages of sin is death” (Rom. 6:23). Adam’s disobedience brought death into the world, but Christ who was without sin died upon the Cross to destroy death itself. Saint Paul proclaims: “Even when we were dead in trespasses, [God] made us alive together with Christ” (Eph. 2:5).

Each time we make the sign of the Cross, we remember both the seriousness of sin and the immeasurable mercy of God, who turned the curse into blessing and death into life. The sign of the Cross becomes both a warning and a deliverance teaching us to flee from sin and to embrace the life that is in Christ.

text.text: 11. Making the sign of Cross as the Measure of God’s Love

text: Above all, the Cross reveals divine love. “For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son” (John 3:16). Saint Paul echoes this: “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom. 5:8). Who can measure this love? Our Lord Himself declared: “Greater love has no one than this, than to lay down one’s life for his friends” (John 15:13). “Therefore, when we make the sign of the Cross, it reminds us of the depth of God’s love for usa love so great that it led Him to die upon the Cross.”

text.text: . Making the sign of Cross as Power and Victory

text: We make the sign of Cross because it is the sign of Christ’s victory over death and Satan. As St. Paul says, “The word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God” (1 Cor. 1:18). text.text: 13. The Cross as the Terror of Demons

text: The devil trembles at the sight of the Cross. For it was upon the tree of Golgotha that his age-long tyranny was shattered, his schemes made void, and his power brought to nothing. Just as in the wilderness the bronze serpent lifted by Moses brought healing to the Israelites (John 3:14), so the Cross of Christ brings deliverance and strikes fear into the enemy. When we make the sign, Satan remembers his defeat and flees. The Cross is for us the weapon of light, and for him the sign of everlasting humiliation.

Therefore, beloved, the glory of the Cross shines in every part of our Orthodox life. It is our faith, our lesson, our proclamation, our remembrance, our love, our power, and our victory. Let us never neglect this holy seal, but make it with reverence, with understanding, and with joy. For through it we confess the Lord who died and rose again for us, and through it we are made heirs of His eternal kingdom.

text: Dear beloved in Christ, peace be multiplied unto you. Today we reflect on the holy mystery of the Cross its glory as proclaimed by the Scriptures and confessed by the Orthodox Church. For the Cross, once a sign of shame, has become for us the throne of victory, the fountain of grace, and the ladder leading to heaven.

text.text: 14.making the sign of Cross as the Source of Blessing

text:
The whole world was once under the curse of sin, condemned to death. But our Lord bore the curse upon Himself on the Cross, that He might grant us blessing in its place reconciliation with God and the gift of new life. As St. Paul teaches: “For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of His Son, much more, having been reconciled, we shall be saved by His life” (Rom. 5:10).

Thus, every blessing of the New Covenant flows from the Cross. For this reason, our priests bless the faithful with the Cross, declaring that it is not from their own hands, but from the Crucified High Priest Himself, Jesus Christ. We venerate the Cross not as wood, but as the sign of Christ’s blessing and grace.

text.text: 15. The cross is present in every mystery.

text:
The mystery of the Cross is present in every mystery of the Church. All the Mysteries draw their power and grace from the blood that our Lord Jesus Christ shed upon the Cross.

Without the Cross, we would not have the blessing of becoming children of God through the sacrament of Baptism. Without the Cross, we would not have the privilege of partaking in His holy Body and Blood in the sacrament of the Eucharist. Without the Cross, we would not receive the grace that flows through the other sacraments of the Church.

Therefore, when our fathers and priests bless the mysteries with the Cross, we too draw near in faith, so that we may receive the grace our Lord has given and honor His holy mysteries.

text.text: 16. The Cross as Our Glory and Fellowship with Christ

text: The Apostle cries: “I have been crucified with Christ” (Gal. 2:20). To be joined to Christ is to share in His sufferings, as St. Paul again says: “That I may know Him and the power of His resurrection, and the fellowship of His sufferings” (Phil. 3:10). The thief, too, who was crucified beside Christ and confessed Him, entered Paradise through the Cross. Thus, we make the sign Cross, for it is the sign of our union and friendship with the Lord.

text.text: 17, Because of the Joy of Our Father, We Make the Sign of the Cross

text:
The Father accepted our Lord Jesus Christ on the Cross as a sin offering and a burnt offering that pleased Him. “It is a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, a sweet savour before the Lord” (Lev. 1:9). Therefore, the prophet Isaiah said, “When He made His soul an offering for sin…the will of the Lord was done in Him” (Is. 53:10).

Our Lord Jesus Christ pleased the Father throughout His earthly life, but He brought this to perfection on the Cross. “And being found in fashion as a man, He humbled Himself and became obedient to death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8). We always look to the Cross, where His perfect obedience was fulfilled, so that we may imitate Christ by becoming obedient even to death. This reminds us of His obedience.

The Cross of our Lord was a joy to the Father and to the crucified Son. Therefore, the apostle explains the joy of the Lord, saying: “For the joy that was set before Him, He endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of God” (Heb. 12:2). The fullness of Christ’s joy was on the Cross, and we too, in order to share in the joy of the Cross of Christ, we make the sign of the Cross.

18. The Cross as Our Reproach and Pilgrimage

text: To follow Christ is to take up His reproach. Moses, the prophet, chose “the reproach of Christ” above the treasures of Egypt (Heb. 11:26). We, too, when we make the sign of the Cross, remember that this life is a pilgrimage: we must endure suffering with the people of God rather than chase the fleeting pleasures of sin. The Cross reminds us that we are on a journey, bearing reproach, until we meet the Lord face to face.

text.text: 19. we make the sign of cross because The Cross is the Sign of His Second Coming

text:

✍🏾Beloved in Christ, let us approach the mystery of the Cross with trembling hearts, for in it is revealed both the depth of human sin and the unfathomable mercy of God.

✍🏾Before our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the Cross was only an instrument of cruelty and shame. History tells us that the practice of crucifixion began in Persia, where they worshipped the earth-god Ormuzd. Believing their god would be defiled if a criminal were executed on the ground, they lifted the condemned above the earth, fastening him to wood. From there, this torment spread until it became the dreaded law of Rome. Furthermore, in the Torah, those who were executed on a cross were considered accursed. “If anyone commits a sin deserving death, and you hang him on a tree, his body shall not remain all night upon the tree, for he who is hanged is accursed of God” (Deut. 21:22–23).

text.text: Then a question rises in our hearts: if those hanged upon wood are cursed, why did our Lord die on the Cross

text:
?

✍🏾Our Lord was crucified because we were under the curse. All humanity had fallen into corruption of body and soul, enslaved to the grave, to sin, and to death. We were condemned, lost, and unable to rise again. Yet our Creator, who leaves the ninety-nine to seek the one that has gone astray (Matt. 18:12–14), descended from heaven to find us.

👉🏾He was conceived by the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin Mary (Luke 1:35).

👉🏾He took flesh from her, our true Mother, and was born in Bethlehem (Luke 2:7).

👉🏾In His incarnation, God became man (Matt. 16:13; 1 John 1:1–2; 5:20).

👉🏾He grew as a child among us (Luke 2:40).

👉🏾At the age of thirty, He was baptized in the Jordan, fasted forty days and nights, chose His apostles, elders, and women disciples (Matt. 3:13–17; Luke 3:21–23; Acts 1:15).

👉🏾For three years and three months, He taught the Gospel of the Kingdom.

👉🏾At last, He gave His body to be broken, His blood to be shed, His soul to be offered, and willingly endured the Cross for our salvation (Mark 15:23–37; John 10:11; 19:30).

✍🏾Thus, He took upon Himself the curse that was ours, so that the curse might be lifted from us. As Isaiah prophesied: “Surely He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; He was wounded for our transgressions, bruised for our iniquities; the chastisement of our peace was upon Him, and with His stripes we are healed” (Is. 53:4–5).

✍🏾

“Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree” (Gal. 3:13). Yet Christ bore that curse to destroy it. Again he said, “He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Cor. 5:21). And in Philippians, “He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, and humbled Himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:7–8).

✍🏾

: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in His mouth. When reviled, He did not revile in return; when He suffered, He did not threaten, but committed Himself to Him who judges righteously. He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live for righteousness by whose stripes you were healed” (1 Pet. 2:22–24).

text: Beloved children of the Holy Orthodox Church, let your hearts be lifted to the mystery of the Cross the tree of life planted anew in the place where Adam fell. Through it, death was slain by death, and corruption was trampled by incorruptibility. Let us behold with trembling joy the purpose of our Lord’s crucifixion and death, for every wound of His flesh became the healing of the nations.

text.text: 2. The Cross Restores the Food of Life

text:
Sin entered the world and brought death because of food.
In Genesis 3:1–24, Adam and Eve ate the fruit of the fig tree and brought death upon humankind. Likewise, in 1 Kings 13:20–25, the man of Judah who was sent to rebuke Jeroboam lost his life because he disobeyed and ate what was forbidden.

The manna that the Israelites ate in the wilderness did not save them from death (John 6:49). Therefore, Jesus gave us His own flesh as the Bread of Life on the cross, so that whoever eats of it may not die. He confirmed this when He said:

“Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, you have no life in yourselves. Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life.” (John 6:53–54)

Thus, the Holy Eucharist, which is offered daily in the Church and received in faith, is the true Body and true Blood of Jesus Christ. The bread is changed and becomes His flesh, and the wine is changed and becomes His blood (Matthew 26:27–29).

That is why the Apostle Paul warned:

“Whoever eats this bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person examine himself, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For whoever eats and drinks in an unworthy manner eats and drinks judgment on himself, not discerning the body of the Lord.” (1 Corinthians 11:27–30)

When the Lord stretched out His hands upon the wood, He bridged heaven and earth. His arms became the measure of reconciliation. “Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you—not as the world gives” (John 14:27). This peace was not written on parchment or decreed by kings; it was written in blood upon the wood of the Cross.

The Apostle Paul reveals this mystery: “Through Him, God reconciled all things to Himself, making peace through the blood of His Cross.” (Col. 1:19–20) The blood that flowed down Calvary is the river that quenched the fire of enmity. Once we were far off wandering in the shadow of wrath but now we have been brought near by the blood of Christ, who Himself is our peace (Eph. 2:13–14).

When the risen Lord appeared to His disciples, His first words were : “Peace be with you.” (John 20:19) Thus, every time the faithful bow before the Cross, they receive not terror, but tranquility the peace purchased at so great a price.

Through the redemption accomplished on the cross, our bodies once burdened by sin and curse have been made new. The Apostle Paul declares,

“We know that our old self was crucified with Him, so that the body of sin might be done away with, that we should no longer be slaves to sin.” (Romans 6:6)

Again, he writes,

“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

As St. Paul teaches, our Lord has renewed us through His redemption, given us a new covenant through the Gospel, promised us a new heaven and a new earth, and prepared for us the eternal kingdom of heaven (Mark 1:15; 2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1).
