Beloved in the Lord, peace be to you in the name of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Let every soul who hears these words incline the ear of the heart, for we speak not of an earthly thing, but of the mystery by which heaven and earth were reconciled the Cross of our Lord, upon which the salvation of all creation was accomplished.

Through the Cross, we have received reconciliation, redemption, and power. That wood, despised by the world, has become our crown of victory and the weapon of the faithful.

text.text: The Cross Is Our Strength and the Power of God

text:
The Cross: Fountain of Power and Glory

“For the word of the Cross is foolishness to those who perish,” says the Apostle Paul, “but to us who are being saved it is the power of God” (1 Cor. 1:18). The Cross is not an ornament of wood or metal; it is the instrument by which death was slain and life restored. The blood that flowed upon it was not the blood of a mere man, but of Him who is both God and Lord. Therefore, the Cross is glorious, not because of its shape or substance, but because upon it the Savior stretched His holy body and poured out His precious blood.

Just as the donkey that bore Christ into Jerusalem was adorned with honor because it carried the King of Glory, so too the Cross, though simple wood, became glorious because it bore the Lord of heaven. Upon it, divine power was revealed. Through it, believers crush the devil, for the prophecy was fulfilled: “He shall crush your head” (Gen. 3:15). This victory was fulfilled upon the Cross. Christ, the second Adam, broke the power of the devil and cast down the dominion of death.

text.text: The Cross: the Cross in the Old Testament

text:
Moses, the chief of the prophets, prefigured this mystery. When he stretched out his hands in the form of a Cross, Israel prevailed over her enemies (Exodus 17:11). Likewise, the faithful spiritual Israel gain victory over the demons through the sign of the Cross.

When Jacob, the father of the twelve tribes, crossed his hands to bless the sons of Joseph (Genesis 48:13–20), he too foreshadowed the blessing of the Cross, through which our bodies and souls are sanctified.

text.text: The Cross: The Devil’s Defeated Enemy

text:
Even now, the adversary seeks to strip the Church of the Cross, saying mockingly, “Is it not wood? Why do you venerate it?” But the faithful do not honor the material wood or metal but the divine power manifest through it. For in every age, God has chosen visible signs to reveal His might:

The rod of Moses turned water into blood and divided the sea (Exodus 4:14).

The mantle of Elijah parted the Jordan (2 Kings 2:7–14).

The Jordan River healed Naaman of his leprosy (2 Kings 5:1–14).

The oil of anointing restored the sick (Mark 6:13; James 5:14).

The pool of

opened the eyes of the blind (John 9:1–12).

The garments of Paul cast out demons and healed diseases (Acts 19:11–12).

If these instruments, touched by grace, became vessels of divine power, how much more the Cross upon which the Blood of God Himself was shed!

text.text: The Cross: Our Shield and Boast

text:
As the Psalmist declared, “You have given a sign to those who fear You, that they may flee from the bow, ” (Ps. 59:4–5). The Cross is this sign. It shields us from the arrows of the evil one, it guards the soul, it fortifies the faithful against despair.

So Paul cried out with holy boldness: “God forbid that I should boast except in the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world is crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). The Cross separates us from the vanity of the world, teaching us to die to sin and live unto righteousness.

Many regard the Cross merely as a symbol but to the faithful it is power, peace, and life. Through it, we are redeemed; by it, we are saved.

The Feast of the Cross and Its Discovery

text:
The Feast of the Cross, celebrated on the 17th of Meskerem, recalls not only Christ’s death and resurrection but also the miraculous rediscovery of the Cross itself.

After Christ’s passion, many were healed by touching the wood of His Cross. But when the unbelieving Jews saw the miracles, they hid the Cross in a garbage heap. Over time, the place was forgotten. In 70 AD, after Jerusalem’s destruction, it became unrecognizable, and for three centuries, the Cross lay buried beneath the dust of men’s indifference.

Then, in the fourth century, holy Queen Eleni, mother of Emperor Constantine, journeyed to Jerusalem, inspired by divine zeal to find the precious Cross. Guided by an aged man named Kyriakos, she poured incense upon the ground, and a fragrant smoke rose like a rainbow, revealing the sacred spot. Excavations began on Meskerem 17 and concluded on Megabit 10, when the Cross was finally raised in triumph. A great church was built there and consecrated again on the 17th of Meskerem the day we celebrate its discovery.

text.text: The Cross in Ethiopia: A Living Witness

text:
we celebrate the Feast of the Holy Cross by lighting candles, praying, and standing in reverence before God. This celebration is not only a tradition but a way to honor the great miracles performed through the Cross.

Historically, when the great kings of that time witnessed the wonders of the Cross, they divided it into four parts so that each could receive a portion. Of these four parts, only the section where the right hand of Christ rested was placed in Debre Kerbe, Geshen Maryam, while the whereabouts of the other three remain unknown.

This sacred Cross was brought to Ethiopia by Emperor David in the 14th century. Upon its arrival, those who sought to build a temple for it found the ground shaking, and no structure could be completed. After many prayers, God revealed, “Place my Cross in the place of Cross.” Miraculously, the place was discovered in the shape of a cross at a place called Debre Kerbe, in Geshen, where it remains to this day.

Because countless people have received blessings from this holy Cross, it is important for us to celebrate this feast with proper reverence and dignity. By doing so, we honor God and participate in the grace that flows from this sacred symbol.

Let us, therefore, hold fast to the Cross, not as an ornament, but as the sign of our salvation. Through it, death was slain, sin was destroyed, and peace was restored between God and mankind.

The Cross is the throne of divine mercy, the key of Paradise, the banner of victory, and the bridge that leads the faithful from death to life. Whoever clings to it with faith partakes of the power that shattered hell and opened heaven.

text: Beloved children of the Orthodox faith, let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the intercession of His Mother, and the blessings of the saints rest upon your hearts. Hear, then, a word concerning the Tsege Fast a season radiant with the light of repentance and adorned with the fragrance of obedience.

text.text: The Time and Meaning of the Tsige Fast

text:
From the 26th day of Meskerem to the 5th day of Hidar, the Church calls these forty days the month of Tsige .

This fast commemorates the journey of the Virgin Mary and the Child Jesus into Egypt, as revealed to Joseph in a dream:

"The angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph, saying, ‘Arise, take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, for they seek the young child’s life.’" (Matthew 2:13)
And so, during these days, the faithful remember the exile and return of the Holy Family, and share in the sorrows and triumphs of that sacred pilgrimage.

text.text: The Nature and Purpose of Fasting

text:
The Fetha Negest declares:

“Fasting is abstinence from food on a certain day and at a certain time, for the forgiveness of sins, obedience to divine command, the weakening of carnal desire, and the subjection of the flesh to the soul.”

Fasting, therefore, is not a burden but a weapon of the spirit, a bridle upon the flesh, and a discipline that grants freedom. The holy Father Isaac writes:

“Fasting is the healing of the soul, the strengthening of the spirit, the mother of prayer, the fountain of tears, the beginning of all virtues, the helper of humility, and the crown of purity.”

Through fasting, the soul learns obedience; the heart softens, and the mind becomes as clear water before the face of God. It is through the hunger of the body that the soul begins to feast upon divine grace.

(Part 1)

Beloved children of the Orthodox faith, let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the intercession of His Mother, and the blessings of the saints rest upon your hearts. Hear, then, a word concerning the Tsege Fast a season radiant with the light of repentance and adorned with the fragrance of obedience.

The Time and Meaning of the Tsige Fast

From the 26th day of Meskerem to the 5th day of Hidar, the Church calls these forty days the month of Tsige .

This fast commemorates the journey of the Virgin Mary and the Child Jesus into Egypt, as revealed to Joseph in a dream:

"The angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph, saying, ‘Arise, take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, for they seek the young child’s life.’" (Matthew 2:13)
And so, during these days, the faithful remember the exile and return of the Holy Family, and share in the sorrows and triumphs of that sacred pilgrimage.

The Nature and Purpose of Fasting

The Fetha Negest declares:

“Fasting is abstinence from food on a certain day and at a certain time, for the forgiveness of sins, obedience to divine command, the weakening of carnal desire, and the subjection of the flesh to the soul.”

Fasting, therefore, is not a burden but a weapon of the spirit, a bridle upon the flesh, and a discipline that grants freedom. The holy Father Isaac writes:

“Fasting is the healing of the soul, the strengthening of the spirit, the mother of prayer, the fountain of tears, the beginning of all virtues, the helper of humility, and the crown of purity.”

Through fasting, the soul learns obedience; the heart softens, and the mind becomes as clear water before the face of God. It is through the hunger of the body that the soul begins to feast upon divine grace.

The Two Great Orders of Fasting

There are, according to the sacred canon, two kinds of fasting: public and private.

Public Fasting

Public fasting is decreed for all the faithful. There are seven such fasts:

1. The Great Fast (Abiy tsom )

2. The Fast of the Apostles ( Tsome Hawaryat )

3. The Fast of the Assumption (St. Mary’s Fast) Tsome Felseta

4. The Fast of the Prophets (Tsome Nebiyat)

5. The Fast of Gehad or gad )

6. The Fast of Nineveh( Tsome Nenewe)

7. Tsome Dihnet :-The Weekly Fast (Wednesdays and Fridays)

Fasting, though appointed for certain months and seasons, is far more than a ritual observance. It is the very foundation of righteousness, the gate that opens toward heaven, and the daily breath of Christian life. For this reason, there are monks and hermits who dwell in monasteries and deserts, fasting not only during the prescribed fasts but throughout the entire year, offering their hunger as a sacrifice of love to God.

Continues 👇🏾

text:
The Holy Scripture declares:

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.” (Matthew 5:6)
“Listen to me, you who seek righteousness, you who seek the Lord.” (Isaiah 41:55)

When practiced rightly, fasting disciplines the body and trains the soul. It strengthens the will, humbles pride, and prepares the heart for divine grace. Thus, the faithful are led from outward fasting to inward fasting from the discipline of the flesh to the training of the spirit. This is the second kind of fasting: personal fasting, offered privately before God, in secret devotion and holy purpose.

Private fasting is a sacred practice performed secretly by believers to whom God has granted strength and spiritual discernment. When a person has a deep need before the Lord, they fast privately disciplining their body, humbling their heart, and seeking divine mercy. This type of fasting is often done under the guidance of one’s spiritual father, especially in times of repentance.

This tradition has existed since ancient times. The great prophets Moses, Daniel, David, and Nehemiah each fasted before God in secret. In the New Testament, Saint Paul and Saint Peter also practiced personal fasting, offering their solitude and hunger as prayer before the Almighty.

Private fasting is divided into two types: penitential fasting and voluntary fasting.

Penitential fasting is undertaken after a believer has confessed their sins and received a canon (a spiritual rule or period of fasting) from their father of confession. It is done privately, without display or announcement, as a hidden act of repentance before God. In this fast, the believer seeks purification of the soul and reconciliation with the Creator, as it is written: “Your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.” (Matthew 6:18)

Voluntary fasting, also called the fast of virtue, is an act of devotion performed either privately or communally. It is observed by those who serve God with diligence individual believers, communities of the faithful, and monks living in monasteries. They fast not out of obligation, but from love and spiritual longing.

Believers practice voluntary fasting for many reasons:
—to remove problems from their personal and family lives, and to lift obstacles that hinder peace in their church and their nation.
—to bring the body under control, as the psalmist David said: “I have humbled my soul with fasting.” (Psalm 35:13)
—for God often grants greater blessings when one asks in humility for little.
—to ask the Creator for strength and guidance in carrying out spiritual duties.

—by remembering sacred events, meditating on the sufferings of the saints, and cleansing the soul from sin.

Throughout the generations, many monks, nuns, and devout believers have kept voluntary fasts with great zeal. Among these are the Tsige Fast (Tsome Tsige) observed from Meskerem 26 to Hidar 5 and the Fast of Yodit (Tsome Yodit), kept during the month of Pagume . These fasts, though not required by law, are embraced out of love, faith, and a longing for deeper communion with God.

text: The Tsige Fast is a holy period observed for forty days, from Meskerem 26 to Hidar 5. This sacred season is called the Month of Tsige a time filled with prayer, hymns, and praise. During these days, the Scriptures read in every church, the psalms sung, the sermons preached, and the homilies delivered all reflect the beauty of the heavens, as though the sky itself were adorned with stars in celebration of God’s glory.

text.text: The Origin of the Tsige Fast

text:
The spiritual foundation of this fast comes from the angelic message delivered to Joseph in a dream:

“Arise, take the young Child and His mother, and flee to Egypt, for they are seeking to destroy the Child.” (Matthew 2:13)

Obedient to the command, Joseph took the Child Jesus and the Virgin Mary and fled into Egypt. After three years of exile, they returned to their homeland, Nazareth, as it is written in Revelation 12:16.
The Tsige Fast, therefore, commemorates this holy journey the suffering, exile, and eventual return of the Virgin Mary and her Son. It is a season to remember her endurance, her faith, and her unwavering obedience to God.

Abba Tsige Birhan, who lived in the 14th century, expressed deep reverence for the Virgin’s suffering, saying:

“O Mary, the fragrance of the pomegranate and the flower of the day, your face pale with fasting and sorrow how I long to share in your hardships, your tears, and your suffering, that I too may share in your endless joy.”

Likewise, Abba Arke Silus, in his Lamentations of the Virgin, wrote:

“O Holy Virgin Mary, daughter of light who wears the sun, when you fled with your Son from the evil Herod, the roads you walked burned with heat, and even the stones wept at your pain.”

These reflections reveal the deep compassion and love with which the faithful remember the Virgin’s trials during her exile.

text.text: The Celebration of the Tsige Fast and Liturgy

text:
The Month of Tsige is observed in the Church with liturgy (Mahelet), hymns, and Zikr (commemorative praise).

Each week, from Saturday evening until Sunday morning, priests perform hymns drawn from St. Yared’s Degwa, Mahelete Tsige, and Sekokawe Dingel. These hymns are arranged from three parts praise ( kidus yared diguwa, mahlete tsige, sekokawe dingl) expressing both the sorrow and the triumph of the Virgin.

Although the Zikr of Tsige has become rare in some urban areas, many rural communities still preserve it. Every Sunday, believers gather in a central place to commemorate the Virgin. The poor, the weak, and travelers are invited to eat and drink in her name, continuing the ancient Ethiopian tradition of hospitality shown to Our Lady when she came to the land of Ethiopia.

text.text: The Story of Abba Tsige Birhan and Abba Gebre Mariam

text:
According to Abune Zena Markos Zena Gedel, Abba Tsige Birhan was a devout father who composed one hundred and fifty hymns for the Mahelet Tsige, following the number of David’s Psalms. His companion and advisor, Abba Gebre Mariam of Wereilu and Debre Hanta, joined him in this holy labor.
Every year, from Meskerem 26 to Hidar 5, they would journey to Debre Bisrat to observe the Mahelete Tsige and keep the fast together in prayer and devotion. Afterward, they would return to their monasteries, renewed in spirit.

From their example, the practice of fasting and celebrating the Tsige Liturgy began to spread slowly among churches, monks, and devout believers. By their witness, a new season of voluntary fasting entered the life of the Ethiopian Church.

text.text: The Practice of the Tsige Fast Today

text: In our own time, the Tsige Liturgy continues to be observed during this holy month. The church bell is rung at three o’clock in the night , calling the faithful men, women, and children to gather in worship. The service is held with the beating of drums and cymbals, and the Mahelete Tsige is sung until twelve o'clock morning , filling the air with the sound of reverence and joy.

text.text: The Nature of the Tsige Fast

text:
The Tsige Fast is voluntary, not obligatory. It is a fast observed out of devotion and love, in remembrance of the Virgin’s suffering and exile. No one is required to keep it by commandment; rather, it is embraced by those who are moved by faith.

Those who fast must not judge those who do not, for fasting is a personal offering. The one who fasts does so unto God; the one who cannot fast should still honor the Virgin in thanksgiving, remembering her pilgrimage and singing her praises.

Whether by fasting or by thanksgiving, every believer is called to remember the Virgin’s faith, her endurance, and the divine mystery revealed in her life.

The second voluntary fast, kept in the month of Pagumen, is the Fast of Yodit (Judith). This fast recalls the righteous Judith who, through fasting and prayer, received strength from God to conquer her enemies (Judith 8:2–7). So the faithful fast in this final month of the year, that they too might receive power over sin and Satan, preparing for the transition from this world to the next just as Pagumen marks the transition of years.

Fasting without humility is an empty shadow. The true fast is not of the lips or stomach alone, but of the heart. The believer must fast with compassion, give alms to the poor, restrain anger, forgive offenses, and keep the tongue from deceit. Let fasting be united with mercy, prayer, and repentance, that it may ascend as sweet incense before the throne of God.

As the fathers teach: “When you fast, do not fast for vain praise, but that your fasting may be a fasting of mercy, wherein you find help, blessing, and the grace of God.”

text: Indeed, my beloved brethren in Christ, let us turn our minds and hearts to the profound mystery of the Holy Cross, that venerable standard of our salvation, upon which our Lord Jesus Christ, the King of Glory, wrought our redemption. Let us delve into the sacred narrative, drawing forth lessons from the very words presented to us, much as a bee gathers nectar from the most fragrant blossoms.

When our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ saw His beloved disciples and His Most Holy Mother standing at the foot of the cross, His heart was not merely concerned with His own suffering, but with the care and comfort of those He loved.

He said to His Mother:

 "Behold your son, your helper, your comforter."

And to His beloved disciple John, He said:

"Behold your Mother, your comforter."

By this sacred act, He gave us all to her, making her the Mother of the faithful. This moment teaches us that the cross, though an instrument of suffering, is also a vessel of divine care, uniting all believers as a family under the protection of the Mother of God.

text.text: The Meaning of the Feast of the Cross

text:
Beyond the beauty and joy that mark the Feast of the Cross, it is important to understand its deeper meaning where it comes from and the blessings it brings through the Holy Word. Like Saint John, whose heart burned with love for the Cross, and Saint Eleni, who was depicted as sharing in its suffering, we are called to look upon the Cross with reverence and gratitude. As the women of Jerusalem stood with the Virgin Mary and heard the words, “Behold, your mother,” so too did Eleni rise up, three centuries later, to bring the Cross out of hiding and share its blessing with the world.

Saint Eleni, who truly understood the mystery and power of the Cross, succeeded in her holy mission. She uncovered the Cross from its burial place, and through her faith, it became a light to the whole world. For whoever glories in the Cross is never ashamed.

The Apostle Paul declared, “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, by whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14). While Saint Eleni was still reflecting deeply on this truth, her son, Emperor Constantine, saw a sign in the sky a radiant Cross bearing the words, “By this sign, you will conquer.”

Throughout her life, Eleni had been grieved that the Cross had been hidden through envy and deceit. Yet she prayed with steadfast faith and longing that it might be revealed once more. God answered her prayer, and through the power of the Cross, the good news of victory and salvation was made known. text:
During the reign of Emperor Diocletian, Christians endured great persecution throughout the Roman Empire. The city of Jerusalem had already been destroyed by the Romans in 70 A.D., and later, under Diocletian’s rule, new decrees were issued to suppress the faith. Churches were closed, temples of idols were opened, holy books were burned, church property was seized, and Christians were dismissed from their jobs. If they were wronged, they were forbidden to seek justice in court. These were days of sorrow and trial for the followers of Christ.

In this dark time, the mercy of God was revealed through a heavenly vision. The cross a symbol of victory appeared in the sky to Emperor Constantine, shining with divine light. Through this miraculous sign, the Lord granted freedom to all Christians who were suffering under the decrees of oppression. Strengthened by the power of the cross, Constantine overcame the pagan rulers who shared authority in the Roman Empire.

After his victory, Constantine abolished the decree of destruction and issued a new decree of freedom. The glory of the Church was restored through the message of the Gospel, which triumphed over the old decree of impurity. He granted the Church exemption from taxes, a share of the state’s revenue, and the right to inherit from those who confessed the faith. Sunday was declared a holy day of rest and worship, and bishops were given full authority to govern the Christian people. Through these acts, the Church found peace and freedom under the protection of the cross.

text.text: Saint Eleni’s Devotion and the Discovery of the Cross

text:
Saint Eleni, the mother of Constantine, was also moved by a deep love for the cross. Like the Virgin Mary and Saint John who stood at Calvary, she set out for that sacred place with devotion and faith. There, she was guided by a man named Kirakos, who instructed her to:

Light a fire (Demera).

Offer incense.

Observe the smoke as a sign.

Dig at the site of cross.

By following these divine instructions, Saint Eleni discovered the exact location of the Holy Cross on Meskerem 16. Excavation began on Meskerem 17 and continued until Megabit 10. At last, the true cross of our Lord Jesus Christ was revealed to the world, bringing joy and light to all believers.

From that time on, history records that countless miracles were performed through the power of the Holy Cross, confirming its truth and sanctity. The love and faith of Saint Eleni stand as a testimony for all generations a reminder that through perseverance and devotion, the glory of God is always revealed to those who seek Him with all their hearts.

text.text: Reflection on the Love of the Cross

text:
As we have seen above, those who truly understood the love of the cross such as Saint Eleni embraced it with deep faith and sacrifice. She sought it not for her own glory, but for the glory of God and for the strengthening of the faithful. Through six long months of tireless searching, prayer, and devotion, she uncovered the hidden cross and revealed it to the world, leaving it as a precious gift for all generations to rejoice in.

We, too, must embrace this love. Christianity demands sacrifice, prayer, and steadfast devotion. We are called to honor the cross and follow Christ with our whole heart.

Saint Paul warns us:

"Men, before whose eyes our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ was clearly set forth, crucified. Who has bewitched you to disobey the truth?" (Galatians 3:1)

Let this admonition pierce our hearts. Are we truly faithful to the cross, or do the cares of the world divert our attention?

May God, in His mercy, grant us understanding of the meaning and love of the cross. Let us receive it with reverence, abide in His house, and inherit His eternal kingdom. The cross is not merely wood or a symbol; it is the source of salvation, the treasure of the faithful, and the path to eternal joy.

Rejoice, beloved, in the cross, for through it we are redeemed, sanctified, and called into eternal fellowship with Christ. Amen.

text.text: The Cross: The Throne of Divine Love

text:
Saint Paul called the love of the Cross “truth,” Under this heavenly truth different from the fleeting truth of the world our Lady stood with St. John at Calvary. Centuries later, St. Eleni, moved by that same love, journeyed from Rome to Jerusalem to find the precious Cross. Many saints carried Calvary within their hearts. Likewise, faithful Ethiopians, enduring great hardship, traveled to Calvary in spirit and fulfilled their vows out of love for the Cross.

Even those who could not go in person journeyed there through faith. In their prayer and devotion, they stood beside the Virgin and St. John, beholding in spirit the crucified Lord and hearing His tender words: “Behold, your Son your help and your comfort.”

text.text: The Mother and the Disciple: A New Household Born at Calvary

text:
When Jesus said to His Mother, “Woman, behold your son,” and to John, “Behold your mother,” He did more than bind two sorrowing hearts together. He inaugurated a new kinship the family of faith gathered at the foot of the Cross.

Mary became mother not to John alone, but to all disciples who would stand by Christ in faith and sorrow. Her motherhood extends to all who receive her Son’s love, all who remain near the Cross when others flee. Thus, when John took her “to his own home,” he carried within that home the heart of the Church itself. The word “your mother” was spoken not to a single disciple but to every soul redeemed by the Crucified.

Even now, two thousand years hence, all who believe and travel in spirit to Calvary find themselves beneath that same Cross. In tears and prayer, they stand beside the Virgin and John, and they too hear the words: “Behold your mother.” For Christ gave her to us that we might not walk alone, but be comforted by her intercession, her steadfast faith, and her maternal love.

text.text: The Pilgrimage of the Heart: Traveling to Calvary in Spirit

text:
Not all can walk the stones of Jerusalem or touch the soil of Golgotha, yet the journey to Calvary is not measured by footsteps but by longing. Saint Eleni journeyed from Rome to Jerusalem because her heart was aflame with the love of the Cross, and God granted her to find the very wood on which the Savior hung. The Ethiopians, through hardship and endurance, made that same pilgrimage not for spectacle, but for love.

Those who cannot travel with their bodies may still journey in spirit, as the saints did, embracing the Cross through prayer, contrition, and love. On the feast of the Holy Cross, the faithful are invited to ascend the hill of Calvary with the heart. It is not by hand or foot that we reach it, but by tears and faith. Even distant lands become holy ground when hearts rise to the Cross.

text.text: The Cross: The House of Divine Wisdom

text:
The Cross is not only the throne of love but the house of wisdom. Solomon, the ancient king, spoke in figures when he said: “Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn her seven pillars; she has prepared her table.” (Proverbs 9:1–2) The fullness of that wisdom was revealed upon the Cross, where the Bread of Life was broken for the salvation of the world.

The true table prepared by Wisdom was the altar of the Cross, upon which Christ, the Lamb without blemish, offered Himself. There the eternal mystery was unveiled: the crucified One is the wisdom of God, despised by the proud but adored by the humble. Thus Saint Paul declared, “The Jews ask for a sign, and the Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified.” (1 Corinthians 1:22–23)

The wisdom of the Cross calls all who would live not to worldly cleverness but to divine understanding to leave ignorance and walk in the light of sacrificial love.

text.text: The Cross: The Banner of Freedom and the Emblem of the Faithful

text:
Every kingdom on earth has its flag, but the Cross is the banner of heaven. To the world it appears as an emblem of suffering; to the faithful it is the sign of victory, freedom, and eternal life. Upon it, Christ conquered death and shattered the tyranny of the devil. It is the flag of liberty for every soul once enslaved by sin.

The Cross marks the Christian as belonging not to this world but to the Kingdom of God. To trace its sign upon our bodies is to confess both our allegiance and our hope. Just as the flag of a nation rallies its people, so the Cross gathers all believers under its shadow. It unites the saints of every age, the martyrs, the mothers, the pilgrims all who have borne its sign in faith and patience.

text.text: The Blessing of the Cross: Living Under Its Shadow

text:
Blessed are they who understand the mystery of the Cross, for they abide in the dwelling of divine love. Whether they walk upon Calvary’s hill or dwell in distant lands, the grace of the Cross reaches them. To desire it, to honor it, to weep beneath its shadow this is to be present with Christ Himself.

Let us, then, take up the Cross not merely as ornament but as calling; not merely as memory but as power. For through it, wisdom descended, truth triumphed, and love reigned forever.

text.text: I. The Glory of the Cross

text:
In our country, the special celebration of Meskere
 16 and 17, which is celebrated together with the beauty of the

, reveals the power of God through the Holy Cross. How wonderful is the Cross! The wood on which it was carved is united with the power of God, forming a remarkable and sacred symbol of the redemption of Christians. Even the demons are powerless before it, and its glorious grace is granted only to those chosen to receive its power.

Saint Paul reminds us, “The word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God” (1 Corinthians 1:18).

text.text: II. The Mother Beneath the Cross

text:
At the foot of the Cross stood the Virgin, the Mother of the Lord, her heart pierced not by iron alone, but by the anguish of divine compassion. In the Gospel of John, it is written: “When Jesus saw His mother and the disciple whom He loved standing by, He said to His mother, ‘Woman, behold your son!’ Then He said to the disciple, ‘Behold your mother!’” (John 19:26–27).

In that sacred moment, the Lord gave to the world two gifts: the maternal love of His Mother and the brotherly care of His beloved disciple. The Virgin, full of grace, became mother not to one Son, but to all who stand beneath the Cross. Her sorrow was deep as the ocean, her heart steadfast as a pillar of light amid the world’s darkness. Her love surpasses all human love combined; her gentleness reflects divine innocence. She is the dove of mercy, interceding for the children of men before her crucified Son.

Who understood pain like her? Let us implore the Virgin Mary as our intercessor, so that we may come to understand the love of the Cross. Let us remember the covenant of her five sorrows, for the trials of this world call us to imitate her. May we follow her example of love, compassion, and gentleness, so that we may please her Son, our Lord. My people, let us abandon grudges, malice, deceit, envy, racism, and all such evils, for they profit neither this world nor the next.

text.text: III. The Beloved Disciple and the Love of the Cross

text:
Today, let us make Saint John a model of the love of the Cross. He understood divine love, rooted himself in the Cross, and bore witness to the depth of the Lord’s suffering. His heart was always with the Cross, and he teaches us to remember the profound mysteries of God’s love for mankind, such as the truth that “God is love,” and to live in the practical guidance of the Holy Spirit.

In light of the story of the Cross, the lives of the Virgin Mary and Saint John were sanctified by their love for God. As Saint John reminds us in his letter: “Do not love the world or the things in the world… The love of the Father abides forever; the world and its desires pass away, but whoever does the will of God abides forever” (1 John 2:15, 17). While living in this world, we must live in love, immersed in the passion of the Cross. Our spiritual service should reflect the light of the Cross, our gatherings should be an invitation to God, and our work should be carried out in love.

text.text: IV. The Virgin and the Disciple: Icons of Perfect Love

text:
In the Virgin’s grief and the disciple’s steadfastness, the Church beholds a union of love and obedience. She represents maternal compassion; he, the loyalty of friendship sanctified by faith. Together, they reveal that the Cross is not only the means of redemption but the school of divine love.

The Virgin’s compassion teaches gentleness in the face of cruelty, patience in sorrow, and intercession for sinners. Saint John’s example calls believers to embrace the Cross daily, to meditate upon its mysteries, and to measure every action by its shadow. In them, divine love and human faith meet the perfect response to divine suffering.

V. The Cross as the Pattern of Christian Life

text:
The Cross is the law of love written in suffering. It is the path through which obedience becomes joy and death becomes life. Christ, by humbling Himself unto death, fulfilled all righteousness. His obedience on the Cross became the cure for Adam’s disobedience. Hence, the Cross stands as the everlasting covenant between heaven and earth, abolishing the curse of sin and restoring the soul’s harmony with its Maker.

The believer who bears his own cross walks in the footsteps of the Savior.Our marriages, too, should be filled with the perfect love of the Cross compassionate, gentle, always ready to forgive, and full of hope for eternal life. May God bless us with a steadfast love for Him and an unwavering spiritual devotion, so that our lives may shine with spiritual awareness and continually remind us of the love of the Cross.

text.text: VI. The Cross as Healing and Resurrection

text:
After His resurrection, the Lord continued His work through the Holy Cross healing the sick and raising the dead. Those who witnessed these wonders and experienced His grace recognized that the Cross is not mere wood, but the source of life and redemption. They worshiped Him with awe and devotion, proclaiming: “The Cross is power, the Cross is redemption, the Cross is the salvation of the soul.”

Indeed, whoever stands at the Cross with steadfast faith finds rest for every affliction. The Cross is not merely a relic of the past; it is the living presence of divine grace in the world. From its wood flows the strength to endure temptation, the courage to forgive, and the hope that does not fade.

text.text: VII. Conclusion: The Call to the Love of the Cross

text:
Saint Yared designated the period from the 17th to the 25th of Meskerem as the Time of the Cross. The Cross is the supreme symbol of love, planted between God and mankind to bring reconciliation. Through the Cross, the curse of the soul and of the body was abolished. Whoever stands steadfast in the hope of the Cross can find comfort for their troubles and salvation for their soul (John 19:25).

The Cross is also the perfect symbol of obedience. Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, by His obedience unto death, bore the sins of many and fulfilled the role of the suffering servant, bringing righteousness to all who believe.

May our merciful God grant us the understanding of the meaning and love of the Cross. May He help us dwell in His house, live in His grace, and inherit His eternal kingdom.

text: Beloved in Christ, let us now turn our hearts and minds to the sacred observance of Zemene Tsige, the Forty Days commemorating the flight and return of the Holy Virgin Mary with her Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. In this holy season, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church gathers to remember, to give thanks, and to glorify God, joining the angels and saints in praise.

text.text: 1. The Meaning and Time of Zemene Tsige

text: ✍🏾The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church designates the period from Meskerem 26 to Hidar 5 as Zemene Tsige, Wereha Tsige the “Season of Blooming.” The term Tsige (ፅጌ), from the Gë`ëz "Tsegeye", means to bloom, to be adorned, to show forth beauty and fruitfulness. It is a sacred time when creation adorns itself with abundance, mirroring divine grace. The earth, clothed in beauty, becomes a visible sermon on the generosity of God.

✍🏾Zemene Tsige is not only a time of natural flourishing but also a reflection of spiritual renewal. The flowering fields and ripened fruits symbolize the Virgin Mary, the Ethiopian Church celebrates not only the glory of creation but also the mystery of the Virgin Mary, she who bore the Word made flesh, the flower of Jesse’s root.

text.text: 3. The Sunday Vigils and Night Prayers

text:
✍🏾During the month of Tsige, which is known as the most cherished and beautiful season of the year, the Ethiopian Orthodox faithful celebrate a time when the earth itself seems to reflect the glory of heaven.

✍🏾In this sacred season, when the fields are green and the air is rich with the scent of flowers and fruit, the priests gather every Sunday from midnight onward in what is called the Tsige assembly. They stand in prayer for many hours, representing Our Lady, the Holy Virgin Mary, the flower of purity and the mother of divine grace.

text.text: 4. Hymns of the Virgin and the Mystery of the Incarnation

text:
✍🏾“…Everything that should happen in the season of flowers has come to pass. The songs of the birds have been hear throughout our land. Our Lady, the Holy Virgin Mary, return so that we may witness peace in you. As you embraced your Son, and as you are adorned with a crown of flowers Mary, my dove, my dove! come. The apostles praise you; the angels send you; the foundation of life comes from Lebanon; the blessing of Shem; the hospitality of Abraham; the fragrance of Isaac; the ladder of Jacob; the comfort of Joseph…”

✍🏾Priests and deacons continue in various styles of singing, while the Debaters (Debteroch) spend the entire night in prayer lighting candles, singing, beating drums, clanging cymbals, chanting, and stamping the ground. Scholars and the faithful join in, praising God and our Lady with words full of power and devotion.

Priests, during the hours of prayer, sing: 

✍🏾(O Mary, who shines like the eastern sun; who gave birth to the Lord, strong as lightning; who carried the mystery of fire. Like the letters of the alphabet, you are abundant with many generations; you bore the Gospel; you carried Christ, the consuming fire. Like the cedar tree, you provide help; O holy Mary, who brings salvation; you gave birth to the Creator, the guest of the world; you save us from the death of punishment; you are the vine, the fruitful vine…)

✍🏾With these words, the faithful praise God and the Holy Virgin Mary, recognizing her unique role in salvation, her strength, and her guidance for the world.

text:

text.text: 8. The Teachings of Master Kifle Wolde Tsadeq: “Tsige Zik”

text:
✍🏾As recorded in Tsige Zik (pp. 1–75) by Master Kifle Wolde Tsadeq, the Tsige season commemorates not only the Virgin and her Son but also the angels, righteous ones, and martyrs.

✍🏾During this time, the Church celebrates:

👉🏾The Holy Trinity and Emmanuel

👉🏾The four beasts of Revelation

👉🏾Archangel Raphael

👉🏾John the Baptist, Stephen, and the Evangelists Matthew and Mark

👉🏾James and John, sons of Zebedee

👉🏾Thomas Zehndeke, Anna, Abune Aregawi, Kirkos, Abba Eustathius

👉🏾Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and many other saints

This harmony of remembrance shows that holiness, like flowers, does not bloom alone it grows in communion.

✍🏾In general, every Sunday during this period, a great celebration is held in all Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo churches, with the faithful participating in the Holy Liturgy . The forty-day celebration of the Feast of Wereha Tsige is dedicated to the Holy Virgin Mary and our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

✍🏾A special service is conducted to commemorate the suffering, thirst, and persecution endured by the Holy Virgin Mary when she was taken to Egypt with her Son, Salome, and Joseph. The service also celebrates her return from Egypt to her homeland, Nazareth.

✍🏾During this period, the Sunday hymns, and liturgy, as well as the hymns of the Holy Spirit, are all centered on the Feast of zemene tsige, reminding the faithful of the trials, devotion, and divine protection surrounding the Holy Family.

✍🏾Fasting without humility is an empty shadow. The true fast is not of the lips or stomach alone, but of the heart. The believer must fast with compassion, give alms to the poor, restrain anger, forgive offenses, and keep the tongue from deceit. Let fasting be united with mercy, prayer, and repentance, that it may ascend as sweet incense before the throne of God.

As the fathers teach: “When you fast, do not fast for vain praise, but that your fasting may be a fasting of mercy, wherein you find help, blessing, and the grace of God.”

text.text:
May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.

text: Beloved in Christ, let us open our minds and hearts to understand the sacred distinctions between images and the holy icons themselves, for knowledge of this truth safeguards the faith and guides the soul in reverent worship.

✍🏾A painting or image is a tangible object, a visible representation of a person or event. Chief Kidane Wold Kifle, in his Sewasew Wegs Dictionary of Grammar, explains that a painting is a “portrait, a shadow of a form, a design, or a representation.” Yohannes Zedamasco further clarifies that a picture contains the likeness of the one represented, yet it remains distinct from the person depicted.

✍🏾In other words, while a painting resembles its subject, it is not the subject itself. Consider a photograph: there is the living person, and there is the photograph. If one asks, “Who is this in the picture?” the answer is the person represented, not the paper or canvas itself. The image points to reality, it reveals, it instructs but it cannot act or live independently.

Thus, images are vehicles of representation, not the essence of the being they depict.

text.text: 2. Three Types of Pictures in the Bible

text:
The Scriptures reveal three distinct categories of images:

a
✍🏾The term “holy” derives from the Gë`ëz verb

, meaning “to separate, honor, or choose.” Holy icons are thus set apart for God, sacred objects that guide the faithful toward spiritual contemplation. They allow us to see, with the eyes of the spirit, the identity and deeds of the saints. Their holiness derives from the saints they depict and the miracles God performs through them.

✍🏾In the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, the following are recognized as holy icons , created according to apostolic tradition and canonical teachings:

👉🏾The Holy God

👉🏾Our Lady, the Holy Virgin Mary

👉🏾The Holy Angels

👉🏾The Holy Prophets

👉🏾The Holy Apostles

👉🏾Other righteous and holy persons

✍🏾These images represent the saints’ lives, their virtue, and their participation in God’s glory. Holy icons are not mere decoration they are windows to the divine, teaching and inspiring the faithful. (Exodus 25:18–22; 36:8–35)

✍🏾In contrast, the Bible warns against images that oppose God’s work and glorify evil. These unclean images are set up for false worship and deception. Among them are:

👉🏾The golden calf worshipped by the Israelites (Exodus 32:1–10)

👉🏾The golden image of Nebuchadnezzar in Babylon (Daniel 3:1)

👉🏾The female deity Astaroth worshipped by the Canaanites

✍🏾Such images are condemned because they lead the heart away from God (Deut. 7:25; 1 Kings 12:28–30; Daniel 11:31; Matthew 24:15–18). They are instruments of idolatry and spiritual corruption, gate of sin.

s

✍🏾Finally, there are images that are neither holy nor intended for worship. These include portraits, photographs, inscriptions, and symbols used in everyday life. Their purpose is informational, decorative, or symbolic, not spiritual. Examples include:

👉🏾Images of rulers on coins (Matthew 22:20)

👉🏾Photographs of people or objects

👉🏾Logos, traffic signs, and organizational symbols

👉🏾Decorative motifs, tattoos, or calligraphy

👉🏾These images are neutral they carry meaning in the material world but do not convey holiness or divine presence.

a) Holy Icons

✍🏾The term “holy” derives from the Gë`ëz verb qedese, meaning “to separate, honor, or choose.” Holy icons are thus set apart for God, sacred objects that guide the faithful toward spiritual contemplation. text:
Beloved in Christ,
Grace and peace be multiplied unto you, who love the Mother of God and her Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.
Let us enter with reverence into the mystery of Zemene Tsige  the Season of Flowers  and the sacred hymn called Mahlete Tsige, which the Fathers of our Church have handed down to us as a treasure of thanksgiving, contemplation, and spiritual renewal.

text.text: Mahlete Tsige (The Hymn of the Season of Flowers)

text:

text.text: The Symbol of Flower and Fruit

text:
✍🏾Abba Tsige written composition is known as “Mahlete Tsige.” Just as fruit comes from a flower and a flower from fruit, so Mahlete Tsige is a composition that describes Our Lady, the Holy Virgin Mary, and her Son, our Savior and God, Jesus Christ, by comparing them with flowers and fruits.

✍🏾When he compares her to a flower, he compares her Son to fruit; and when he compares her to fruit, he compares her Son to a flower. As the prophet Isaiah said, “There shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a branch shall grow out of his roots” (Isaiah 11:1), thus portraying Our Lady, who is from the seed of Jesse, as the rod, and Christ, who is born of her, as the branch that springs forth.

Abba Tsige Dengel also composed his Melk-e in this light, combining each Melk-e of Our Lady and her Child, and representing them in Tsige and Fre. In doing so, he united the wonderful work of God—revealed in mystery, history, prayer, and related aspects—in a truly beautiful and harmonious way.

✍Just as Our Lady expressed her praise and liturgy to Saint Ephrem and Abba Hiriakos, who longed for her love and guidance, she also allowed this Mahele Tsige to be written by abba Tsige Dengel, who was yearning for her love.

text: Dear followers of the Orthodox teachings, we greet you with the peace of God. Today, we explore the sacred meaning of Holy Icons, a teaching entrusted to all who seek to understand the mysteries of faith.

✍🏾The term “Holy’ Icons” is a combination of two words: “Holy” and “Icons.”

✍🏾Holy refers to the sacred and special.

✍🏾Icons are a language of communication, speaking to the eyes and inspiring the heart.

✍🏾Thus, Holy Icons are not mere images. They are a divine language through which we communicate with the Holy One, God Himself, who is unique in all creation. What sets Holy Icons apart from worldly images is that God speaks to us through them, revealing His presence and making His voice heard.

✍🏾The drawing of holy icons did not arise from human desire alone. It is commanded by God. When God instructed Moses to make the Ark of the Covenant, He also commanded the depiction of icons:

👉🏾“You shall make two cherubim of gold on the two sides of the mercy seat… I will meet with you and speak with you from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim.” (Exodus 25:18-22)

Thus, the first holy icons were not for decoration but for divine encounter.

✍🏾Later, Moses and Solomon the Wise followed God’s command in the construction of the temple:

👉🏾“And the cherubim shall be above them, as the skilled worker makes the work of the tabernacle… he overlaid its doors with gold, and carved cherubim on its walls.” (Exodus 26:1; 2 Chronicles 3:7)

✍🏾These passages show that icons were created by God’s command, not by human whim. Consequently, icons continued in the New Testament and are still created today, honoring God and His saints.

text.text: Holy Iconss in the New Testament

text:
👉🏾In the New Testament, holy icons preserved memory and devotion:

👉🏾Tiberius Caesar received an icon of our Lord crucified to remember His love for mankind.

👉🏾The king of Edessa, Abgar Uqama, was healed by an icon of our Lord.

👉🏾Saint Luke painted an icon of the Holy Virgin Mary.

These examples demonstrate that holy icons are not only commemorative but also channels of God’s grace.

✍🏾Early Christians, persecuted by Roman emperors, painted their faith in caves and secret places as testimony to God’s power. By the 8th century, conflicts arose between iconoclasts, who opposed icons, and the defenders of holy icons.

✍🏾In 784 AD, a council established the canon of icons, affirming their honor and worship while prohibiting sculptures.

✍🏾Since the Old Testament, various sacred images crosses, flowers, pomegranates, fig trees, angels, and more have been drawn in unity, either openly or secretly, to convey holiness and spiritual teaching.

✍🏾The first person who use palm in painting was Solomon the Wise (2 Chronicles 3). These figures were used to distinguish one image from another, to highlight the dignity and significance of each, and to organize them according to day, time, chapter, or title. Such usage is frequently seen in manuscripts and sacred books

Holy Icons are far more than art; they are a divine language through which God communicates His presence, grace, and love. From the cherubim on the Ark to the images of Christ and the Holy Virgin, icons guide the faithful in prayer, worship, and remembrance of God’s wondrous works. They are sacred mirrors reflecting the glory of God and His saints, inviting us to encounter the divine with our eyes and hearts.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.

text.text: 2.1. As for the story of Michal:

text:
when King David, the prophet of Israel, brought the Ark of the Covenant, he sang and pray before it with all his might. Michal(Milkol), the daughter of Saul, saw him rejoicing before the Ark of the Lord and despised him in her heart. Because of this, she was punished and remained childless for the rest of her life (2 Samuel 6:12–23).

✍🏾The author, after recalling this story, says, “I will sing to you, O Virgin, as David sang before the Ark of Zion, which is a symbol of our Lady. So I will sing to you before your image. text.text: The Call to True Fasting and Worship

text:
Fasting, when done for human praise, is empty; when done in obedience and mercy, it becomes a ladder to heaven. The lesson concludes with a call:

“When we fast, let us fast not for vain praise, but for the sake of the law and order. Let us fast for mercy, where we can find help, blessings, and abundance through fasting.”

Through prayer, fasting, and the intercession of the Virgin, the faithful are renewed and strengthened to walk in humility before God.

In Zemene Tsige, we are reminded that faith kindles miracles, that the Virgin is the living bush who bore divine fire, and that those who honor her with pure hearts will find mercy through her Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

text:
Beloved brothers and sisters in the faith of the Orthodox Church, peace be unto you in the name of our Lord. Today, we meditate upon the sacred word spoken to the prophet Ezekiel:

“And you, son of man, take a brick and lay it before you, and draw a picture of the city of Jerusalem on it; and circle it.” (Ezekiel 4:1)

This divine instruction, filled with profound mystery, opens to us the deep origin and sanctity of sacred images within the Church of God.

text.text: 1. The Beginning of Sacred Images in Divine Revelation

text:
From the earliest times, God used visible signs to reveal invisible truths. In the days of Moses, the Lord Himself commanded that cherubim be carved upon the Ark of the Covenant:

“And you shall make one cherub on one side and another cherub on the other side... and the cherubim shall spread out their wings, covering the mercy seat.” (Exodus 25:19–20)

Likewise, Solomon adorned the Holy Temple with images of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, all overlaid with gold. (1 Kings 6:23–29) These were not idols, but sacred representations of heavenly realities symbols of the divine presence among His people.

Ezekiel, following this divine tradition, was commanded to draw Jerusalem upon a brick. This act was not mere artistry; it was prophecy through image. The brick became a message from God showing the siege, the judgment, and the redemption of the Holy City. Thus, the drawing of images became a form of sacred teaching.

text.text: 2. The Sacred Purpose of Holy Icons

text:
From the caves of early believers to the sanctuaries of today, holy images have served as visible gospels teachers for the eyes, guiding the faithful toward unseen truth. The ancients painted the stories of Scripture, the struggles of the martyrs, and the triumphs of faith, so that even those who could not read might behold the works of God.

Through time, the Church faced division over this holy practice. In the eighth century, two errors arose:
, those who worshiped the images as gods,

, those who rejected the use of images altogether.

But the Holy Spirit guided the Church to truth at the Second Council of Nicaea (787 A.D.), where it was declared that holy images are to be venerated, not worshiped. They are windows into heaven, revealing the glory of God, His saints, and His mysteries.

text.text: 3. The Canon and Meaning of Holy Icons

text:
The sacred images used in the Holy Church were painted by people chosen by God. For example, the first to paint the crucifixion of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ for Emperor Tiberius was Saint John the Evangelist. The canon of sacred images is based on the Church’s rules for painting and use. Since they are placed in the church, the faithful stand before the images and offer their petitions.

When painting sacred images, one must first ask God, the Owner of Holiness, in prayer. Since He is the source of knowledge and wisdom, He will grant us the grace to paint the image. The use of colors in sacred images is also part of the Church’s tradition and not arbitrary. For example:
represents the blood of martyrdom, the courage of the saints.
represents purity and holiness, seen in the Resurrection and the Virgin Mary.
symbolizes divinity and eternal majesty, used in depictions of the Holy Trinity.

text.text: 4. Reverence and Responsibility in Using Holy Icons

text:
The size of holy icons can be increased or decreased as needed. In prayer books, it depends on They size of the book, and in a church building, it can be adjusted according to the size of the building.

There are things we should keep in mind when using holy icons for prayer and various services. It is important to keep them in a dignified manner so that they do not become damaged or faded. Since the icons represent the one depicted God, a saint, or a martyr it is necessary to show them proper respect and reverence.

text.text: 5. The Caution Against Confusion and Imitation

text:
Artists should paint holy icons correctly so that the faithful can recognize the true subjects of the icons and pray to them. However, this practice is not always followed in some places of worship.

Two or three different images are sometimes painted to imitate the likeness of a saint. An example of this is the image of St. Arsema. This became a controversial topic among believers, and sources emerged claiming that it was not her true image. Eventually, it was concluded that the painting widely accepted as that of Saint Arsema was actually of Saint Barbara.

text.text: 6. The Eternal Message of Ezekiel’s Brick

text: Just as Ezekiel’s brick carried a prophetic message to Jerusalem, so too do our sacred images bear divine lessons to every generation. The brick was not a mere object it was a teaching tool through which God revealed His judgment and mercy. Likewise, the Church’s icons are silent preachers of faith, teaching through color what words cannot contain.

Artists should paint holy icons correctly so that the faithful can recognize the true subjects of the icons and pray to them. However, this practice is not always followed in some places of worship.

Two or three different images are sometimes painted to imitate the likeness of a saint. An example of this is the image of St. Arsema. This became a controversial topic among believers, and sources emerged claiming that it was not her true image. Eventually, it was concluded that the painting widely accepted as that of Saint Arsema was actually of Saint Barbara.

6. The Eternal Message of Ezekiel’s Brick

Just as Ezekiel’s brick carried a prophetic message to Jerusalem, so too do our sacred images bear divine lessons to every generation. The brick was not a mere object it was a teaching tool through which God revealed His judgment and mercy. Likewise, the Church’s icons are silent preachers of faith, teaching through color what words cannot contain.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

text.text: V. The Legacy of the Saint: Judgment, Healing, and Veneration

text:
After Saint Arsema was martyred with the twenty-seven virgins, King Dirtades fell seriously ill. Saint Gregory had already prisoned by him. (Tradition says he was her elder brother.) Later he released Saint Gregory and cured him of his illness. The holy virgins, Saint Arsema, and the holy martyrs were to be buried here, in Saint Gregory, on the sixth day of Tahisas. Likewise, the one hundred and nineteen martyrs who are called her companions are commemorated. Then they built a beautiful church in her name and honored it there, so we should honor them.

The feast day of Saint Arsema, is celebrated on this day every month. Her story serves as a testament to the strength of faith, the preservation of purity, and the power of spiritual devotion in the face of adversity and temptation.

Beloved faithful in the Orthodox Church, peace and grace be multiplied unto you. We greet you in the name of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

Today, through the blessings of God, we share with you a series on the mystery of Zemene Tsige. this lesson, drawn from the lives of the saints and the wisdom of our Fathers,may this lesson inspire repentance, humility, and love for God in every heart that reads it.

text.text: 2.2.The poor man Aulōgis and Abba Daniel’s remorse and the cry for intercession

text:
✍🏾Aulōgis was a poor man who lived on the small income he earned by grinding millstones and selling them. After spending a little on himself, he would use the rest to help those who were in greater need than he.

✍🏾One day, while doing this, he saw a monk named Abba Daniel. This monk said within himself, “If this man can help the poor even in his poverty, how many people would he help and how many good deeds would he do if he had great wealth?” So Abba Daniel prayed to God to give this man wealth.

✍🏾Although God told him that riches would not be good for Aulōgis, Abba Daniel, following his own will, continued to beg God to grant him wealth. After this, Abba Daniel, as was his custom, while digging stone, found gold buried in a pot. He took the gold and gave it to the king. When the king saw his honesty, he said, “How loyal is this man who brought the treasure to me rather than keeping it for himself?” The king then appointed him to serve in his palace.

✍🏾After Aulōgis was appointed, his honor and wealth increased, and he left his previous work. However, he became a judge who did not judge rightly or defend the oppressed.

✍🏾At this time, Abba Daniel saw God’s anger in a dream God judging Aulōgis for his sins. Realizing that his own prayer had brought this upon Aulōgis, Abba Daniel fell at the feet of the Virgin Mary icon and begged her to intercede for mercy and forgiveness

Abba Daniel was deeply troubled by the vision he saw in his dream. He feared that perhaps Aulōgis had acted unjustly toward the poor and had violated the law of God. Because of this, he chose to speak to him 

"As you pray to your Son who died out of love for mankind, have mercy also on me to the son of tsige, that I too may receive forgiveness."

This teaches us that the Virgin Mary, through her intercession, seeks mercy even for those who are unaware of the punishment awaiting them so that all may find forgiveness through repentance and the compassion of God.

text.text: 2.3.The miracles recorded by Saint Deksios and the sobriety of sacred signs

text:
✍🏾 The miracles of our Lady were gathered and written by Saint Deksios. Our Lady also gave him a blue chair that no one else could sit on, and a robe that no one else could wear.

✍🏾 After the death of Saint Deksios, the bishop who succeeded him wanted to sit on this chair and wear the episcopal robe. But when he tried, they said to him, “This was given only to Deksios,” but out of pride he sat down, saying, “I am a bishop like him why should I not take what was his?” He immediately died.

The above account shows the holiness and divine favor granted to Saint Deksios.

✍🏾“O Mother of God, helper of the weak and defender of the needy You who have no need of help from others just as You received the man who sat upon his throne  of Your faithful servant Deksios, so now arise with the power of Your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, to drive away my enemies, both demons and sins.”

👉🏾This prayer, drawn from the story, teaches us to call upon our Holy Mother to deliver us from all spiritual enemies. Through her intercession and the strength of her Son, we find protection, mercy, and victory over the powers of darkness.

2.4.Paradise, the Seraph, and the unique role of Christ and the Virgin

text:
👉🏾“Without You, O Lord, there is no creature that can open the garden guarded by the Seraphim except Christ.”
(Genesis 3:24)

✍🏾Eve, who was restored to her former glory and place by Christ, rejoiced as one who finds again her mother’s embrace.

✍🏾 This teaches us that no one can open the gate of Paradise except Christ, who redeemed mankind by His cross. It was Christ who opened the closed door of Paradise and restored the grace of sonship that humanity had lost and this same Christ was born of our Lady, the Virgin Mary.

✍🏾 God said through Isaiah: “My salvation will not delay; I will bring salvation to Israel that I may be glorified in Zion.” (Isaiah 46:13)

✍🏾The Savior, Jesus Christ, through whom fallen mankind was glorified and saved, came forth from our Lady called Zion the Holy Virgin Mary. She is the one who gave this medicine of life to the world.

✍🏾Fasting without humility is an empty shadow. The true fast is not of the lips or stomach alone, but of the heart. The believer must fast with compassion, give alms to the poor, restrain anger, forgive offenses, and keep the tongue from deceit. Let fasting be united with mercy, prayer, and repentance, that it may ascend as sweet incense before the throne of God.

As the fathers teach: “When you fast, do not fast for vain praise, but that your fasting may be a fasting of mercy, wherein you find help, blessing, and the grace of God.”

✍🏾Eve, who was restored to her former glory and place by Christ, rejoiced as one who finds again her mother’s embrace.

✍🏾 This teaches us that no one can open the gate of Paradise except Christ, who redeemed mankind by His cross. It was Christ who opened the closed door of Paradise and restored the grace of sonship that humanity had lost and this same Christ was born of our Lady, the Virgin Mary.

4.1. The Covenant with Abraham

“You shall keep my covenant, you and your descendants after you.
Every male among you shall be circumcised.
It shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you.” (Genesis 17:9–11)

✍🏾 The promise made to Abraham “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” was not fulfilled through Isaac.

text.text: 4.2. The Lamb and the Tree of Life

text:
The Virgin Mary, the Mother who gave birth to Christ, is prefigured in the Old Testament. When Abraham offered Isaac, a ram was found caught in a thicket.

“Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw a ram caught by its horns in a thicket.
He took the ram and offered it in place of his son.” (Genesis 22:13)

✍🏾Isaac represents the world,
the ram represents Christ,
and the tree of life where the ram was caught symbolizes the Virgin Mary

Just as the ram was bound in the tree and became a ransom for Isaac, so Christ took flesh from our Lady, was bound upon the Cross, and became the ransom for the sins of the world.

✍🏾Thus, the parable of Isaac and the ram is fulfilled in Christ and His Mother. The Virgin Mary is the living Tree of Life, bearing the fruit that brought salvation to all.

✍🏾The prophet Balaam foresaw this mystery and said:

“A star shall rise from Jacob,
and a scepter shall spring from Israel,
and He shall remove sin and unrighteousness.”
(Numbers 24:17; Isaiah 27:9; Romans 11:26)

This “star” is Christ, born from the “East of Jacob,” the radiant Virgin who gave light to the world.

“The prophets who saw the heavens declared,
‘A garden enclosed is my sister, my spouse;
a spring shut up, a fountain sealed.’” (Song of Solomon 4:12)

This prophecy speaks of the Virgin Mary, the sealed and holy dwelling in which the Word of God took flesh. She is the enclosed garden of purity, the living fountain from which the waters of salvation flow to all who believe.

Today we reflect upon the mystery of Zemene Tsige, the Season of the Flower a time that reveals to us the hidden beauty of the Virgin, the Mother of God, and the fulfillment of divine prophecy.

text.text: King Solomon says in the Song of Songs:

text:
👉🏾“My Beloved , my bride, is a locked garden, a sealed spring.” (Song of Songs 4:12)

👉🏾In this, the prophet speaks of Our Lady, the Virgin Mary, using the imagery of a garden and a fountain. Why does he call her “locked” and “sealed”?

✍🏾There is a garden within, but no one can enter it; it is locked. Since our Lady is enclosed in purity and virginity, only our God and Savior, Jesus Christ, was born from her.

✍🏾 A garden cannot bear fruit without seeds being sown or plants being tended. Yet this garden is locked, inaccessible to all, and still it bears fruit. Our Lady, remaining ever-virgin and pure, carried within her the Son of God and gave birth to Christ.
✍🏾The spring is sealed, yet it contains water. Likewise, our Lady, preserving her virginity and purity, gave birth to Christ through motherhood.

text.text: The Prophet Ezekiel spoke of this mystery:

text:
👉🏾“Then He brought me to the outer gate of the sanctuary which faces east, and it was shut. And the Lord said to me, ‘This gate shall remain shut; it shall not be opened, and no man shall enter by it, for the Lord, the God of Israel, has entered by it; therefore it shall remain shut.’” (Ezekiel 44:1–3)

✍🏾The meaning of this vision is clear: the “Gate of the East” is the Virgin Mary. The Lord, the God of Israel Christ the Son.entered through her and was born as a perfect man.

✍🏾This vision should not be taken as referring to a literal temple. For what purpose would a temple be built, only to be closed forever? As it is written:

👉🏾“Let them build Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them.” (Exodus 25:8)

👉🏾Ezekiel’s temple represents the Virgin, through whom God chose to dwell among His people. Later, in Ezekiel 46:12, the prophet adds:

👉🏾“When the prince enters, the gate facing east shall be opened for him.”

✍🏾Solomon and Ezekiel both spoke prophetically of her. Their words were fulfilled in Mary, the Mother of God (Theotokos).

God Himself gave a sign concerning her:

👉🏾“The Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call His name Immanuel.” (Isaiah 7:14)

✍🏾This was the divine mark of forgiveness and the fulfillment of the covenant promise.

When the angel announced the birth of Christ to the shepherds, he said:

👉🏾“This will be a sign to you: You will find a baby wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger.” (Luke 2:12)

When the wise men arrived, Scripture says:

👉🏾“They saw the child with His mother Mary.” (Matthew 2:11)

✍🏾In all these signs, the pattern is clear: the true Christ is found with His Mother. The Virgin’s role is inseparable from the mystery of salvation and the revelation of the true faith.

text.text: 3. Mary in the Fulfillment of Prophecy

text:
✍🏾Our Lady was not only the Mother of Christ she remained united with Him in every trial: during His ministry, His suffering, His crucifixion, and even at Pentecost, when He sent the Holy Spirit upon the apostles.

✍🏾Therefore, as the prophets praised her under many names, we too honor her for the mystery revealed through her. Her praise is constant, and it brings spiritual benefit to those who honor her in truth.

text.text: 4. 4 The Flower in the Time of Harvest

text:
There is no harvest or gathering during the flowering season, because their times are different. For example, in Meskerem, which is the season of flowers, there is no harvest or gathering.

✍🏾 “You are the harvest of prophecy, O Mary, who has brought to fruition the promises of the prophets and removed the time of famine.” Just as in the days of famine the prophecy of Joel the prophet of Elda spoke of blessings mountains flowing with honey and milk the seed of prophecy spoken by the prophets was fulfilled in our Lady. The prophets foretold the coming of the Messiah in various ways, and she became the fulfillment of these divine words.

✍🏾 The prophecies spoken by the Lord’s prophets were fulfilled, and the apostles, chosen to witness this fulfillment, understood:

“One sows and another reaps. I sent you to reap that for which you have not labored. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labors.” (John 4:37)

✍🏾 Thus, the prophets sowed their words, and in the time of the apostles, their labor bore fruit. This fruit of prophecy is Mary. Moreover, it is written:

“A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and the fruit of Christ will appear.”

Therefore, our Lady is like a flower appearing in the harvest season. Since flowers do not usually bloom at this time, she is called “a strange flower; a strange flower.” This is also a fulfillment of the prophecy of Joel.

✍🏾 In Joel’s time, the people suffered a severe famine. Yet the prophet declared that God would visit them with mercy and bring an end to the famine:

“You shall eat in plenty and be satisfied. After this, the mountains shall drip with wine, and the hills shall flow with milk, and all the springs of Judah shall flow with water.” (Joel 3:18)

Through Mary, the seed of prophecy was fulfilled, and the mercy of God flowed into the world as promised.

The Virgin Mary is the sealed garden, the fountain of life, and the strange flower that blooms in the harvest season. In her, the prophets’ words are fulfilled, and the promise of salvation is realized. Through her, heaven was opened, and God came to dwell among men.

text_entities.text: 4. 4 The Flower in the Time of Harvest

There is no harvest or gathering during the flowering season, because their times are different. For example, in Meskerem, which is the season of flowers, there is no harvest or gathering.

✍🏾 “You are the harvest of prophecy, O Mary, who has brought to fruition the promises of the prophets and removed the time of famine.” Just as in the days of famine the prophecy of Joel the prophet of Elda spoke of blessings mountains flowing with honey and milk the seed of prophecy spoken by the prophets was fulfilled in our Lady. The prophets foretold the coming of the Messiah in various ways, and she became the fulfillment of these divine words.

✍🏾 The prophecies spoken by the Lord’s prophets were fulfilled, and the apostles, chosen to witness this fulfillment, understood:

“One sows and another reaps. I sent you to reap that for which you have not labored. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labors.” (John 4:37)

✍🏾 Thus, the prophets sowed their words, and in the time of the apostles, their labor bore fruit. This fruit of prophecy is Mary. Moreover, it is written:

“A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and the fruit of Christ will appear.”

Therefore, our Lady is like a flower appearing in the harvest season. Since flowers do not usually bloom at this time, she is called “a strange flower; a strange flower.” This is also a fulfillment of the prophecy of Joel.

✍🏾 In Joel’s time, the people suffered a severe famine. Yet the prophet declared that God would visit them with mercy and bring an end to the famine:

“You shall eat in plenty and be satisfied. After this, the mountains shall drip with wine, and the hills shall flow with milk, and all the springs of Judah shall flow with water.” (Joel 3:18)

Through Mary, the seed of prophecy was fulfilled, and the mercy of God flowed into the world as promised.

The Virgin Mary is the sealed garden, the fountain of life, and the strange flower that blooms in the harvest season. In her, the prophets’ words are fulfilled, and the promise of salvation is realized. Through her, heaven was opened, and God came to dwell among men.

Beloved in Christ, peace to your souls. Today we turn our minds to a word vast in meaning: intercession. It is a bridge between weakness and mercy, a sacred act by which the frailty of man seeks the favor of God through the help of the righteous.

The word intercessor is derived from gë`ëz the verb "malede", which means “to beg” or “to pray.”

Intercession means to plead or to reconcile, and an intercessor is one who performs this sacred act. The act itself is called intercession.

Intercession is the act of appealing to someone who has the power to do what another cannot. The intercessor does not fulfill the request by his own strength or will, but stands before the one who has authority pleading on behalf of the person in need. The success of intercession depends on the will of the one being asked and the closeness of the intercessor to that person. At times, intercession may not be granted, not because the intercessor lacks favor, but because of the sinfulness or hardness of heart of the one seeking help.

The one who seeks intercession must have faith and reverence toward the intercessor. The saints are honored not only because they are righteous, but because they offered their very lives in faith. They pray before the Creator, and He hears them. Yet there were kings such as Pharaoh and Diocletian whose hearts were hardened and could not be saved. This was not because the intercession of the saints was rejected or that God lacked mercy, but because of the stubbornness and wickedness of those who refused to repent.

As the Lord declared through the prophet Jeremiah:
“Even if Moses and Samuel stood before Me, My heart would not be toward this people; let them go out of My sight.” (Jeremiah 15:1)

Through this, we understand that intercession is powerful, yet it bears fruit only when the heart of the one seeking mercy is humble and repentant before God.

text.text: The Place of Intercession in the Church

text:
✍🏾Intercession is one of the sacred parts of prayer in our Holy Church. The Church, guided by the Holy Spirit, offers different kinds of prayer, among which are:

👉🏾Prayer of Thanksgiving

👉🏾 Prayer of Intercession

She offers these prayers through readings, spoken words, and songs of praise.

👉🏾As it is written:
“The Lord is near. In everything, by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.” (Philippians 4:6)

✍🏾Our Holy Church is herself an intercessor. Therefore, she includes prayers of intercession within her worship. For example, in the Liturgy we pray, “For rulers and all in authority, that they may be granted wisdom and the fear of God.” This prayer has a firm biblical foundation, for the Apostle Paul teaches:

👉🏾“I urge, then, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people for kings and all who are in authority that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.” (1 Timothy 2:1–2)

✍🏾A true Christian offers prayer and thanksgiving not only for himself but also for others. This is the harmony of personal supplication and intercession. Though they are distinct, they are like two sides of the same coin. Personal supplication expresses one’s own need before God, while intercession lifts up the needs of others. The Holy Church keeps both in balance.

✍🏾Thus, intercession means to reconcile, to present the needs of others before God, to seek peace and mercy, and to instruct the faithful in compassion and unity through prayer.
