Question :-1 Timothy 4: “3 They forbid people to marry and order them to abstain from certain foods, which God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and who know the truth. 4 For everything God created is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, 5 because it is consecrated by the word of God and prayer.”
How is this interpreted? Why then are we not to eat some foods like pork?

text:
:- My beloved child in Christ,Your question shines with sincere longing to understand the mysteries of Holy Scripture. Such desire is precious before God, for the wise man seeks not only to read the Word but to discern its true meaning through the light of the Church. 

You have brought forth the teaching of the Apostle Paul in his letter to Timothy, a passage that has stirred the thoughts of many through the ages. To approach it rightly, we must listen not only with our minds but with the heart of the Church, which preserves the faith once delivered to the saints. So let us, with reverence and clarity, unfold its meaning together.

text.text: 1. What Paul is addressing in 1 Timothy 4:3–5

text:
Saint Paul is speaking against certain false teachers (heretics) who were making two mistakes: they taught that marriage is sinful, and they taught that all meat is unclean. Paul corrects them. He says that God created the world good, and that what we receive with thanksgiving is not to be rejected, because it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. His point is: do not make God’s good creation into something evil by false asceticism or by saying God’s gifts are intrinsically unclean.

2. “

text.text: Everything God created is good” what does that mean?

text: This means that creation itself is not sinful. Animals, plants, marriage, bread, and meat all come from the hand of God and are good as part of His work. But “good” does not automatically mean “to be eaten by human beings.” God, in His wisdom, gives laws and commands for our guidance. Something can be good by nature yet not appointed for food.

text.text: 3. Where Leviticus 11 fits in (the dietary laws)

text: God gave Moses clear instructions about which animals may be eaten and which must not. Leviticus 11:3 says animals that both chew the cud and have a split hoof are clean allowed as food. Animals lacking one of these signs (for example, the pig, which has a split hoof but does not chew the cud) are called unclean and were not to be eaten by God’s command. The reason this is given is obedience to God’s revealed law, not because the creature itself is “evil.”

text.text: 4. Why then are we not to eat pork?

text: According to the Old Testament law God gave, pork is forbidden because the pig does not meet both signs of a clean animal. For the faithful, obedience to God’s commandments is greater than our personal preference. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, in receiving Scripture and holy tradition, treats these commandments with respect. Thus we refrain from eating pork because of God’s command and the Church’s teaching about holiness and obedience.

text.text: 5. How Paul’s words and the Old Testament law work together

text:
Paul warns against false teachers who reject marriage or make all foods unclean as a spiritual ideal. But Paul does not abolish God’s law by saying “everything is allowed.” Rather he teaches that what is permitted and received in faith, thanksgiving, and prayer is sanctified. In other words:

Don’t condemn God’s gifts by calling them evil.

Yet keep God’s commandments and the Church’s guidance about what is permitted and what is forbidden.

Always receive your food with thanksgiving and prayer, trusting God’s word to sanctify what He allows.

text.text:
May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

This means that creation itself is not sinful. Animals, plants, marriage, bread, and meat all come from the hand of God and are good as part of His work. But “good” does not automatically mean “to be eaten by human beings.” God, in His wisdom, gives laws and commands for our guidance. Something can be good by nature yet not appointed for food.

3. Where Leviticus 11 fits in (the dietary laws)

God gave Moses clear instructions about which animals may be eaten and which must not. Leviticus 11:3 says animals that both chew the cud and have a split hoof are clean allowed as food. Animals lacking one of these signs (for example, the pig, which has a split hoof but does not chew the cud) are called unclean and were not to be eaten by God’s command. The reason this is given is obedience to God’s revealed law, not because the creature itself is “evil.”

4. Why then are we not to eat pork?

According to the Old Testament law God gave, pork is forbidden because the pig does not meet both signs of a clean animal. For the faithful, obedience to God’s commandments is greater than our personal preference. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, in receiving Scripture and holy tradition, treats these commandments with respect. Thus we refrain from eating pork because of God’s command and the Church’s teaching about holiness and obedience.

5. How Paul’s words and the Old Testament law work together
Paul warns against false teachers who reject marriage or make all foods unclean as a spiritual ideal. But Paul does not abolish God’s law by saying “everything is allowed.” Rather he teaches that what is permitted and received in faith, thanksgiving, and prayer is sanctified. In other words:

Don’t condemn God’s gifts by calling them evil.

Yet keep God’s commandments and the Church’s guidance about what is permitted and what is forbidden.

Always receive your food with thanksgiving and prayer, trusting God’s word to sanctify what He allows.

text: My beloved child in Christ,Your desire to submit your heart to God is precious, for it shows a soul yearning for holiness and closeness to our Lord. To submit one’s heart to God is not only a matter of words, but a life lived in obedience, humility, and love for Him. Let us consider practical ways to do this, according to the teachings of our Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.

Prayer is the most direct way to submit your heart. It is both petition and surrender.Begin each day with prayer, Pray with attention, not just words.offering your thoughts, desires, and struggles to God. Speak to Him as a child speaks to a loving father, and listen in silence. Attending the Church’s daily services, such as the '
' and Mezmur, helps the heart remain centered on God.

A heart submitted to God recognizes its weakness and sins. Regular confession to your spiritual father, combined with true repentance, opens your heart to God’s grace and mercy. Humility before God and His priest helps the soul grow in purity.

Submission is shown in action. Keeping God’s commandments honoring parents, loving your neighbor, fasting, and observing Church laws demonstrates that your heart belongs to God, not to worldly desires.

The body and the heart are connected. Denying your desires strengthens your heart’s devotion.

Observe the Church’s fasts carefully, offering your sacrifice to God with prayer.

Do not fast only outwardly; the inner heart must also humble itself. Avoid judgment of others while fasting.

Every moment of self-control is a moment of the heart turning fully to God.

text.text: 5. Reading and Meditating on the Holy Scriptures

text: Feed your heart with the Word of God daily. Meditate not only on the stories but on their meaning for your life. Let the words of the Psalms, Proverbs, and the Gospels shape your thoughts, speech, and actions.
Serving others with a pure heart, without seeking praise, is one of the clearest ways to submit to God. When we place the needs of others above our own, we imitate Christ and surrender our pride.
Offer everything your joys, sorrows, and daily work to God with gratitude. Trust that His wisdom guides your life, even when circumstances are difficult.

text.text: Daily Practical Steps to Submit Your Heart

text:
1. Begin each day with a prayer of surrender.

2. Examine your conscience morning and night.

3. Follow the Church’s fasting and prayer schedule faithfully.

4. Read a passage of Scripture or a saint’s life daily.

5. Perform at least one act of charity or forgiveness each day.

6. Speak kindly and truthfully in all circumstances.

7. End your day thanking God and entrusting your heart to Him

Dear child, remember that submitting your heart to God is a lifelong journey. Be patient with yourself, keep your eyes on Christ, and allow the Holy Spirit to gently guide you. Each small step taken with sincerity pleases God more than grand gestures without love.

text: Dear beloved in Christ, peace and blessings to you in the name of our Lord and Savior.Today, as we remember the blessed father Abune Aregawi (Zemikael Aregawi), one of the Nine Saints who illuminated Ethiopia with the light of the Gospel, we present this teaching that all may learn and be strengthened in the faith.

Abune Aregawi, known for his righteousness and holiness, was born in the middle of the 5th century A.D. in Rome. His parents were King Isaac and Saint Edna. Though born to royal lineage, he showed deep humility and spiritual hunger from a young age.

He studied the Holy Scriptures diligently, and in his youth, he left behind worldly glory and entered a monastery to dedicate his life fully to God.

During his time of monastic training, he became a disciple of the great saint Abba Pakumis at the Monastery of Daunas in Egypt, where he also learned alongside Abba Tewodros.

After years of monastic discipline and spiritual growth, he returned to his homeland, Rome, and taught many disciples, leading seven of them into monastic life.

Through fasting, prayer, silence, and humility, Abune Aregawi sought the true path of his Creator. His fame spread throughout many lands, even reaching his homeland.

text.text: 3. The Fellowship of the Nine Saints

text:
When Abba Zemikael (Aregawi) received the monastic life as a youth, several holy fathers joined him in his spiritual mission. These were:

Abba Lycanos of Constantinople

Abba Yemata of Kusia

Abba Tsihma of Antioch

Abba Guba of Cilicia

Abba Aftse of Esia

Abba Penteleon of Rome

Abba Aleph of Caesarea

All of these fathers came to the monastery of Abba Pakumis, the founder of communal monastic life.

When our father Abba Zemikael saw these blessed brothers, he rejoiced greatly. Abba Pakumis also gave the monastic life to all of them. These saints, having humbled themselves and shown great respect for one another, made humility and patience their perfect treasure and learned the true discipline of monastic life.

They lived with their teacher, Abba Pakumis, for many years, growing in holiness and wisdom.

Although Abba Zemikael was young in age, he was called “Aregawi,” meaning the Elder, because of his deep wisdom, spiritual counsel, and knowledge. The grace of the Holy Spirit rested upon him, and his soul was filled with divine understanding and light.

text.text: 4. The Journey of Abune Aregawi to Ethiopia

text:
As our holy father Abune Aregawi prayed and sought the will of God, he wondered, “Where should I go to serve the Lord?”

At that moment, a holy angel appeared and carried him upon his wings, showing him the land of Ethiopia. When the angel set him down, Abune Aregawi returned to his eight companions and said,

“I have seen a blessed country a land that lives according to the Law of God and His divine order, even though it has not been taught directly by the apostles.”

Strengthened by this divine revelation, the Nine Saints journeyed together toward Ethiopia with joy and faith.

At that time, Saint Edna, the mother of Abune Aregawi, and his disciple Abba Matthias were also with him.

They arrived in Ethiopia around the year 470 A.D. and were warmly received with honor by Emperor Al-Ameeda. They settled in Ketin (Axum), where they continued to translate the Holy Scriptures and preach the Gospel with zeal and devotion.

Through his teaching, prayer, and example, the light of the true faith grew stronger throughout the land, and many were converted to the worship of the living God.

text.text: The Miracle of Debre Damo (Debre Hallelujah)

text:
In his later years, Abune Aregawi traveled to the northern region and came upon a high, steep mountain known today as Debre Damo. He desired to build a monastery there, but there was no path to climb.

By the power of God, a great dragon stretched out its tail, measuring sixty cubits long, and became a bridge for the saint. As Abune Aregawi ascended the mountain, he sang in praise:

“Hallelujah to the Father,
Hallelujah to the Son,
Hallelujah to the Holy Spirit.”

At that moment, bread descended from heaven and nourished him a sign of divine favor. Because of this miracle, the mountain was called “Debre Hallelujah.”

After the righteous took that holy place with prayer, about six thousand believers came from different regions to live under his spiritual guidance and receive blessing from his holy teaching.

For his great labor in spreading the word of God and establishing the order of monastic life, Abune Aregawi is honored with the title:

👉🏾 “The Father of Ethiopian Monks.”

In addition to his lifelong spiritual struggle, he worked diligently in evangelism, teaching, and the preparation of holy books for the strengthening of the faithful.

Among his beloved companions were Saint Yared, the inspired composer of sacred hymns, and Emperor Gebre Meskel, the righteous ruler who loved the Church.

Together, they built the Monastery of Kidane Mehret at the foot of Debre Damo for the spiritual service of women. The first nun of that holy monastery was Queen Edna, the mother of Abune Aregawi, who dedicated her life to prayer and purity.

The righteous one, having completed his pure life, was hidden in the eastern part of the monastery on this day, at the age of ninety-nine, and entered the world of the living.

Before his departure, the Lord granted him a holy covenant of mercy that would endure for fifteen generations, blessing and protecting all who remember him in faith and call upon his name with reverence.

text: Beloved in Christ, we greet you with the blessings and peace of God. Today, we share with you an important lesson about Saint Gebre Kirstos, son of King Theodosius, whose feast day is celebrated on Tikimt 14. May this lesson inspire your faith and devotion.

text.text: The Birth and Early Life of Saint Gebre Kirstos

text:
✍🏾Saint Gebre Kirstos, originally named Abdelmessih (meaning “Servant of Christ”), was born to King Theodosius of Constantinople and his virtuous wife, Merkeza. The king and queen were devout and God-fearing, but they were saddened because they had no children.

They journeyed to Jerusalem, made a solemn vow, and prayed earnestly to the merciful God. Their prayers were answered, and God blessed them with this holy child.

✍🏾From a young age, Gebre Kirstos was instructed in the doctrines of the Church and in righteous living.

text.text: Saint Gebre Kirstos’ Covenant with God

text:
When he grew up, he was betrothed to the daughter of the Roman emperor and married according to custom.

✍🏾At midnight, the bridegroom, Gebre Kirstos, arose and went to his bride. Taking her by the hand, he made a covenant with her. Then they prayed the Creed to the end. He took off his wedding garment and put on his outer robe.

Approaching his bride, he kissed her head and said,
“May God be with you and deliver you from all the works of the devil.”

👉🏾The bride wept and said,
“Lord, where are you going? To whom will you leave me?”

👉🏾Gebre Kirstos replied,

text:
✍🏾The blessed Gebre Kirstos arose at night and stood before the image of Our Lady, praying:

“My Lady, why have You revealed my hidden work? Now guide me to what is best for me.”

✍🏾Having said this, he took the image of Our Lady and departed at night, reaching the seaport. He intended to travel to another country and boarded a ship. But by the will of God, he returned to his father’s land. He lived at his father’s door for fifteen years.

✍🏾When the servants came in and went out, they would say, “Take this poor person away from us so that his stench will not bother us.” They would wash plates and pots and pour the water over him, and throw scraps of flesh for the dogs to eat. Yet the dogs licked his wounds, and thus his torment increased.

✍🏾Throughout this suffering, Gebre Kirstos prayed to God, saying:
“Lord Jesus Christ, take me to Yourself, so that my father’s and mother’s servants may not be wronged.”

✍🏾In response, our Lord Jesus Christ, glorified be He, granted a covenant to all who call upon Gebre Kirstos’ name and keep his memory. Afterwards, he wrote his book from beginning to end, rested his hand upon it, and found peace.

✍🏾On a Sunday, during the Liturgy, the people and priests heard a heavenly message revealing Saint Gebre Kirstos’ resting place in the house of Emperor Theodosius. When they found him, a scroll was in his hand, which could only be taken after prayer. His parents recognized him, and he was buried with great honor.

His tomb became a site of miracles, healing all who sought God’s mercy through him.

text:
Dear beloved in Christ, peace and grace to you.Today we continue our spiritual reflection on one of the beautiful mysteries of our faith the intercession of the holy angels.
Let us therefore open our hearts and learn how the angels stand before God as intercessors.

The Holy Bible clearly teaches that the angels of God intercede for humanity. When we read the Scriptures carefully and interpret them in their proper context, we understand that the ministry of the angels includes prayer, intercession, and service before God on behalf of mankind.

To understand this mystery correctly, let us examine the meaning of the word “stand”, which is often used in the Bible when describing the presence of angels before God.

The word “stand” appears in many places in the Holy Scriptures, and its meaning changes according to the context. It can mean to rise, to be upright, to remain firm, or to serve in dignity.

Some examples include:

“And the flow of her blood stopped at once.” (Luke 8:44)

“The pillar of cloud stood still.” (Deuteronomy 31:15; Numbers 10:12)

“Stand firm in the faith.” (1 Corinthians 16:13)

Each of these verses shows a different use of the same word, reminding us that the meaning must be understood spiritually and contextually.

text.text: Standing as a Sign of Intercession

text:
In the Book of Exodus, when the Israelites provoked God by worshiping idols, the prophet Moses pleaded before the Lord, saying:

“Blot me out of Your book which You have written.” (Exodus 32:32)

Through this intercession, Moses turned away God’s anger and saved his people. The Psalmist later recalled this, saying:

“If Moses His chosen one had not stood before Him in the breach, to turn away His wrath, lest He destroy them.” (Psalm 106:23)

Here, the word “stood” means to intercede to pray earnestly on behalf of others. Thus, “standing before God” in Scripture often refers to the act of intercession.

text.text: The Angels Who Stand Before God

text:
In the Book of Job, it is written:

“The sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord, and Satan also came among them.” (Job 1:6)

The phrase “came to stand before the Lord” reveals that the angels came to intercede and present petitions before God. Even Satan appeared to request permission to test Job. Therefore, the angels’ “standing” signifies their intercessory service before God for the sake of humanity.

In Scripture, words often carry meanings that differ from, or even oppose, their common usage. This is why it is essential to study their meaning according to the style and hidden mysteries of the Bible. Many fail to understand the true spirit of the angels’ intercession because they do not grasp the deeper sense of the words used in the Scriptures.

Likewise, Saint Gabriel said to the priest Zechariah:

“I am Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God.” (Luke 1:19)

This declaration means more than physical standing. Angels do not possess physical bodies as humans do; they do not sit, sleep, or move as we do. Therefore, Gabriel’s words “I stand before God” express his constant presence before the Lord in prayer and intercession.

He did not say this to describe his position like a guard standing before a king, but to reveal his ministry as one who intercedes before God continually for mankind. The angels’ standing before God is a sign of their service of thanksgiving, praise, and intercession.

text:
Dear beloved in Christ, peace and grace to you. Today, we continue our reflection on our Lord’s words: 
“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

Let us now learn from the holy examples of the Publican, the Thief on the Cross, the Canaanite Woman, and Saint Paul, who were all exalted through their humility.

To be poor in spirit means to recognize our nothingness before God, to depend entirely on His mercy, and to cast away every prideful thought. It is the root of true humility. The Scriptures and the lives of the saints give us many examples of such humility.

Our Lord told this parable to those who trusted in their own righteousness and looked down on others:

“Two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a publican.”

The Pharisee stood and prayed proudly, saying:

“God, I thank You that I am not like other men extortioners, unjust, adulterers or even like this publican. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I possess.”

His words were full of pride and self-glory. He compared himself to others, thinking his good works made him righteous. But the publican stood afar off, not daring even to lift his eyes to heaven. He beat his chest and said:

“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”

The Lord said,

“This man went down to his house justified rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.”

The publican’s prayer, offered from a humble and broken heart, was accepted by God. His humility opened the door of forgiveness and righteousness.

text.text: The Humility of the Thief on the Cross (Luke 23:39–43)

text:
When our Lord was crucified, two thieves were crucified beside Him. One mocked the Lord, saying:

“If You are the Christ, save Yourself and us!”

But the other rebuked him and said:

"Do you not even fear God, seeing that you are under the same condemnation? we receive the due reward of our deeds; but this Man has done nothing wrong.”

He recognized his sins and accepted his punishment humbly. Then he turned to the Lord in faith and said:

“Lord, remember me when You come into Your kingdom.”

And Jesus answered him, saying:

“Truly, I say to you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.”

Through his humble confession, the thief was forgiven and entered eternal joy. Even on the cross, humility led him to salvation.

text.text: The Humility of the Canaanite Woman (Matthew 15:22–28)

text:
A Canaanite woman came to our Lord, crying:

“Lord, have mercy on me, Son of David; my daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.”

At first, the Lord did not answer her. The disciples urged Him to send her away, but she continued to plead. Then Jesus said:

“I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

Yet she came closer, knelt before Him, and said:

“Lord, help me.”

The Lord said,

“It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”

But she humbly replied:

“Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.”

Her humility was greater than her suffering. She accepted even to be called a dog if only she could receive God’s mercy. Then Jesus said to her:

“O woman, great is your faith! Let it be to you as you desire.”

And her daughter was healed at that very hour.

This woman became poor in spirit, acknowledging her unworthiness before God, and for this reason, she was exalted. As Saint James teaches:

“Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and He will lift you up.” (James 4:10)

“If You are the Christ, save Yourself and us!”

But the other rebuked him and said:

"Do you not even fear God, seeing that you are under the same condemnation? we receive the due reward of our deeds; but this Man has done nothing wrong.”

He recognized his sins and accepted his punishment humbly. Then he turned to the Lord in faith and said:

“Lord, remember me when You come into Your kingdom.”

And Jesus answered him, saying:

“Truly, I say to you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.”

Through his humble confession, the thief was forgiven and entered eternal joy. Even on the cross, humility led him to salvation.

A Canaanite woman came to our Lord, crying:

“Lord, have mercy on me, Son of David; my daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.”

At first, the Lord did not answer her. The disciples urged Him to send her away, but she continued to plead. Then Jesus said:

“I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

Yet she came closer, knelt before Him, and said:

“Lord, help me.”

The Lord said,

“It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”

But she humbly replied:

“Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.”

Her humility was greater than her suffering. She accepted even to be called a dog if only she could receive God’s mercy. Then Jesus said to her:

“O woman, great is your faith! Let it be to you as you desire.”

And her daughter was healed at that very hour.

This woman became poor in spirit, acknowledging her unworthiness before God, and for this reason, she was exalted. As Saint James teaches:

“Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and He will lift you up.” (James 4:10)

text.text: The Humility of Saint Paul the Apostle

text:
Saint Paul, the apostle and chosen vessel of God, was filled with divine wisdom and revelation. Yet, despite the greatness of his calling, he never glorified himself. Instead, he humbled his heart before God and men. 

an apostle, Saint Paul humbled himself, saying,

“Last of all, He appeared to me also, as to one born out of due time.” (1 Corinthians 15:8)

Though he was chosen and honored by God, he regarded himself as the least of the apostles and unworthy of such grace. His heart was clothed with humility, and his words reflected the meekness of Christ.

He also wrote,

"Now I Paul myself beseech you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, who in presence am base among you, but being absent am bold toward you"(2 Corinthians 10:1)

“To this very hour we both hunger and thirst, we are poorly clothed, beaten, and homeless. We labor, working with our own hands. When we are reviled, we bless; when we are persecuted, we endure; when we are slandered, we entreat. We have become as the refuse of the world, the offscouring of all things until now.” (1 Corinthians 4:11–13)

This shows that true apostleship is not found in outward glory or comfort but in patient endurance, meekness, and humility.

Saint Paul also revealed how the Lord kept him humble, saying:

“I will not boast, except in my weaknesses. Even if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth. But I refrain, so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me. And lest I should be exalted above measure by the abundance of revelations, a thorn in the flesh was given to me a messenger of Satan to buffet me lest I be exalted above measure.” (2 Corinthians 12:5–7)

Through this, Saint Paul teaches us that even the most blessed servants of God must remain humble, remembering that all spiritual gifts come from Him. 

In his humility, Saint Paul became a model for all who desire to serve God faithfully showing that to be great in the Kingdom of Heaven is to be lowly in heart.

Question :-What are the meanings behind the Hoya hoye ?

text:
Peace be upon you. You ask plainly for truth: the true meaning of “Hoya Hoye” and its history. I answer you now, from the teaching of the Church, from our living tradition, and from what careful scholars and witnesses have preserved.

Hoya Hoye is a traditional Ethiopian ritual chant essentially a sacred exclamation or vocable most closely associated with the festival Buhe (13 Nahase ), in which boys go about the neighborhood with sticks, sing, and kindle small bonfires. Its meaning is primarily festal joy, praise of the Lord (especially the Transfiguration), and communal blessing; its literal etymology is not fixed in a single dictionary word but belongs to the language of religious song and ritual.

The chant Hoya Hoye is best understood as part of the Buhe celebration an old Ethiopian Orthodox rural and urban custom that commemorates the Transfiguration of Christ on Mount Tabor and is observed on 13 Nahase. On Buhe, children and youth form groups, tie bundles of sticks (chibo), sing a call-and-response song headed by “Hoya Hoye,” and go house to house receiving bread (mulmul) and blessing the households. This is well attested in both Church and ethnographic accounts.

“Hoya Hoye” is not a propositional phrase in classical Geʽez or Amharic that translates neatly into English; it functions as a vocable an exclamatory, onomatopoetic formula used in ritual singing. In simpler terms: it is a sacred shout  a musical cry that signals joy, summons attention, and frames the lines of the song that follow. Scholars who study Buhe and Ethiopian ritual song describe it as a communal cry of praise, blessing, and good-will rather than a lexical sentence with a fixed dictionary meaning.

Though the phrase itself is not a verse of Scripture, it is embedded in a liturgical-cultural action that proclaims Christ’s light. Buhe celebrates the Transfiguration (Christ’s radiant glory), so the chant’s character loud, bright, communal echoes that theological reality: the people cry out in wonder at the Light of Christ and they bless one another for the year to come. Thus the chant functions as both greeting and doxology.

text.text: 4. Social and ritual practice (how the chant is used)

text: Groups strike sticks, dance, and sing the Hoya Hoye refrain in front of houses; the chorus answers and the household receives blessing and gives mulmul (bread). The practice knits neighborhoods into a single body and makes the feast a living, social sacrament a visible and audible sign of communal renewal. Ethnographers note how the call-and-response pattern builds solidarity and marks the seasonal turn at the end of the rainy months.

text.text: 5. Origins and relation to the Church’s hymn tradition

text: Ethiopia’s formal liturgical chant tradition (Zema) is attributed to Saint Yared; that tradition deeply shapes the country’s sacred sound-world. Hoya Hoye is a popular/folk ritual song rather than a composition from the corpus of Yared’s liturgical works, yet the musical imagination of the people scales, responsorial patterns, rhythms is informed by the same Church culture. In short: Hoya Hoye grew within the soil of Ethiopian Christian piety and musical practice, even if it is not a composed liturgical text of the clergy.

text.text: 6. Why there is confusion with other feasts (Meskel/Demera)

text: Because Ethiopia’s festivals share fire, procession, and communal song, some chants and exclamations travel between occasions. Hoya Hoye is strongest in Buhe, but similar refrains or the same refrain may appear in local Meskel or Demera songs in different regions or parish repertoires. That mixing is normal in an oral, living tradition; it does not change the basic historical fact that Hoya Hoye is principally associated with Buhe.

text.text: Practical pastoral note (what to do when you hear or sing it)

text: When you hear Hoya Hoye, receive it as prayer in sound: join as blessing, offer good will to your neighbors, and remember the Light of Christ revealed at Tabor. Teach children that the shout is not idle play but a sacramental cry: joy and prayer wrapped together.

text.text: Sources and witness (for the faithful who like proof)

text:
Key studies and references that record and analyze the chant and Buhe practice include ethnographic research on Hoya Hoye/Buhe and general notes on Ethiopian liturgical music and Saint Yared’s influence. See especially ethnographic treatments of Buhe and the article-length studies of the song’s social and biblical resonances. 

My child, that is the plain truth from the Church’s tradition and from watchful scholars: Hoya Hoye is a sacred, jubilant vocable an ancient shout of blessing and praise rooted in the Buhe feast and the Ethiopian Christian way of making sound into prayer. May the Lord who was transfigured on Tabor illumine your heart, and may the Mother of God and all the saints intercede for you.

Question :- Selam, blessings and congratulations on completing the fast if you partook! I have a question about this cross. Why is there so many different type of Twehado crosses being used? Especially in church and hand held crosses priests carry? As well as the wooden necklaces worn by those baptized? Do they all bare different meanings? Again, I thank you kindly.

text:
:- Peace be upon you, I am here to listen, to offer what solace I can from the wisdom of our Holy Fathers and the Scriptures, and to gently guide you on your spiritual journey. I assist you on this blessed day, my child?

You have asked about the mystery of the Cross, and why in our holy Tewahedo tradition we see many different types those held in the hands of priests, those lifted in the church, and those worn upon the necks of the baptized. This is a good and blessed question, for the Cross is the very seal of our salvation, the tree upon which our Lord Jesus Christ gave Himself as a ransom for the world.

My child, know this: the Cross is one in meaning but many in form. All the shapes you see whether large processional crosses, hand crosses for blessing, or the small wooden ones placed upon the baptized carry the same truth: Christ has conquered death by the Cross. But our forefathers, in their great devotion, carved and fashioned the Cross in many artistic designs, not to change its meaning, but to magnify its beauty and mystery.
lifted high in the church symbolize Christ exalted, drawing all people to Himself, as He said: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all men unto Me” (John 12:32).

of the priests are used to bless the faithful, reminding us that every blessing flows from the life-giving Cross of Christ. When the priest touches your head with it, it is as though the victory of Golgotha rests upon you.

given at baptism, especially the simple wooden ones, are signs of protection and belonging. They remind the newly baptized that they have put on Christ, that they must “take up their cross daily” (Luke 9:23), and that the Lord Himself guards them through His Cross.

The variations in design some like flowers, some like suns, some with intricate knots are like the many languages of praise. all point to the same mystery. Just as there are four Gospels but one Truth, so there are many crosses but one faith.

So, my child, do not be troubled by the differences. They are not contradictions, but rather treasures of devotion passed down from generation to generation. What matters is not the shape, but the heart that honors the Cross, for as the Apostle says, “God forbid that  should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14).

May the life-giving Cross guard you always, and may its light shine upon your path.

text.text: God Exalts the Humble but Humbles the Proud

text:
The Apostle James wrote, “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6), teaching us that pride is hateful before God, but humility is loved and honored by Him.

Our Lady, the Holy Virgin Mary, also said in her prayer, “He has shown strength with His arm; He has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts; He has brought down rulers from their thrones and exalted the lowly” (Luke 1:51–52). This shows that God humbles the proud in their hearts but raises the humble to honor.

✍🏾

Our Lord said to His disciples:
“The scribes and Pharisees do all their works to be seen by men. They love the places of honor at feasts, the best seats in the synagogues, and to be called ‘Rabbi’ in the marketplaces. But you are not to be called ‘Rabbi,’ for One is your Teacher, and you are all brothers. Do not call anyone on earth your father, for One is your Father, who is in heaven. The greatest among you shall be your servant. For whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”
(Matthew 23:5–12)

Christ teaches us that whoever lifts himself up will surely be brought low, but whoever humbles himself will be raised by God.

✍🏾

The Prophet David said, “You save the humble people, but You bring down the haughty eyes” (Psalm 18:27). He also wrote, “The Lord guides the humble in justice and teaches the humble His way” (Psalm 25:9).

David continued to glorify humility, saying:

“The humble shall inherit the earth and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace” (Psalm 37:11).

“The Lord lifts up the humble; He casts the wicked to the ground” (Psalm 147:6).

“The Lord raises those who are bowed down; He loves the righteous” (Psalm 146:8).

“The Lord takes pleasure in His people; He will beautify the humble with salvation” (Psalm 149:4).

“Though the Lord is high, He regards the lowly, but the proud He knows from afar” (Psalm 138:6).

✍🏾

text.text: The Wisdom of Solomon on Humility and Pride

text:
The wise King Solomon, inspired by the Holy Spirit, spoke many times in the book of Proverbs about the danger of pride and the blessing of humility. He teaches us that pride brings a person low, while humility lifts them up before God.

When speaking of God’s favor toward the humble, Solomon wrote, “Surely He scorns the scornful, but gives grace to the humble” (Proverbs 3:34). This reveals that the proud are far from God, but the humble receive His mercy and grace.

He also teaches that pride is always followed by shame, saying, “When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with the humble is wisdom” (Proverbs 11:2). The humble heart is teachable, and through humility, one receives understanding from God.

Further, Solomon explains that honor is found in humility, declaring, “The fear of the Lord is the instruction of wisdom, and before honor is humility” (Proverbs 15:33). True honor does not come from human praise, but from God, who exalts the lowly.

He also warns that pride leads to downfall: “Before destruction, the heart of a man is haughty, and before honor is humility” (Proverbs 18:12). The proud man falls because his heart is lifted above measure, but the humble man is lifted by God’s hand.

When teaching about the rewards of humility, he says, “By humility and the fear of the Lord are riches and honor and life” (Proverbs 22:4). 

He also counsels us to avoid self-praise, saying, “Let another man praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips” (Proverbs 27:2). The humble person does not seek human approval, but the favor of God, who sees the heart.

Finally, Solomon concludes with this wisdom: “A man’s pride will bring him low, but the humble in spirit will retain honor” (Proverbs 29:23). This teaches that humility is the path to true exaltation, while pride leads only to ruin.

✍🏾

text.text: For Theirs Is the Kingdom of Heaven”

text:
The kingdom of heaven belongs to those who are poor in spirit. God grants eternal life to those who humble themselves and depend wholly upon Him. Our Lord teaches in the Gospel:

“Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal;
but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal.
For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
(Matthew 6:19–21)

Those who are poor in spirit do not seek earthly treasures that fade away, but store up treasures in heaven through fasting, prayer, and almsgiving. Their hearts are not attached to worldly riches, but to the grace of God.

As a witness to this truth, the Lord gives us the story of Lazarus and the rich man (Luke 16:19–31). Lazarus, though poor and despised on earth, was rich in humility and faith. Because of this, he was received into Abraham’s bosom in heaven. The rich man, however, though wealthy in possessions, was proud and unmerciful, and for this he was condemned.

It was not Lazarus’s material poverty that made him righteous, but his humility of heart. Likewise, it was not the rich man’s wealth that condemned him, but his pride and hardness of heart.

text.text: Christ, the Perfect Example of Humility

text:
Our Lord Jesus Christ, who for our salvation became poor in His incarnation, is the refuge of the poor and the source of eternal life. When a man said to Him, “Lord, I will follow You wherever You go,” Jesus replied,

“Foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head.”
(Luke 9:58)

The Creator of heaven and earth chose to live without a resting place, teaching us that true riches are not found in worldly comfort but in obedience to the will of God.

Yet the same Lord, who had nowhere to rest His head on earth, spoke of an eternal home prepared for His faithful ones, saying:

“In My Father’s house are many mansions; if it were not so, I would have told you.

I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and receive you to Myself;that where I am, there you may be also.”(John 14:2–3)

Dear beloved in Christ, peace and grace to you.Today we continue our spiritual reflection on one of the beautiful mysteries of our faith the intercession of the holy angels.
Let us therefore open our hearts and learn how the angels stand before God as intercessors.

text.text: The Meaning of “Standing” Angels as Intercessors

text:
If an angel were to say, “I stand in the presence of God to intercede for all people,” would this be difficult to believe?

The Archangel Gabriel himself said, “I am Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God” (Luke 1:19). This clearly shows that to “stand before God” means to serve and to intercede.

Likewise, the prophet Daniel speaks about Saint Michael the Archangel:

“And at that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people.”(Daniel 12:1)

In this verse, Saint Michael is described as the one who stands for the people of God. For what purpose does he stand? It is not to defend God who needs no defender but to plead and intercede for God’s people.

If we interpret the phrase “he stands for the children of the people” without understanding its spiritual meaning, we may fall into confusion. The proper understanding is that Saint Michael stands before the Creator as an intercessor and protector for humanity.

Daniel further confirms the presence of countless angels standing before God in heavenly service:

“A thousand thousands ministered unto Him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before Him.”(Daniel 7:10)


Here, “standing” clearly represents the act of ministering, serving, and interceding before God.

✍🏾

text.text: The Meaning of “Seeing” Angels as Witnesses and Intercessors

text:
Just as the word “stand” carries deep spiritual meaning, the word “see” also bears multiple sacred meanings in the Bible. It can signify not only physical sight but also understanding, compassion, sorrow, hope, fear, and repentance.

The Psalmist says:

👉🏾 “The eyes of all wait upon You, O Lord” (Psalm 144:15).

Here, the act of “seeing” expresses trust, expectation, and prayer. In many places, the Holy Scriptures use the word “see” to mean to listen, to examine, to have mercy, to forgive, or even to become angry.

When it is said, “God looked upon me with favor,” it means that He remembered me, visited me, had mercy on me, heard my cry, and forgave me. The same word can also express divine displeasure, for when God “looks upon” sin, it can be a gaze of judgment.

Let us observe a few examples:

“And the Lord looked with favor upon Abel and his offering” (Genesis 4:4).

“Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear Him” (Psalm 32:18).

“The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and His ears are open to their cry” (Psalm 33:15).

From these verses, we understand that when God “sees,” He acts - He listens, accepts, blesses, or corrects.

Similarly, when man or creation “sees,” the meaning changes according to context. The Psalmist prays, “Look upon me, O Lord my God, and hear me” (Psalm 12:3), which means, “Have mercy on me.”

In the Gospel, our Lord says, “Show yourself to the priest” (Matthew 8:4). The command “Show yourself” here means to be examined or to be made pure again through repentance. Even in common speech, we find this reflected when people say, “Let me see my doctor,” meaning to be examined or healed.

By understanding these deeper meanings of “seeing,” we can also understand how the angels intercede for us.

text.text: The Guardianship and Intercession of Angels

text:
God, in His mercy,has appointed angels to guard every human being. As it is written:

👉🏾 “He shall give His angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways” (Psalm 91:11).

This verse reveals that the Creator has prepared heavenly guardians to protect the children of men.

Our Lord Jesus Christ also confirmed this divine truth through the parable of the gardener (Luke 13:6–9), teaching that every person is cared for by a heavenly guardian, as the gardener tends the fig tree. This is why in the book of Daniel the angel is called “a holy watcher” or “a holy guardian” (Daniel 4:13, 4:23).

Moreover, in the Gospel of Matthew, the Lord Himself bears witness to the existence of guardian angels when He says:

👉🏾 “See that you do not despise one of these little ones, for their angels always behold the face of My Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10).

This verse clearly reveals the intercession of the angels. The phrase “their angels” means that every person has a guardian angel assigned to them by God. These angels continually behold the face of the Father that is, they stand in His presence, praying and interceding for the souls entrusted to their care.

✍🏾

text.text: The Angels as Our Heavenly Family

text:
The angels are not distant or foreign beings. They are our elder brothers in the divine household. They are called the sons of God (Job 1:6; 2:1), created before humanity, while we, too, are made children of God (John 1:12). Just as children of one father are brothers and sisters, so are we united with the angels in the household of God.

The angels are also said to be “ours” our angels not because we possess them by authority, but because God has appointed them to serve and protect us. They rejoice when we repent, they grieve when we sin, and they continually present our prayers before the throne of God.

When the Gospel says, “Their angels always behold the face of My Father,” it means that they constantly pray for us, intercede for our salvation, and even bear witness against those who despise others made in the image of God. The verse also serves as a warning: those who mistreat others will one day be judged by the very angels who prayed for the ones they wronged.

The intercession of the holy angels is therefore a truth revealed in Scripture and upheld by the Holy Church.They stand before God in unceasing prayer, offering intercession for humanity.
They are our heavenly guardians, our companions in worship, and our protectors in the unseen battle of the spirit.

text: Dear faithful, we greet you with the peace and blessing of God. Today, based on the above-mentioned topic, we share with you this important teaching about Saint Stephen, the first martyr of our Lord Jesus Christ. May all who read and learn from it be strengthened in faith and love.
The name Stephen means “light” He is called the first martyr, for he was the first to die for his faith in Christ after the Lord commanded His disciples to be free from all fear and oppression.

When the apostles were teaching in Jerusalem, the number of believers became very large, and it became difficult to serve everyone. Therefore, seven deacons were chosen to care for the community and manage the ministry of service. Saint Stephen was the first to be chosen and was appointed as chief among the seven that is, the first Archdeacon (Acts 6:5, 6:15).

Saint Stephen was one of the most remarkable Israelites of the first century. His parents were named Simon and Mary (some others gives different names). From his childhood, he loved truth and grew up studying the Torah.

When he reached maturity, he entered the school of the great Jewish teacher Gamaliel, who is mentioned in Acts 5:33. Tradition tells us that this Gamaliel taught several righteous men among them Saint Stephen, Saint Paul, Nathanael, and Nicodemus. Gamaliel himself is believed to have become a secret believer in Christ.

Under Gamaliel’s guidance, Saint Stephen became deeply learned in the Law and the Prophets. Though his generation was filled with sin and moral decay, the saint waited for the coming of the Messiah with patience, prayer, and steadfast hope.

text.text: His Discipleship under Saint John the Baptist

text:
When Saint Stephen heard that Saint John the Baptist was preaching the baptism of repentance by the River Jordan, he went to examine his teaching. Having discerned that John’s message was truly from God, Saint Stephen became his devoted disciple and served him faithfully for six months.

After his study and service, our Lord Jesus Christ was baptized by john . Witnessing the great miracles that occurred during the Lord’s ministry, he was deeply moved and asked his teacher, Saint John, to explain them to him. Saint John replied humbly, saying, “It is better to hear it from the mouth of the Creator Himself than from me.”

Obedient to this counsel, Saint Stephen went to the Lord Jesus Christ, raised his hands in reverence, and received divine instruction. (Luke 7:18) From that time forward, he became one of the Lord’s disciples. The Lord made him one of the Seventy-Two Apostles, sending him out to serve and to proclaim the Gospel. Through the power of Christ, even demons were subject to him (Luke 10:17).

Wherever Saint Stephen went, he taught the Good News of salvation and revealed the mysteries of the faith. After the Lord willingly died for our sake, rose from the dead, and ascended into heaven, He blessed His disciples and sent them forth to shepherd the Church.

Dear faithful, we greet you with the peace and blessing of God. Today, based on the above-mentioned topic, we share with you this important teaching about Saint Stephen, the first martyr of our Lord Jesus Christ. May all who read and learn from it be strengthened in faith and love.

The Meaning of His Name

The name Stephen means “light” He is called the first martyr, for he was the first to die for his faith in Christ after the Lord commanded His disciples to be free from all fear and oppression.

His Election as Archdeacon

When the apostles were teaching in Jerusalem, the number of believers became very large, and it became difficult to serve everyone. Therefore, seven deacons were chosen to care for the community and manage the ministry of service. Saint Stephen was the first to be chosen and was appointed as chief among the seven that is, the first Archdeacon (Acts 6:5, 6:15).

His Early Life and Education

Saint Stephen was one of the most remarkable Israelites of the first century. His parents were named Simon and Mary (some others gives different names). From his childhood, he loved truth and grew up studying the Torah.

When he reached maturity, he entered the school of the great Jewish teacher Gamaliel, who is mentioned in Acts 5:33. Tradition tells us that this Gamaliel taught several righteous men among them Saint Stephen, Saint Paul, Nathanael, and Nicodemus. Gamaliel himself is believed to have become a secret believer in Christ.

Under Gamaliel’s guidance, Saint Stephen became deeply learned in the Law and the Prophets. Though his generation was filled with sin and moral decay, the saint waited for the coming of the Messiah with patience, prayer, and steadfast hope.

Saint John replied humbly, saying, “It is better to hear it from the mouth of the Creator Himself than from me.”

(Luke 7:18) From that time forward, he became one of the Lord’s disciples. The Lord made him one of the Seventy-Two Apostles, sending him out to serve and to proclaim the Gospel. Through the power of Christ, even demons were subject to him (Luke 10:17).

Continues 👇🏾

text:
At that time, Saint Stephen was ordained as a priest like his brothers, the apostles through the grace of the Holy Spirit. When the Holy Spirit descended on the Feast of Pentecost, no one among the seven deacons spoke as many languages as Saint Stephen, nor did anyone receive as many divine revelations. Filled with wisdom and courage, he preached the Gospel with great boldness.

When the early Church faced challenges regarding the distribution of food and care among believers, Saint Stephen was among the seven deacons chosen by the Holy Spirit to serve. Among them, he was the chief of the six deacons and the administrator of more than eight thousand believers.

To guide and protect so many souls from the temptations of the evil one is no small task. Yet, as the Scripture testifies, “He was a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 6:5). Truly, it is a great challenge even to guide one soul toward salvation, but he who is filled with the Spirit of God is made strong to do it.

Some may think that Saint Stephen’s title “Chief Deacon” was only a matter of rank in his time. Yet, in truth, he was more than a deacon: he was also a priest, a preacher, and an apostle, serving both at the altar and among the people. His service at the table was not mere physical labor it was a spiritual ministry, performed in humility, faith, and love.

text.text: The Discovery of His Holy Relics

text:
About three hundred years after his martyrdom, a righteous man named Lucian lived in Jerusalem. Saint Stephen appeared to him several times in a vision, saying, “Take up my body.”

Lucian informed the Pope, who gathered priests and faithful, and they went to the place known as Atsede Gamaliel (the estate of his ). When they began to dig, a sweet fragrance filled the air, angels were heard singing, and a radiant light appeared.

The people and clergy bowed down and took up the holy relics with great joy and hymns of praise. The relics were placed in the city of Zion, where a righteous man named Alexander built a church in his honor.

After five years, Alexander passed away, and his body was placed beside Saint Stephen out of love and devotion.

Later, when Alexander’s wife returned to her homeland, Constantinople, she mistakenly took the relics of Saint Stephen, thinking they were her husband’s. On the journey, she heard angelic singing from the casket and realized it was the saint’s body. Rejoicing, she brought it to Emperor Constantine, and the entire city celebrated the miracle.

“Peace and blessings to all followers of the Orthodox faith. Today, we reflect on the profound teaching of our Lord about humility and the blessedness of the poor in spirit. As we study the Scriptures and the examples of the saints, may our hearts be opened to receive wisdom, and may we learn to live a life of true humility before God.

✍🏾Humility in the Covenant

When God gave the covenant to wise Solomon, He said:

“If my people, who are called by my name, humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land.” (2 Chronicles 7:14)

This teaches us that humility before God brings forgiveness, healing, and restoration.

✍🏾

text.text:
The Reward of the Humble

The Apostle Paul wrote:

text: “These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off and embraced them. They were strangers and pilgrims on the earth, seeking a heavenly country. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them.” (Hebrews 11:13-16)

“Do not love the world or the things in the world. For the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life are not from the Father. Whoever loves the world does not have the love of the Father in them. The world is passing away, but he who does the will of God abides forever.” (1 John 2:15-17)

Doing God’s will, therefore, brings eternal wealth and blessing in heaven.

“Truly I tell you, there is no one who has left house, parents, siblings, spouse, or children for the sake of the kingdom of God who will not receive many times more in this present time and, in the age to come, eternal life.” (Luke 18:30)

Here, Christ affirms that those who leave everything for their faith in Him will inherit the kingdom of heaven. A powerful testimony to this promise is the thief crucified on Jesus’ right, who, being poor in spirit, said:

“Lord, remember me in your kingdom.” (Luke 23:42)

Jesus answered him:

“Today you will be with me in paradise.”

This shows that the Lord grants eternal life to those who humbly believe and serve Him.

The Apostle Paul further instructs:

“As God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience.” (Colossians 3:12)

We are called to put on humility, for without it, our spiritual nakedness is revealed. Likewise, the Scriptures encourage us to treasure humility in our relationships:

“With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, endeavoring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” (Ephesians 4:2-3)

Through these teachings, we learn that humility is essential not only for our spiritual life but also for living in love and harmony with others.

text:
Spiritual service is a service of humility. It is a service in which the servant humbles themselves and exalts God. A service is only truly valuable when it is offered with genuine humility.

✍🏾Our Lord Himself taught this lesson in practice. He washed the feet of His disciples, took up His garments, sat down, and said to them:

“Do you understand what I have done to you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and rightly so. If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. I have given you an example, that you also should do as I have done to you. Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor a messenger greater than the one who sent him. If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” (John 13:12-17)

Blessed, therefore, are those who not only understand humility but also practice it in their lives.

The humility most often mentioned in the Bible is spiritual humility, which guides righteous deeds. Humility is also important in physical work, but we must not confuse spiritual humility with self-revelation in physical knowledge and skills.

✍🏾 True humility is not self-deprecation. It is knowing ourselves accurately and giving glory to God and others rather than focusing on ourselves. It is not a lack of humility to describe our abilities and achievements truthfully, recognizing that God is our helper. However, we must be careful not to exaggerate beyond our knowledge or skills.

✍🏾 In a competitive world, presenting ourselves beyond our true ability is arrogance, not humility. Arrogance occurs when we see ourselves as superior to our own abilities and wisdom, and begin to regard others as inferior. This is why Solomon wisely wrote:

“Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will direct your paths. Do not be wise in your own eyes; fear the Lord and turn away from evil.” (Proverbs 3:5-7)

✍🏾 Sincere humility is a life in which we:

👉🏾Trust that only God can accomplish everything

👉🏾Give priority and honor to others rather than our own desires

👉🏾Focus on spiritual service and the praise of God

True humility is not about self-centered knowledge or confidence; it is about trusting God and placing others before ourselves.

✍🏾 True humility is also not pretended. We cannot imitate Christ if we merely claim humility with our words while hiding pride in our hearts. Pride leads to spiritual ruin, as with the devil, and without humility, there can be no Christianity or holiness.

✍🏾 The Gospel teaches humility through the lives of the saints. No one is justified except those who reject pride. Understanding this truth, we should treasure heartfelt humility in our lives.

✍🏾 Let us not pretend to be poor in spirit. Instead, we must walk humbly before God and also before all people, whether considered great or small by worldly standards.

Dear followers of the Orthodox teachings ,we greet you with the peace and blessings of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Today, based on the above-mentioned topic, we present to you this important spiritual lesson. We ask all of you to read carefully and learn from it with humility and faith.

✍🏾

text.text: “I will open my mouth in a parable.” (Psalm 77:2)

text: To fulfill this prophecy, our Lord and God Jesus Christ taught many things in parables during His earthly life. Among these parables is one that reveals the mystery of the intercession of the holy angels.

text.text: ✍🏾 The Parable of the Barren Fig Tree

text:
“A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none.
He said to the vinedresser, ‘Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and find none. Cut it down; why should it use up the ground?’

✍🏾The vinedresser answered to his master, “Let it alone this year also.” This reveals an act of intercession. The master could have demanded simple obedience, saying, “I hired you to obey, not to plead.” Yet the worker’s words were a petition, a plea made not for himself but for the fruitless fig tree. What is remarkable is that the fig tree itself did not beg for mercy; it remained silent. The worker, moved by compassion, spoke on its behalf.

If the worker interceded freely, out of his own kindness and will, how much greater would his plea have been? Even a person who is not accustomed to ask for mercy can still do so when love compels them. In the same way, this worker’s humble request shows the depth of mercy that dwells in those who serve the Lord.

The master’s response is even more revealing. He did not say, “I hired you to obey,” but rather allowed the worker’s request and accepted it. This shows that God is the Lord who welcomes supplication and rejoices in intercession. He is not a tyrant who delights in punishment, but a Father who listens when His servants plead for mercy.

✍🏾

The Lord (owner) of the fig tree represents God the Creator.

The fig tree represents first the people of Israel, and by extension, all of humanity.

The worker represents the guardian angel appointed to protect and intercede for each person.

The fruit expected from the fig tree symbolizes the good faith, repentance, and righteous works that the Creator desires from every soul.

The three years during which the owner came seeking fruit represent the three main stages of human life in which God expects spiritual fruit:

👉🏾 Childhood, 

👉🏾Youth,

👉🏾 Adulthood,

The command, “Cut it down,” signifies the divine judgment that comes upon the soul that remains fruitless and unrepentant. Yet the worker’s plea shows the intercession of angels, who beg mercy on behalf of humanity.

Our Lord Himself teaches through this parable that the angels continually pray for us, just as the vinedresser pleaded for the fig tree. Scripture confirms this truth, saying:

“Behold, a watcher, a holy one, came down from heaven.”
(Daniel 4:13, 23)

and again:

“He will command His angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways.”(Psalm 91:11)

Each word of this parable holds deep spiritual meaning. But since our subject is the intercession of angels, let us focus on this mystery alone.

✍🏾 “I will open my mouth in a parable.” (Psalm 77:2)

To fulfill this prophecy, our Lord and God Jesus Christ taught many things in parables during His earthly life. Among these parables is one that reveals the mystery of the intercession of the holy angels.

✍🏾 The Parable of the Barren Fig Tree

“A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none.
He said to the vinedresser, ‘Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and find none. Cut it down; why should it use up the ground?’

✍🏾The vinedresser answered to his master, “Let it alone this year also.” This reveals an act of intercession. The master could have demanded simple obedience, saying, “I hired you to obey, not to plead.” Yet the worker’s words were a petition, a plea made not for himself but for the fruitless fig tree. What is remarkable is that the fig tree itself did not beg for mercy; it remained silent. The worker, moved by compassion, spoke on its behalf.

If the worker interceded freely, out of his own kindness and will, how much greater would his plea have been? Even a person who is not accustomed to ask for mercy can still do so when love compels them. In the same way, this worker’s humble request shows the depth of mercy that dwells in those who serve the Lord.

The master’s response is even more revealing. He did not say, “I hired you to obey,” but rather allowed the worker’s request and accepted it. This shows that God is the Lord who welcomes supplication and rejoices in intercession. He is not a tyrant who delights in punishment, but a Father who listens when His servants plead for mercy.

✍🏾 The Interpretation of the Parable

The Lord (owner) of the fig tree represents God the Creator.

The fig tree represents first the people of Israel, and by extension, all of humanity.

The worker represents the guardian angel appointed to protect and intercede for each person.

The fruit expected from the fig tree symbolizes the good faith, repentance, and righteous works that the Creator desires from every soul.

The three years during which the owner came seeking fruit represent the three main stages of human life in which God expects spiritual fruit:

👉🏾 Childhood, 

👉🏾Youth,

👉🏾 Adulthood,

The command, “Cut it down,” signifies the divine judgment that comes upon the soul that remains fruitless and unrepentant. Yet the worker’s plea shows the intercession of angels, who beg mercy on behalf of humanity.

Our Lord Himself teaches through this parable that the angels continually pray for us, just as the vinedresser pleaded for the fig tree. Scripture confirms this truth, saying:

“Behold, a watcher, a holy one, came down from heaven.”
(Daniel 4:13, 23)

and again:

“He will command His angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways.”(Psalm 91:11)

Each word of this parable holds deep spiritual meaning. But since our subject is the intercession of angels, let us focus on this mystery alone.

Continues 👇🏾

text:
If someone were to question this, asking, “Does the worker have more mercy than the master?” the answer is clear: No. The mercy of the worker is born from the mercy of the master. The worker’s compassion is a reflection of the divine compassion that already exists in the Creator’s heart.

It was the master who gave the worker permission to plead. It was the master who created the opportunity for mercy. Even before the worker spoke, the master knew he would intercede and He had already decided to accept that intercession.

Thus, the parable is symbolic, revealing both the power and the mercy of God. The Creator shows His full authority over creation, yet also His deep desire that His servants His angels participate in His merciful work.

The Lord who said, “Cut it down,” is the same Lord who knew from eternity that the tree would be spared through the plea of His servant. In this, we see the wisdom, sovereignty, and compassion of God, and the sacred ministry of His holy angels, who intercede continually for the salvation of mankind.

The parable teaches us that:

God, the Creator, is just and merciful.

The holy angels are His servants who intercede for humanity.

Intercession is not an act that opposes God’s will but a part of His divine plan to lead us to repentance and salvation.

Let us therefore give thanks to God, who appoints holy angels to watch over us, pray for us, and protect us in every trial.

May we, through their intercession and by the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, be found fruitful in faith and righteousness on the day of judgment.

text:
Dear followers of the Orthodox teaching we greet you with the peace and blessing of God. Today, based on the topic mentioned above, we present to you the following important teaching, and we encourage you all to read, reflect, and learn from it.

✍🏾

“Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.”
(Matthew 5:4; Luke 6:21)

Is the Christian life a life of sorrow and mourning? Is joy a sin? Absolutely not. Joy is not a sin. In fact, the Holy Bible considers joy a fruit of the Spirit, as written in Galatians 5:22.

Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ taught His disciples about spiritual joy, saying:

“I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.”
(John 16:22)

Likewise, the Apostle Saint Paul said of eternal joy:

“Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice.”(Philippians 4:4)


Our Lord also spoke of the heavenly joy that comes from repentance:

“There will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.”
(Luke 15:7)

Another spiritual joy is found in seeing others grow in their spiritual lives. Thus, the Apostle John said:

“I rejoiced greatly when the brothers came and testified of your truth, that you walk in the truth. I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in the truth.” (3 John 2–4)

When our Lord said, “Blessed are those who mourn,” He was not speaking of physical sorrow, but of spiritual sorrow.

Physical sorrow is the sadness we feel when a parent, child, relative, or friend dies, or when we lose something we hoped for. But spiritual sorrow is much deeper. It is the sorrow a person feels for his own sins, for the sins of others, and for the suffering of the Son of God. This sorrow is not despair but repentance that leads to salvation.

Saint Paul teaches:

“Godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation, not to be regretted; but worldly sorrow produces death.”(2 Corinthians 7:10)

✍🏾

While we live on this earth, we must come to repentance through mourning and tears for our sins. When our Lord carried the Cross to Calvary, He said to the women who were weeping for Him:

“Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for Me, but weep for yourselves and for your children. For the days are coming when they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren, the wombs that never bore, and the breasts that never nursed.’”
(Luke 23:28–29)

The Apostle Paul also teaches us to share in the sorrows of others:

“Weep with those who weep.”
(Romans 12:15)


And Saint James exhorts us to weep over our sins:

“Cleanse your hands, you sinners; purify your hearts, you double-minded. Be afflicted and mourn and weep; let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will lift you up.”(James 4:8–10)

He further warns the rich, saying:

“Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you.”(James 5:1)

✍🏾

Many holy prophets, apostles, and saints wept deeply over their sins and the sins of others. Even our Lord Jesus Christ wept for humanity.

The Prophet Samuel grieved over King Saul because Saul disobeyed the command of God. The Scripture says:

“The word of the Lord came to Samuel, saying, ‘I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned back from following Me and has not performed My commandments.’ And Samuel was distressed and cried out to the Lord all night.”(1 Samuel 15:10–11)

text:
“Does the Lord delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as much as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of divination, and stubbornness is as idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, He has rejected you as king.”
(1 Samuel 15:22–23)

Saul’s repentance was not sincere, and therefore Samuel saw him no more. Yet the Scripture tells us:

“Samuel mourned for Saul; and the Lord regretted that He had made Saul king over Israel.”
(1 Samuel 15:35)

Finally, the Lord said to Samuel:

“How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him as king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and go; I am sending you to Jesse the Bethlehemite, for I have provided Myself a king among his sons.”(1 Samuel 16:1)

Thus, the kingship was taken from Saul and given to David, the son of Jesse.

Therefore, beloved, spiritual mourning is not hopeless sadness but holy repentance. The tears of the righteous cleanse the heart, humble the soul, and open the path to salvation. Those who mourn their sins with sincere hearts will indeed be comforted by the mercy of God, for His promise is true:

“Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.”

text: Dear followers of the Orthodox teachings, we greet you with the peace and blessings of God.Today, based on the above-mentioned topic, we bring you this important lesson. We ask you all to read it carefully and learn from the examples of the saints and prophets who wept before God.

The noble Prophet David wept for his sins, for the sorrows he suffered, and for the mercy of God.

David, who was pursued by King Saul, mourned deeply even when Saul his pursuer died. 2 Samuel 1:12 teaches us that we should weep not only for our friends but also for our enemies.

When his son Absalom rebelled against him, David went up the Mount of Olives barefoot and weeping, wearing sackcloth. Those who were with him also wept. (2 Samuel 15:30) When Absalom was later killed, David cried bitterly, saying:

“O my son Absalom my son, my son Absalom! Would God I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son!” (2 Samuel 18:33)

After Ziklag was captured by the Amalekites and burned, David and his men lifted up their voices and wept until they had no strength left to weep. (1 Samuel 30:3–5)

David also mourned for the death of Uriah, for the sin he committed with Bathsheba, and for the death of their child. (2 Samuel 12:22)

Because of all this, Saint David lamented for himself, for the people of Israel, and for Jerusalem, saying:

“I am weary with my groaning; all night I make my bed swim, I drench my couch with my tears.” (Psalm 6:6)

“My tears have been my food day and night.” (Psalm 42:3)
“For I have eaten ashes like bread and mingled my drink with weeping.” (Psalm 102:9)
“Rivers of water run down from my eyes because they do not keep Your law.” (Psalm 119:136)

David wept both for his own repentance and for the sins of his people.

The Prophet Isaiah lamented his own sinfulness, saying:

“Woe is me, for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the Lord of hosts!” (Isaiah 6:5)

He also mourned the destruction of Moab:

“Therefore I will weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vine of Sibmah; I will water you with my tears, O Heshbon and Elealeh; for the shouting has fallen over your summer fruits and your harvest.” (Isaiah 16:9)

Isaiah lamented the destruction of Jerusalem, saying:

“Turn away from me; let me weep bitterly. Do not try to comfort me because of the destruction of the daughter of my people.” (Isaiah 22:4)

When King Hezekiah became sick and was told he would die, he turned his face to the wall and prayed to the Lord:

“Remember now, O Lord, I pray, how I have walked before You in truth and with a loyal heart.”

Hezekiah wept bitterly, and the Lord said through Isaiah:

“I have heard your prayer and seen your tears; I will add fifteen years to your life.” (Isaiah 38:1–6)

The Prophet Jeremiah wept for his people, saying:

“For the hurt of the daughter of my people I am hurt; I am mourning; astonishment has taken hold of me.” (Jeremiah 8:21)

He lamented greatly:

“Oh, that my head were waters, and my eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!” (Jeremiah 9:1)

His grief was deep and constant:

“My sorrow is beyond healing; my heart is faint within me.” (Jeremiah 8:18)

In the Book of Lamentations, Jeremiah mourned the destruction of Jerusalem and begged God for mercy. Through him, we learn that when people sin and God’s anger comes upon them, believers must weep for themselves, for their people, and seek forgiveness from the Lord.

text:
The righteous Job, who endured great trials, prayed to God with a pure and faithful heart, saying:

“O earth, do not cover my blood, and let my cry find no resting place.” (Job 16:18)

God permitted him to face deep suffering to test his faith. When his trials became severe, Job cried out:

“Behold, I cry out of wrong, but I am not heard; I cry aloud, but there is no justice.” (Job 19:7)

He reflected on the fate of the wicked, asking:

“What is the hope of the hypocrite, though he may gain much, if God takes away his life? Will God hear his cry when trouble comes upon him?” (Job 27:8–9)

Through these words, Job teaches us that one should weep and turn to God while still in this life, before it is too late.

When Job was in great distress and felt abandoned, he said:

"I cry out to you, but you do not answer me; I stand up, and you only look at me.” (Job 30:20)

Even in his anguish, Job’s compassion extended beyond himself:

“Did I not weep for him who was in trouble? Has not my soul grieved for the poor?” (Job 30:25)

Thus, the righteous Job shows us that tears offered in faith whether for our own suffering or for the suffering of others are never forgotten by God. His patience and sorrow became his path to righteousness and his witness of steadfast trust in the Lord.
